The bill prohibits criminal prosecutions or civil actions based on a school bus operator's failure to ensure seat belt use, directly affecting the types of cases that can be brought before the state judiciary.

Synopsis: Expanding the definitions of "abuse" and "sexual abuse" for purposes of provisions relating to the reporting and investigation of child abuse and neglect.
Title: Family Law - Child Abuse - Definitions
Status: In the House - Hearing canceled

NarrowSubjects.Name: Investigations and Inquiries -see also- Crim Bckgrnd Invest

bill_summary: This bill expands the definitions of "abuse" and "sexual abuse" as they relate to child abuse and neglect reporting and investigations. It removes specific limitations on the perpetrator's relationship to the child, effectively allowing for the reporting and investigation of abuse or sexual abuse committed by any individual, rather than only those in specific roles such as parents, household members, or persons in authority.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Human Services (Social Services Administration)
stakeholders: Children in Maryland, the Social Services Administration, local departments of social services, law enforcement agencies, and mandated reporters including health practitioners, educators, and human service workers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to increase the number of child abuse and neglect reports and subsequent investigations by expanding the definition of abuse to include any perpetrator. This will likely result in an indeterminate increase in state and local expenditures for the Social Services Administration and local departments of social services to handle the increased caseload. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the text provided.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department's Social Services Administration is the primary agency responsible for child abuse and neglect investigations and maintaining the centralized confidential database. Expanding the definition of 'abuse' directly increases the volume and scope of investigations conducted by local departments.

As a primary law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police is responsible for investigating child abuse. The bill's expansion of the 'abuse' and 'sexual abuse' definitions impacts their investigative workload and reporting requirements under the Family Law Article.

The Office of the Attorney General is explicitly included in the definition of a 'law enforcement agency' in the bill. Additionally, the OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Human Services regarding child welfare laws and investigations.

Expanding the legal definitions of child abuse is expected to increase the number of cases filed in the court system, particularly Child in Need of Assistance (CINA) and other protective proceedings, impacting judicial workload.

Educators and professional employees of public and private schools are mandatory reporters of child abuse. Expanding the definitions of 'abuse' and 'sexual abuse' directly affects the reporting obligations of these employees.

Health practitioners and employees of health institutions are mandatory reporters. The expansion of the 'abuse' definition changes the threshold for what these professionals are legally required to report to authorities.

Staff at the Department of Juvenile Services are classified as human service workers and mandatory reporters. The expanded definitions affect their reporting duties for youth within their care or supervision.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill defines employees of correctional institutions as 'educators or human service workers' who are mandatory reporters, impacting their legal responsibilities regarding suspected child abuse.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office coordinates public safety and victim services. Expanding the definitions of child abuse impacts the state's criminal justice strategy and the allocation of resources for victim support services.
As the agency coordinating the well-being of Maryland's children, the Governor's Office for Children is involved in policy development regarding child protection and reducing trauma.
The Center develops resources and training for school safety. Expanded definitions of abuse in educational settings would require updates to training protocols for school safety personnel.

Due to the potentially significant increase in investigations and caseloads for the Department of Human Services, this bill may have a notable fiscal impact requiring budget adjustments for personnel and resources.

Synopsis: Altering the date from December 31, 2025, to December 31, 2030, by which certain community solar energy generating systems must be approved by the Public Service Commission in order for land that is used by the community solar energy generating systems to qualify for the agricultural use assessment.
Title: Property Tax - Agricultural Use Assessment - Community Solar Energy Generating Systems
Status: In the House - Hearing canceled

NarrowSubjects.Name: Agriculture -see also- Agritourism; Cannabis Prd; Farm; etc.
Energy Matters -see also- Fuel; NuclearMatt; PwrPlnts; etc.

bill_summary: This bill extends the deadline from December 31, 2025, to December 31, 2030, for community solar energy generating systems to be approved by the Public Service Commission so that land used for agrivoltaics can qualify for the agricultural use property tax assessment.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation
stakeholders: Landowners of community solar energy generating systems, agricultural property owners, the Public Service Commission, and the Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill extends the qualification period for agricultural use property tax assessments for certain solar energy lands through 2030. This likely results in an indeterminate reduction in potential property tax revenue for the state and local governments compared to assessing the land at market value, but specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires community solar energy generating systems to be approved by the Public Service Commission under § 7-306.2 of the Public Utilities Article to qualify for the tax assessment extension.
The bill concerns the criteria for land to be assessed as actively used for farm or agricultural purposes, a core area of expertise and policy leadership for the Department of Agriculture.

The agency promotes renewable energy and coordinates energy planning; extending the eligibility for community solar and agrivoltaics projects directly aligns with its mission to advance clean energy technologies.

As the independent body that hears appeals regarding property tax assessments and exemptions, this board will be responsible for resolving disputes related to the new agricultural use assessment criteria for solar land.
The Tax Court serves as the highest level of administrative review for tax-related disputes, including factual determinations regarding real property assessments and agricultural use qualifications.
As the state's chief financial officer and tax collector, the Comptroller oversees the fiscal integrity of tax laws and monitors the revenue impact of changes to the property tax code.
The agency promotes sustainable growth and provides policy guidance on land use, which includes the intersection of agricultural preservation and renewable energy infrastructure like agrivoltaics.
This department is responsible for long-term fiscal planning and estimating the impact of tax law changes on state and local revenues.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the Public Service Commission and assessment bodies, regarding the implementation and enforcement of the bill's provisions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Agricultural & Resource-Based Industry Development Corp.
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MARBIDCO supports the economic viability of farming and rural businesses, many of which may utilize agrivoltaics as a tool for financial sustainability.
The Governor's Office oversees executive branch policy initiatives and the administration of state laws, including those related to environmental protection and agricultural assessment.

Synopsis: Adding convictions for resisting arrest, making a false statement to a law enforcement officer, and making a false statement to a law enforcement officer when under arrest to the list of misdemeanor convictions that a person may expunge under certain circumstances.
Title: Criminal Procedure - Expungement of Records - Resisting Arrest and Making a False Statement to a Law Enforcement Officer
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/03 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Courts -see also- AppCt; Circuit; District; Orphans'; etc.
Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
Investigations and Inquiries -see also- Crim Bckgrnd Invest
Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill adds convictions for resisting arrest and making a false statement to a law enforcement officer to the list of misdemeanors for which an individual can petition for the expungement of their records.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and State and local law enforcement agencies
stakeholders: Individuals with misdemeanor convictions for resisting arrest or making false statements to law enforcement officers
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. However, expanding the list of offenses eligible for expungement typically results in increased administrative workloads for the Maryland Judiciary and law enforcement agencies to process petitions, and it may also lead to an increase in revenue from petition filing fees.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Administrative Office of the Courts is responsible for the operations of the judicial branch. This bill requires court clerks to process new types of expungement petitions and judges to review and grant orders for the removal of court records related to resisting arrest and false statements.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency maintains the Criminal Justice Information System (CJIS), the state's central repository for criminal records. They are the primary entity responsible for executing expungement orders and ensuring that the relevant criminal history is removed from state and federal databases.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Public Defender provides legal representation to indigent individuals. Expanding the list of expungeable offenses directly impacts their caseload, as they assist eligible clients with the petition process for these specific misdemeanors.

As a primary law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police maintains arrest and investigative records. They must comply with court-ordered expungements by removing or shielding records of the newly eligible offenses from their internal systems.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies and represents the state in legal matters. They would be responsible for providing guidance on the implementation of the new expungement criteria and handling any related litigation.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office coordinates state criminal justice strategies and policy. The expansion of expungement eligibility for these misdemeanors is a significant policy shift in the criminal justice system that falls under their advisory and coordination scope.

Synopsis: Requiring any person involved in a motor vehicle accident that results in the death of, or a life threatening injury to, another person to submit to breath and blood testing for impaired driving.
Title: Motor Vehicles - Accidents - Required Testing for Impaired Driving (Mateo's Law)
Status: In the House - Hearing 1/28 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Death -see also- Homicide; Murder; Wrongful Death
Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police

bill_summary: This bill requires any driver involved in a motor vehicle accident that results in the death of, or life-threatening injury to, another person to submit to breath and blood testing for potential alcohol or drug impairment, regardless of whether a police officer has reasonable grounds to suspect impairment.
stakeholders: Drivers involved in motor vehicle accidents resulting in death or life-threatening injury, law enforcement agencies, and the Maryland court system.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by 1,295,049 in fiscal 2027 for the Department of State Police to hire forensic scientists and procure testing supplies. Costs are projected to rise to approximately 1,789,700 by fiscal 2031. State and local revenues may increase minimally due to additional fines for impaired driving offenses, while local expenditures may increase slightly to cover blood kit purchases.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of State Police is the primary agency responsible for enforcing traffic laws and conducting the forensic testing of blood kits related to impaired driving. The fiscal note identifies a significant expenditure increase for the department to hire additional forensic scientists and procure testing supplies to handle the increased volume of mandated blood and breath tests.

As an agency within the Maryland Department of Transportation, the MVA is responsible for administrative sanctions related to driving, including the suspension of licenses for refusal to submit to the chemical tests mandated by this bill. It also manages the Ignition Interlock System Program mentioned in the fiscal analysis.

The bill directly amends the Transportation Article of the Maryland Code. MDOT, through its modal administrations like the MVA and State Highway Administration, oversees the state's motor vehicle laws and highway safety initiatives impacted by these new requirements.

The Judiciary, supported by the Administrative Office of the Courts, will handle the anticipated increase in criminal charges and violations filed in the District Court resulting from the expanded testing requirements.

The OAH is explicitly mentioned in the fiscal note as being responsible for handling administrative hearings related to license suspensions and ignition interlock orders that may arise from test refusals under the bill.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the state and law enforcement agencies regarding the constitutional implications of mandatory testing, particularly concerning Fourth Amendment protections and U.S. Supreme Court precedents like Birchfield v. North Dakota mentioned in the fiscal note.

Synopsis: Requiring the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services to transmit a list that includes the name and new residential address of individuals released from incarceration at a State correctional facility to the State Board of Elections on a weekly basis; requiring the State Board to automatically restore the voter registration of certain individuals released from State correctional facilities who were registered to vote in the State before being incarcerated; etc.
Title: Election Law - Individuals Released From State Correctional Facilities - Automatic Restoration of Voter Registration
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/04 at 2:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Public Safety and Correctional Services, Department of
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records
Voting -see also- Absentee and Mail-In Voting

bill_summary: This bill requires the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services to provide the State Board of Elections with weekly electronic lists of individuals released from State correctional facilities. The State Board of Elections is then required to automatically restore the voter registration status of individuals who were registered to vote in Maryland before their incarceration and who currently reside in the state.
responsible_party: State Board of Elections and Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Individuals released from State correctional facilities who were previously registered to vote in Maryland
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not expected to materially affect State finances. However, local government expenditures are estimated to increase collectively by $400,000 in fiscal 2027 only to cover one-time development costs for modifying the statewide voter registration system to enable automatic registration restoration and updated notification cards.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: SBE is the primary agency responsible for identifying individuals eligible for voter registration restoration, automatically updating the statewide voter registration system, and coordinating with local boards to issue notification cards.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS is mandated to electronically transmit weekly lists of individuals released from State correctional facilities to the State Board of Elections, providing the essential data for the automatic restoration process.

As the chief legal officer for the State, the OAG provides legal counsel on the implementation of election laws, constitutional voting rights, and the specific Public Information Act non-disclosure provisions included in the bill.

The Judiciary currently reports felony convictions and sentences to the State Board of Elections; this bill establishes the complementary data flow for restoration upon release, requiring system coordination between judicial and executive reporting.

DBM oversees the fiscal performance of executive agencies and will monitor the implementation of the bill's fiscal requirements, including one-time development costs for the statewide voter registration system.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, including the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services, and coordinates the implementation of state policies regarding voter rights.

Synopsis: Requiring the reporting of certain procurement contracts and memoranda of understanding entered into by certain public elementary and secondary education systems in the State; and requiring each local school system to make publicly available on the local school system's website certain in-kind services agreements, procurement contracts, and memoranda of understanding.
Title: Education - Agreements, Procurement Contracts, and Memoranda of Understanding - Reporting and Publication
Status: In the House - Hearing 1/29 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Education -see also- ContEd; DrvEd; HigherEd; etc.
Primary Schools -see also- Private Schools; Public Schools
Secondary Schools -see also- Private Schools; Public Sch

bill_summary: This bill requires various entities within Maryland's public education system, including local school boards, superintendents, and the State Board of Education, to report annually on memoranda of understanding and procurement contracts. Additionally, it mandates that local school systems publish in-kind services agreements and memoranda of understanding on their official websites for public access.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education and the State Superintendent
stakeholders: Public elementary and secondary education systems, county boards of education, county superintendents, and the State Board of Education.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Fiscal Note indicates there is no State fiscal impact as the requirements can be handled with existing resources. Similarly, local school systems are expected to manage the reporting and website publication requirements using existing resources. While some local systems initially expressed concerns about administrative capacity, the Fiscal Note clarifies that the definition of "procurement contract" in the bill excludes local boards, limiting their reporting burden primarily to memoranda of understanding.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill identifies the State Board of Education and the State Superintendent of Schools as 'covered entities' required to report their own procurement contracts and memoranda of understanding. Furthermore, the State Superintendent is responsible for receiving reports from all local school systems, compiling a statewide report for the General Assembly, and ensuring compliance with public disclosure requirements.

As the chief legal officer for state agencies, the OAG will likely provide legal counsel to the Department of Education regarding the bill's exemptions for information that may be withheld or is prohibited from disclosure by law.

The IAC oversees the planning and funding of public school construction and capital improvement projects. The bill's focus on procurement contracts in the education sector overlaps with the IAC's role in facility procurement and reporting as noted in the fiscal note.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency for the state. As noted in the fiscal note, local school boards already report certain payments to DBM; the bill establishes a parallel reporting requirement for MOUs and procurement contracts within the education system.

The Board of Public Works oversees significant state procurements. While the bill focuses on reports to the State Superintendent, it involves units of the Executive Branch (the State Board and State Superintendent) whose procurement activities are subject to BPW oversight.

DGS is the central procurement authority for the state. While the bill primarily affects local school systems, the inclusion of the State Board and State Superintendent as 'covered entities' involves procurement reporting from units that fall under state-level procurement coordination.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, including the Department of Education. The bill introduces new reporting mandates for leadership within the executive branch (the State Superintendent and State Board).

Synopsis: Requiring each county board of education to establish a policy to obtain at least one airway clearing device per school and to authorize school nurses and other school personnel to use an airway clearing device in certain emergency situations; and requiring the State Department of Education to develop and disseminate a form for public schools to report each incident requiring the use of an airway clearing device.
Title: Public Schools - Airway Clearing Device Availability and Use - Policy (Bowen Levy Airway Clearing Device Act)
Status: In the House - Hearing 1/29 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Job Training -see also- Continuing Ed; Vocational Rehab
Nurses -see also- Nurse Practitioners; Nursing Assistants
Public Schools -see also- Primary Schools; Secondary Sch

bill_summary: The Bowen Levy Airway Clearing Device Act requires each county board of education to establish a policy for public schools to obtain at least one airway clearing device per school and authorizes school personnel to use the device during choking emergencies. It mandates training for staff, specific storage requirements in dining areas, and establishes a reporting system for incidents involving the device's use.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education and local county boards of education
stakeholders: Public school students, school nurses, school personnel, and local school systems
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures for the Maryland State Department of Education are expected to be handled within existing budgeted resources. Local school system expenditures will increase by approximately 85200 dollars statewide to purchase at least one airway clearing device for each of the more than 1,400 public schools. Additional local costs include minimal training expenses and periodic replacement of device components every two to three years.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MSDE is the primary agency tasked with implementing the bill, including developing and disseminating the standard reporting form, collecting incident data from all public schools, and providing guidance to local boards of education on policy requirements.

MDH collaborates with MSDE to develop school health standards and guidelines; the agency also oversees local health departments that provide the school nurses mentioned in the bill's training and authorization requirements.
The OAG provides legal counsel to MSDE and MDH regarding the implementation of the bill and the interpretation of the liability immunity clause for school personnel responding to emergencies.

As an independent unit within MSDE focused on school safety training and resources, MCSS may be involved in developing or distributing the mandated training procedures for the use of airway clearing devices.

As a state agency that functions as a public school, MSD is directly affected by the mandate to obtain emergency devices, train its staff, and report any incidents requiring the use of the devices to MSDE.

Synopsis: Altering, for a certain licensing requirement, the definition of "money transmitter" under the Maryland Money Transmission Act to exclude a certain person designated as an agent of a payor for the purpose of the agent's provision of payroll processing services under certain circumstances.
Title: Maryland Money Transmission Act - Definition of Money Transmitter - Alteration
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/03 at 1:30 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Financial Institutions -see also- Banks; Credit Unions; etc.
Licenses -see also- AB Lic; Certifications; DrLic; Permits
Salaries and Compensation -see also- Overtime; Reimb. Rates

bill_summary: This bill narrows the definition of a money transmitter under the Maryland Money Transmission Act to exclude certain payroll processors. To qualify for the exemption, the processor must be a designated agent of the payor under a written agreement, be represented to payees as an agent of the payor, and the payor must remain legally obligated to payees even if the agent fails to remit the funds.
stakeholders: Payroll processing companies, employers, employees, and the Maryland Department of Labor Office of Financial Regulation
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund revenues for the Maryland Department of Labor are estimated to decrease by $6,000 annually beginning in fiscal 2027. This impact results from approximately three payroll processing companies no longer being required to pay the $2,000 annual licensing fee. The bill has no impact on state expenditures or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Labor's Office of Financial Regulation is the primary agency responsible for licensing money transmitters. The bill specifically alters the definition of 'money transmitter' within the Act they administer and will result in a direct decrease in special fund licensing revenue for the department.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the Department of Labor, on the interpretation and enforcement of state financial laws such as the Maryland Money Transmission Act.

The Department of Budget and Management is responsible for supervising budget execution and estimating revenues. The bill has a fiscal impact on state special fund revenues, decreasing them by an estimated $6,000 annually starting in FY 2027.

The Office of Legislative Audits performs fiscal compliance audits of executive agencies. They are responsible for auditing the Department of Labor's adherence to licensing definitions and the resulting changes in fee collections to ensure financial accountability.

The Office of Administrative Hearings adjudicates contested cases for state agencies. Any legal disputes regarding a company's licensing status or regulatory enforcement under the revised definition of a money transmitter could be heard by an Administrative Law Judge at this agency.

Synopsis: Requiring a public body that enters into an energy performance contract to comply with certain provisions of law regarding energy performance contracts; requiring the Maryland Clean Energy Center to hire or contract with navigators to assist a public body in creating an energy performance contract; altering the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Loan Program and the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Fund to allow for the issuance of certain grants and loans to certain public bodies; etc.
Title: Energy Performance Contracts - Navigators, Funding, and Requirements
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/03 at 2:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Energy Matters -see also- Fuel; NuclearMatt; PwrPlnts; etc.
Higher Education -see also- Comm Colleges; Med Schools; etc.
Technology -see also- AeroT; BioT; EnergyT; InfoT; MedT; etc
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Clean Energy Center to hire or contract with regional navigators to assist public bodies, such as local governments, schools, and hospitals, in developing energy performance contracts. It renames the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Loan Program to the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Grant and Loan Program, authorizing the Maryland Energy Administration to provide grants to public bodies in addition to loans. The bill establishes a mandated annual appropriation of $1,500,000 from the Strategic Energy Investment Fund to support the navigator program.
responsible_party: Maryland Clean Energy Center and Maryland Energy Administration
stakeholders: Public bodies including State agencies, counties, municipalities, public higher education institutions, local boards of education, State and local hospitals, and small businesses providing energy conservation services.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund expenditures from the Strategic Energy Investment Fund increase by $1,500,000 annually beginning in FY 2027. Nonbudgeted revenues and expenditures for the Maryland Clean Energy Center increase by the same amount. Additionally, the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Fund will experience indeterminate impacts as a portion of its funds transitions from loans (which are repaid) to grants (which are not), potentially reducing long-term revenue from loan repayments. Local governments and State agencies may experience net energy cost savings.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates the Maryland Clean Energy Center to hire or contract with navigators to assist public bodies in creating energy performance contracts and provides $1.5 million in annual mandated funding for this purpose.

The Maryland Energy Administration administers the Jane E. Lawton Grant and Loan Program and the Strategic Energy Investment Fund, both of which are significantly altered and utilized for funding under the bill.
The bill explicitly requires the Department of General Services to monitor the status of active energy performance contracts and review measurement and verification reports from units.
The Board of Public Works oversees and approves energy performance contracts and receives annual reports on their status from the Department of General Services.
The Treasurer serves as the custodian of the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Fund and is responsible for financing state energy performance contracts through capital leases.
The Department of Budget and Management is responsible for the state budget process, which must now include the $1.5 million mandated appropriation for the navigator program.
The Governor is required to include a $1.5 million appropriation from the Strategic Energy Investment Fund in the annual budget bill to support the navigator program.
The Comptroller is responsible for accounting for the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Fund and serves as a member of the Board of Public Works, which oversees these contracts.
Local boards of education are specifically included in the definition of public bodies eligible for grants and technical assistance for energy performance contracts.
State and local hospitals are defined as public bodies eligible for grant funding and navigator assistance to improve energy efficiency.
Public institutions of higher education are defined as public bodies that can enter into energy performance contracts and receive technical assistance and grants.
As a public institution of higher education, Morgan State University is a public body eligible for grant funding and navigator assistance under the bill.
As a public institution of higher education, St. Mary's College is a public body eligible for the grant and assistance programs established by the bill.
The Commission coordinates policies for public higher education institutions, which are public bodies eligible for the energy performance contract assistance and grants.
The definition of public bodies includes units of state government, including those within the judicial branch, making them eligible for programs under the bill.
The bill affects the Strategic Energy Investment Fund, which also provides funding for the Air and Radiation Administration within the Department of the Environment.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a person from constructing a data center in the State; prohibiting a unit of State or local government from approving a proposal for the construction of a data center in the State; providing for the termination of the Act if the General Assembly enacts legislation regarding the co-location of data centers with a new or existing natural gas power generation facility, nuclear power generation facility, or small module reactor; applying the Act prospectively; etc.
Title: Moratorium on Construction of New Data Centers - Co-Location and Generation Contingency
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/03 at 2:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Energy Matters -see also- Fuel; NuclearMatt; PwrPlnts; etc.

bill_summary: This emergency bill establishes a moratorium on the construction of new data centers in Maryland and prohibits state and local government units from approving new data center proposals. The moratorium remains in effect until the General Assembly enacts legislation requiring all new data centers to be co-located with specific power generation facilities (such as natural gas, nuclear, or small module reactors) that can provide sufficient power to meet the data center's needs.
stakeholders: Data center developers, state and local government agencies, electric utilities, electricity ratepayers, and small businesses providing construction or operational services to data centers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not directly affect State or local finances, but is expected to have significant indirect effects. These include potential reductions in tax and fee revenues from data center development and operation, as well as possible impacts on electricity rates. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as they are considered beyond the scope of the fiscal note, though the impact is anticipated to be significant.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MEA is responsible for advising the state on energy policy and maximizing energy efficiency. The bill's abrogation is contingent on legislation requiring data centers to be co-located with specific power generation facilities (natural gas, nuclear, or small module reactors), and MEA is required by prior law to assess the energy impacts of data center development.

The PSC regulates public utilities and sets electricity rates. The bill's abrogation clause directly concerns the construction of power generation facilities and managing the large electrical loads required by data centers, which impact utility rates for all Maryland residents.

As the state's primary economic development agency, the Department of Commerce is responsible for attracting and retaining businesses. A moratorium on constructing a specific industry's facilities (data centers) directly conflicts with its mission to stimulate economic growth and job creation.

MDE is responsible for environmental protection and permitting. It is also mandated by current law to assess the environmental impacts of data centers, making a construction moratorium and the potential for new co-located power plants highly relevant to its oversight.

The Department of Planning promotes sustainable growth and resource management through land use policy. The bill imposes a state-wide land use restriction on a specific facility type, which falls under the agency's planning and policy guidance role.

The OPC represents residential utility consumers in proceedings regarding rates and service quality. The fiscal note highlights the OPC's position that data center power needs significantly impact retail electricity rates, a core concern of this bill.

The Governor's Office oversees executive branch policy and coordinates state initiatives. This bill is an emergency measure with significant implications for the Governor's energy, environmental, and economic priorities.

The Comptroller is the state's principal tax collector. The bill uses definitions from the Tax - General Article and will have significant indirect effects on state tax and fee revenues derived from data center construction and operation.

DBM is responsible for long-term fiscal planning and budget execution. The fiscal note indicates the bill will have significant indirect effects on state and local finances, which DBM monitors to ensure government efficiency.

MEDCO assists in the attraction and expansion of industry through real estate development and financing. The prohibition of data center construction affects its ability to support these large-scale industrial projects.

DNR manages public lands and natural resources. Large-scale data center construction and co-located power generation facilities have significant environmental and conservation impacts on state land and waterways.

The Department of Labor oversees workforce development and small business support. The fiscal note indicates the moratorium could meaningfully affect small businesses and laborers involved in the development and construction of data centers.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies. The office would be responsible for advising units of government on the legality and enforcement of the moratorium and its prospective application.

DoIT manages the state's IT strategy and infrastructure. While the bill focuses on private construction, the overall availability and development of data center infrastructure in Maryland is relevant to the state's digital ecosystem.

Synopsis: Providing that certain authorization for the holders of certain licenses to sell alcoholic beverages for off-premises consumption in a certain manner applies only if the Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore County has adopted certain regulations; authorizing the holders of certain licenses in Baltimore County that authorize the sale of alcoholic beverages at a restaurant or bar to sell certain alcoholic beverages for off-premises consumption under certain circumstances; etc.
Title: Baltimore County - Alcoholic Beverages - Sale for Off-Premises Consumption
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/23 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes
Food -see also- Meat, Poultry, & Seafood; Milk; etc.
Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore County to allow Class B and Class D license holders, such as restaurants and bars, to sell mixed drinks or cocktails for off-premises consumption. Such sales are only permitted if the Board adopts specific regulations after considering public health impacts. Conditions for sale include a requirement that the drink be purchased with prepared food, sold in a sealed container, and sold before 11:00 p.m. to an individual at least 21 years old. The Board is prohibited from charging additional fees for this authorization but may limit the quantity of beverages sold per transaction.
responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore County
stakeholders: Class B and Class D alcoholic beverage license holders (restaurants and bars) and consumers in Baltimore County
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text. However, the bill explicitly prohibits the Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore County from charging an additional fee for the off-premises sale permit, indicating that no new permit revenue will be generated. Any administrative costs for the Board to develop regulations and oversee the permits are not specified.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is the primary state agency responsible for regulating the alcohol industry and enforcing state tax laws related to alcoholic beverages. This bill directly modifies the regulatory framework for alcohol sales in Baltimore County.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies, boards, and commissions, including the local boards of license commissioners. It would be responsible for advising the Baltimore County Board on the legalities of the new regulations and ensuring compliance with the state's Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article.

The bill explicitly mandates that the Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore County consider public health impacts before adopting regulations to authorize off-premises sales. As the state agency overseeing public health policy and coordinating with local health departments, the Department of Health is relevant to these policy considerations.

The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in appointing members to various state boards and commissions, including the Board of License Commissioners for Baltimore County. Changes to the statutory authority and regulatory duties of the Board are relevant to the office's mission in managing state leadership roles.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a unit of State government or other State entity that provides State aid from providing State aid to a nonprofit entity unless the nonprofit is current with certain obligations under federal, State, and local law.
Title: State Aid - Nonprofits - Status
Status: In the House - Hearing 1/27 at 2:00 p.m.
bill_summary: This bill prohibits Maryland State agencies and entities from providing State aid—including contributions, grants, or subsidies—to any nonprofit entity unless the nonprofit meets specific criteria: it must be in good standing with the IRS, current on federal, State, and local tax obligations, have a current charter on file with the State Department of Assessments and Taxation, and have filed its most recent tax forms such as IRS Form 990 or a personal property tax return.
responsible_party: Maryland State agencies and departments that provide State aid to nonprofit entities
stakeholders: Nonprofit organizations seeking or receiving State aid and Maryland State agencies that administer grant programs.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Fiscal Note indicates that the bill may have an operational impact on State agencies providing aid to nonprofits as they must verify compliance with the new requirements, but it is unlikely to materially affect State expenditures. State revenues and local government finances are not affected. Some agencies noted potential needs for additional staff or IT resources, but the Department of Legislative Services assumes grantors can largely fulfill requirements through existing resources or grantee affidavits.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DBM is the principal fiscal agency responsible for supervising budget execution and state expenditures. It manages the reporting framework for State aid provided to grantees and determines the format for reports required from all grantors.

DoIT is mandated to develop and operate the searchable public website that tracks State aid and grantees. Any changes to the conditions for receiving aid may require adjustments to tracking and reporting systems managed by this department.

As the state's principal tax collector, the Comptroller is responsible for verifying that entities are current on state tax obligations, which is a key requirement for nonprofits under the bill. The Comptroller also manages social organization reporting for State aid expenditures.

The department is a major grantor that provides significant State aid to nonprofits for behavioral health, developmental disabilities, and public health services. It would be responsible for verifying the compliance status of these numerous partners.

DHCD provides extensive State aid through grants and subsidies to nonprofits for affordable housing, community revitalization, and small business development, necessitating a robust verification process for all recipients.

DHS distributes State aid to nonprofit partners providing food assistance, energy assistance, and protective services. It will need to ensure all such entities meet the bill's tax and registration requirements.
Commerce provides grants and financial assistance to nonprofits in the arts, tourism, and economic development sectors. The bill adds a layer of compliance verification to their funding process.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Service and Civic Innovation
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This department relies heavily on nonprofit partnerships to create paid service opportunities and workforce pathways. It would be required to verify the standing of all nonprofit participants before providing aid.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office manages and allocates significant state and federal funding to nonprofit organizations for victim services, law enforcement support, and youth programs.
RMC administers the Rural Maryland Prosperity Investment Fund and other grants to nonprofit entities in rural counties, making them a primary grantor affected by the bill's restrictions.

As a state-chartered grant-making organization, the Trust awards numerous grants to nonprofits for environmental restoration and education, all of which must now meet the bill's specific compliance criteria.
MSDE provides State aid to various nonprofit educational partners, including those involved in early childhood development and special education services.
MDEM coordinates with nonprofits for disaster recovery and hazard mitigation, often involving the distribution of state funds that would fall under the definition of State aid.
MDE provides technical and financial assistance for environmental infrastructure and cleanup, which may involve grants to nonprofit environmental organizations.
DNR manages grant programs for conservation and restoration often executed by nonprofit stewardship organizations.
MDP, through entities like the Maryland Historical Trust, provides grants to nonprofits for cultural and historical preservation efforts.
The department provides State aid for workforce development and adult learning programs frequently operated by nonprofit entities.
MDoA oversees programs for older adults that are often delivered via nonprofit Area Agencies on Aging or community service providers.
MDA provides funding and support for agricultural promotion and soil conservation that may involve nonprofit grant recipients.
The department coordinates services for residents with disabilities, which includes funding nonprofit organizations that provide integrated community living and assistive technology services.
MDOT provides grants and technical assistance to various entities, including nonprofits involved in transit and transportation safety initiatives.
This department partners with and supports nonprofit organizations that provide advocacy and services to veterans and their families.
DJS provides funding for community-based treatment and rehabilitation programs often run by nonprofit service providers.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS provides aid to nonprofits that facilitate rehabilitation and recidivism reduction programs for justice-involved individuals.
GOCI acts as a primary liaison between the state and the nonprofit community, advising the Governor on community service policies and facilitating partnerships that involve state funding.
This office coordinates support networks and initiatives like the ENOUGH Initiative, which often involve providing state funds to nonprofits addressing child poverty.
GGO provides technical assistance and resources to state agencies regarding grant management and compliance, making them a key advisory body for implementing the bill's new requirements.
The library agency administers state and federal grants to support public library systems and related nonprofit educational initiatives.
OAG would provide legal counsel to all state agencies on how to interpret and implement these new statutory compliance requirements for nonprofit grantees.
BPW oversees and approves significant state expenditures and procurement contracts, ensuring that all executive decisions involving state funds comply with the law.
DGS is the central procurement authority and may oversee certain types of state aid or contracts with nonprofits that would fall under the bill's scope.
As a state entity, USM institutions may provide grants or aid to affiliated nonprofits or community partners, requiring adherence to the bill's verification standards.
MSP was identified in the fiscal note as an agency that may provide forms of aid or support to nonprofits that would require status verification.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MIEMSS coordinates the state's emergency medical services and may provide grants or equipment to nonprofit volunteer rescue squads.

Synopsis: Including institutions and programs of higher education in which a student is enrolled as part of a dual enrollment program in the definition of "school system"; adding certain offenses to the list of offenses a law enforcement agency must report to certain school personnel under certain circumstances; and authorizing State's Attorneys to make a certain notification if a student is arrested for certain offenses.
Title: School Systems - Reportable Offenses - Alterations
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/05 at 1:00 p.m. (Ways and Means)

NarrowSubjects.Name: Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
Higher Education -see also- Comm Colleges; Med Schools; etc.
Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police
Pornography -see also- Nudity and Sexual Displays; Obscenity
Violence -see also- Domestic Violence; Hate Crimes

bill_summary: This bill expands the list of 'reportable offenses' that law enforcement must report to school officials to include crimes such as stalking, distributing revenge porn, and threats of mass violence. It also includes institutions of higher education within the definition of a school system for students in dual enrollment programs and authorizes State's Attorneys to notify school officials of a student's arrest if law enforcement has not already done so.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE), local school superintendents, school principals, and State's Attorneys
stakeholders: Maryland public and nonpublic school students (ages 5–22), students in dual enrollment programs, school administrators, law enforcement agencies, and State's Attorneys
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE) can adjust its reporting requirements within existing resources, resulting in no state fiscal impact. Local government finances are not anticipated to be materially affected by the changes to notification requirements and procedures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MSDE is the primary agency responsible for overseen the Maryland public education system, adopting regulations for the handling of student information, and preparing the mandated annual report on reportable offenses.
MCSS, as an independent unit within MSDE, is directly responsible for coordinating school safety policies, managing safety grants, and training school safety personnel.

The bill expands the definition of 'school system' to include institutions of higher education for dual enrollment students, necessitating coordination of reporting policies and student data by the commission.
As the primary state law enforcement agency, MSP is mandated to notify school officials within 24 hours when a student is arrested for the expanded list of reportable offenses.
The bill authorizes State's Attorneys to notify school systems of arrests and requires judicial oversight for the release of confidential information about student reportable offenses.

DJS supervises youth in the justice system; changes to reporting requirements and the expanded list of offenses directly affect the coordination between justice and educational systems for their rehabilitation.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP serves as the state's coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice policy, advising on strategies related to the reporting of criminal acts and juvenile delinquency.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires school officials to invite a student's attorney (often a Public Defender) to participate in conferences regarding the student's removal or exclusion from school programs.
As a state-governed higher education institution, MSU is impacted by the bill's expanded definition of school systems and the requirement to receive notifications for dually enrolled students.
As an independent public college, St. Mary's is subject to the bill's new notification requirements for students dually enrolled in its programs.
USM member institutions that enroll dual enrollment students are included in the expanded definition of school systems for arrest reporting and safety coordination.
The Governor's Office receives the annual report on reportable offenses and student outcomes, and the office oversees the executive branch departments implementing these changes.
As a state education agency serving students ages 5-21, the Maryland School for the Deaf must adhere to state-mandated safety and reportable offense notification procedures.
OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like MSDE and MHEC regarding the legal implementation of reporting mandates and confidentiality protections.

Synopsis: Allowing, subject to certain limitations, a subtraction modification under the Maryland income tax for certain personal casualty losses of certain retirement assets from theft or a fraud scheme; and applying the Act to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.
Title: Income Tax - Subtraction Modification - Losses From Theft or Fraud
Status: In the House - Hearing 1/29 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes
Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police

bill_summary: This bill establishes a subtraction modification under the Maryland income tax for personal casualty losses that occur as a result of theft or a fraud scheme involving assets in a qualified retirement plan. Taxpayers are required to submit a police report and documentation of the impacted assets to claim the subtraction.
stakeholders: Maryland taxpayers who experience theft or fraud involving their qualified retirement plan assets
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues may decrease by more than $1,000,000 annually beginning in fiscal 2027. Additionally, local income tax revenues are estimated to decrease by more than $700,000 annually starting in fiscal 2027. The Comptroller’s Office is expected to handle the implementation with existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's principal tax collector, the Comptroller is responsible for implementing the new subtraction modification, updating tax forms, and processing claims for losses related to theft or fraud schemes.

The bill is projected to decrease general fund revenues by more than $1 million annually starting in fiscal 2027, which impacts the department's core duties of revenue estimation and long-term fiscal planning.

The bill requires taxpayers to provide a police report to qualify for the subtraction modification. As the primary state law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police is involved in investigating such crimes and provided data for the fiscal analysis.

The Office of the Attorney General's Consumer Protection Division provided information for the fiscal note and is responsible for investigating the types of fraud schemes and financial exploitation that the bill addresses.

The fiscal note specifically identifies elder financial exploitation as a significant source of the losses addressed by the bill, making it relevant to the department's mission to protect the rights and assets of older adults.
The Maryland Tax Court would be responsible for hearing appeals from final decisions made by the Comptroller regarding the eligibility of specific subtraction modification claims under this act.

Synopsis: Requiring that a motor vehicle be at least 25 years old in order to be eligible for registration as a historic motor vehicle.
Title: Vehicle Laws – Historic Motor Vehicles – Minimum Age
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/27 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Age -see also- Age of Maj; Children; Elderly; Inf&Tod.; etc
Historical Matters -see also- Archives; Monumts; Museum; etc
Motor Vehicles -see also- Aband Veh; Ambulances; Buses; etc.

bill_summary: This bill updates the eligibility criteria for registering a vehicle as a historic motor vehicle. It replaces the fixed model year requirement of 1999 or earlier with a rolling requirement that the vehicle be at least 25 years old. The bill maintains existing restrictions on vehicle use, such as prohibiting daily commuting or commercial use, and preserves the current registration fee structure.
stakeholders: Owners of motor vehicles at least 25 years old and the Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill changes the pool of vehicles eligible for historic registration by establishing a rolling 25-year age requirement. While the bill specifies an annual registration fee of $55.50 and a one-time fee of $50.00 for vehicles at least 60 years old, a formal fiscal impact estimate is unavailable because the Fiscal Note was not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Motor Vehicle Administration is the primary agency responsible for the bill's implementation, as it manages vehicle registration, issues historic license plates, and adopts regulations to determine vehicle eligibility.
As the parent agency of the Motor Vehicle Administration, MDOT oversees the state's transportation network and the collection of registration fees that fund the Transportation Trust Fund.

The bill impacts environmental regulations because historic vehicles are exempt from emissions inspections, a program co-administered by the Maryland Department of the Environment to ensure air quality standards.

The Comptroller acts as the state's chief financial officer and principal tax collector, overseeing the collection of state revenues including the registration fees impacted by this change in vehicle classification.
DBM is responsible for revenue estimation and fiscal planning; changes to the volume of historic vehicle registrations will affect the state's revenue projections.

The Maryland State Police enforce motor vehicle laws on state highways, and changes to the definition and equipment requirements for historic vehicles affect their law enforcement and safety inspection duties.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Motor Vehicle Administration and other state agencies regarding the drafting and enforcement of regulations related to vehicle registration laws.

Synopsis: Exempting a sale, rental, or transfer of a regulated firearm from the seven-day waiting period requirement if the purchaser, renter, or receiver of the firearm is a law enforcement officer, a retired law enforcement officer who retired in good standing, or an individual with a permit to wear, carry, or transport a handgun.
Title: Regulated Firearms - Seven-Day Waiting Period - Exceptions
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/04 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police
Licenses -see also- AB Lic; Certifications; DrLic; Permits
Transfer of Goods -see also- Goods&Svc; Leas&Rnt; RetailSale

bill_summary: This bill creates an exception to the seven-day waiting period for purchasing, renting, or transferring a regulated firearm for specific individuals, including law enforcement officers, retired law enforcement officers in good standing, and individuals with a handgun wear, carry, or transport permit.
stakeholders: Law enforcement officers, retired law enforcement officers, handgun permit holders, and regulated firearm licensees.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the primary legal representative for the state and provides counsel to the Maryland State Police regarding the enforcement and legal interpretation of firearm statutes and regulatory exemptions.

bill_summary: This bill defines and prohibits deed fraud, including the unauthorized sale, conveyance, or lease of real property and the acquisition of property through deception or intimidation. It establishes the Deed Fraud Prevention Grant Fund, administered by the Department of State Police, to aid law enforcement, support legal services for victims, and provide emergency housing assistance. It also creates a Task Force to Study Deed Fraud and mandates new crime reporting requirements.
stakeholders: Real property owners, victims of deed fraud, state and local law enforcement agencies, and the Maryland Legal Services Corporation.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $48,900 in FY 2027 for administration. A mandated $200,000 general fund appropriation is required in FY 2028 to capitalize the Deed Fraud Prevention Grant Fund. One-time IT programming costs to update the National Incident-Based Reporting System are estimated to exceed $1,000,000 for the Department of State Police, with additional significant costs likely for local law enforcement agencies.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of State Police (referred to as the Department in the Public Safety Article) is the primary agency responsible for administering the new Deed Fraud Prevention Grant Fund. The agency must also collect, analyze, and disseminate disaggregated crime data specifically regarding deed fraud violations.

The Administrative Office of the Courts is mandated by the bill to provide staffing for the newly established Task Force to Study Deed Fraud. Additionally, a representative of the Judiciary, designated by the Chief Justice, is a member of the Task Force.

The Attorney General (or a designee) is a required member of the Task Force to Study Deed Fraud. As the state's chief legal officer, the OAG is also relevant to the establishment of new criminal prohibitions and the prosecution framework for deed fraud.

The Secretary of Housing and Community Development (or a designee) is a required member of the Task Force. Furthermore, the Deed Fraud Prevention Grant Fund is authorized to provide emergency housing assistance to displaced victims, which aligns with this department's mission.

The Governor is responsible for appointing members to the Task Force to Study Deed Fraud and designating its chair. The Governor is also required to include a mandated appropriation of $200,000 for the Grant Fund in the fiscal year 2028 budget.

The bill includes a mandated appropriation of $200,000 in fiscal year 2028 and establishes a new special fund. DBM is responsible for overseeing state budget development and supervising the execution of these funds.

The Comptroller is responsible for accounting for the new Deed Fraud Prevention Grant Fund and ensuring interest earnings are appropriately credited or distributed.

The bill updates Section 8-601 of the Criminal Law Article, which specifies the Register of Wills as a location for filing counterfeit instruments and as a potential venue for criminal prosecution.
The Task Force to Study Deed Fraud includes a representative from the land title insurance industry, a sector regulated by the Maryland Insurance Administration.

stakeholders: Individuals with expunged criminal records (particularly for cannabis possession), educational institutions, and state and local government agencies
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures for the Judiciary increase by approximately $175,607 in FY 2027 for one-time computer programming costs to remove references from the MDEC system. There is no expected material fiscal impact on local government operations or finances.

The bill prohibits educational institutions from using a person's refusal to disclose expunged criminal charges as a reason for expulsion or denial of admission. MSDE oversees the state's public schools and sets educational policies relevant to these admission and disciplinary standards.

The bill prohibits educational institutions, including public and private colleges, from denying admission or expelling individuals for refusing to disclose expunged records. MHEC coordinates policies for these institutions and ensures adherence to academic and financial standards.

The Comptroller's office regulates and licenses various industries (alcohol, tobacco, motor fuel). The bill's provisions regarding the denial of licenses based on nondisclosure of expunged records applies to its regulatory functions.

bill_summary: This bill allows for the admissibility of intercepted wire, oral, or electronic communications and evidence derived from them in criminal trials or hearings under specific circumstances. For such evidence to be admitted, the court must determine that the case involves a crime against an individual, the evidence is material and highly probative, the interception was not conducted by or for Maryland law enforcement, and its admission serves the interests of justice, provided that notice is given to the adverse party at least 14 days before trial.
stakeholders: Defendants, victims, and legal professionals within the Maryland criminal justice system
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the text. There are no explicit funding mandates or revenue changes described in the bill, and specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the Maryland Judicial Branch by establishing new criteria and procedures for judges in District and Circuit Courts to determine the admissibility of intercepted communications in criminal trials and hearings.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the agency providing legal representation to indigent defendants, the bill significantly impacts their work by expanding the types of evidence (intercepted communications) that can be admitted against their clients in criminal proceedings.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer and represents the state in criminal appeals. This bill changes evidentiary rules that would be central to criminal prosecutions and subsequent appeals handled by the office.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency is the state's primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategies. A change in the admissibility of intercepted communications is a significant policy shift relevant to their mission of reducing crime and recidivism.

The OSP investigates and prosecutes criminal offenses related to official misconduct and election integrity. The ability to use intercepted communications in criminal trials is highly relevant to their prosecutorial functions in Circuit Court.

As the primary state law enforcement agency, the MSP is involved in the investigations that lead to the criminal trials affected by this bill, even if the specific exception in the bill applies to interceptions not conducted by state law enforcement.

DJS manages youth in the juvenile justice system. While the bill specifies 'criminal trials,' intercepted communications are often relevant in the court proceedings involving youth supervised by this agency.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency oversees the rehabilitation and supervision of justice-involved individuals. Changes in evidentiary standards that affect trial outcomes have a downstream impact on the population managed by DPSCS.

DBM is responsible for the state's fiscal planning. Changes in court procedures and admissibility rules can impact the duration of trials and the resources required by the Judiciary and the Office of the Public Defender.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes state policy. This bill represents a notable change in criminal law policy that intersects with the Governor's public safety initiatives.

bill_summary: House Bill 133 reduces several major Maryland taxes: it establishes a flat 3% individual income tax rate for most taxpayers, lowers the corporate income tax rate from 8.25% to 3%, and reduces the general sales and use tax rate from 6% to 3%. Additionally, it increases the capital gains surtax to 3% while exempting the first $10,000 of gains for individuals aged 65 and older, and repeals the sales and use tax on data and information technology services.
stakeholders: Maryland individual and corporate taxpayers, retail consumers of goods and services, senior citizens, and information technology service providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill will result in a net decrease in State revenues and expenditures of approximately 14016600000 in fiscal 2027. General fund revenues are estimated to decrease by 13253000000, while special fund revenues will decrease by 843200000. Local government revenues are projected to decrease by 96900000 in fiscal 2027 due to reduced distributions from corporate income taxes and cannabis sales taxes.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the administrative support for the Governor, who proposes the annual state budget and coordinates policy initiatives, this office is highly relevant as the bill proposes a massive overhaul of the state's tax structure resulting in an estimated $13.3 billion general fund revenue decrease, fundamentally altering the state's fiscal landscape.

As the state's chief financial officer and principal tax collector, the Comptroller is the primary agency responsible for implementing and enforcing the proposed changes to the individual income tax, corporate income tax, and sales and use tax rates, including the repeal of specific IT-related sales taxes.

As the state's primary economic development agency, the bill's significant reduction in corporate and individual income tax rates and the repeal of sales taxes on IT services are highly relevant to the Department's mission of attracting and retaining businesses.

The bill repeals the sales and use tax on data or information technology services and software publishing. As the agency responsible for the state's IT strategy and digital services, these changes directly impact the economic environment of the technology sector.

MEA manages the Strategic Energy Investment Fund, which receives a portion of corporate income tax revenue. The bill's reduction of the corporate tax rate will impact SEIF funding for renewable energy and efficiency programs.

As a state-funded research university, Morgan State is impacted by the bill's changes to the corporate income tax, which funds the Higher Education Investment Fund, and the broader reduction in general fund revenue.

OLA is responsible for conducting fiscal compliance audits. The massive changes to tax collection and distribution proposed in this bill will require significant oversight and auditing to ensure financial accountability and legal compliance.
As a public college and independent unit of state government, the college is relevant due to the bill's significant impact on state general fund revenues, which support higher education institutions.

The USM is impacted by the bill's reduction of the corporate income tax rate, which directly decreases revenue for the Higher Education Investment Fund used to support the system's institutions and research.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a legal process allowing family members and other interested parties to petition the court for reasonable visitation with an adult who is alleged to be incapacitated or a protected person. stakeholders: Alleged incapacitated or protected adults, their spouses, adult children, adult grandchildren, parents, adult siblings, legal guardians, and health care facilities

stakeholders: Maryland local governments, property owners in areas designated as blighted, and small businesses in the construction and development sectors.

The agency provides technical assistance and policy guidance for land use planning and sustainable growth, including the designation of development districts within political subdivisions.

Synopsis: Altering an exemption that allows an official of the Legislative Branch to accept a gift of food or beverages as part of a meal or reception to which a legislative unit is invited to instead allow an official of the Legislative Branch to accept a gift of food or beverages at a meal or reception to which all members of the General Assembly are invited and that was open to the public; altering the written invitation and registration report requirements a regulated lobbyist must meet under certain circumstances; etc.

bill_summary: This bill restricts the conditions under which Maryland Legislative Branch officials may accept gifts of food and beverages. It limits the current exemption to only those meals or receptions where every member of the General Assembly is invited and the event is open to the public, effectively removing exemptions for smaller groups like committees or regional delegations. The bill also requires regulated lobbyists to provide 14 days of advance notice for such events instead of 5, and it mandates that the Department of Legislative Services post event details on the General Assembly website within one business day of registration.
responsible_party: Department of Legislative Services and the State Ethics Commission
stakeholders: Members of the Maryland General Assembly, officials of the Legislative Branch, regulated lobbyists, and the general public.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the source text. Financial implications identified in the bill text include administrative costs for the Department of Legislative Services to update the General Assembly website and manage new registration reports, as well as modifications to reporting procedures for the State Ethics Commission and regulated lobbyists.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Ethics Commission is the primary agency responsible for the administration and enforcement of the Maryland Public Ethics Law. This bill directly amends provisions of that law related to gift exemptions, financial disclosure schedules, and lobbyist reporting, requiring the Commission to update its systems and oversight procedures.

The Office of the State Prosecutor has the mandate to investigate and prosecute violations of the Maryland Public Ethics Law. By altering the legal standards for accepting gifts and the requirements for lobbyist registration, the bill directly impacts the OSP's enforcement and investigative activities.

OLA is an agency within the Department of Legislative Services (DLS). The bill specifically tasks DLS with receiving lobbyist registrations for meals/receptions and posting that information on the General Assembly website. Furthermore, OLA audits state agencies for compliance with the public ethics laws amended by this bill.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for the state, providing counsel to the General Assembly and the State Ethics Commission. They would be responsible for advising on the implementation of these ethics law changes and potentially defending the regulations in court.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, which includes the State Ethics Commission. As this bill proposes amendments to the statewide Public Ethics Law, the Governor's Office would be involved in the policy coordination and potential budgetary adjustments required for implementation.
