Public Officials -see also- Atty Gen; Compt; Coun Admin; etc

bill_summary: The Congressional Stock Trading Transparency Act requires the Maryland State Board of Elections to add an option to the certificate of candidacy form for candidates for the U.S. Senate or U.S. House of Representatives to indicate whether they and their spouses will refrain from buying, selling, or exchanging individual stocks during their term of office. The State Board must also publish a list of candidates who make this indication on its website.
stakeholders: Candidates for the office of United States Senator or Representative in Congress and their spouses
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill has no state or local fiscal impact, and the State Board of Elections can implement the requirements using existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the State Board of Elections to modify the certificate of candidacy forms for congressional candidates to include a stock trading pledge and requires the Board to publish this information on its official website.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies like the State Board of Elections and would be responsible for reviewing the legality of the new form requirements and providing guidance on their implementation.

The bill references the existing requirement for candidates to file financial disclosure statements with the State Ethics Commission (or other required reports) as a condition of a valid certificate of candidacy, which is the primary subject of this legislation.

Synopsis: Establishing that certain documentation relating to real property may be used to establish a rebuttable presumption of ownership of the property in certain court proceedings.
Title: Courts - Evidence - Proof of Ownership of Real Property
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/04 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill allows a new owner of real property to use specific documentation, such as a deed submitted for recordation, a HUD-1 settlement statement, or a closing disclosure, to establish a rebuttable presumption of ownership in court proceedings. The purpose is to allow property owners to engage in legal actions to protect their property during the administrative period required to officially record a deed.
stakeholders: New real property owners and parties involved in legal proceedings regarding real property ownership
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local operations or finances, and no specific dollar estimates for revenue or expenditures are provided in the fiscal note.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes new evidentiary standards for court proceedings and grants the Supreme Court of Maryland, which the Administrative Office of the Courts supports, the authority to adopt implementing rules and forms.

As the agency responsible for supporting homeownership and community development, this department is a primary stakeholder in property ownership verification and was consulted during the fiscal analysis of the bill.
The Maryland Tax Court adjudicates property assessment and tax disputes where the rebuttable presumption of ownership created by this bill would be directly applicable.
The Register of Wills manages probate and estate administration, where establishing real property ownership during the processing time for a deed transfer is frequently necessary.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the state and its agencies on the interpretation and application of new evidentiary statutes in civil and criminal litigation.
Administrative Law Judges at the OAH may be required to apply this rebuttable presumption of ownership in contested administrative cases involving state agencies and property interests.
As the primary manager of state-owned real estate and acquisitions, the agency is impacted by rules governing the legal protection of property during the transition period before a deed is recorded.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a health care provider from using the health care provider's human reproductive material when providing assisted reproductive treatment without the consent of the recipient of the treatment; prohibiting a health care provider from using a donor's human reproductive material to provide assisted reproductive treatment without the donor's informed consent or in a manner that is inconsistent with the donor's consent; etc.
Title: Health Care Providers - Assisted Reproductive Treatment - Informed Consent and Fraud
Status: In the House - Unfavorable Report by Health; Withdrawn

NarrowSubjects.Name: Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records
Reproductive Matters -see also- Abortion; BrthCntr; Preg

bill_summary: This bill establishes strict informed consent requirements for health care providers performing assisted reproductive treatments (ART), such as in vitro fertilization and insemination. It prohibits providers from using their own human reproductive material without the recipient's consent and requires separate written consent from both donors and recipients. The bill also forbids providers or their employees from misrepresenting donor identity, genetic history, or the quality of reproductive material. Unauthorized use of a provider's own material is classified as a felony, and the bill creates civil liability for damages, including liquidated damages of up to $50,000 and attorney's fees.
responsible_party: Maryland health care provider licensing boards and the state court system
stakeholders: Health care providers performing assisted reproductive treatments, fertility clinic employees, sperm and egg donors, patients receiving fertility treatments, and children born as a result of assisted reproductive treatment.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the bill text. However, the bill establishes a new felony offense for unauthorized use of a provider's reproductive material, punishable by a fine of up to $5,000. Additionally, health care providers may be subject to civil lawsuits for violations, with potential liquidated damages of up to $50,000 per violation, as well as compensatory damages and legal fees. Specific state-wide expenditure and revenue estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill adds a new section to the Health - General Article and requires health care providers to report misuses or errors in human reproductive material to their respective licensing boards, which are housed under the Maryland Department of Health.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Health Care Alternative Dispute Resolution Office
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates new civil causes of action for medical liability and damages against health care providers for unauthorized use of human reproductive material. As the office responsible for mandatory arbitration of medical malpractice claims, HCADRO would likely manage the initial filing of these claims.

The bill establishes new civil causes of action with specific statutes of limitations and creates a new felony offense for unauthorized use of a provider's own reproductive material, which will impact court caseloads and judicial procedures.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the health occupations licensing boards and the Department of Health, and would likely be involved in advising on the implementation and enforcement of the new reporting and fraud requirements.

The bill requires reporting violations to licensing boards. Contested disciplinary actions taken by these boards against health care providers for violations of this section would be adjudicated through the Office of Administrative Hearings.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a new felony offense punishable by up to 10 years in prison, which could impact the state's correctional system population and parole/probation caseloads.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a new felony offense. The Office of the Public Defender would be responsible for representing indigent health care providers charged with this crime.
As the primary law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police may be involved in investigating allegations of health care provider fraud and criminal violations of this section.

Synopsis: Requiring each county and municipal automated traffic enforcement program to submit to the Vision Zero coordinator a quarterly report containing certain information regarding each citation issued under the program during the quarter to a motor vehicle registered in another state.
Title: Motor Vehicles - Out-of-State Drivers - Automated Enforcement (Out-of-State Driver Accountability Act)
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/12 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
License Plates -see also- Motor Vehicle Registration

bill_summary: The Out-of-State Driver Accountability Act requires Maryland county and municipal automated traffic enforcement programs to submit quarterly reports to the State Vision Zero coordinator regarding citations issued to vehicles registered in other states. These reports must include the registration plate number, the state of registration, payment status, and a cumulative summary of out-of-state citations and payments.
responsible_party: The Maryland Department of Transportation (Vision Zero coordinator) and local county and municipal automated traffic enforcement programs.
stakeholders: Out-of-state motor vehicle owners, Maryland county and municipal governments, and the Maryland Department of Transportation.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note with specific revenue or expenditure estimates was not provided in the text. However, the bill creates administrative requirements for local governments to compile, update, and report citation data on a quarterly basis. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly tasks the MDOT-designated Vision Zero coordinator with receiving quarterly reports from all local automated traffic enforcement programs and collaborating with them on implementation.
SHA is the primary agency responsible for the state's roadway safety and the operational implementation of Vision Zero. They also oversee work zone speed control systems mentioned in the bill.

MVA manages the state's vehicle registration data and inter-state reciprocity agreements. The bill's focus on identifying and tracking out-of-state registrations for citation payment accountability directly involves MVA data and policy interests.
As the primary state law enforcement agency for traffic laws, MSP collaborates with MDOT on safety initiatives and manages certain automated systems, such as work zone speed enforcement.
The bill includes school bus monitoring cameras in the reporting mandate. MCSS, which oversees school-related safety and transportation security, has a direct interest in this data.

DBM oversees state personnel and fiscal policy. The new reporting mandate will likely have a fiscal and operational impact on MDOT staff who must manage and process the quarterly reports from local jurisdictions.
The bill includes reporting requirements for noise abatement monitoring systems, an area where MDE sets environmental standards and provides technical guidance.
MSDE is the parent agency of the Maryland Center for School Safety and oversees public education transportation standards, including policies related to school bus monitoring cameras.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP coordinates statewide public safety strategies and manages related funding, which may be informed by the data collected on traffic law violations and payment compliance.

Synopsis: Authorizing the governing body of Baltimore County to grant, by law, a property tax credit against the county property tax imposed on certain real property owned by the Fraternal Order of Police Lodge 34.
Title: Baltimore County – Property Tax Credit – Fraternal Order of Police Lodge 34
Status: In the House - Hearing 1/20 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the governing body of Baltimore County to grant a 100% property tax credit against the county property tax for real property owned by the Fraternal Order of Police Lodge 34, specifically the location at 730 Wampler Road in Middle River, Maryland.
stakeholders: Fraternal Order of Police Lodge 34 and Baltimore County
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no impact on State finances. To the extent the credit is granted, Baltimore County property tax revenues may decrease by approximately $9,600 annually beginning in fiscal 2027. This estimate is based on the fiscal 2027 assessment of the property and the current county property tax rate.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board is the state entity responsible for hearing and adjudicating disputes regarding local property tax assessments, exemptions, and credits, such as the one authorized by this bill for Baltimore County.

The Maryland Tax Court is the highest level of administrative review for tax disputes in the state, hearing appeals from the decisions of local taxing authorities and the Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board regarding property tax matters.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation passed by the General Assembly, including local property tax authorizations.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Governor on the constitutionality of legislation and represents state agencies and boards in legal matters related to the enforcement of tax laws.

Synopsis: Establishing a certain process for bringing vehicles owned by State residents that are improperly registered in another state into compliance with the Maryland Vehicle Law; providing that if a vehicle's owner fails to properly register the vehicle within 60 days after issuance of a warning, the Administration will begin to assess a civil fine of $7 per day up to 60 days; providing that if the vehicle is not registered within 120 days after the warning, the vehicle may be immobilized by towing and impoundment or by booting.
Title: Vehicle Laws - Out-of-State Vehicles - Improper Registration
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/12 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Motor Vehicles -see also- Aband Veh; Ambulances; Buses; etc.
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

bill_summary: This bill establishes an enforcement process for Maryland residents who fail to properly register their vehicles in the State. The Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA) is authorized to issue warnings, assess civil fines of $7 per day for up to 60 days for non-compliance, and eventually refer persistent cases to local State's Attorneys for civil actions resulting in vehicle immobilization, impoundment, or booting.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Transportation Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA) and County State's Attorneys
stakeholders: Maryland residents with vehicles improperly registered out-of-state, the Motor Vehicle Administration, and local government law enforcement agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State special fund revenues (primarily for the Transportation Trust Fund) are estimated to increase by $15,375,437 in fiscal 2027, with ongoing annual increases of $6,224,537. Additional significant revenue from vehicle excise taxes could range from $26.2 million to $65.5 million. State expenditures increase by $379,365 in fiscal 2027 to hire five customer service agents for administration. Local governments will realize increased revenues from a portion of registration fees (local highway user revenues) and the required payment of outstanding automated enforcement citations prior to new registration.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA) is the primary implementing agency for this bill. It is responsible for identifying probable cause for improper registration, issuing warnings, assessing civil fines, and managing the nonresident permit process.

As the parent agency of the Motor Vehicle Administration, MDOT oversees the Transportation Trust Fund (TTF), which is projected to receive millions of dollars in increased revenue from registration fees, titling, and fines under this bill.

The bill establishes a civil action in rem process that will be handled by the Maryland court system. Additionally, existing penalties for registration violations are adjudicated and collected through the courts.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MIEMSS oversees the Maryland Emergency Medical System Operations Fund (MEMSOF), which is projected to receive nearly $1 million in additional annual revenue from registration surcharges resulting from the bill's enforcement.
DBM is responsible for the personnel management and budget execution for the five additional customer service positions the MVA requires to manage the workload created by this bill.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the MVA and would likely assist in establishing the legal standards for 'probable cause' and 'residency' required to issue the warnings and assess fines mandated by the bill.

As the primary law enforcement agency for motor vehicle laws on state highways, the Maryland State Police are involved in the enforcement of registration compliance and the identification of out-of-state vehicles.
The MHCC oversees the Maryland Trauma Physician Services Fund, which is specifically identified in the fiscal note as a recipient of increased surcharge revenue from newly registered vehicles.
The OAH would likely serve as the venue for administrative appeals if vehicle owners contest MVA's residency determinations or the assessment of daily civil fines.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and MDOT/MVA, coordinating the policy initiatives that drive large-scale enforcement programs like the one proposed in this bill.
The State Treasurer acts as the custodian of state funds, managing the reception and investment of the significant new revenue flowing into the Transportation Trust Fund and other special funds.

Synopsis: Providing that it is lawful for a person to intercept an oral communication if the person is working as a fair housing tester for a fair housing testing program operated by the federal government, the State, a local government, or a nonprofit civil rights organization under certain circumstances; and providing that the contents of an intercepted oral communication may be used only for the purpose of enforcing federal, State, or local fair housing laws.
Title: Evidence – Interception of Oral Communications – Fair Housing Testing
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/24 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
General Assembly -see also- AELR Cmte; LegislativePolCmte
Housing -see also- Apartments; Condos; Mobile & Manuf  Homes
Investigations and Inquiries -see also- Crim Bckgrnd Invest
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill allows fair housing testers working for government programs or specific nonprofit civil rights organizations to intercept oral communications without the consent of all parties, provided the tester is a party to the communication and the recording is intended to gather evidence of fair housing violations. The intercepted evidence is only admissible for enforcing federal, state, or local fair housing laws.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and state and local fair housing enforcement agencies
stakeholders: Fair housing testers, nonprofit civil rights organizations, property owners and managers, and government agencies involved in fair housing enforcement
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local finances or operations. No specific revenue or expenditure figures are provided as the impact is considered negligible.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article to establish new rules for the admissibility of evidence obtained through the interception of oral communications. It specifically affects how courts must handle evidence in trials or hearings involving fair housing violations.

The Commission is the primary state agency responsible for enforcing anti-discrimination laws in housing. The bill specifically empowers fair housing testing programs—which the Commission may operate or oversee—by allowing testers to record communications as evidence of violations.

The department is responsible for ensuring residents have access to safe and secure housing. Fair housing testing is a critical tool for identifying discrimination that prevents residents from securing housing, directly aligning with the department's mission.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Under current law, intercepting oral communications without consent is a felony. By creating a lawful exception for fair housing testers, the bill directly impacts the criminal statutes that the Office of the Public Defender would navigate when representing indigent individuals who might otherwise face surveillance-related charges.

As the state's primary law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police are responsible for enforcing criminal laws, including those related to illegal electronic surveillance. This bill creates a statutory exception to the wiretap felony for housing testers, which impacts police investigative and arrest protocols.

The Office of Administrative Hearings adjudicates contested cases for state agencies, including those involving regulatory enforcement and potential housing discrimination claims where this type of recorded evidence might now be introduced.

The OAG serves as the chief legal representative for the state and provides counsel to the Commission on Civil Rights and other state agencies. They would be responsible for interpreting these new evidentiary rules and using this evidence in civil rights litigation.

Synopsis: Requiring institutions of higher education to develop and implement an academic forgiveness policy on or before August 1, 2026, that applies to applicants who earned unsatisfactory or failing grades at a prior institution of higher education under certain circumstances.
Title: Higher Education - Academic Forgiveness Policy - Established
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/24 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Higher Education -see also- Comm Colleges; Med Schools; etc.
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill requires Maryland institutions of higher education that receive State funding to establish an academic forgiveness policy by August 1, 2026. The policy allows applicants to elect to have unsatisfactory or failing grades earned seven or more years prior to their application disregarded during the admissions process.
responsible_party: Maryland institutions of higher education that receive State funding
stakeholders: Prospective higher education students with academic records older than seven years and Maryland institutions of higher education receiving State funds.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. However, the mandate for institutions to develop and implement a new academic forgiveness policy by August 2026 suggests that these institutions would likely incur administrative costs.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's regulatory and coordinating board for postsecondary education, the Commission is responsible for establishing and overseeing statewide policies for public and private institutions, including the implementation of the mandated academic forgiveness policy.

As the primary public higher education system in the state, the University System of Maryland must develop and implement the required academic forgiveness policies across its 12 member institutions that receive state funds.

As a state-funded public university independent of the University System, Morgan State University is directly required by the bill to implement an academic forgiveness policy for its admissions process.
As Maryland's public honors college and an independent state agency receiving state funds, the college is mandated to develop and implement the academic forgiveness policy described in the bill.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Maryland Higher Education Commission and the public institutions of higher education, and would likely assist in drafting and reviewing the required academic forgiveness policies for legal compliance.

This agency collects and analyzes student performance data from the Higher Education Commission and partner institutions. Changes in how prior grades are treated in the admissions process may impact data collection, reporting, and longitudinal studies of student outcomes.

The department advocates for veterans' educational benefits. Veterans are often non-traditional students who may have prior academic records from 7+ years ago and could significantly benefit from the academic forgiveness policies established by this bill.

Synopsis: Requiring the Department of Aging to conduct an annual financial stress test for each continuing care in a retirement community provider; requiring a continuing care in a retirement community provider to meet with a resident association at least quarterly and in a certain manner; requiring a provider to make agendas and minutes of certain meetings accessible to the provider's subscribers; etc.
Title: Continuing Care Providers - Financial Stress Tests, Transparency, and Governing Bodies
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/05 at 1:45 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Continuing Care -see also- Long-Term Care; Nursing Homes

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of Aging to conduct annual financial stress tests for continuing care retirement community providers and publish financial stability grades on its website. It also mandates that providers meet with resident associations at least quarterly, provide meeting agendas and minutes to subscribers, and requires that subscriber members of a provider's governing body be elected by the resident association rather than selected by the provider.
stakeholders: Subscribers (residents) of continuing care retirement communities, continuing care retirement community providers, and the Maryland Department of Aging.
fiscal_impact_summary: State special fund expenditures increase by at least $270,500 in FY 2027 for the Maryland Department of Aging to hire two analysts and secure contractual services for a financial grading system. Ongoing annual expenditures are estimated to range from $200,900 to $228,300 through FY 2031. Special fund revenues to the Continuing Care Fund may increase by an indeterminate amount if provider fees are raised to offset these administrative costs. There is no impact on local finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the Department of Aging to conduct annual financial stress tests for continuing care providers, hire analysts to perform these tests, and manage the results through its Financial Review Committee.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill assigns a specific new duty to the Department of Aging's Financial Review Committee, which is a permanent advisory body composed of experts appointed to evaluate the financial condition of providers.

The bill requires the hiring of two new analysts and involves a significant increase in special fund expenditures, which falls under the oversight of the Department of Budget and Management for personnel and fiscal planning.

As the chief legal officer for state agencies, the OAG would be responsible for providing legal counsel to the Department of Aging regarding the implementation of the new stress tests and the public grading system for private providers.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and the Department of Aging, and is responsible for the overall state budget process which includes the new special fund expenditures and personnel required by this bill.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a person from knowingly recruiting, harboring, transporting, or obtaining an individual for the purpose of appropriating the government benefits of an individual for the benefit of the person or another through deception, coercion, exploitation, isolation, or any other means; prohibiting a person from aiding, abetting, or conspiring with one or more persons to violate a certain provision of the Act; establishing that a violation of the Act is a felony; etc.
Title: Criminal Law - Benefits Exploitation
Status: In the House - Hearing 1/27 at 2:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty
Public Benefits -see also- Housing; MedAsst;  SupplNutrAsstP

bill_summary: This bill creates the felony crime of benefits exploitation, which prohibits a person from knowingly recruiting, harboring, transporting, or obtaining an individual for the purpose of appropriating their government benefits through deception, coercion, exploitation, or isolation. Government benefits covered include Medicare, Medicaid, SNAP, Social Security, and veterans benefits, among others. Violators are subject to a maximum penalty of 25 years imprisonment and/or a fine of $15,000.
stakeholders: Recipients of government benefits (including the elderly and disabled), law enforcement, and the state court system
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State general fund expenditures will increase by $1,573 in fiscal 2026 only for the Judiciary to implement one-time programming changes. The bill is not expected to materially affect local finances or operations, and other state agencies like the Office of the Public Defender are expected to handle workloads within existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note explicitly identifies a general fund expenditure for the Judiciary to implement one-time programming changes related to the new criminal charge. As the central support agency for the Judicial Branch, it must manage the operational impacts of this new felony legislation.

The OAG has existing authority and specialized units (Senior and Vulnerable Adult Asset Recovery Unit) to handle civil and criminal matters related to the exploitation of vulnerable adults. This bill directly expands the criminal framework for benefit-related exploitation, which aligns with OAG's enforcement and consumer protection roles.

DHS administers several of the programs specifically listed as 'government benefits' in the bill, including TANF, SNAP, TDAP, and Public Assistance to Adults (PAA). The agency is directly impacted by crimes targeting the benefits it provides to vulnerable populations.

MDH is responsible for administering Medicare, Medicaid, and likely WIC benefits, which are explicitly listed as 'government benefits' targeted for exploitation under the bill. The agency's role in public health and Health Care Financing makes it highly relevant to benefit integrity.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender

bill_summary: The Maryland Voting Rights Act of 2026 prohibits voter intimidation, deception, and obstruction while preventing local governments from implementing election policies that create material disparities for protected classes based on race, color, or language. It enhances public notice requirements for changes to administrative policies affecting voting rights, establishes civil causes of action for enforcement, and authorizes the Attorney General to approve local remedies for potential violations.
responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Elections, local boards of elections, municipal corporations, and the Office of the Attorney General.
stakeholders: Maryland voters (particularly members of protected classes), local governments, county boards of education, and election administrators.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. However, the bill specifies financial implications including costs for local governments to meet expanded public notice requirements, the potential for local governments to reimburse reasonable costs for notification letters, and liability for court-awarded damages and attorney's fees in cases of successful enforcement actions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency for election administration, the State Board is directly responsible for the bill's expanded public notice requirements, maintaining the central web repository for election policy changes, and overseeing the administrative policies affected by the act.

The bill grants the Attorney General significant enforcement and regulatory authority, including the power to file civil actions, approve local government remedies to address violations, and adopt regulations to carry out the act.

The bill specifies the Circuit Court for Anne Arundel County as the exclusive venue for certain actions and establishes mandatory judicial standards, expedited pretrial and trial proceedings, and specific remedy requirements that the court must follow.

The bill's definition of 'Local Government' and 'Governing Body' explicitly includes county boards of education and their elected members, subjecting school board election policies and boundary changes to the act's anti-suppression and notice requirements.

The bill defines voting assistance for people with disabilities as an 'administrative policy affecting voting rights' and requires local governments to take appropriate steps to provide meaningful notice of proposed changes to residents with disabilities.

The department is relevant due to the fiscal impact of the bill, which includes potential state liability for attorney's fees and litigation costs in enforcement actions and the administrative costs associated with new notice and reporting requirements for state boards.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees the agencies tasked with implementing and enforcing this emergency legislation, and the office manages the broader policy initiatives related to civil rights and state governance.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the installation of individual water submeters in apartment houses and mobile home parks to ensure fair allocation of water costs. fiscal_impact_summary: The Fiscal Note states that the bill's requirements can be handled with existing budgeted resources and that state and local revenues will not be materially affected. Small business impacts are expected to be minimal.

The Department of Housing and Community Development must consult with MDE on submeter regulations and is specifically required to approve the installation of individual submeters by local housing authorities.
The bill authorizes the Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General to handle complaints from occupants regarding violations of the submetering and billing requirements.
The bill requires the Board of Public Works to approve the installation of individual submeters for apartment houses or dwelling units by local housing authorities.
The bill prohibits treating unpaid water bills as unpaid rent in eviction proceedings, which directly affects judicial procedures for summary ejectment and landlord-tenant litigation.

The bill defines 'water service providers' to include water companies regulated by the Commission and concerns submetering, a regulatory area where the Commission already oversees other utilities like gas and electricity.
As a member of the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller is responsible for the oversight and approval of submetering installations by local housing authorities as mandated by the bill.
The State Treasurer, as a member of the Board of Public Works, is required to approve submetering projects initiated by local housing authorities under the provisions of the bill.

The Governor chairs the Board of Public Works, which has approval authority under the bill, and oversees the executive departments (MDE and DHCD) responsible for implementing the new submetering regulations.

fiscal_impact_summary: If approved by voters in the 2026 general election, the bill is expected to increase State and local expenditures beginning in FY 2028 for primary election implementation. The bill requires that all returns from the constitutional amendment vote be made to the Governor and mandates that the Governor issue a formal proclamation declaring the amendment adopted if it is ratified by the voters.

The agency would be responsible for reviewing the constitutional amendment for legal sufficiency and representing the state in any legal challenges regarding the implementation of the new primary election rules.

The Secretary of State is the principal custodian of the state's official records, including laws and constitutional amendments. If ratified and proclaimed by the Governor, the Secretary of State would be responsible for recording the amendment.

bill_summary: The bill increases the debt capacity limit of the Maryland Transportation Authority (MDTA) from $4.0 billion to $5.0 billion. This increase is primarily intended to provide the agency with financial flexibility for the reconstruction of the Francis Scott Key Bridge, particularly to manage the timing of federal reimbursements, and to support other capital preservation projects.
stakeholders: Maryland Transportation Authority, Maryland Department of Transportation, users of Maryland toll facilities, and construction contractors for state transportation projects.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill increases the MDTA revenue bond debt limit by $1,000,000,000. MDTA nonbudgeted revenues will increase significantly as additional bonds are issued, potentially beginning in fiscal 2029 when debt is projected to exceed the current $4,000,000,000 limit. Nonbudgeted expenditures will increase accordingly to account for debt service on the new bonds. This additional debt capacity may help MDTA avoid toll increases that would otherwise be necessary to fund its capital program.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly increases the MDTA's revenue bond limit from $4.0 billion to $5.0 billion, allowing the agency to issue more debt to fund capital projects like the Francis Scott Key Bridge reconstruction and other preservation activities.

MDTA is a modal administration within MDOT. The bill is a departmental request from MDOT, and the increased bonding capacity supports the department's broader transportation capital program and infrastructure recovery efforts.

As the state's chief financial agency responsible for debt management and oversight of bond issuances, the Treasurer's Office is involved in the fiscal implications of increasing state-related debt limits and was consulted as an information source for the fiscal note.

The Governor oversees the executive branch and MDOT. This bill is a departmental request submitted on behalf of the administration to support major infrastructure priorities, such as the Key Bridge reconstruction.

bill_summary: The Transportation Investment Priorities Act of 2026 requires the Maryland Department of Transportation (MDOT) to develop and implement a project-based scoring system to evaluate and prioritize major surface transportation projects for inclusion in the Consolidated Transportation Program (CTP). The bill defines major surface transportation projects as those exceeding $5 million in total cost. Additionally, it restructures the Maryland Transportation Commission by altering its membership to 13 members, changing the chair to the Secretary of Transportation, and expanding its duties to include reviewing budget updates and prioritization guidelines.
stakeholders: Local governments, metropolitan planning organizations, transit agencies, and Maryland residents who utilize state highways and transit systems.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill mandates a new prioritization and scoring process for transportation projects with total costs exceeding $5,000,000. While the bill text does not provide specific appropriation amounts or revenue changes, it requires MDOT to identify available funds for these projects biennially after accounting for department operating costs, maintenance, and other mandatory grants. A formal Fiscal Note with specific dollar estimates was not provided in the text, so specific state and local fiscal impacts are indeterminate beyond the procedural requirements.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary department responsible for the Consolidated Transportation Program (CTP), the Department of Transportation (MDOT) is the lead agency implementing the bill's requirements for a new project-based scoring system and restructuring the Maryland Transportation Commission.

Projects within the State Highway Administration (SHA) are specifically identified as 'major surface transportation projects' that must be evaluated and scored using the new prioritization system before being included in the CTP.
Projects within the Maryland Transit Administration (MTA) are classified as 'major surface transportation projects' and are subject to the new project-based scoring system for capital prioritization.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill significantly alters the membership, chair, meeting frequency, and responsibilities of the Maryland Transportation Commission, which is a body encompassed by this collective designation.

The bill includes Maryland Transportation Authority projects in the definition of capital projects and requires their capital and operating programs to be summarized in the CTP. Their funding needs are also considered before determining available funds for the surface project scoring cycle.

While its projects are excluded from the new surface scoring system, the administration's capital funding needs must be identified and accounted for before the Department determines available funds for the project-based scoring cycle.
The administration's projects are excluded from the scoring process, but its capital funding needs are explicitly factored into the prioritization cycle's budget determination.
The MVA is an administration under MDOT whose capital funding needs must be identified and prioritized prior to the allocation of funds for the major surface transportation project scoring process.

The Governor is responsible for appointing eight members to the Maryland Transportation Commission under the new structure and oversees the executive branch departments implementing the CTP scoring system.
This office will be responsible for vetting and recommending the eight members appointed by the Governor to the restructured Maryland Transportation Commission.
The bill includes 'sustainable land use' as a policy goal for project evaluation, and MDOT is required to coordinate with local planning efforts during its annual county visits regarding the CTP.
The project evaluation process must consider climate change, environmental goals, and the Greenhouse Gas Emissions Reduction Act, which are primary focus areas for the MDE.
The bill maintains the requirement for MDOT to consult with the Department of Natural Resources regarding water access for recreational activities when developing projects for the CTP.
The Consolidated Transportation Program must specifically include a summary of plans to increase commuter access between University of Maryland campuses, which is a core component of the USM.

As the agency responsible for developing the state's budget and long-term fiscal planning, DBM is impacted by the restructuring of transportation investment priorities and the financial forecasts associated with the CTP.

bill_summary: This departmental bill updates the administrative and regulatory framework for public school construction in Maryland. It clarifies the State Superintendent's role in approving school facility projects involving student-occupied spaces, increases the cost threshold for change order approvals from $50,000 to $200,000, and repeals the requirement for the Interagency Commission on School Construction (IAC) to approve 75% of preliminary funding by December 31. Additionally, the bill refines criteria for state debt service reimbursement on unused school buildings and aligns statutory reporting for facility assessments and alternative energy systems.
responsible_party: Interagency Commission on School Construction and the State Superintendent of Schools
stakeholders: Local education agencies, county governments, and Maryland public school students.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill is largely procedural and does not have a direct fiscal impact on State or local finances. While the bill adjusts reporting deadlines and alters the timeline for funding allocations, these administrative changes are expected to be managed with existing resources and may allow for more efficient use of agency funds.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Interagency Commission on School Construction is the primary agency implementing the bill. It is responsible for adopting regulations for state funding eligibility, conducting maintenance and facility assessments, managing project allocations, and establishing an appeals process for local jurisdictions regarding project funding.

The bill mandates that the State Superintendent of Schools (the head of MSDE) or their designee must approve school site proposals, construction plans for new buildings, and significant renovations or additions to existing school facilities that affect student-occupied spaces.

The bill clarifies the Department of General Services' role in reviewing design and construction documents for major school construction and systemic renovation projects, as well as its collaboration with the IAC to develop submission and approval timelines.

The Board of Public Works oversees significant state expenditures, including the capital funding for school construction, and plays a role in the reimbursement of state debt service for school buildings that are no longer used for eligible educational purposes.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for the state's capital budget, which includes the school construction allocations and debt service management affected by the bill's procedural and reporting changes.

The Maryland Stadium Authority is involved in school construction financing and implementation (such as through the Built to Learn Act), and its projects are subject to the IAC approval processes and terminology updates outlined in this bill.

The Governor's Office receives mandated reports from the IAC regarding maintenance effectiveness and facility assessments. Additionally, the Governor chairs the Board of Public Works, which manages school construction funding and debt reimbursement.

The Comptroller is a member of the Board of Public Works, which oversees school construction spending and debt service reimbursement. The agency also monitors the fiscal integrity of state revenues used for these projects.

The State Treasurer serves on the Board of Public Works and manages state bonds and insurance. The bill's provisions concerning the reimbursement of outstanding state debt service for transferred school property directly intersect with the Treasurer's financial management duties.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the IAC, MSDE, and other state agencies regarding the implementation of new regulations, contract requirements, and legal procedures for debt service reimbursement.
The bill requires school facility assessments to include data on lead paint and asbestos, hazards for which the Department of the Environment maintains regulatory oversight and safety standards.

responsible_party: Maryland Heritage Area Authority and the Maryland Department of Planning
stakeholders: Local jurisdictions, state departments (including Agriculture and Education), heritage area management entities, and applicants for heritage project grants and loans.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill does not materially affect State finances. While the Maryland Heritage Area Authority Financing Fund receives up to $6,000,000 annually through Program Open Space, the bill does not change this total allocation. Local jurisdictions and other eligible entities may benefit from the Authority's new discretion to reduce or adjust the currently mandated 50% matching fund proportion for grants and loans.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Heritage Area Authority (MHAA) is an independent unit within the Department of Planning. The Secretary of Planning serves as the Chair of the Authority, and this is a departmental bill requested by the agency to alter MHAA's operations and membership.

The bill adds the Secretary of Agriculture as a new voting member of the Maryland Heritage Area Authority and requires the Secretary to support and assist activities regarding agricultural resources within certified heritage areas.

The bill adds the State Superintendent of Schools (head of the Department of Education) as a new voting member of the Maryland Heritage Area Authority and requires the Superintendent to support and assist activities regarding educational resources within certified heritage areas.

The Secretary of Commerce is an existing member of the Authority. The bill alters the Secretary's duties from preparing program statements to actively supporting and assisting activities in certified heritage areas related to the State tourism program and economic development.

The Secretary of Housing and Community Development is an existing member of the Authority. The bill alters the Secretary's duties to support and assist activities in certified heritage areas regarding housing and neighborhood revitalization.

The Secretary of Natural Resources is an existing member of the Authority. The bill updates the Secretary's duties and also replaces a member from the Maryland Greenways Commission (a DNR-related entity) with a public member experienced in natural resource stewardship or climate resiliency.

The Secretary of Transportation is an existing member of the Authority. The bill updates the Secretary's duties to support and assist activities in certified heritage areas regarding access, scenic byways, and special signage.

The Secretary of Higher Education is an existing member of the Authority. The bill updates the Secretary's duties to support and assist activities in certified heritage areas regarding educational resources and their interpretation.
The bill updates the duties of the Secretary of General Services to support and assist activities in certified heritage areas regarding the management and disposition of State property.

The Governor's Office is responsible for appointing ten members of the Authority. The bill modifies the qualifications and categories for these appointments, including adding requirements for natural resource stewardship or climate resiliency expertise.
As part of the Governor's Office, this office will be responsible for recruiting and vetting candidates for the modified board positions created by the bill.

The bill repeals the requirement that the Authority send copies of boundary maps to the office of the county clerk (who are judicial officials). This reduces a minor administrative filing task for the courts.

Synopsis: Prohibiting local jurisdictions from adopting or enforcing certain zoning provisions relating to lot size, dimensions, setback requirements, lot coverage, and design or architectural elements for certain single-family homes; prohibiting local jurisdictions from prohibiting certain housing types in certain zones; and prohibiting local jurisdictions from prohibiting certain subdivisions of certain lot types.

bill_summary: The Starter and Silver Homes Act of 2026 prohibits local jurisdictions from adopting or enforcing certain zoning restrictions for single-family homes and townhouses. Specifically, it limits minimum lot sizes to 5,000 square feet in areas with public water and sewer, sets maximum front/rear and side setbacks, and prohibits requirements for minimum square footage, lot coverage maximums, and specific architectural or design elements. The bill also allows owners of improved residential lots to subdivide their property into up to three smaller lots and prevents local governments from prohibiting townhouses in areas zoned for single-family use. Certain exemptions apply for historic districts, agricultural land, and conservation property.
responsible_party: Local legislative bodies and the Maryland-National Capital Park and Planning Commission
stakeholders: Local governments, residential property owners, home developers, and Maryland residents looking for housing
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is absent from the provided text, and specific dollar estimates are unavailable. The bill likely creates local fiscal impacts including administrative costs for local jurisdictions to update zoning codes and potential long-term changes to property tax revenues resulting from increased housing density and lot subdivisions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill was requested by the Department of Housing and Community Development and is the primary agency responsible for affordable housing and community revitalization, making it the lead implementing department for this policy.

This agency oversees sustainable growth and land use planning in Maryland, providing technical assistance to local governments on the exact zoning and subdivision regulations that this bill seeks to modify.

As a major departmental initiative affecting state-local land use relations and addressing housing supply, the Governor's Office would be responsible for high-level policy coordination and legislative oversight.

The bill involves significant state preemption of local zoning authority, which may require legal review by the OAG to ensure constitutional compliance and to defend against potential legal challenges from local jurisdictions.

The bill specifically references 'Silver Homes,' indicating a focus on housing for older adults, which falls within the department's mission to improve housing assistance and quality of life for seniors.
The density requirements in the bill are triggered by connections to public water and sewer systems, which are regulated and supervised by MDE.

The bill includes specific exemptions for agricultural land, requiring coordination with MDA's land preservation and soil conservation programs to ensure protected farmlands are not negatively impacted.

Changes in local zoning density and residential development patterns directly affect infrastructure needs, traffic management, and highway access planning overseen by MDOT's State Highway Administration.
The department works to advance accessible housing; changes to zoning for townhouses and smaller homes impact the inventory and accessibility of housing options for people with disabilities.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM monitors the fiscal impact of departmental legislation and would oversee any budgetary adjustments required for state agencies to implement these zoning oversight duties.

The bill impacts zoning and land use across all Maryland counties, including rural jurisdictions where changes to lot sizes and subdivision rules significantly affect regional development and agriculture.

Synopsis: Requiring a local planning commission to notify the Department of Planning when beginning the review of the local jurisdiction's comprehensive plan; requiring the Department, within 60 days of receiving the notification, to provide guidance materials relating to State law, best practices for local comprehensive plans, and any other resources to support the plan's review; and requiring the Department to develop and maintain certain guidance materials in consultation with certain other State agencies and offices.
Title: Local Comprehensive Plans - Guidance Materials and Notification to the Department of Planning
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/12 at 1:00 p.m.

bill_summary: This bill requires local planning commissions to notify the Maryland Department of Planning (MDP) when beginning a review of their comprehensive plans. MDP must provide guidance materials, including state laws and best practices, within 60 days of notification to support the review or amendment process. Additionally, the bill updates terminology in the Land Use Article by replacing references to "visions" with "planning principles."
stakeholders: Maryland Department of Planning, local planning commissions, and local governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Department of Planning will incur administrative costs to develop and maintain guidance materials. Local jurisdictions will face minor procedural requirements to notify the Department when starting plan reviews. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as no formal Fiscal Note was included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency for state land use policy, the Department of Planning is tasked with receiving notifications from local planning commissions, developing and maintaining guidance materials on state laws and best practices, and consulting with other agencies to support local comprehensive plan reviews.

This initiative is grounded in the state planning visions that this bill renames to 'planning principles.' It coordinates land use and resource conservation efforts across the agencies that the Department of Planning must consult to create guidance materials for local jurisdictions.

The Department of the Environment is likely to be consulted by the Department of Planning to develop guidance materials for local comprehensive plans, particularly regarding environmental protection, water quality, and sensitive areas elements.

The Department of Natural Resources is likely to be consulted to provide expertise for the guidance materials regarding the conservation of natural resources and the management of sensitive areas within local comprehensive plans.

The Department of Transportation is a key stakeholder in land use planning and is likely to be consulted to provide guidance on transportation elements and infrastructure integration within local comprehensive plans.
The Department of Agriculture is likely to be consulted regarding land preservation and agricultural elements that are integral to local comprehensive planning guidance.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies and would likely be involved in reviewing the guidance materials developed by the Department of Planning to ensure they accurately reflect State laws.

bill_summary: This bill extends the termination dates for five professional licensing boards and commissions within the Maryland Department of Labor until July 1, 2032, including those for barbers, cosmetologists, professional land surveyors, real estate appraisers, and individual tax preparers. It also mandates that the Department submit a report regarding these entities to the Joint Audit and Evaluation Committee by July 1, 2030.
stakeholders: Barbers, cosmetologists, professional land surveyors, real estate appraisers, appraisal management companies, home inspectors, and individual tax preparers.
fiscal_impact_summary: Special fund revenues and expenditures are maintained through fiscal 2032 as the bill extends the authority of several regulatory boards. The Maryland Department of Labor and the Joint Audit and Evaluation Committee can manage the required reporting and implementation using existing resources. No specific dollar estimates were provided in the fiscal note.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary implementing agency, the Maryland Department of Labor oversees the five licensing boards and commissions whose termination dates are being extended and is responsible for submitting required reports to the Joint Audit and Evaluation Committee.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill directly extends the statutory and regulatory authority of five specific state regulatory boards and commissions, which fall under this category of executive-branch entities.

The bill requires reports to be submitted to the Joint Audit and Evaluation Committee (JAEC). OLA is the legislative agency that supports the JAEC through fiscal and performance audits and evaluations.

The bill extends the State Board of Individual Tax Preparers, which regulates professionals involved in the tax filing processes central to the Comptroller's revenue collection and enforcement duties.
As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM oversees the budget execution and long-term planning for the special funds that support the operation of the boards being extended.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive departments (including Labor) and has the authority to propose the budget and appoint members to the state boards and commissions extended by this bill.

The Office of Appointments is responsible for recruiting and vetting candidates for state boards and commissions; extending these boards ensures their ongoing need for membership recruitment and vacancy management.

bill_summary: This bill updates Maryland's unemployment insurance laws to align with federal confidentiality requirements regarding the protection and disclosure of claimant and employer information. It defines confidential unemployment insurance information, establishes protocols and safeguards for its disclosure to public officials and third parties, and expands criminal penalties for the unauthorized disclosure of such data by current or former employees of the Maryland Department of Labor and other recipients.
stakeholders: Unemployment insurance claimants, employers, current and former employees of the Maryland Department of Labor, third-party data recipients, and child support enforcement units.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill has a beneficial operational impact on the Maryland Department of Labor and can be implemented with existing budgeted resources. State revenues are not affected, and there is no material fiscal impact on local governments. While the bill expands criminal penalties for unauthorized data disclosure, any resulting fine revenue is expected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency responsible for administering the state's unemployment insurance (UI) program, the Department of Labor is the central subject of this departmental bill. The bill directly alters how the Department manages, protects, and discloses confidential UI and wage information to ensure compliance with federal law.

The bill explicitly references child support enforcement units and their agents, who are overseen by the Department of Human Services. It establishes protocols for these units to access confidential claim information for the purpose of locating individuals and collecting child support obligations.

The Maryland Longitudinal Data System Center collects and links student and workforce data from the Department of Labor. This bill's definitions and confidentiality standards directly impact the information that the Department of Labor provides to the Center for research and performance accountability.

The bill specifically addresses the use of confidential unemployment insurance information for performance accountability under the federal Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA), which the Governor's Workforce Development Board oversees as the state's chief policy body for the workforce system.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Labor regarding compliance with federal and state confidentiality laws. Additionally, the bill establishes new criminal penalties for the unauthorized disclosure of information, which may involve the OAG's prosecutorial or advisory functions.

The bill defines 'public official' to include public postsecondary educational institutions and allows for the disclosure of confidential unemployment insurance information to these entities for workforce training program performance accountability and reporting.

As a public postsecondary educational institution, Morgan State University is specifically included in the bill's definition of 'public official' and may receive confidential UI data for federal and state performance reporting requirements.

As a public postsecondary educational institution, St. Mary's College is specifically included in the bill's definition of 'public official' and may receive confidential UI data for federal and state performance reporting requirements.

The bill applies to 'state educational authorities' regarding data usage for performance accountability. MSDE manages workforce-related educational programs that require tracking and reporting on student and trainee employment outcomes.

The Commission serves as a state educational authority and coordinating board for higher education, making it a relevant entity under the bill's provisions regarding data sharing for education and workforce training accountability.

The bill allows for the disclosure of confidential information to elected officials in the performance of official duties or constituent services, which includes the Governor's role in overseeing executive branch operations and assisting Maryland residents.

bill_summary: This bill standardizes and updates the required elements for local comprehensive and general plans in Maryland. It replaces previous requirements with eight mandatory elements: Land, Transportation, Housing, Economy, Equity, Resilience, Place, and Ecology. The bill requires the Maryland Department of Planning to provide guidelines and technical assistance, and mandates that various State agencies provide relevant data and analysis to help local jurisdictions prepare and update their plans in alignment with established planning principles.
stakeholders: Local governments (including charter counties and municipalities), local planning commissions, Maryland residents, and small businesses.
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Department of Planning and other involved State agencies can implement the bill's requirements using existing resources, with no impact on State revenues. Local government expenditures may increase for some jurisdictions to conform their comprehensive plans to the new requirements, particularly those that rely on contractual services or additional staff for the mandated 10-year plan reviews. Specific dollar estimates for local fiscal impacts are not provided in the fiscal note.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency requesting the bill, the Department of Planning (MDP) is responsible for facilitating state agency assistance, providing guidelines and best practices for comprehensive plans, and supplying local jurisdictions with population, demographic, and land use data.

The bill requires the Department of the Environment (MDE) to review mineral resources, sensitive areas, and water resources elements; provide technical assistance on water resources; and supply environmental justice data for the equity element.

The Department of Natural Resources (DNR) is mandated to provide statewide forest resource inventories, review sensitive areas elements, and coordinate with MDP on information regarding habitat connectivity and wildlife crossings.

The Department of Transportation (MDOT) is required to provide state-level transportation data and coordinate through its State Highway Administration (SHA) on habitat connectivity and wildlife crossing information for local plans.
The Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) is required to provide state-level housing data and, in consultation with MDP, technical assistance for the housing element of local plans.
The Department of Commerce is mandated to provide local jurisdictions with state-level data on economic development to inform the newly required Economy element.
The Department of Labor is required to provide local jurisdictions with state-level data on the labor force for the preparation of the Economy element.

Local Resilience elements must be informed by the State Resilience Strategy and the State of Maryland Hazard Mitigation Plan, which are primary responsibilities of the Maryland Department of Emergency Management (MDEM).

The Land element may include priority preservation area subelements developed per the Agriculture Article, and the Ecology element specifically addresses agricultural resources and the protection of prime agricultural land.

The bill specifically references state-rated capacity standards established by the Interagency Commission on School Construction (IAC) for the assessment of public schools in the municipal growth subelement.
The Economy element of local plans must be informed by the Maryland State Plan for Postsecondary Education, which is established and managed by the Higher Education Commission.

Local plans must address community facilities including schools, and the municipal growth subelement requires consideration of public school capacity in coordination with standards from the IAC (an independent unit within MSDE).

The bill's Community Facilities subelement includes hospitals and medical facilities, and the Place and Equity elements address public health, social cohesion, and health risks in underserved communities.

The Land and Community Facilities elements require planning for the location and extent of public buildings, grounds, and administrative facilities, which are managed by the Department of General Services.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Community Facilities subelement specifically lists jails as a type of public facility that local jurisdictions may address in their comprehensive plans.
The Community Facilities subelement specifically lists police stations as a type of public facility that local jurisdictions may address in their comprehensive plans.
The Community Facilities subelement specifically lists social welfare facilities, which are relevant to the mission and operations of the Department of Human Services.

Title: Natural Resources – Vessel Transfers – Transfer–on–Death Beneficiary Designation
Status: In the House - Unfavorable Report by Environment and Transportation; Withdrawn

NarrowSubjects.Name: Death -see also- Homicide; Murder; Wrongful Death
Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes

bill_summary: This bill allows an individual who is the sole owner of a vessel to designate a beneficiary to take ownership of the vessel upon the owner's death. This process allows the transfer of vessel ownership to occur outside of traditional estate administration and probate, provided the beneficiary survives the owner.
stakeholders: Sole owners of vessels in Maryland and their designated beneficiaries.
fiscal_impact_summary: Special fund revenues for the State Boat Act Fund may increase by an estimated $265,540 in fiscal 2027, assuming 10% of the 132,770 eligible sole owners apply for a new certificate of title and pay the $20 fee. General fund revenues may decrease minimally each year because vessels transferred via beneficiary designation are removed from the probate estate, potentially reducing probate fees and inheritance tax collections. There is no anticipated impact on state expenditures or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary implementing agency, the Department of Natural Resources is responsible for processing vessel beneficiary designations, issuing new certificates of title, and collecting the associated fees. The bill is a departmental request from DNR.

The bill allows vessels to be transferred outside of estate administration through a transfer-on-death designation. This reduces the number of assets subject to probate, potentially impacting the workload of the Registers of Wills and reducing the collection of probate fees and inheritance taxes.

The Judicial Branch, supported by the Administrative Office of the Courts, manages the probate system. The bill's provision to bypass probate for certain vessels affects judicial operations regarding estate administration.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of Natural Resources and would be involved in drafting regulations and ensuring the new titling process complies with state law.

DNR will likely require assistance or oversight from the Department of Information Technology to update its electronic titling and registration systems to accommodate beneficiary designations and 'Transfer-on-Death' markers.

The Department of Budget and Management monitors state revenue impacts. This bill is expected to increase special fund revenues for DNR while potentially causing a minimal decrease in general fund revenues from probate fees.

Synopsis: Transferring the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Loan Program from the Maryland Energy Administration to the Maryland Clean Energy Center; repealing the authority of the Maryland Energy Administration to adopt regulations to implement the Program; and altering reporting requirements for the Maryland Strategic Energy Investment Fund.
Title: Maryland Energy Administration - Jane E. Lawton Conservation Loan Program and Maryland Strategic Energy Investment Fund
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/03 at 2:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Energy Matters -see also- Fuel; NuclearMatt; PwrPlnts; etc.

bill_summary: This bill transfers the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Loan Program from the Maryland Energy Administration to the Maryland Clean Energy Center. It also modifies the annual reporting requirements for the Strategic Energy Investment Fund by requiring detailed accounting only for disbursements exceeding $10,000 and changing the metric for program evaluation from electricity savings to greenhouse gas emissions reductions.
stakeholders: Nonprofit organizations, local jurisdictions, State agencies, and eligible businesses
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, State special fund expenditures from the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Fund will increase by $131,300 in fiscal 2027. This reflects the net increase in costs for the Maryland Clean Energy Center to hire an additional employee to manage the program, offset by a reduction in administrative expenses at the Maryland Energy Administration. Projected annual expenditures increase to approximately $165,100 by fiscal 2031 due to inflation. The bill has no direct impact on local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MEA is the requesting agency and currently administers the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Loan Program being transferred. It also manages the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF), for which the bill alters annual reporting requirements, including grant thresholds and performance metrics.

MCEC is the primary agency impacted by the transfer; the bill designates MCEC as the new administrator of the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Loan Program and the associated Jane E. Lawton Conservation Fund.

The bill explicitly mandates that the State Treasurer continue to hold, invest, and reinvest the money of the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Fund, even as management of the program moves to the Maryland Clean Energy Center.

The bill requires the Comptroller to account for the Jane E. Lawton Conservation Fund, which remains a special, nonlapsing fund in the state treasury following its transfer to the Maryland Clean Energy Center.

DBM is impacted by the fiscal and personnel changes associated with transferring a program from a budgeted executive agency (MEA) to a nonbudgeted entity (MCEC), including the net increase in special fund administrative expenditures.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive agencies involved in the transfer and receives the annual report from MEA regarding the Strategic Energy Investment Fund.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies regarding statutory transfers, the repeal of existing regulations, and the enforcement of the misdemeanor provisions for false statements included in the bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Strategic Energy Investment Advisory Board is a statutory recipient of the annual report concerning the uses and expenditures of the Strategic Energy Investment Fund, which the bill modifies.
