Synopsis: Authorizing a minor who is the parent of a child to initiate or defend an action for child support, whether pendente lite or permanently.
Title: Child Support - Capacity of Minors to Initiate and Defend an Action
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/05 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Minors -see also- Age of Majority; Youth

bill_summary: This bill authorizes a minor who is the parent of a child to independently initiate or defend a legal action for child support, whether the support is requested on a temporary or permanent basis, notwithstanding existing court rules that usually require a guardian or next friend to act on behalf of a minor.
stakeholders: Minors who are parents of a child
fiscal_impact_summary: State general and federal fund expenditures for the Department of Human Services increase by an estimated $1,174,680 in fiscal 2027 only for one-time programming updates to the Child Support Management System and the Eligibility and Enrollment System. Federal fund matching revenues increase by $797,062 accordingly. The bill does not materially affect local government operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Human Services (DHS) is the primary agency impacted by this bill. Its Child Support Administration (CSA) oversees child support enforcement, and the fiscal note identifies a one-time cost of approximately $1.2 million for DHS to update the Child Support Management System and the Eligibility and Enrollment System to accommodate minor parents.

The bill directly impacts judicial proceedings by changing the capacity of minors to initiate or defend child support actions in court. The Administrative Office of the Courts provides operational and legal support to the judicial branch and was consulted for the fiscal analysis.

The Department of Budget and Management is responsible for state budget development and execution. This bill requires a significant one-time general and federal fund expenditure in FY 2027 to implement the necessary IT system changes for DHS.

As the agency responsible for statewide IT strategy and infrastructure, the Department of Information Technology would likely oversee the major programming updates required for the Child Support Management System and the Eligibility and Enrollment System.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies, including DHS and the Judiciary, and would be involved in interpreting the legal implications of granting minors the capacity to sue or be sued in child support matters.

The Governor's Office for Children coordinates efforts to improve the well-being of children and families and reduce child poverty. This bill, which alters legal rights for minor parents regarding child support, falls within their policy focus.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and the state budget. The Governor would be responsible for the policy direction and budgetary approval for the system updates and programmatic changes within the Department of Human Services.

Synopsis: Establishing a rebuttable presumption in an action for personal injury or wrongful death that a medical bill from a health care provider or an agent of the health care provider is authentic, fair, and reasonable if the bill was properly provided in discovery; and establishing that a party may overcome the presumption that a medical bill is authentic, fair, and reasonable by proving, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the medical bill, or any charge in a medical bill, is not authentic, is unfair, or is unreasonable.
Title: Courts and Judicial Proceedings - Evidence - Rebuttable Presumption of Medical Bills
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/11 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Death -see also- Homicide; Murder; Wrongful Death
Health Care Facilities -see also- Clinics; Hospices; etc
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill establishes a rebuttable presumption in personal injury and wrongful death lawsuits that medical bills provided during discovery are authentic and the charges listed are fair and reasonable. It removes the necessity for expert testimony to admit these bills as evidence, although opposing parties may challenge the presumption by providing a preponderance of evidence that the bill is not authentic or the charges are unfair.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary (Administrative Office of the Courts)
stakeholders: Plaintiffs and defendants in personal injury or wrongful death litigation, healthcare providers, attorneys, insurance companies, and State and local government entities involved in tort claims.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures may increase for the State Insurance Trust Fund (SITF) and the Transportation Trust Fund (TTF) to address additional claims or to hire experts to rebut the presumption of medical bill fairness. Local governments may experience similar increases in litigation-related expenditures. Specific dollar estimates are not provided in the fiscal note.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note explicitly mentions that the bill may increase expenditures for the State Insurance Trust Fund (SITF), which is administered by the Maryland State Treasurer's Office, due to shifts in litigation burdens for claims against the state.

This bill modifies the rules of evidence for civil actions (personal injury and wrongful death) in Maryland courts, establishing new rebuttable presumptions that the Judiciary must implement and follow.

As the primary legal representative for the state, the OAG will be directly affected by changes in evidentiary rules for civil litigation when defending state agencies in personal injury and wrongful death claims.

The fiscal note highlights that the MTA's tort liability is paid out of the Transportation Trust Fund (TTF) and does not have the same liability limits as the Tort Claims Act; thus, easier authentication of medical bills could increase MTA's litigation costs.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Health Care Alternative Dispute Resolution Office
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency was identified as a source of information for the bill's analysis and deals with medical-related legal claims, although the bill applies broadly to civil personal injury rather than just medical malpractice.
As the parent department for the Maryland Transit Administration, MDOT is relevant due to the potential fiscal impact on the Transportation Trust Fund (TTF) used for transit-related tort settlements.
DBM is the principal fiscal agency and monitors legislation that may increase state expenditures through the State Insurance Trust Fund or other agency-level fiscal impacts.

Synopsis: Requiring the Governor to withhold 35% of the annual appropriation for grants to the Washington Suburban Transit District under certain circumstances; altering the calculation of the amount that the Governor is required to include in the annual budget each year to provide grants to the Washington Suburban Transit District to pay the capital costs of the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority; making the Act contingent on enactment of certain legislation by the Commonwealth of Virginia and the District of Columbia; etc.
Title: Metro Funding Modification Act of 2026
Status: In the House - Reassigned to Appropriations and Environment and Transportation

NarrowSubjects.Name: Transportation -see also- Aircraft; Airports; Boats; etc

bill_summary: This bill modifies Maryland's funding for the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority (WMATA) by creating a new annual grant starting in fiscal 2029 to cover the State's share of the Metrorail Operating Subsidy Allocation Formula. It also adjusts existing capital grant structures by repealing a 3% annual increase on standard grants and requires WMATA to implement a workforce transition plan for rail automation by July 2028 to avoid funding penalties.
stakeholders: Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority (WMATA), Washington Suburban Transit District, transit riders in the Washington metropolitan area, and WMATA employees.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill is expected to increase total capital grant funding for WMATA by a net amount of 145,100,000 dollars in fiscal 2029. This results from a new 150,000,000 dollar mandate (with a 3% annual growth rate) offset by the repeal of an existing 3% escalator on standard capital grants. Funding will likely be drawn from the Transportation Trust Fund, which may require redirecting resources from other state transportation projects.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the Governor to include specific appropriations in the annual State budget for grants to the Washington Suburban Transit District and requires the Governor to withhold 35% of those funds under certain performance and labor-related conditions.

The Maryland Department of Transportation (MDOT) is the primary agency responsible for the Transportation Trust Fund (TTF), which funds these grants, and the bill requires MDOT to certify WMATA's performance reports and manage the grant withholding process.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for developing the budget, estimating revenues for the TTF, and ensuring the execution of the mandated appropriations and formula adjustments established by the bill.

The MTA, as a modal administration within MDOT, coordinates regional transit operations and funding; the bill's focus on Metrorail operating subsidies and workforce transition plans directly overlaps with the MTA's transit leadership role.

The OAG would be responsible for providing legal counsel regarding the bill's impact on the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority Compact and the legal sufficiency of the contingency requirements involving Virginia and the District of Columbia.
The Comptroller serves as the state's chief financial officer and a member of the Board of Public Works, overseeing the revenue flow and large-scale expenditures related to major transit grants.

The Treasurer's Office manages the state's cash flow, investments, and bonds; the fiscal note indicates that the funding for these transit grants could involve bond revenues or impact the long-term management of the Transportation Trust Fund.

The Board of Public Works oversees and approves significant state expenditures and contracts, including major capital grants and property transfers that may arise from the modified funding structure for the Washington Suburban Transit District.

The bill requires detailed performance and condition assessments, including operational efficiency and reliability reports; GOPI coordinates these types of data-driven strategies and performance metrics across the executive branch.

Synopsis: Prohibiting an entity from including in a contract for certain State public art a provision requiring artists to waive copyright rights; defining "State public art" as public art commissioned for a project that receives State funding, regardless of whether the State funding directly paid for the public art; requiring certain State public art to be registered with the Maryland State Arts Council; and applying the Act prospectively.
Title: Commissioned Public Art - Artist Rights and Registration of Art
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/03 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Art, Music, and Cultural Affairs -see also- EthAff; Mus; etc

bill_summary: This bill prohibits any entity from including a provision in a contract for State public art that requires an artist to waive copyright protections or federal rights under the Visual Artist Rights Act, though artists may voluntarily waive these rights in writing. Additionally, any entity commissioning State public art must register the artwork—including details about the artist, location, and type of art—with the Maryland State Arts Council.
stakeholders: Artists and entities (including State and local agencies) commissioning public art for projects receiving State funding
fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland State Arts Council can implement the bill's registration requirements using existing resources. According to the Fiscal Note, the bill does not materially affect State or local governmental operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill applies to State public art commissioned for projects receiving State funding, which includes capital projects for judicial branch facilities managed by the Administrative Office of the Courts.

The Board of Public Works oversees and approves significant state procurement contracts and capital projects; these contracts would be subject to the bill's restrictions on artist rights waivers and registration requirements.
The Department of Commerce oversees the Maryland State Arts Council (MSAC), which is the agency explicitly designated by the bill to serve as the registry for all commissioned State public art.

As the primary agency for state facility construction and central procurement, DGS frequently commissions public art for state buildings and will be responsible for modifying its contracts and ensuring the art is registered with MSAC.

MDOT manages large-scale infrastructure and transit projects that often incorporate commissioned public art, making the agency responsible for adhering to the bill's new contracting and registration rules.
The Commission oversees state-funded public school capital improvement projects, which may include commissioned art subject to the bill's provisions.

As an independent state university with significant capital projects, Morgan State commissions public art on its campus that will be subject to the bill's contract restrictions and registration requirements.
The OAG reviews state contracts for legal sufficiency and will be responsible for ensuring that agencies comply with the bill's prohibition on mandatory artist rights waivers in public art contracts.
The college manages state-funded construction and renovation projects that may include commissioned public art, requiring compliance with the bill's mandates.
USM coordinates and manages state-funded capital projects across its 12 institutions, many of which involve commissioned art that must now be registered and governed by the bill's contract rules.

Synopsis: Authorizing supervisory employees of the Baltimore County Public Library to form, join, and participate in an employee organization and engage in certain other activities related to collective bargaining; authorizing certain bargaining units for the employees of the Baltimore County Public Library; and altering certain provisions to provide that an employee may be deemed a certain management employee, rather than a supervisory employee, under certain circumstances.
Title: Baltimore County Public Library - Collective Bargaining - Supervisory Employees
Status: In the House - First Reading Government, Labor, and Elections

NarrowSubjects.Name: Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill grants supervisory employees of the Baltimore County Public Library the right to organize and engage in collective bargaining. It establishes two distinct bargaining units: one for supervisory employees and one for non-supervisory employees, and clarifies that certain employees previously classified as supervisory may be designated as management employees.
stakeholders: Supervisory and non-supervisory employees of the Baltimore County Public Library
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill has no impact on State revenues or expenditures. Locally, Baltimore County Public Library expenditures may increase minimally to cover the costs of outside mediators and any potential salary increases resulting from collective bargaining negotiations. The library can manage payroll deductions for union fees using its existing resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Education Article of the Maryland Code which governs the state's library systems. As the agency responsible for providing strategic leadership and coordination for Maryland's 24 public library systems, the Maryland State Library is directly concerned with the administrative and labor structures of the Baltimore County Public Library.

The bill authorizes the creation of new collective bargaining units and expands bargaining rights to supervisory employees. The Public Employee Relations Board is the state agency responsible for overseeing union representation, certifying bargaining units, and adjudicating labor disputes within the public sector workforce.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the Maryland State Library and the Public Employee Relations Board, and may be involved in interpreting the legal requirements of the expanded collective bargaining rights.

Synopsis: Altering and establishing certain provisions relating to the detention, confinement, and transportation of children arrested, convicted, or awaiting trial on certain charges.
Title: Juveniles - Detention and Confinement - Limitations on Juvenile Contact With Incarcerated Adults
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/05 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Minors -see also- Age of Majority; Youth

bill_summary: This bill restricts the detention and confinement of juveniles in adult facilities, requiring that children (including those charged as adults) be kept separate from incarcerated adults by sight and sound. It limits temporary holds in adult jails for processing to six hours and prohibits the transportation of children alongside adults charged with or convicted of crimes.
stakeholders: Juveniles under the age of 18 who have been arrested or convicted, and personnel at Maryland's State and local correctional and detention facilities.
fiscal_impact_summary: Maryland State general fund expenditures for the Department of Juvenile Services will increase significantly beginning in FY 2029, with illustrative construction costs of $45,000,000 per new facility and annual operating expenses between $12,000,000 and $15,000,000. The bill is expected to prevent the annual loss of approximately $173,000 in federal grant funding. Local government expenditures are expected to decrease as fewer juveniles are housed in local jails.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DJS is the primary agency responsible for the detention and confinement of juveniles in Maryland. The bill shifts the detention of youth from adult jails to secure juvenile facilities managed by DJS, necessitating a significant increase in the agency's operational capacity and the potential construction of new facilities.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS oversees state correctional facilities and pretrial detention centers. The bill prohibits the housing of juveniles in these adult facilities (with very limited exceptions for temporary processing) and mandates strict sight and sound separation from incarcerated adults.

The bill amends the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article and the Criminal Procedure Article, altering the procedures and standards the judiciary must follow when ordering the detention or transfer of juveniles.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP manages federal juvenile justice grants (JJDPA). The bill is explicitly designed to bring Maryland into compliance with JJDPA 'sight and sound' and 'jail removal' requirements to prevent the loss or restriction of federal funding managed by this office.

DGS is responsible for the planning, design, and construction of state-owned facilities. As DJS will likely require new juvenile detention centers to accommodate the expanded population under this bill, DGS would lead the capital improvement projects.

As the primary state law enforcement agency, MSP is impacted by the bill's new restrictions on the transportation and processing of juveniles, specifically the prohibition against transporting children with incarcerated adults.

DBM oversees state budget execution and fiscal planning. The bill's significant projected costs for new DJS facilities and expanded staffing will require DBM's involvement in budget development and revenue estimation.
OAG provides legal counsel to DJS and DPSCS. They would be responsible for advising these agencies on the legal and constitutional implications of the new detention and separation standards.
BPW must approve significant state expenditures and procurement contracts, including those related to the design and construction of any new juvenile facilities necessitated by the bill.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch departments involved (DJS, DPSCS, GOCPP) and is responsible for proposing the annual state budget, which would need to reflect the bill's fiscal impact.

bill_summary: This bill is the State of Maryland's annual budget for Fiscal Year 2027. responsible_party: Maryland Department of Budget and Management
stakeholders: Maryland residents, state employees, local government entities, and recipients of state-funded programs and services.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill authorizes a total appropriation of $70,941,598,613 for fiscal year 2027 across general, special, and federal funds. This total includes a net subtotal of $70,841,598,613 after estimated reversions. Additionally, the bill includes deficiency appropriations for fiscal year 2026 totaling $2,996,838,102 to address funding shortfalls in the prior year.

The bill includes the constitutional salary for the Lieutenant Governor of Maryland in the salary schedule (Section 3).

Synopsis: Authorizing the creation of a State Debt in the amount of $1,824,782,000, the proceeds to be used for certain necessary building, construction, demolition, planning, renovation, conversion, replacement, and capital equipment purchases of the State, for acquiring certain real estate in connection therewith, and for grants to certain subdivisions and other organizations for certain development and improvement purposes; etc.
Title: Creation of a State Debt – Maryland Consolidated Capital Bond Loan of 2026, and the Maryland Consolidated Capital Bond Loans of 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, and 2025
Status: In the House - First Reading Appropriations
bill_summary: This bill authorizes the creation of State debt through the Maryland Consolidated Capital Bond Loan of 2026, totaling $1,824,782,000. The proceeds are intended for capital projects including the construction, renovation, and equipping of State facilities, public schools, community colleges, and healthcare infrastructure. The act also modifies or reduces debt authorizations from prior capital bond loans (2015-2025) and provides grants to local governments and non-profit organizations for various development and improvement projects.
stakeholders: Maryland state agencies, local school systems, nonpublic schools, community colleges, public libraries, nonprofit organizations, healthcare facilities, and Maryland residents.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill authorizes a total State debt of $1,824,782,000 through the issuance of general obligation bonds. When accounting for $74,782,000 in reductions to prior bond authorizations, the net new debt authorized is $1,750,000,000. Repayment of the debt is supported by a state tax on all assessable property, with the principal to be discharged within 15 years. Local governments and organizations benefit from significant grant allocations for capital projects, though many grants require matching funds and must be expended or encumbered by June 1, 2033.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill is submitted at the request of the Administration (the Governor) and concerns the Maryland Consolidated Capital Bond Loan, which funds the executive branch's major construction and policy priorities.

The Comptroller is a member of the Board of Public Works, which is authorized to borrow the money, and is specifically required by the bill to make transfers, adjustments, and reconciliations of project funds.

The State Treasurer is a member of the Board of Public Works and is responsible for determining the amount of bond premiums to be transferred and managing the issuance and sale of general obligation bonds.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Governor and all state agencies involved in the capital projects, and ensures the legal sufficiency of the bond issuance and grant agreements.
The bill includes amendments to prior bond acts that fund the Senior Centers Capital Grant Program, which is administered by this department.
The bill provides funding for the Maryland Agricultural Cost-Share Program to implement best management practices on farms.
DBM is the principal agency for budget execution and is authorized by the bill to approve the use of design funds for construction and oversee capital project spending.
The bill provides funding for the Maryland Arts Capital Grant Program, which is overseen by this department to support cultural infrastructure.
The bill funds the Access Maryland program, which improves accessibility for persons with disabilities at state-owned facilities.
MSDE is responsible for administering several grant programs mentioned in the bill, including the Nonpublic Aging Schools Program and grants for public school construction.
The bill provides significant funding for the Bay Restoration Fund, Water Quality Revolving Loan Fund, and other environmental infrastructure programs managed by MDE.

DGS is the primary operational support agency responsible for the design, construction, and management of state-owned facilities funded by this bill, and it must record correct information in grant agreements.
The bill funds community health facilities, federally qualified health centers, and major renovations at the Clifton T. Perkins Hospital Center.
The bill funds a wide range of DHCD programs including neighborhood revitalization, rental housing programs, and the Strategic Demolition Fund.
The bill provides funding for the Maryland FiRST Public Safety Radio System, which is managed by DoIT.

bill_summary: The Budget Reconciliation and Financing Act of 2026 adjusts the Maryland state budget by altering mandated appropriations, authorizing fund transfers, and modifying revenue distributions to ensure fiscal balance. Key provisions include transferring over $491 million from special funds to the General Fund, updating higher education funding formulas, and increasing the amount counties must pay for teacher retirement costs.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits Maryland state and local agencies from using persistent aerial surveillance—defined as aircraft recording video or images that show a person's actions over time—to gather evidence in criminal investigations. Exceptions are provided for search warrants, arrest warrant execution, fresh pursuit, search and rescue, locating escaped prisoners, preventing imminent serious bodily harm, or countering terrorist risks.
responsible_party: Maryland State and local government agencies and their law enforcement units.
stakeholders: Maryland law enforcement agencies, individuals subject to criminal investigations, and the general public.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because no formal Fiscal Note was provided. The bill text does not explicitly identify financial allocations, revenue changes, or spending mandates.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's primary law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police utilize aircraft and drones for criminal investigations. This bill directly prohibits persistent aerial surveillance for gathering evidence in such investigations, fundamentally impacting their operational tactics and use of aviation technology.

The Natural Resources Police (NRP) within this department utilize aircraft for conservation enforcement and search and rescue. The bill's restrictions on surveillance for criminal investigations would apply to NRP's enforcement activities, although they may benefit from the search and rescue exception.

The Maryland Transportation Authority (MDTA) maintains its own police force which enforces laws on toll facilities and bridges. This agency's use of aerial surveillance for criminal investigation purposes would be restricted under the bill.

The OAG provides legal counsel to all state agencies and boards. They would be responsible for advising law enforcement and other units on the legal boundaries of the new surveillance restrictions and representing the state in challenges related to evidence gathered via aerial means.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The department is responsible for correctional facilities and the pursuit of escapees. The bill contains a specific exception allowing persistent aerial surveillance to locate an escaped prisoner, making the bill directly relevant to their security operations.

The bill includes an exception for persistent aerial surveillance if a high risk of a terrorist attack is identified by the U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security. This office coordinates Maryland's homeland security efforts and would be involved in the intelligence and response related to this exception.

The department coordinates state preparedness and response. The bill provides an exception for aerial surveillance used to assist in an active search and rescue operation, which is a core function coordinated by MDEM.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates state policy. This bill creates a new regulatory framework for state agencies' law enforcement practices, which the Governor's Office would oversee through policy initiatives and intergovernmental relations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office advises the Governor on criminal justice strategies and coordinates public safety policies. The restriction on aerial surveillance in criminal investigations is a significant shift in criminal justice policy that falls within their advisory scope.

The bill allows an exception for persistent aerial surveillance conducted in accordance with a valid search warrant issued by a judge. This places the judiciary and its administrative support in the role of overseeing the legal authorization process for such surveillance.

The DGS manages the Maryland Capitol Police, which provides security for state-owned facilities. The bill's restrictions on aerial surveillance for criminal investigations would apply to their security and investigative operations.

The Maryland National Guard may be activated for search and rescue operations or domestic emergencies. The bill includes exceptions for search and rescue and imminent bodily harm, which are scenarios where National Guard aerial assets might be deployed.

USM institutions maintain their own campus police departments. These units would be prohibited from using persistent aerial surveillance for criminal investigations except under the specified circumstances.
As a state agency with its own police force, Morgan State University's law enforcement activities are subject to the restrictions on persistent aerial surveillance for criminal investigations.
As an independent unit of state government, the college and its security/police functions would be subject to the prohibitions outlined in the bill regarding aerial surveillance.

bill_summary: This bill extends the reporting deadline and termination date for a workgroup convened by the State Retirement Agency to study the requirements and processes for transferring member service between State and local retirement and pension systems. The reporting deadline is moved from December 1, 2025, to October 1, 2026, and the workgroup is now set to expire on June 30, 2027.
stakeholders: Members of State and local retirement and pension systems and the State Retirement Agency.
fiscal_impact_summary: The fiscal note indicates no State or local fiscal impact, as extending the reporting date for the workgroup does not affect governmental operations or finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly names the State Retirement Agency as the entity responsible for convening the workgroup, studying the transfer of member service between retirement systems, and submitting the final report and recommendations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill extends the duration and reporting mandate of a specific workgroup, which falls under this category of temporary bodies created to study specific government issues and provide recommendations.
The State Retirement Agency is required to submit the workgroup's report and legislative recommendations to the Governor.

As the state's central personnel agency responsible for managing employee benefits and policies, DBM has a secondary interest in policies regarding the transfer of retirement service credits for the state workforce.

Synopsis: Converting the Biotechnology Investment Incentive Tax Credit to be the Biotechnology Investment Incentive Grant Program in the Department of Commerce; requiring the Department to disburse a grant within a certain time period; allowing a subtraction modification under the Maryland income tax for certain grants received during the taxable year; establishing the Biotechnology Investment Incentive Grant Program Fund; requiring the Governor to include an appropriation of $10,000,000 in the annual budget bill for the Fund; etc.
Title: Biotechnology Investment Incentive Tax Credit - Conversion to Grant Program
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/12 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.

bill_summary: This bill converts the existing Biotechnology Investment Incentive Tax Credit into the Biotechnology Investment Incentive Grant Program, which is administered by the Maryland Department of Commerce. It establishes the Biotechnology Investment Incentive Grant Program Fund as a special, nonlapsing fund to provide grants to qualified investors who invest in early-stage Maryland biotechnology companies and creates an income tax subtraction modification for the received grants.
stakeholders: Qualified investors and Maryland-based early-stage biotechnology companies with fewer than 50 full-time employees.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill mandates an annual appropriation of $10,000,000 to the Biotechnology Investment Incentive Grant Program Fund starting in fiscal 2028. According to the Fiscal Note, while overall expenditures for biotechnology incentives may remain consistent with historic levels, general fund expenditures could increase to meet the mandated funding level or due to increased demand. Additionally, the Department of Commerce may incur between $68,000 and $77,000 in administrative costs for a temporary contractual grants associate. There is no reported impact on local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary implementing agency, the Department of Commerce will administer the Biotechnology Investment Incentive Grant Program, moving it from a tax credit system. Commerce is responsible for certifying companies and investors, issuing grant eligibility certificates, disbursing funds, and managing the new special fund.

The bill creates a new income tax subtraction modification for grants received through the program, which the Comptroller must administer. Additionally, the Comptroller is responsible for accounting for the Biotechnology Investment Incentive Grant Program Fund.
The State Treasurer is designated as the custodian of the new Biotechnology Investment Incentive Grant Program Fund, responsible for holding the fund separately and investing its assets.
The bill creates a mandated annual appropriation of $10,000,000 that the Governor must include in the annual state budget for the grant program fund.

DBM is responsible for state budget development and must manage the $10,000,000 mandated appropriation and the fiscal transition from a tax credit (revenue reduction) to a grant program (expenditure).

The bill provides for an appeal process for qualified investors if the Department of Commerce revokes a grant or eligibility certification; such contested administrative cases are typically adjudicated by the OAH.

The OLA is responsible for auditing state agencies and special funds; it will be required to audit the newly created Biotechnology Investment Incentive Grant Program Fund and the Department of Commerce's administration of the grant program.

The bill includes provisions for Opportunity Zone enhancements that require verification of property registration and lead-based paint compliance with the Department of the Environment as part of the grant eligibility criteria.

Synopsis: Authorizing the placement and use of speed monitoring systems on Maryland Route 5 in Prince George's County, subject to placement and signage requirements; requiring certain revenue collected by Prince George's County as a result of violations enforced by a speed monitoring system on Maryland Route 5 to be used for State and local highway and pedestrian safety improvements on and in the vicinity of Maryland Route 5 in Prince George's County; etc.
Title: Prince George's County - Speed Monitoring Systems - Maryland Route 5 PG 315-26
Status: In the House - First Reading Environment and Transportation

BroadSubjects.Name: Vehicle Laws - Rules of the Road

NarrowSubjects.Name: Laws and Ordinances -see also- Pub Local Laws; Uniform Laws

bill_summary: This bill authorizes Prince George’s County to place and use speed monitoring systems on Maryland Route 5. It requires that fines collected from these systems, after recovering administrative costs, be remitted to the State Comptroller for distribution to the State Highway Administration to fund highway and pedestrian safety improvements on or near Maryland Route 5. The bill also mandates that these systems include signage and a real-time display of a driver's speed.
responsible_party: Prince George’s County and the Maryland State Highway Administration
stakeholders: Motorists traveling on Maryland Route 5 in Prince George’s County, pedestrians and residents near the route, and the Prince George’s County government.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a revenue stream from civil penalties for speeding violations on Maryland Route 5, with fines ranging from $40 to $425 depending on the speed recorded. These funds are designated to cover the costs of implementing the systems, with the remaining balance used for State and local highway and pedestrian safety improvements. A specific total estimate of revenue or expenditures is not provided in the bill text, and the formal Fiscal Note is absent from the provided material.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly tasks the State Highway Administration with receiving fine revenue remitted by the Comptroller and using it to implement highway and pedestrian safety improvements on and near Maryland Route 5 in Prince George's County.

As the parent department of the State Highway Administration (SHA) and the Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA), MDOT is responsible for the overall management and safety of the state's transportation network, which includes the projects authorized by this bill.
The bill mandates that Prince George's County remit fine revenue to the Comptroller, who is then responsible for distributing those funds to the State Highway Administration.
The bill involves civil penalties for speed monitoring system violations, which are adjudicated within the District Court system supported and managed by the Administrative Office of the Courts.

The MVA is responsible for driver services and vehicle registration, which are impacted by traffic enforcement and the administration of civil citations. Additionally, the MVA's Highway Safety Office coordinates safety initiatives relevant to the bill.
As the primary law enforcement agency for the state, the Maryland State Police are responsible for traffic safety and enforcing motor vehicle laws on state highways such as Maryland Route 5.
The bill amends notice and signage requirements that apply to the Maryland Transportation Authority for the speed monitoring systems it is authorized to operate.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP coordinates public safety strategies and manages funding for law enforcement and victim services, aligning with the bill's focus on public safety and enforcement revenue usage.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the State Highway Administration and the Department of Transportation regarding the implementation and enforcement of new traffic safety regulations.
The department is responsible for supervising budget execution and revenue estimation, which will be affected by the collection and distribution of fine revenue for state highway projects.

Synopsis: Establishing the Common Ownership Community Ombudsman Unit in the Division of Consumer Protection in the Office of the Attorney General to receive and respond to certain complaints; requiring common ownership communities to file certain governing documents with the Department of Housing and Community Development, which the Department must use to create a publicly accessable database; and establishing requirements for a local common ownership commission established by the local government of a county.
Title: Common Ownership Communities - Ombudsman Unit, Governing Document Database, and Local Commissions

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Common Ownership Community Ombudsman Unit in the Office of the Attorney General to handle complaints and assist members of common ownership communities. It also requires common ownership communities, including condominiums, cooperative housing corporations, and homeowners associations, to file their governing documents with the Department of Housing and Community Development for the creation of a public database and sets operational standards and dispute resolution requirements for local commissions established by counties.
responsible_party: Office of the Attorney General and the Department of Housing and Community Development
stakeholders: Residents and governing bodies of condominiums, cooperative housing corporations, and homeowners associations; local county governments; and property managers.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures will increase for the Attorney General to staff the Ombudsman Unit and for the Department of Housing and Community Development to maintain a public database of governing documents. State revenue will increase via DHCD filing fees (up to $100 for initial filings and $25 for amendments) and a $500 fine for noncompliance. Local governments that establish commissions will incur administrative costs, which can be offset by authorized per-unit fees and dispute resolution charges. Specific total fiscal estimates from a Fiscal Note are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Common Ownership Community Ombudsman Unit within the Division of Consumer Protection in the Office of the Attorney General. The agency is responsible for appointing the Ombudsman, staffing the unit, responding to complaints, and reporting on activities.

The bill requires the department to establish and maintain a public database of governing documents for common ownership communities, receive filings from these communities, and collect associated fees.

The bill mandates that local common ownership commissions include at least one member who is a licensed common ownership community manager; the Department of Labor is the agency responsible for licensing and regulating this profession in Maryland.

The Secretary of State is currently responsible for the registration and oversight of condominiums. The bill creates overlapping or new filing and oversight requirements for condominiums through the Department of Housing and Community and the Office of the Attorney General.

As the principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM is responsible for the budget execution and staffing approvals required to establish the new Ombudsman Unit and the statewide governing document database.

The bill impacts the judicial branch by defining the standard of review for appeals of commission decisions, providing for the stay of civil actions during commission proceedings, and clarifying the relationship between local commission disputes and civil litigation.

The mandate for the Department of Housing and Community to develop and maintain a public-facing digital database of governing documents requires alignment with the state's IT strategy, cybersecurity standards, and data governance policies managed by DoIT.

Synopsis: Requiring a custodian to deny inspection of certain records pertaining to a divorce proceeding; and requiring a custodian to release records pertaining to a divorce proceeding to certain applicants under certain circumstances.
Title: Public Information Act - Divorce Records
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/24 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill requires a custodian of public records to deny inspection of specific records related to divorce proceedings, including divorce applications, financial records, settlement records, and custody orders. The bill does not apply to final divorce decrees. Custodians are required to release these records to a person in interest, their attorney, or an individual authorized by a court order.
responsible_party: State and local public record custodians
stakeholders: Individuals involved in divorce proceedings, attorneys representing these individuals, and custodians of public records in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the fiscal note, the bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local government operations or finances. There are no specific revenue or expenditure estimates provided as the impact is expected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Divorce proceedings are judicial matters handled within the Maryland court system. As the primary support agency for the judiciary and overseer of the clerks of the circuit courts, the Administrative Office of the Courts is the chief custodian of the divorce proceeding records (applications, financial records, settlements, and custody orders) specifically targeted by the bill's privacy requirements.

The OAG serves as the chief legal counsel to all state agencies, providing guidance on compliance with the Public Information Act (PIA). Additionally, the OAG is responsible for publishing the Public Information Act Manual and maintaining the statewide list of PIA custodians, both of which would require updates to reflect the new mandatory denial provisions for divorce records.

The Department of Human Services, particularly through its Child Support Services and social service programs, regularly utilizes and maintains copies of divorce settlements, custody orders, and financial records from divorce proceedings. As a custodian of these records, the department must adhere to the new bill's restrictions regarding their inspection by the public.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This collective entity includes the Public Information Act Compliance Board (PIACB), which is mandated to resolve disputes between record applicants and custodians. The board would be responsible for adjudicating complaints related to the denial of divorce proceeding records under this new legislation.

The Maryland Department of Health manages vital records, including reports of divorce, and frequently uses divorce proceeding information to determine eligibility for state assistance programs such as Medicaid. The agency is a relevant custodian of divorce-related data and is impacted by shifts in PIA disclosure rules for such information.

The Maryland State Archives is the central depository for permanent state and court records. As historical divorce proceeding records are transferred from the courts to the Archives, the agency becomes the custodian responsible for enforcing the bill's privacy protections against public inspection requests.

Synopsis: Altering certain terminology relating to State parks that preserve and interpret the history of certain populations.
Title: Natural Resources - State Parks - Terminology
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/11 at 1:00 p.m.

Historical Matters -see also- Archives; Monumts; Museum; etc
Natural Resources -see also- Coal; For&Pks; Rivers; etc.
Racial Matters -see also- Ethnic Affairs; Minorities

bill_summary: This bill updates the terminology used for State parks that focus on preserving the history of underrepresented populations, including African American, Asian, Indigenous, and Hispanic communities. Specifically, it renames 'Freedman’s State Historical Park' to 'Freedman’s State Park' and 'Port of Deposit State Historical Park' to 'Port Deposit State Park,' while also changing references from 'State historical parks' to 'State parks' in relevant statutes without altering the parks' historical purposes.
stakeholders: Underrepresented communities including African American, Asian, Indigenous or Native American, and Hispanic or Latino populations; local governments in Montgomery, Cecil, and Charles counties and Baltimore City; and nonprofit organizations involved in park partnerships.
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, the bill does not directly affect State or local finances. Because signs and publications for the renamed parks have not yet been produced, the Maryland Department of Natural Resources will not incur costs to update existing materials. There are no small business impacts.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency responsible for managing the state park system and the Maryland Park Service, the Department of Natural Resources is the lead agency for implementing the terminology changes and managing the specific parks and advisory committees established in the bill.

The bill explicitly requires the Department of Natural Resources to seek input from the Commission on African American History and Culture, the Governor’s Commission on Asian Pacific American Affairs, and the Commission on Indian Affairs, all of which are coordinated through this office.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates the creation and specifies the composition of stakeholder advisory committees for Freedman’s State Park, Port Deposit State Park, and Gwynns Falls State Park, and requires coordination with several existing state commissions.

The Secretary of Planning and the Director of the Maryland Historical Trust (which is overseen by the Department of Planning) are designated members of the stakeholder advisory committee for Port Deposit State Park.
The bill requires input from the Office of Immigrant Affairs, which is part of the Executive Department, regarding decisions related to the establishment of certain state parks.
The Chief Archaeologist of the State Highway Administration (a modal administration under MDOT) is a designated member of the stakeholder advisory committee for Port Deposit State Park.

The Secretary of the Environment is a designated member of the Port Deposit State Park stakeholder advisory committee, and the Commission on Environmental Justice and Sustainable Communities provides input on park establishment.
The Secretary of Commerce is designated as a member of the stakeholder advisory committee for the Port Deposit State Park.

Synopsis: Prohibiting provisions of the governing documents of a condominium or homeowners association from unreasonably restricting the governing body from installing or authorizing the installation of electric vehicle recharging equipment; establishing that the installation or authorization of electric vehicle recharging equipment by a governing body is subject to the ordinary budgeting processes of the condominium or homeowners association; applying the Act retroactively; etc.
Title: Condominiums and Homeowners Associations - Governing Documents - Electric Vehicle Recharging Equipment
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/19 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Licenses -see also- AB Lic; Certifications; DrLic; Permits
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill prevents condominium and homeowners association (HOA) governing documents from unreasonably blocking the association's governing body from installing electric vehicle (EV) charging stations in common parking areas. It mandates that governing bodies must account for existing parking needs and use standard budget procedures for these installations, and applies these rules retroactively to existing governing documents.
responsible_party: Governing bodies of condominiums and homeowners associations
stakeholders: Residents of condominiums and homeowners associations, association governing boards, and electric vehicle owners.
fiscal_impact_summary: Financial impacts are limited to the private budgets of condominiums and homeowners associations, as the bill requires installations to follow ordinary budget processes. No specific state or local government fiscal impact is mentioned, and specific dollar estimates are unavailable because a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Secretary of State is responsible for the registration and oversight of condominiums. Since this bill directly impacts the governing documents and bylaws of condominiums, it falls under the agency's regulatory scope.

The Maryland Energy Administration promotes renewable energy and efficiency. This bill concerns the implementation of electric vehicle recharging infrastructure, which is a significant part of the agency's policy and planning mandate.

The Office of the Attorney General enforces consumer protection laws and provides legal counsel to the state. This bill involves changes to real property law that affect the rights of residents within community associations and requires legal interpretation.

The Maryland Clean Energy Center works to advance the adoption of clean energy technologies like EV charging stations. This bill facilitates the installation of such equipment in residential communities.

The Department of Housing and Community Development is responsible for residential housing policy and supporting thriving communities, which includes the regulatory and infrastructure standards for condominiums and HOAs.
The bill introduces a standard of 'unreasonable restriction' in governing documents, which may lead to litigation in the state's judicial system that the Administrative Office of the Courts supports.

Synopsis: Adding Class B (on-sale) beer and wine and Class B (on-sale) beer, wine, and liquor licenses to the list of alcoholic beverages licenses for which the prohibition against issuing multiple licenses for the same person or premises in Prince George's County does not apply.
Title: Prince George's County - Alcoholic Beverages - Multiple Licenses Prohibition - Exceptions PG 313-26
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/23 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.

bill_summary: This bill creates an exception to the prohibition in Prince George’s County against an individual or entity holding multiple alcoholic beverages licenses. It specifically permits a person to have an interest in more than one Class B (on-sale) beer and wine license or Class B (on-sale) beer, wine, and liquor license.
responsible_party: Prince George’s County Board of License Commissioners
stakeholders: Potential and existing alcoholic beverage licensees in Prince George’s County and the Prince George’s County Board of License Commissioners.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to increase local license fee revenue for Prince George’s County by allowing the issuance of additional Class B licenses. However, specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the Fiscal Note was not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller of Maryland is the principal state agency responsible for regulating the alcohol industry and enforcing state tax laws. This bill amends the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article regarding license restrictions in Prince George's County, which falls under the Comptroller's broad regulatory and industry oversight responsibilities.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the chief legal officer for the state, providing counsel to the General Assembly and state boards and commissions. This includes the interpretation of the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article and representing local boards of license commissioners in legal disputes regarding the issuance of multiple licenses.

Synopsis: Prohibiting the Board of License Commissioners for Prince George's County from approving the transfer or sale of a Class A beer, wine, and liquor license; requiring a Class A license holder to return the license to the Board if the license expires or the license holder no longer wishes to hold the license; and prohibiting the Board from reissuing a Class A beer, wine, and liquor license.
Title: Prince George's County - Alcoholic Beverages Licenses - Prohibition on Transfer of Class A Beer, Wine, and Liquor License PG 314-26
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/23 at 1:00 p.m.
bill_summary: This bill prohibits the Board of License Commissioners for Prince George’s County from approving the transfer or sale of Class A beer, wine, and liquor licenses. It mandates that these licenses must be returned to the Board if they expire or if the holder no longer wishes to maintain them, and it further prohibits the Board from reissuing any such returned licenses.
responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Prince George’s County
stakeholders: Class A beer, wine, and liquor license holders in Prince George’s County
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will likely result in a gradual decrease in local revenue for Prince George's County as Class A licenses (which have an annual fee of $910) are retired and cannot be reissued or transferred. Specific aggregate fiscal estimates from a formal Fiscal Note were not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly regulates the authority and operations of the Board of License Commissioners for Prince George’s County, which is a permanent body established to address specific governmental regulatory issues (alcoholic beverages) within that jurisdiction.

The Comptroller is the state's principal regulator of the alcohol industry and is responsible for collecting alcoholic beverage taxes. This bill, by prohibiting the transfer or reissuance of certain licenses, directly impacts the regulatory landscape and the potential revenue base for state alcohol taxes.

The Governor is responsible for overseeing the executive branch and appointing members to various boards and commissions, including local boards of license commissioners. This bill limits the statutory powers of a board whose members are appointed by the Governor.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state boards and commissions. It would be responsible for advising the Board of License Commissioners on the implementation of these new restrictions and defending the board in potential litigation related to license transfer denials.

The Office of Appointments vets candidates for state boards and commissions. It is relevant as it manages the recruitment of the individuals who serve on the Board of License Commissioners for Prince George's County.

DBM is responsible for estimating state revenues and supervising budget execution. The eventual reduction in the number of active Class A licenses in Prince George's County could impact fee-based revenue and long-term fiscal planning.

Synopsis: Authorizing Prince George's County to retain, by local law, a portion of a certain fee, not to exceed 10 cents for each bag, that retail establishments in the county are required by local law to charge a customer for providing a single-use or reusable carryout bag.
Title: Prince George's County - Authority to Retain Fee for Single-Use and Reusable Bags PG 403-26
Status: In the House - First Reading Government, Labor, and Elections and Economic Matters

NarrowSubjects.Name: Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes
Laws and Ordinances -see also- Pub Local Laws; Uniform Laws

bill_summary: This bill authorizes Prince George’s County to enact local legislation allowing the county to retain a portion of the fee (up to 10 cents per bag) that retail establishments charge customers for single-use or reusable carryout bags. The funds collected by the county under this authority must be directed to the county’s General Fund.
stakeholders: Retail establishments and customers in Prince George’s County
fiscal_impact_summary: Prince George's County may experience an increase in General Fund revenue from retaining up to 10 cents per carryout bag fee. The total fiscal impact is indeterminate as it is contingent upon the county enacting a local law and the subsequent volume of bag sales; a formal Fiscal Note with specific dollar estimates was not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the head of the executive branch, the Governor must review and sign this bill into law; the office also coordinates policy initiatives that may include local sustainability efforts.
As the state's chief financial officer and tax collector, the Comptroller monitors point-of-sale transactions and fees that may intersect with sales tax administration or retail auditing.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the state and reviews the legality of legislation, ensuring that the proposed expansion of local government fiscal authority is consistent with state law.
This bill impacts the economic operations of retail establishments in Prince George's County, which falls under Commerce's mission to support and advise the state's business community.
The bill relates to land and water quality by discouraging single-use bags through fiscal policy, aligning with the department's mission of environmental protection and waste reduction.
Planning provides data analysis and policy guidance to local governments regarding sustainable growth and effective resource management.
This multi-agency initiative coordinates efforts to reduce the state's carbon footprint and promote environmental preservation, which is supported by legislation targeting bag waste.

Synopsis: Altering the jurisdiction of the juvenile court by repealing provisions specifying that the juvenile court does not have jurisdiction over a child alleged to have committed any crime punishable by life imprisonment.
Title: Juvenile Court - Jurisdiction (Youth Charging Reform Act)
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/12 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: The Youth Charging Reform Act expands the jurisdiction of the juvenile court by repealing provisions that automatically sent children charged with certain serious crimes—including kidnapping, robbery, and various firearm offenses—to adult criminal court. Under the bill, these cases will now originate in juvenile court, though children 16 and older charged with crimes punishable by life imprisonment will still be excluded from juvenile jurisdiction and tried in adult court.
stakeholders: Juveniles under the age of 18 charged with criminal offenses, the Department of Juvenile Services, the Office of the Public Defender, and local State's Attorneys' offices.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures for the Office of the Public Defender are estimated to decrease by as much as $1,400,000 in FY 2027 and $1,850,000 annually thereafter due to a reduction in adult court transfer hearings. The Department of Juvenile Services may experience significant cost savings from operational efficiencies, though these could be partially offset by an increased demand for juvenile services. Local expenditures for State's Attorneys' offices are expected to increase significantly, with several jurisdictions reporting the need for dozens of additional personnel to manage the shifted caseload and expedited juvenile timelines.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill significantly expands juvenile court jurisdiction, directly shifting more youth from the adult system into the care, supervision, and rehabilitative programs of the Department of Juvenile Services.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note indicates a significant potential decrease in agency expenditures of up to $1.4 million due to a projected 75% reduction in mandatory juvenile transfer hearings.
The bill alters the original jurisdiction of the court system for specific crimes committed by youth, requiring significant operational and administrative updates across the judiciary.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The jurisdictional shift is expected to reduce the number of youth held in adult pretrial detention centers and sentenced to adult correctional facilities managed by the department.
The bill modifies the definition of 'reportable offenses' in the Education Article, which is a core component of the agency's mission to manage school safety reporting and data.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's primary coordinating body for public safety, this agency advises on criminal justice strategies and manages funding for programs that support youth involved in the justice system.
The bill amends the Education Article regarding the definition and reporting of off-campus offenses, impacting state education policy and safety protocols for local school systems.
The agency is involved in the reporting of delinquency adjudications and the state-mandated fingerprinting of children for certain delinquent acts identified in the bill.
As the chief legal officer, the OAG provides counsel to executive agencies and the Governor on the implementation of these significant changes to criminal and juvenile procedure.
The department is responsible for overseeing the significant fiscal shifts and resource reallocations between the adult and juvenile justice systems identified in the fiscal note.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates high-level policy initiatives, including major reforms to the state's juvenile justice and criminal laws.

Synopsis: Establishing requirements and prohibitions regarding food and milk product labeling; and requiring the Maryland Department of Health to create a marketing program and educational materials to inform consumers about the meaning of quality dates and safety dates for food labels by July 1, 2027, and to post the information on the Department's website.
Title: Public Health - Food and Milk Product Labeling - Requirements
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/03 at 3:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Food -see also- Meat, Poultry, & Seafood; Milk; etc.
Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.

bill_summary: This bill establishes standardized labeling for food and milk products in Maryland by requiring manufacturers and retailers to use specific phrases for 'quality dates' (Best if used by) and 'safety dates' (Use by) while prohibiting the use of 'sell by' dates on labels intended for consumers. It also requires the Maryland Department of Health to develop and post educational materials to explain these date labels to the public.
stakeholders: Food manufacturers, processors, and retailers; Grade A milk plants and processors; Maryland consumers; and local health departments.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund expenditures increase by $125,000 in fiscal 2027 and 2028 for contractual services to update regulations and create a consumer marketing program. Local health departments may experience a minimal increase in expenditures to enforce retail compliance. Small businesses may face meaningful compliance costs for updating product labels.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Maryland Department of Health to create an educational program, marketing materials, and a website presence regarding food labeling. MDH is also responsible for adopting regulations and overseeing the enforcement of the new quality and safety date labeling requirements for both food and milk products.

The Maryland Department of Agriculture oversees food quality assurance and supports the economic viability of the agricultural community. The bill's specific requirements for Grade A milk product labeling directly impact the dairy industry and processors under the agency's broader agricultural and food quality purview.

The Comptroller regulates the alcohol industry in Maryland. The bill contains specific exemptions for beer and malt beverages and provides specific labeling allowances for wine and distilled spirits, necessitating coordination or awareness within the Comptroller's regulatory framework.

The Authority operates regional food distribution facilities, such as the Maryland Wholesale Produce and Seafood Markets. Wholesalers and distributors operating within these state-managed facilities will be required to comply with the bill's prohibitions on 'sell by' dates and new requirements for 'quality' and 'safety' dates.

As the independent agency that adjudicates contested cases for state departments, the OAH would be responsible for hearing appeals related to regulatory enforcement actions or penalties issued by the Maryland Department of Health under the new labeling laws.

The Council addresses challenges facing Maryland's rural counties, where agricultural production and milk processing are vital economic drivers. Changes to dairy labeling requirements and the associated compliance costs for rural food processors fall within the Council's interest in supporting rural economic development.

Synopsis: Increasing the amount of the standard deduction allowed for certain individuals from $3,350 to $4,100 under the Maryland income tax; and applying the Act to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.
Title: Income Tax - Standard Deduction - Alteration

bill_summary: This bill increases the Maryland individual income tax standard deduction from $3,350 to $4,100 for individual filers and from $6,700 to $8,200 for heads of household, surviving spouses, and joint filers. bill_summary: This bill exempts property managers from the requirement to obtain a collection agency license when they are collecting rent, utilities, or fees from residential tenants on behalf of a property owner, provided that the collection happens during the lease or holdover period and debt collection is not the manager's primary business activity for that property.
stakeholders: Property managers, residential tenants, property owners, and the State Collection Agency Licensing Board
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a licensure exemption for certain property managers, which is expected to result in a decrease in licensing fee revenue for the State Collection Agency Licensing Board. However, specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the associated Fiscal and Policy Note was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly concerns the State Collection Agency Licensing Board, which is a regulatory unit within the Maryland Department of Labor. The department is responsible for the licensing and regulation of various professions and financial industries, including collection agencies.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the Department of Labor and its licensing boards. Furthermore, the OAG's Consumer Protection Division enforces laws regarding debt collection practices, which are directly impacted by new licensing exemptions for property managers.

As the agency responsible for supporting rental housing and ensuring residents have access to secure housing, DHCD is impacted by legislation that defines and regulates the activities of property managers in their interactions with residential tenants regarding rent and fee collection.

The OAH adjudicates contested administrative cases for state agencies. If a property manager's status or eligibility for this licensing exemption is challenged by the Department of Labor, the OAH would likely handle the resulting administrative hearing.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits residential landlords from using algorithmic software to set rent, occupancy levels, or lease terms if that software relies on nonpublic competitor data. Such use is classified as an unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practice under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act, making it subject to the state's existing enforcement mechanisms and civil penalties.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Residential landlords, tenants, property management companies, and developers of rent-pricing software.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific fiscal estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the text. The bill creates a new violation under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act, which may lead to an indeterminate increase in State general fund revenue from civil penalties and potential enforcement-related expenditures for the Office of the Attorney General.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly makes the use of certain algorithmic devices by landlords an unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practice under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act. The Office of the Attorney General is the primary agency responsible for enforcing this Act through its Consumer Protection Division.

As the state's lead agency for residential housing policy and ensuring access to affordable housing, the Department of Housing and Community Development is directly impacted by regulations concerning how rent, occupancy, and lease terms are determined in the Maryland rental market.

The bill creates new prohibitions within the Real Property and Commercial Law articles and allows for enforcement and penalties. This is likely to result in increased civil litigation and enforcement actions that must be processed through the state judicial system.

Synopsis: Decreasing from eight to four the number of screens in a motion picture house above which the motion picture house is required to provide open movie captioning.

bill_summary: This bill reduces the threshold for movie theaters required to provide open movie captioning from those with eight or more screens to those with four or more screens. Such theaters must provide at least two open-captioned screenings per week for movies available with that technology during the first three weeks after a movie premieres.
stakeholders: Owners and operators of motion picture houses with four or more screens and moviegoers, specifically those with hearing impairments.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is not anticipated to materially affect State or local government operations or finances. Small business movie theaters with four or more screens may experience a meaningful fiscal impact through potential changes in revenue based on viewer preferences for open captioning, though specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Commission on Civil Rights is the primary agency responsible for enforcing laws that prohibit discrimination in public accommodations. This bill directly amends the state's public accommodation statutes regarding movie captioning requirements.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency advocates for equal access and the general welfare of the deaf and hard of hearing community. The bill's expansion of open movie captioning requirements directly addresses the accessibility needs of this agency's primary constituency.

As the principal agency coordinating services and policies for residents with disabilities, the Department of Disabilities is a key stakeholder in ensuring public accommodations are accessible and inclusive.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Commission on Civil Rights and oversees the enforcement of state laws, including those related to civil rights and consumer protection in places of public accommodation.
The OAH adjudicates contested administrative cases, which may include disputes or enforcement actions brought by the Commission on Civil Rights regarding movie captioning compliance.
The AOC supports the judicial branch, which would handle any civil appeals or legal challenges arising from the enforcement of movie captioning laws in state courts.
Older adults are a significant demographic with hearing impairments who rely on captioning services. The department monitors policies that improve the quality of life and accessibility for seniors.
The bill impacts the operational requirements and potential revenues of motion picture houses, which are part of the state's commercial landscape monitored by the Department of Commerce.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The fiscal note identifies a potential meaningful impact on small businesses (theaters with four to seven screens). This office is concerned with the economic environment and regulatory impact on small businesses.
The school serves deaf and hard-of-hearing students and their families, who are the primary beneficiaries of increased accessibility at motion picture houses.

bill_summary: This bill increases the annual compensation for the members of the Anne Arundel County Board of Education. The president's compensation increases from $17,000 to $25,000, the vice president's from $16,000 to $24,000, and the other members' from $15,000 to $23,000.
