bill_summary: This bill expands the requirement for a Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) to include all transmission lines designed to carry more than 69,000 volts, effectively removing the previous limitation that only applied to overhead lines. It replaces a mandatory CPCN waiver for construction on existing lines with a discretionary waiver based on 'good cause,' requiring the Public Service Commission to consider environmental impacts and costs to ratepayers. Additionally, the Commission must adopt regulations by July 1, 2027, to establish specific criteria for these waivers.
stakeholders: Electric utility companies, Maryland electricity ratepayers, environmental advocacy groups, the Maryland Aviation Administration, and local municipal and county governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. However, the bill creates new administrative requirements for the Public Service Commission, including the development of new regulations and the review of a potentially higher volume of CPCN applications and waiver requests. Ratepayers may be financially impacted as the Commission is now required to consider the cost of construction during the waiver evaluation process.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission (PSC) is the primary regulatory body responsible for issuing Certificates of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) for transmission lines. This bill directly modifies the PSC's regulatory authority by expanding the CPCN requirement to all transmission lines (not just overhead), establishing new criteria for waivers, and requiring the PSC to adopt new regulations.

The bill explicitly requires the PSC to consider aviation safety as determined by the Maryland Aviation Administration (MAA) and requires MAA's concurrence with Federal Aviation Administration determinations regarding transmission lines located near public airport runways.

The Department of Planning is specifically named as an entity that must receive immediate notice of any CPCN application and is responsible for evaluating the proposal's significance to State and local plans.

The Office of the People's Counsel represents residential utility consumers. The bill adds 'the cost of the construction on ratepayers' as a mandatory consideration for the PSC when determining whether to waive CPCN requirements, which is a core advocacy area for this agency.

The bill requires the PSC to consider environmental impacts, air and water quality, and climate change commitments (specifically citing the Environment Article) when reviewing CPCN applications. MDE is the primary agency for enforcing these standards.

The bill impacts the Maryland Aviation Administration, a modal unit of MDOT, regarding airport safety. It also affects the construction of utility infrastructure that often intersects with state-owned transportation rights-of-way.

DNR typically serves as a 'State unit' in the CPCN review process, evaluating the impact of energy infrastructure on natural resources, fisheries, and wildlife, all of which are considerations under the bill's expanded criteria.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the PSC and other state agencies involved in the CPCN process and would be involved in the drafting of new regulations and any legal challenges related to eminent domain or regulatory changes.

The Department of Agriculture is concerned with the impact of large-scale infrastructure projects on agricultural land and soil conservation, which are components of the environmental and site-use evaluations required by the bill.

Transmission lines frequently traverse rural counties. The Council advocates for rural interests regarding infrastructure development, economic impact, and land preservation, all of which are impacted by changes to CPCN requirements.

The bill references the right of condemnation in accordance with Title 12 of the Real Property Article. Changes to CPCN applicability directly affect the frequency and legal basis for eminent domain cases heard in the state court system.

The bill requires the PSC to consider the effect of transmission lines on 'historic sites.' The Archives and its Commission on Artistic Property are involved in identifying and preserving Maryland's historical record and assets.

The Governor oversees the executive branch agencies (PSC, Planning, MDE, MDOT) involved in the implementation of the bill and is responsible for the overall policy direction regarding state energy infrastructure and climate goals.

The construction of transmission lines and the resulting cost to ratepayers can impact Maryland's economic competitiveness and business environment, which are key concerns for the Department of Commerce.
The bill maintains provisions for emergency repairs to avoid imminent safety hazards or reliability risks, which relates to the department's role in statewide disaster and emergency preparedness.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a regulatory framework for 'large load customers' (commercial or industrial entities with at least 25 MW demand and an 80% load factor). It requires the Public Service Commission to develop specialized interconnection processes and a Demand Response Program for these customers, exempts specific projects from the Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity requirement, and mandates a load study fee of at least $1,000 per megawatt to fund low-income energy assistance programs. stakeholders: Large load commercial and industrial electricity customers, data center developers, electric utility companies, and low-income residents who benefit from state energy assistance programs.

Specific aggregate dollar estimates for revenue or expenditures are unavailable as they depend on the number and size of future large load customer applications. The Public Service Commission and Maryland Energy Administration will also incur administrative costs to implement the new processes and conduct the required study.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates the Public Service Commission to establish a new interconnection process for large load customers, regulate a new Demand Response Program, set load study fees, and manage the prioritization of interconnection and permitting for specific customers.

The bill requires the Maryland Energy Administration to conduct a comprehensive study of surplus interconnection potential at generating facilities across the State and report its findings to the General Assembly.

The bill provides a direct fiscal impact by allocating 50% of the fees collected from large load customer load studies (not less than $1,000 per megawatt) to the EmPOWER Maryland Limited Income Energy Efficiency Program administered by DHCD.

The bill allocates 50% of the fees collected from large load customer load studies to the Electric Universal Service Program, which is a major energy assistance program managed by the Department of Human Services.

The bill specifies that large load customers must pay the prevailing wage rate to receive prioritization for load studies and interconnection, which falls under the regulatory and enforcement domain of the Department of Labor.

As the representative for residential utility consumers, the Office of the People's Counsel would be concerned with the grid impacts, ratepayer implications, and demand response incentives associated with high-demand 'large load' industrial and commercial users.

The bill impacts 'large load customers,' which are primarily industrial or commercial entities like data centers, and the facilitation of their interconnection is a significant factor in Maryland's economic development and business attraction strategies.

The bill addresses significant state energy policy, grid management, and economic development priorities, requiring coordination across the executive branch and alignment with the Governor's climate and economic goals.

The bill exempts certain projects from the Certificate of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN) process and emphasizes carbon-free assets and behind-the-meter storage, which intersect with MDE's environmental regulation and climate goals.

DNR typically participates in the CPCN process through the Power Plant Research Program; exemptions from CPCN requirements for large load customers and storage facilities would impact their regulatory review workload.

Large load customers with high load factors are often data centers or major IT infrastructure hubs; the bill's provisions on interconnection directly impact the deployment of this critical digital infrastructure in Maryland.
The OAG would provide legal counsel to the PSC and MEA regarding the new regulations, study mandates, and the dispute resolution process established for the Demand Response Program.

bill_summary: This bill requires health care entities—including hospitals, ambulatory surgical facilities, and provider organizations—with at least $10,000,000 in assets or annual revenue to provide 90 days' notice to the Maryland Health Care Commission (MHCC) and the public before completing a material change transaction such as a merger, acquisition, or affiliation. It repeals certain Certificate of Need (CON) exemptions for mergers and establishes a public interest review process. Under this process, the MHCC Executive Director evaluates transactions for their impact on market competition, costs, quality, equity, and access to care, and has the authority to approve, deny, or impose conditions on the transactions.

Additionally, the Commission may contract with independent experts or consultants to conduct public interest reviews, the costs of which must be paid by the parties to the transaction. The Commission is also authorized to impose civil penalties for violations, not exceeding 1% of the transaction's value. Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note were not provided in the bill text, so specific state revenue and expenditure figures are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Health Care Commission (MHCC) is the primary agency responsible for implementing this bill. The bill regulates transactions involving organizations that administer contracts with health insurance carriers. These consolidations in the health provider market can influence insurance rates and market stability, which are overseen by the MIA.

The bill explicitly references and provides specific exceptions for health care facilities owned and operated by the Maryland Department of Veterans and Military Families in the context of certificate of need requirements.

This bill will likely have a fiscal impact requiring new personnel or resources for the Maryland Health Care Commission to conduct technical public interest reviews, monitor compliance, and manage the new regulatory workload.
The bill establishes a formal judicial review process in the Circuit Courts for parties aggrieved by the Commission's decisions regarding material change transactions, impacting court operations.

The bill authorizes the Commission to impose civil penalties of up to 1% of the value of a material change transaction, which represents a potential source of state revenue that the Comptroller's office manages.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Office of Appointments to collect demographic data and produce an annual report regarding applicants and nominees for judicial positions.

As the Appointments Office is an administrative unit within the Governor's Office (the Executive Department), the Governor's Office is responsible for overseen compliance with this statutory reporting requirement.

This bill pertains to judicial selection; the Administrative Office of the Courts provides operational and legal support to the judicial branch and may be involved in coordinating data related to judicial applicants and candidates.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Judicial Nominating Commissions, which are advisory bodies that receive judicial applications and make recommendations to the Governor, are the source of the data required for the reporting mandate.

The requirement to make the demographic report publicly available likely requires technical coordination with DoIT regarding data governance and online publication standards.

bill_summary: This emergency bill renames the commercial blue and flathead catfish finfish trotline license to the commercial blue and flathead catfish license. It expands the authorized gear for catching blue catfish in Maryland's tidal waters to include gill nets with a mesh size of 7 inches or less, in addition to trotlines, while flathead catfish may still only be caught using trotlines.
stakeholders: Commercial fishers in Maryland's tidal waters targeting invasive catfish species
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill maintains an annual license fee of $15. There may be a minor increase in state revenue for the Department of Natural Resources if the expanded gear authorization for blue catfish attracts more license applicants. Specific aggregate fiscal estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are unavailable in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary implementing agency, DNR is responsible for administering the commercial blue and flathead catfish license, defining gear regulations (such as gill net mesh sizes), and managing the tidal fisheries impacted by this bill.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Natural Resources regarding the drafting of regulations and the enforcement of the new gear requirements and license alterations specified in the bill.

MDA oversees the marketing of local agricultural and seafood products; it is actively involved in promoting the commercial harvest and consumption of invasive species like blue catfish to support the economic viability of Maryland's farming and agribusiness sectors.

DBM oversees state revenue estimation and budget execution; it would be responsible for tracking the fiscal impact of changes in license fees and the potential increase in commercial license applications.

OAH adjudicates administrative disputes and contested cases for state agencies; it would handle appeals related to the issuance, suspension, or revocation of the licenses modified by this legislation.

MFCA manages wholesale seafood distribution facilities; an increase in commercial blue catfish landings resulting from the authorized use of gill nets could impact the volume and operations of food distribution within the state.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Agricultural & Resource-Based Industry Development Corp.
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MARBIDCO provides financial services and support to Maryland's seafood and agricultural industries; changes in commercial fishing regulations can affect the profitability and capital needs of the businesses they support.

This multi-agency initiative coordinates environmental protection and Bay restoration efforts; the bill's focus on managing invasive catfish species aligns with the initiative's goals for ecological health and sustainable resource management.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Council on the Chesapeake Bay
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Council advises the Governor on the management and restoration of the Chesapeake Bay; the expansion of commercial harvest techniques for invasive species is a key policy area for Bay management and restoration strategies.
As the state's economic development agency, Commerce is interested in the growth of the commercial fishing industry and the creation of jobs related to the harvest and processing of seafood products.

fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the text; therefore, specific dollar estimates are unavailable. agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency overseeing Maryland's public education system, MSDE is responsible for setting policies and standards for local school systems, including the grading rubrics regulated by this bill.
The Maryland School for the Deaf provides tuition-free public education and would be directly subject to the bill's restrictions and authorizations regarding grading rubrics for its students.

DJS operates residential facilities and educational programs for youth in the juvenile justice system; these programs typically follow public school standards and would need to comply with the new grading rubric requirements.
The bill includes a specific exception for students who require special education services, aligning with this department's role in coordinating services and policies for residents with disabilities.
Changes to statewide grading rubrics affect student performance data, which the MLDS Center links and analyzes to inform state education and workforce policy decisions.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Education and the General Assembly, and would be involved in interpreting and ensuring the legal implementation of this grading policy.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and educational policy initiatives, and would be responsible for the ultimate execution of the law.

Synopsis: Requiring the Department of Agriculture, based on a finding of Palmer amaranth on land, to issue an order to an owner of the land to eradicate the Palmer amaranth within 2 weeks after the order was issued and requiring the Department to inspect the land every 2 weeks until the Department determines that the Palmer amaranth has been eradicated.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of Agriculture to order landowners to eradicate Palmer amaranth within two weeks of discovery and mandates biweekly follow-up inspections until the weed is eradicated. It also establishes specific administrative penalties for noncompliance, ranging from $500 to $2,000, which are deposited into a special fund for noxious weed control.
stakeholders: Maryland landowners, agricultural managers, and the Maryland Department of Agriculture
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a potential increase in state special fund revenue through administrative penalties ranging from $500 to $2,000 per violation. State expenditures will increase for the Maryland Department of Agriculture to perform mandatory biweekly inspections. Specific total dollar estimates are unavailable as no formal Fiscal Note was included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Agriculture (MDA) is the primary agency responsible for enforcing the Maryland Noxious Weed Law. This bill explicitly tasks the Department with inspecting land for Palmer amaranth, issuing eradication orders, and conducting follow-up inspections every two weeks.

The Department of Natural Resources manages over 500,000 acres of public land. The bill specifically includes 'landowners of public land' in the requirement to eradicate or control noxious weeds, making the DNR responsible for compliance on the vast acreage it oversees.

The Department of Transportation, particularly the State Highway Administration (SHA), manages extensive land along highway rights-of-way. As a landowner of public land, MDOT would be responsible for eradicating Palmer amaranth on its property and would be subject to MDA inspections and orders.

The bill's requirement for the MDA to conduct inspections every two weeks until eradication is confirmed will likely require significant additional personnel and operational resources. DBM is responsible for the fiscal oversight and budget allocation required to support these new duties.

The OAG serves as legal counsel for state agencies. It would be responsible for representing the MDA in enforcement actions related to eradication orders and for providing legal advice to other state agencies regarding their compliance obligations as public landowners.

The bill introduces specific administrative penalties for violating eradication orders. Contested penalties and enforcement actions issued by the MDA would be adjudicated by Administrative Law Judges within the OAH.

The University System of Maryland, including institutions like the University of Maryland, College Park, manages significant agricultural research acreage and campus grounds. As a public landowner, the USM must comply with the new mandates and MDA's inspection regime.

The DGS is responsible for the maintenance and landscaping of many state-owned facilities and grounds. It would be responsible for ensuring that the properties it manages are compliant with noxious weed eradication requirements to avoid penalties.

As the state's chief financial officer and collector of revenues, the Comptroller's office would be involved in the accounting and distribution of the administrative penalties collected under the bill, which are directed to a special fund.

The Treasurer's Office is responsible for the management and protection of state funds. The bill mandates that collected penalties be distributed to a special fund for noxious weed control, which falls under the Treasurer's broader fiscal management duties.

bill_summary: The County and Municipal Street Lighting Investment Act authorizes Maryland counties and municipalities to acquire street lighting equipment from electric companies via purchase or condemnation. The bill requires local governments to pay the net book value of the equipment and the costs of any necessary preparation work (make-ready work). It mandates that electric companies establish a specific tariff for customer-owned street lighting that excludes certain maintenance fees, allowing local jurisdictions to manage their own lighting infrastructure and potentially implement energy-efficient upgrades like LED technology.
stakeholders: Maryland counties and municipalities, electric companies, and residential and commercial electricity customers.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text. However, the bill specifies that local governments will face initial capital expenditures to acquire street lighting equipment at its net book value and cover make-ready costs. These jurisdictions may see long-term savings through reduced maintenance and electricity charges under the new customer-owned lighting tariffs. The Public Service Commission will incur administrative costs to review new tariffs and resolve acquisition disputes.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill designates the Public Service Commission (PSC) as the primary regulatory and adjudicative body for this initiative. The PSC is responsible for receiving notices of street lighting acquisition, resolving disputes regarding the net book value of equipment or other acquisition terms through its complaint procedures, and issuing final determinations on the adoption of the mandatory customer-owned street lighting tariffs filed by electric companies.

The bill's findings explicitly state that street lighting upgrades provide opportunities to reduce carbon footprints and address climate change through energy-efficient technologies like LED lamps. As the agency dedicated to maximizing energy efficiency and advising the state on energy policy, the MEA is directly relevant to the implementation and policy goals of transitioning to more efficient, customer-owned lighting systems.

The Maryland Department of Transportation, specifically through the State Highway Administration (SHA), manages thousands of miles of roadways. While the bill empowers counties and municipalities to acquire utility-owned streetlights, these local jurisdictions often coordinate infrastructure and safety resources with MDOT SHA along state-numbered highways that run through their boundaries.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Public Service Commission and other state agencies. It would likely be involved in providing legal guidance on the implementation of the new tariff regulations and representing the state in any legal matters or appeals arising from the condemnation and acquisition processes established by the bill.

The bill authorizes counties and municipalities to use condemnation proceedings under Title 12 of the Real Property Article if they cannot reach a purchase agreement with an electric company. The Administrative Office of the Courts supports the judicial branch where these condemnation cases and jury trials for determining property value would be conducted.

bill_summary: This bill removes the requirement that deeds and other instruments submitted for recording include specific margin sizes and requires clerks of the circuit court to record the date of any changes or corrections made to the general alphabetical index for land records.
stakeholders: Property owners, real estate professionals, and clerks of the circuit court
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not provided. The bill may reduce revenue from penalty fees collected for non-conforming documents by eliminating margin requirements and may cause a minor increase in administrative workload for clerks to date index corrections.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates operational changes for the Clerks of the Circuit Court regarding the dating of changes in land record indices and the technical requirements for recorded instruments. The Administrative Office of the Courts provides the central operational and technological support for the Maryland Judicial Branch, including the land record systems.

The Maryland State Archives serves as the central depository for judicial records and land records. Changes to indexing protocols and recordation standards directly impact the agency's mission to preserve and provide public access to these historical and legal documents.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Judiciary and state agencies regarding real property law and administrative procedures. They would be responsible for advising on the implementation of these statutory changes to recordation practices.

As the agency responsible for the acquisition, management, and real estate leasing of state-owned facilities, the Department of General Services is a frequent user of land records and the general alphabetical index for state property transactions.

The Department of Planning uses land use data and historical records for statewide planning and historic preservation through the Maryland Historical Trust; changes to indexing protocols for real property affect the data resources they utilize.

The Department of Budget and Management oversees the fiscal execution of state agencies. While the impact is likely minimal, any procedural changes that affect the personnel or operational costs within the clerks' offices could have a minor fiscal implication.

The Comptroller's office collects state revenues related to property transactions, such as recordation taxes. While the bill's changes are primarily clerical and procedural, they affect the legal instruments used in the revenue collection process.

bill_summary: House Bill 952 regulates artificial intelligence companion chatbots by requiring operators to establish safety protocols regarding self-harm, suicide, and sexually explicit content. It mandates clear user warnings, usage time alerts for minors, and annual reporting to the Maryland Department of Health's Office of Suicide Prevention. Violations are classified as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health (Office of Suicide Prevention) and the Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Companion chatbot operators, users of social AI systems (particularly minors), and the Maryland Department of Health.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text. The bill creates administrative responsibilities for the Maryland Department of Health to compile and publish annual reports. Additionally, classifying violations as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices may lead to an indeterminate increase in State revenue from civil penalties.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill defines a violation of the companion chatbot regulations as an unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practice subject to the enforcement and penalty provisions of the Maryland Consumer Protection Act, which is primarily enforced by the Consumer Protection Division within the Office of the Attorney General.

The bill specifically tasks the Office of Suicide Prevention within the Maryland Department of Health with receiving annual reports from chatbot operators, compiling data regarding self-harm protocols and crisis notifications, and publishing this data on its website. It also requires chatbot operators to refer users to the Maryland Behavioral Health Crisis Response System.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch departments, including the Maryland Department of Health, and coordinates policy initiatives related to public health and safety, such as the digital safety and mental health protocols established by this bill.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM will be responsible for managing the fiscal impact and potential personnel requirements for the Maryland Department of Health and the Office of the Attorney General as they implement and enforce these new regulatory and reporting mandates.

The bill regulates artificial intelligence systems and references specific AI definitions within state law; as the agency responsible for the state's IT strategy and data governance, DoIT may provide technical guidance regarding the evidence-based methods used by operators for detecting user distress.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Governor, with the approval of the Board of Public Works, to transfer funds from the Revenue Stabilization Account (commonly known as the Rainy Day Fund) to the State Disaster Recovery Fund. Such transfers are only permitted if the remaining balance in the Revenue Stabilization Account stays at or above 5% of the estimated General Fund revenues for that fiscal year.
responsible_party: The Governor and the Board of Public Works
stakeholders: Maryland residents, local governments, and communities impacted by disasters requiring state recovery assistance.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes a mechanism to transfer existing state funds between the Revenue Stabilization Account and the State Disaster Recovery Fund. No specific dollar amounts for these transfers are provided in the bill text, and a formal Fiscal Note with expenditure estimates was not included in the source material. The bill requires that any transfer must leave a balance of at least 5% of estimated General Fund revenues in the Revenue Stabilization Account.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill grants the Governor the authority to initiate the transfer of funds from the Revenue Stabilization Account to the State Disaster Recovery Fund.
The bill explicitly requires the approval of the Board of Public Works for any transfer of funds from the Revenue Stabilization Account to the State Disaster Recovery Fund.
This agency coordinates Maryland's disaster recovery efforts and oversees the State Disaster Recovery Fund, which would receive funds under this legislation.
DBM is responsible for the state's budget execution and the management of the Revenue Stabilization Account (Rainy Day Fund), which is the source of the transfers.
The State Treasurer is a member of the Board of Public Works and is responsible for the management and protection of state funds, including the Revenue Stabilization Account.
The Comptroller is a member of the Board of Public Works and serves as the state's chief financial officer, overseeing the collection and distribution of state revenues.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Governor and the Board of Public Works regarding the legality and implementation of statutory fund transfers.

bill_summary: This bill requires that undisputed retention proceeds held by a Maryland State procurement unit or a contractor under a State construction contract be paid within 90 days after the date of substantial completion, as defined by the relevant contract or subcontract.
responsible_party: Maryland State procurement units and the Maryland Transportation Authority
stakeholders: Construction contractors, subcontractors, lower-tier subcontractors, and State agencies involved in construction procurement.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text. The bill mandates the timing of payments for undisputed retention proceeds but does not explicitly authorize new State spending or revenue generation, focusing instead on the administrative timeline for existing contract payments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary procurement authority for the state and the agency responsible for the design and construction of state-owned facilities, DGS is directly responsible for implementing the new 90-day payment timeline for retention proceeds on its construction contracts.

MDOT is a primary procurement unit that manages extensive infrastructure and construction projects. The bill's requirement to pay out retainage within 90 days of substantial completion will directly impact its financial management and project close-out procedures.

MDTA is explicitly named in the bill text (amending Section 13-225) as one of the entities governed by these retention and payment regulations. The agency will be required to update its payment practices for all major toll facility and infrastructure projects.

The Board of Public Works oversees and approves significant state procurement contracts and sets general procurement policies. This bill amends the State Finance and Procurement Article, which governs the contracts the Board must review and authorize.

The IAC oversees the funding and execution of public school construction projects. Since the bill regulates retention payments for construction contracts, it will impact the administration of capital projects funded and supervised by the IAC.

The Maryland Stadium Authority manages large-scale construction projects for sports facilities and public schools. The new requirements for the timely release of retention proceeds will apply to their numerous high-value construction contracts.

As a primary procurement unit for the state's public universities, USM manages its own construction contracts and will be required to comply with the 90-day deadline for paying out retention proceeds to contractors.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS is designated as a primary procurement unit for construction related to correctional facilities. The agency will need to adjust its contract administration to ensure retention proceeds are paid within the new statutory timeframe.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency and a primary procurement unit. It oversees budget execution and procurement policies, and will be responsible for ensuring that the fiscal impact of accelerated retainage payments is managed within the state budget.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Board of Contract Appeals
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MSBCA adjudicates contract and bid disputes. Establishing a strict 90-day window for retention payments may lead to an increase in claims or disputes brought before the Board if 'substantial completion' or the 'undisputed' status of funds is contested.

The OAG provides legal counsel to all state agencies regarding procurement law. They will be responsible for advising units on the definition of 'substantial completion' as applied in various contracts and ensuring that standard contract language aligns with the new requirements.
Morgan State University acts as an independent procurement unit for its own campus construction projects and will be required to adhere to the 90-day retainage payment mandate for its vendors.

stakeholders: Residents, governing bodies, and property management of residential condominiums and homeowners associations in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: There is no state or local fiscal impact associated with this bill. The legislation governs internal administrative procedures for private associations and does not involve state or local government expenditures or revenues. While it may reduce election-related costs for private associations during uncontested elections, no specific dollar estimates for these private savings are provided.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Secretary of State is explicitly responsible for the registration and oversight of condominiums and time-shares in Maryland. This bill directly amends the Maryland Condominium Act regarding election procedures, which falls under the agency's oversight domain.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel on the interpretation of the Maryland Condominium Act and the Maryland Homeowners Association Act. Additionally, their Consumer Protection Division often addresses grievances related to the governance and election practices of these residential associations.

As the primary agency for housing policy in the state, DHCD has a general interest in the governance and stability of residential communities, including condominiums and homeowners associations, although it does not directly regulate their internal elections.

The Governor's Office is responsible for overseen the executive branch and reviewing all legislation passed by the General Assembly, including changes to real property laws affecting residential governance.

responsible_party: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
stakeholders: Condominium unit owners in buildings over 40 years old, condominium associations, and the Department of Housing and Community Development
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will increase State expenditures for the Department of Housing and Community Development to conduct the study and report findings. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because no formal Fiscal Note was included with the bill text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Department of Housing and Community Development to conduct the study on 40-year-old condominiums, manage the data collection on unit owners, and report findings to the General Assembly.

The Secretary of State is the primary agency responsible for the registration and oversight of condominiums in Maryland, making them a critical source of data and a primary stakeholder for any study concerning condominium buildings.

The study requires determining the annual income of each condominium unit owner; as the state's chief tax collector, the Comptroller would likely be the necessary source or partner for obtaining this financial data.

The Department of Planning provides data analysis and technical assistance regarding land use and resource management; they are a likely source for the historical property records needed to identify buildings more than 40 years old.

The bill requires the collection of age-related data for condominium owners. This information is relevant to the Department of Aging's mission to protect and improve the quality of life for older adults who may be impacted by building safety or financial reserve requirements.
As the principal fiscal agency, DBM would oversee the budget execution and potential personnel costs associated with DHCD conducting a significant statewide study that was not originally budgeted.

Synopsis: Requiring each local school system to designate a local point of contact for certain communications, to comply with, and certify compliance with, the State minimum cybersecurity standards, and to conduct a cybersecurity maturity assessment every 2 years; repealing the requirement that county boards of education prioritize the purchase of digital devices with certain funds; requiring the Office of Security Management within the Department of Information Technology to annually update the State minimum cybersecurity standards; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires Maryland local school systems to designate a cybersecurity point of contact, comply with State minimum cybersecurity standards by 2027, and conduct biennial cybersecurity maturity assessments. responsible_party: The Maryland Department of Information Technology (DoIT), its Office of Security Management, and local school systems (county boards of education).
stakeholders: Students, teachers, and administrative staff within Maryland's local school systems, as well as the Department of Information Technology.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes new cybersecurity compliance and assessment mandates for local school systems. agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill designates the Department (DoIT) and its Office of Security Management as the primary bodies responsible for establishing, reviewing, and updating state minimum cybersecurity standards. DoIT is also mandated to support local school systems with compliance, maturity assessments, and remediation efforts, and to receive certifications of compliance.

The bill directly mandates local school systems (which are overseen by MSDE) to comply with cybersecurity standards and conduct assessments. It also amends the Education Article regarding the target per-pupil foundation amount to include cybersecurity and requires county boards to report cybersecurity expenditures to the Department.

Local school systems are required to create or update cybersecurity preparedness and response plans in consultation with local emergency managers and report cybersecurity incidents to them. MDEM oversees and coordinates these emergency management activities at the state level.

The bill modifies the allocation of funds within the target per-pupil foundation amount, adding cybersecurity as an explicit cost component. As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for the oversight of budget execution and fiscal planning related to these funding formulas.

OLA is responsible for auditing local school systems and state agencies. The new statutory requirements for cybersecurity compliance, maturity assessments, and certification will fall under the scope of future fiscal and compliance audits conducted by this agency.

As an independent unit within MSDE focused on school safety, the Center may be involved in the training or technical assistance required to help schools meet the new safety-related cybersecurity standards mandated by the bill.

bill_summary: The Secure the Vote Act of 2026 repeals the use of ballot drop boxes and permanent absentee ballot lists in Maryland. Shortfalls in meeting the standard require electricity suppliers to pay compliance fees (e.g., 1.5 cents per kilowatt-hour for Tier 2) into the Maryland Strategic Energy Investment Fund. The bill may also impact retail electricity rates for consumers based on changes to utility compliance costs.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary agency responsible for implementing and regulating the Renewable Energy Portfolio Standard (renamed Clean Energy Portfolio Standard by this bill). They oversee electricity suppliers, manage the credit trading system, and verify compliance.

The MEA manages the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF), which receives compliance fees from electricity suppliers who fail to meet the standard. They are also consulted by the Commission on certain energy performance ratings and coordinate statewide energy planning.

The bill links the energy standard to the state's greenhouse gas emissions reduction goals, which are overseen by MDE. Additionally, MDE is responsible for verifying that thermal biomass systems meet air quality standards to qualify for credits.
DGS is specifically authorized by the bill to enter into power purchase agreements for offshore wind energy and associated credits to meet the State's energy needs for its facilities.

The bill mandates that the Maryland Department of Labor regulate and enforce specific labor provisions, including wages, benefits, and apprenticeship requirements for geothermal system installations seeking energy credits.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The office is tasked with consulting on the development of minority business enterprise (MBE) participation goals and procedures for qualified offshore wind projects under the new standard.

The bill amends the Natural Resources Article to update terminology regarding forests as a resource for the Clean Energy Portfolio Standard, which falls under DNR's conservation and management purview.
The OAG is required to consult with the Governor's Office of Small, Minority, and Women Business Affairs in establishing minority business enterprise goals for offshore wind projects.

As the state's green bank, the expansion of the portfolio standard to include nuclear energy and the shift to a 'clean' energy framework impacts MCEC's mission to advance and finance clean energy technologies.

The Executive Director of the Commission serves as an ex-officio member of the Maryland Medicaid Advisory Committee, and a representative of the Commission is mandated to serve on the newly established Workgroup to Study the Adoption of a Fee-for-Service Model.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards

The Secretary of Human Services is designated as an ex-officio member of the Maryland Medicaid Advisory Committee, which is responsible for reviewing Medicaid programs that often intersect with human services populations (e.g., TANF recipients).

bill_summary: The Maryland Fair and Agricultural Education Promise Act establishes the Maryland Fair and Agricultural Education Promise Fund to support agricultural fairs and education through annual grants. The bill mandates that $1,450,000 from State lottery proceeds be distributed to this fund each year starting in fiscal 2027, replacing previous funding mechanisms derived from the horse racing Special Fund. The fund is administered by the Comptroller and provides specific grant amounts to the Maryland Agricultural Fair Board, the Maryland Agricultural Education Foundation, the Maryland State Fair and Agricultural Society, and the Maryland FFA Association.
stakeholders: Maryland Agricultural Fair Board, Maryland Agricultural Education Foundation, Inc., Maryland State Fair and Agricultural Society, Inc., Maryland FFA Association, 4-H Clubs, and local/county agricultural fair organizers.
fiscal_impact_summary: Starting in fiscal 2027, the bill redirects $1,450,000 annually from the State Lottery Fund to the newly created Maryland Fair and Agricultural Education Promise Fund, resulting in a $1,450,000 annual decrease in General Fund revenue. The bill also repeals existing grant mandates totaling $1,450,000 from the horse racing Special Fund. The new fund is directed to pay out annual grants totaling $1,500,000, which is supported by the lottery proceeds, interest earnings, and potential supplemental budget appropriations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly designates the Comptroller to administer the Maryland Fair and Agricultural Education Promise Fund, account for the fund, and distribute the annual grants to the designated recipients.

The bill adds a new subtitle to the Agriculture Article and provides significant funding to the Maryland Agricultural Fair Board, which is an entity within the Department of Agriculture, to promote state and county agricultural fairs.
The State Treasurer is required to hold the new special fund separately and invest its money in the same manner as other state money.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates that $1,450,000 from the State Lottery Fund be allocated annually to the Maryland Fair and Agricultural Education Promise Fund before remaining proceeds are sent to the General Fund.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is impacted by the creation of a new special fund, the diversion of lottery revenue from the General Fund, and the requirement that expenditures from the fund follow the state budget process.

The bill provides specific grant funding for the Maryland FFA Association and the Maryland Agricultural Education Foundation, which support agricultural education and youth programs that align with the department's oversight of public education and vocational programs.
The OAG would provide legal counsel to the Comptroller, Treasurer, and Department of Agriculture regarding the establishment, administration, and regulatory compliance of the new grant fund.

bill_summary: This bill expands the scope of the Open Meetings Act's enhanced requirements to include the Maryland State Department of Education (MSDE), the Accountability and Implementation Board (AIB), and all county boards of education. These entities are required to post meeting agendas and materials online at least 48 hours in advance, publish minutes within two business days of approval, and provide live video streaming of open sessions. Additionally, the bill mandates that all public bodies subject to these enhanced requirements must retain meeting minutes and video recordings for a minimum of 15 years.

bill_summary: The Freedom From Monopolies Act repeals various regulations and licensing requirements for retail electricity and gas suppliers, salespersons, and vendors. The bill eliminates price caps and contract duration limits for residential energy suppliers, reduces the maximum assessment the Public Service Commission (PSC) can levy against utilities for its operating costs, and abolishes a specific division within the PSC. It also renames and modifies the purpose of the Education and Protection Fund to focus specifically on retail choice education.
stakeholders: Retail electricity and gas suppliers, public service companies (utilities), residential and small commercial energy consumers, and the Maryland Public Service Commission.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will result in a significant but indeterminate decrease in state revenue due to halving the maximum assessment rate (from 0.50% to 0.25% of gross operating revenues) that the Public Service Commission may charge public service companies to fund its operations. Additionally, potential revenue from civil penalties will decrease as the maximum fine for violations is lowered from $25,000 to $10,000. Administrative expenditures will be impacted by the abolition of a specific PSC division and the subsequent reassignment of staff, though the bill mandates no diminution in pay or benefits for those employees. Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission (PSC) is the primary agency affected by this bill. It oversees the licensing of electricity and gas suppliers, manages the newly named Retail Choice Customer Education and Protection Fund, and is responsible for standard offer service transitions. The bill also reduces the PSC's assessment cap and abolishes a specific division within the Commission.

The bill directly impacts the funding of the Office of the People's Counsel (OPC) via the modified public service company assessment. Additionally, OPC is explicitly named as a party involved in customer complaints, licensing investigations, and market status reporting.

The bill affects the Maryland Energy Administration (MEA) through its Strategic Energy Planning Office, which is funded by the assessments modified in the bill. The bill also repeals several provisions related to green energy and renewable energy credits which align with MEA's energy policy role.

The bill requires the Public Service Commission to consult with the Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General before issuing consumer protection regulations. The OAG also maintains enforcement authority over consumer protection violations related to energy suppliers.

The bill repeals specific provisions that allowed the Department of General Services (DGS) to sell energy under certain conditions and removes them from the definition of energy salespersons/vendors under specific sections.
The State Treasurer's Office is responsible for holding the Retail Choice Customer Education and Protection Fund and managing its investments as specified in the bill.

The Comptroller is responsible for accounting for the newly named Retail Choice Customer Education and Protection Fund and has a general interest in the fiscal assessments on public service companies.

The bill involves the transfer and reassignment of state employees within the Public Service Commission and modifies state fund structures, which falls under DBM's personnel and fiscal management oversight.

The bill repeals specific requirements for the Education and Protection Fund to address the State's climate commitments under the Environment Article and modifies reporting requirements for renewable energy credits.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires electricity suppliers to document the participation levels of minority business enterprises in activities supporting the creation of renewable energy credits, a reporting requirement relevant to this office's mission.

Synopsis: Prohibiting licensed massage therapists, registered massage practitioners, and third parties directed by licensed massage therapists or registered massage practitioners from placing, publishing, or distributing certain advertisements; and requiring certain advertisements for massage therapy to include the full name, as stated on the license or registration application, and the license number or registration number of the licensed massage therapist or registered massage practitioner providing massage therapy services.

bill_summary: This bill establishes advertising standards for massage therapy services, requiring practitioners to include their full name and license or registration number in most advertisements. It explicitly prohibits advertisements that offer prostitution or sexual services, advertisements placed on websites known for such services, or content that implies sexual activity is part of the therapy. The State Board of Massage Therapy Examiners is required to adopt regulations defining prohibited language and establishing reporting procedures for violations.
responsible_party: State Board of Massage Therapy Examiners
stakeholders: Licensed massage therapists, registered massage practitioners, massage therapy businesses, and third-party advertisers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The State Board of Massage Therapy Examiners can implement the bill's requirements, including the adoption of regulations, using existing budgeted resources. State revenues are not affected, and there is no fiscal impact on local governments. Small business impacts are expected to be minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health oversees the State Board of Massage Therapy Examiners, which is the primary body responsible for implementing the bill, adopting the required regulations, and enforcing the new advertising standards through its licensing and disciplinary powers.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as legal counsel to the Maryland Department of Health and its various boards; it would provide legal advice on the drafting of the new advertising regulations and represent the Board of Massage Therapy Examiners in disciplinary proceedings against licensees.

The Office of Administrative Hearings adjudicates contested cases and disciplinary actions taken by state boards; any massage therapist facing license suspension or revocation due to the advertising violations established by this bill would likely have their case heard by an Administrative Law Judge at this agency.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office coordinates public safety and criminal justice strategies for the state. Since the bill specifically targets the use of massage therapy advertisements to mask illegal prostitution, escort, and sexual services, it aligns with the agency's mission to reduce crime and address human trafficking.

bill_summary: The Education Funding Accuracy Act alters the calculation for State education aid by redefining full-time equivalent enrollment. Instead of using a single student count from September 30, the new definition uses an average of the student counts from September 30 and May 31 of the prior school year. The bill also requires the Maryland State Department of Education to publish an annual report disaggregating enrollment counts by county and detailing per-pupil funding allocations.
stakeholders: K-12 students in Maryland public schools and local school systems
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text. The bill's change to the enrollment count calculation—averaging fall and spring counts instead of a single fall snapshot—will likely result in a decrease in the calculated enrollment numbers for many school systems. This would lead to a reduction in State education aid expenditures and a corresponding decrease in revenue for local school systems starting in fiscal 2028.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency responsible for the oversight of Maryland's public education system, MSDE is directly tasked with implementing the new enrollment count formula and producing the annual reports required by this bill.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for budget execution and long-term planning. Altering the education funding formula significantly impacts the state's annual budget and fiscal projections.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the annual state budget. Changes to the foundation program formula affect a major portion of the executive budget proposal.

The MLDSC links student performance and workforce data. The bill's requirement for detailed enrollment reporting, including specific categories like 'whereabouts unknown,' directly involves the data sets managed by this agency.

OLA conducts fiscal and performance audits of state agencies and local school systems. They would be responsible for auditing the accuracy of the new May 31 enrollment counts and the resulting state aid allocations.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, including MSDE. They may be required to review the new formula's implementation and the regulatory changes needed to define full-time equivalent students under the new average count.
The Comptroller serves as the state's principal tax collector and pays state bills. Changes in state aid distributions to counties would be managed and recorded by this office.
The Treasurer's Office manages and distributes state funds. Changes to the education foundation program affect the distribution of significant portions of the state's cash reserves.

GOPI utilizes data-driven strategies to oversee the implementation of state priorities. The bill's focus on 'funding accuracy' and reporting directly aligns with GOPI's mandate for accountability and measurable results.
This team is charged with identifying strategies to reduce child poverty and enhance economic mobility. Educational funding is a critical component of these policy priorities.
The GOC focuses on child well-being and reducing poverty. Educational aid levels and accurate student counts are central to the comprehensive support networks they coordinate.
While this bill addresses operating aid, enrollment counts are a fundamental metric used by the IAC for planning, funding, and assessing the educational sufficiency of school facilities.

bill_summary: This bill regulates individuals or businesses not accredited by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs that charge for assistance with veterans' benefits claims. It requires these entities to use written fee agreements that include specific disclosures regarding the availability of free services, mandates that these disclosures be provided orally, and prohibits charging fees if the claimant dies before the claim is processed. Violations are categorized as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices, subject to civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation and a potential one-year ban on providing such services.
responsible_party: Maryland Attorney General and the Maryland Department of Veterans and Military Families
stakeholders: Veterans, their dependents and survivors, and non-V.A. accredited individuals or businesses providing veterans' benefits services for compensation.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a potential revenue increase for the Maryland Veterans Trust Fund through civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation. It also grants the Attorney General enforcement authority under the Consumer Protection Act. Specific total fiscal estimates are not provided as a formal Fiscal Note was not included with the bill text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the Maryland Department of Veterans and Military Families (DVMF) as it regulates services related to veterans benefits matters, defines such matters in the context of the department's administration, and mandates that civil penalties be deposited into the Maryland Veterans Trust Fund, which the department manages.

The Office of the Attorney General (OAG) is tasked with enforcing the provisions of the bill, particularly regarding consumer protection and bringing civil actions in District Court for violations related to unaccredited claim servicers.

The bill grants jurisdiction to the District Court to order civil penalties for violations, which involves the judicial branch's operations and workload overseen by the Administrative Office of the Courts.

As the state's chief financial officer and tax collector, the Comptroller is responsible for the oversight of state revenues, including the collection and accounting of civil penalties directed to the Maryland Veterans Trust Fund.

The State Treasurer's Office is responsible for the management and protection of state funds, including the Maryland Veterans Trust Fund, which will receive revenues from civil penalties established by this bill.

The Department of Budget and Management is relevant due to its role in supervising budget execution and fiscal planning related to the Maryland Veterans Trust Fund and the resources required for enforcement by the Attorney General.

bill_summary: Known as Kanaiyah’s Law, this bill establishes the Office of the Child Welfare Ombudsman within the Office of the Attorney General to investigate complaints, uphold the rights of children, and ensure their protection within the state welfare system. The legislation prohibits placing children in unlicensed settings such as hotels or office buildings, expands criminal history records check requirements to include all adults residing in a guardian's home, and creates a 24-hour toll-free helpline for child welfare concerns.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General and the Department of Human Services
stakeholders: Children and families involved in the child welfare system, legal guardians, adults residing in guardian households, and state and local social services agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will result in increased state expenditures to establish and operate the Office of the Child Welfare Ombudsman, including salaries for the Ombudsman and staff, and the maintenance of a 24-hour helpline and website. There are also potential costs for local departments of social services to monitor guardian households and facilitate expanded criminal background checks. Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are not provided in the bill text, though it mandates that the Governor include sufficient funds in the state budget.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Office of the Child Welfare Ombudsman specifically within the Office of the Attorney General (OAG). The Attorney General is responsible for appointing the Ombudsman and overseeing the office's budget and staffing coordination.

The bill directly impacts DHS and its local departments by prohibiting the placement of children in unlicensed settings, expanding criminal history records check requirements for guardians, and establishing an independent Ombudsman to oversee and investigate the department's child welfare activities.

The bill authorizes juvenile courts to co-commit children to the Maryland Department of Health (MDH) and requires MDH to provide plans for clinically appropriate services in the least restrictive setting.

The bill modifies procedures for juvenile courts, requiring specific directives in guardianship orders, setting strict timelines for review hearings, and establishing a new petition process for reviewing guardianships based on criminal history findings.

The bill requires the Attorney General to cooperate with the Secretary of Budget and Management to set minimum salaries, qualifications, and training standards for positions within the new Office of the Child Welfare Ombudsman.

The bill explicitly directs the Ombudsman to use the services and personnel of the Department of State Police to the extent practicable and mandates that the Department cooperate with the Ombudsman's investigations.

The bill expands criminal history records check requirements to include adults residing in homes known by the State Department of Education (MSDE) for providing family child care or informal child care.

The bill authorizes the Child Welfare Ombudsman to apply to the Board of Public Works for additional money from the General Emergency Fund if the office's budget is insufficient to perform its duties.

The bill’s primary focus on child well-being, child protection, and the creation of an oversight body for the child welfare system is directly aligned with the mission of the Governor's Office for Children to coordinate statewide efforts for children and families.

fiscal_impact_summary: The bill's specific financial impact is unknown as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text. agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary agency responsible for implementing the bill, as it must determine equity market returns and adjust utility rates during base rate proceedings.

The OAG serves as the chief legal representative for state agencies, including the PSC, and would provide legal counsel regarding the implementation and defense of the new rate-setting regulations.

fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will likely result in an indeterminate decrease in tuition revenue for public institutions of higher education due to an increase in the number of students eligible for tuition waivers. The University System's 12 institutions are public institutions of higher education that must implement the tuition exemption for eligible students, which directly impacts their tuition revenue.

bill_summary: This bill alters, caps, or repeals various Maryland tax credits, modifications, and exemptions to increase revenue and reduce tax expenditures. Key provisions include terminating the Enterprise Zone Program on January 1, 2031, and the One Maryland Economic Development Tax Credit on January 1, 2027. It establishes a $2,000,000 annual aggregate cap for Enterprise Zone income tax credits and a $500,000 per-property cap for associated property tax credits. Additionally, the bill requires an addition modification for dividends paid by Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs), repeals the 0.5% motor fuel tax discount for dealers, eliminates various sales and use tax exemptions, and reduces the tobacco tax exemption for consumers.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Commerce and the Comptroller of Maryland
stakeholders: Maryland business entities (including REITs, film producers, technology firms, and industrial manufacturers), motor fuel dealers, tobacco consumers, and local governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to increase State revenue and decrease expenditures by capping or repealing numerous tax incentives. Explicit annual limits introduced include a $2,000,000 cap on Enterprise Zone income tax credits and a $12,000,000 limit for film production activity credits. It also repeals the 0.5% motor fuel tax discount and various sales and use tax exemptions. While these measures indicate a significant revenue increase, a formal Fiscal Note with an aggregate total dollar estimate was not provided in the source text.

The bill specifically tasks the Comptroller with joint regulation of the film production tax credit and modifies several tax categories under the Comptroller's direct jurisdiction.

DBM is responsible for revenue estimation and long-term fiscal planning. This bill has significant fiscal impacts due to the repeal and alteration of multiple state tax credits and exemptions, which affects state revenue and budget execution.

It is also required to perform a formal evaluation of the film credit.
The bill repeals a sales and use tax exemption for target redevelopment areas defined by participation in the Voluntary Cleanup Program, which is administered by the Department of the Environment.

As the parent agency of the Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA), MDOT is impacted by changes to vehicle registration credits. Additionally, the repeal of the motor fuel tax discount for licensed dealers impacts the revenue of the Transportation Trust Fund.

GOPI's mission to enhance efficiency and data-driven performance aligns with the bill's intent to evaluate and sunset potentially under-performing tax credits, as well as the requirement for new reporting metrics for business entities.
The bill requires the Maryland Insurance Commissioner to compute and certify the amount of State tax credits authorized for business entities against the insurance premiums tax.

The Maryland Tax Court provides the highest level of administrative review for tax disputes. Changes to income, sales, motor fuel, and property tax credits are likely to result in appeals that fall under the court's jurisdiction.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the state agencies (Commerce, Comptroller, MDH, etc.) tasked with implementing and enforcing the new tax regulations and program terminations.

PTAAB hears appeals regarding property tax assessments and credits. The bill's significant changes to Enterprise Zone property tax credits and the new $500,000 credit cap per property are likely to generate assessment disputes.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Mattress Stewardship Program to manage the collection, transportation, and recycling of postconsumer mattresses in Maryland. It requires mattress producers to develop and fund stewardship plans, prohibits mattress disposal in landfills and incinerators by 2035, and introduces a mattress stewardship assessment on all mattresses sold in the state. The program includes oversight by the Maryland Department of the Environment and a newly created Mattress Stewardship Advisory Board, with a focus on environmental justice and social equity in the waste management system.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of the Environment, Office of Recycling
stakeholders: Mattress producers, retailers, consumers, recycling and waste management entities, and local governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: The program is funded by a consumer-paid stewardship assessment on mattress sales. The Maryland Department of the Environment will receive revenue from plan and report review fees and civil penalties (up to $1,000 per day for producers and $100 per day for retailers), which are deposited into the State Recycling Trust Fund to cover administrative oversight costs. Local jurisdictions may experience reduced expenditures for mattress disposal and illegal dumping as these responsibilities shift to the producer-funded program. Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are unavailable in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) is the primary implementing and regulatory agency for the Mattress Stewardship Program. Its Office of Recycling is specifically tasked with reviewing and approving stewardship plans, annual reports, and assessments, as well as providing staff for the newly created Advisory Board.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Mattress Stewardship Advisory Board, a multi-stakeholder body tasked with advising on the implementation, sustainability, and evaluation of the program.

The bill explicitly requires the Maryland Environmental Service to coordinate with the Office of Recycling to study and report on recycling centers, waste disposal economics, and progress in diverting mattresses from landfills.

The Comptroller or their designee is a mandated member of the Mattress Stewardship Advisory Board. Additionally, the Comptroller is responsible for accounting for the State Recycling Trust Fund, which will receive new fees from this program.

The Governor is responsible for appointing ten members to the Mattress Stewardship Advisory Board, representing various industries and advocacy groups. The office also receives mandated reports on the program's progress.
The State Treasurer is the custodian of the State Recycling Trust Fund, which the bill expands to include plan and report review fees collected from the Mattress Stewardship Program.

The bill provides immunity from state and federal antitrust and unfair trade practice claims for producers acting in accordance with the program, a legal provision that would involve the oversight of the state's chief legal officer.

The Secretary of Health or their designee is a mandated member of the Mattress Stewardship Advisory Board. The bill addresses environmental health issues, such as hazardous chemicals in mattresses leaching into drinking water.
The Secretary of Commerce or their designee is a mandated member of the Mattress Stewardship Advisory Board, reflecting the program's impact on mattress manufacturers and retailers.

The bill emphasizes creating jobs for disadvantaged populations and requires stewardship plans to prioritize entities that hire individuals reentering society, those in recovery, or those experiencing homelessness, which aligns with the department's workforce development mission.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill specifically requires that the program's stewardship plan describe how Minority Business Enterprises (MBEs), women-owned businesses, and veteran-owned businesses will be solicited and supported.

The bill includes goals for hiring individuals with disabilities within the mattress waste management stream and mandates that collection infrastructure must be accessible to residents with disabilities.

bill_summary: This bill repeals the Building Energy Performance Standards program, which required commercial and multifamily residential buildings with at least 35,000 square feet to report energy usage data and meet specific greenhouse gas emission reduction targets (20% by 2030 and net-zero by 2040). The legislation eliminates reporting requirements, the $100 annual reporting fee, and the authority of the Department of the Environment to assess alternative compliance fees for failure to meet emission targets.
stakeholders: Owners and managers of commercial and multifamily residential buildings with 35,000 square feet or more, State agencies that own large buildings, and the Maryland Department of the Environment.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will result in a decrease in State revenue due to the repeal of the $100 annual reporting fee per covered building and the removal of alternative compliance fees based on the social cost of greenhouse gases. Additionally, the bill will lead to a decrease in State expenditures as the Maryland Department of the Environment will no longer be required to develop, implement, or enforce building energy performance standards. Because a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the bill text, specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of the Environment was the primary agency tasked with developing standards, adopting regulations, and collecting data for the Building Energy Performance Standards program being repealed.

DGS is the primary agency responsible for managing state-owned facilities; the repeal removes energy performance compliance and reporting mandates for large state buildings under its care.
The bill repeals a mandate requiring electric and gas companies regulated by the PSC to provide aggregate energy data to building owners for benchmarking purposes.
As the agency managing energy efficiency incentives and policy, MEA is impacted by the removal of a primary regulatory driver for building energy transitions in the state.
As the state's fiscal agency, DBM is impacted by the removal of program fees and administrative costs at MDE, as well as the fiscal impact on compliance requirements for other state agencies.
The department's modal administrations operate large state-owned facilities, including airports and transit hubs, which were categorized as covered buildings under the repealed standards.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services

The University System manages a vast portfolio of state-owned buildings that were required to meet the direct greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets established by the repealed law.

The Board of Public Works oversees significant state property transactions and capital projects; the repeal of these standards changes the requirements for state-funded construction and facility management.
The Stadium Authority manages large state-owned facilities, such as stadium complexes and convention centers, that were classified as covered buildings under the standards being repealed.
