bill_summary: This bill establishes the Electronic Device Producer Responsibility Program in Maryland, which requires manufacturers of covered electronic devices to participate in a producer responsibility organization (PRO) to fund and manage the statewide collection, recycling, and reuse of their products. Manufacturers must register with the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE), pay registration fees into a dedicated account within the State Recycling Trust Fund, and submit comprehensive plans to ensure equitable access to collection sites across the state. The bill also establishes an advisory council to provide recommendations on program administration and requires retailers to provide recycling information to consumers at the point of sale.
stakeholders: Electronic device manufacturers, retailers, recyclers, Maryland households, small businesses or nonprofit organizations with 10 or fewer employees, and local governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill increases state revenue through new registration and review fees paid by electronic device manufacturers and producer responsibility organizations into the State Recycling Trust Fund. Specifically, manufacturers must pay initial registration fees of $10,000 (for 1,000+ units sold) or $5,000 (for 100-999 units sold). These funds are designated to cover MDE’s costs for program administration, oversight, and enforcement. Additionally, PROs are required to provide fair financial compensation to collection sites and local public sector agencies for the management and transportation of electronic devices. A formal Fiscal Note with aggregate dollar estimates was not included in the provided text.

As the chief legal officer for state agencies, the OAG will provide legal counsel to MDE regarding the new regulations and represent the state in enforcement actions and appeals related to the program.

The bill defines 'covered entity' to include public sector agencies. As the agency responsible for state IT strategy and infrastructure, DoIT is impacted by the requirements for the disposal and recycling of state-owned electronic devices.

This multi-agency initiative includes MDE and Planning to reduce the state's carbon footprint and promote sustainable development, goals which are shared by the electronic device recycling program.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits behavioral health care providers from using artificial intelligence (AI) for clinical purposes, such as assessment, diagnosis, treatment, and therapeutic communication. It permits the use of AI for administrative support tasks—including scheduling, billing, and record management—provided the provider ensures compliance with confidentiality laws, signs security agreements with AI vendors, and notifies patients of the potential risks. Providers must also obtain written informed consent if AI systems could materially affect clinical decision-making, and they remain subject to disciplinary action by their respective health occupation boards for violations.
stakeholders: Behavioral health care providers, patients receiving behavioral health services, and Maryland health occupation regulatory boards.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. MSDE oversees the public education system, which employs various behavioral health providers, such as school psychologists and licensed clinical social workers. These professionals are subject to the bill's restrictions when providing services within the school environment.

bill_summary: This bill updates Maryland's laws regarding business entities. It permits boards of open-end investment companies to take actions by majority consent without a meeting, simplifies corporate procedures during bankruptcy proceedings, and repeals criminal misdemeanor penalties for officers of unregistered foreign corporations. fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland State Department of Education is required to provide staff for the workgroup. Members of the workgroup receive no compensation but are entitled to reimbursement for travel expenses under Standard State Travel Regulations. Specific fiscal estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Education is the primary agency impacted as it is responsible for providing staff for the workgroup, appointing a representative, and receiving the final report. The workgroup's focus on public school students directly aligns with the department's oversight of the state's public education system.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards

The Governor's Office is responsible for appointing two executive branch members to the workgroup and is one of the primary recipients of the final report and recommendations.
The Office of Appointments within the Executive Department is responsible for vetting and recommending candidates for the Governor's appointments to state task forces and commissions.
The Attorney General is required to appoint an advisory member to the workgroup, likely to provide legal counsel on statutory and regulatory policy recommendations.
The bill entitles workgroup members to travel reimbursement as provided in the state budget, which is overseen by the Department of Budget and Management as the state's principal fiscal agency.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes Maryland counties and municipalities to establish multidisciplinary suicide fatality review teams. These teams investigate suicide deaths to identify systemic risk factors, coordinate prevention and crisis response efforts, and develop recommendations to reduce suicide rates. The bill mandates coordination with the State Suicide Fatality Review Committee and establishes strict confidentiality requirements for records and meetings involving individual cases.
responsible_party: County Health Officers, local health authorities, and the State Suicide Fatality Review Committee.
stakeholders: County and municipal governments, local health departments, social services, law enforcement agencies, healthcare providers, and the general public.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill authorizes rather than mandates the establishment of local suicide fatality review teams, meaning fiscal impact is contingent on local government participation. Counties opting to establish teams may face increased administrative and staffing costs. The bill also establishes a misdemeanor fine of up to $500 for confidentiality violations, which could generate minimal local revenue. Because no formal Fiscal Note was provided with the text, specific dollar estimates for State or local expenditures are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates that local suicide fatality review teams coordinate with and operate subject to guidance from the State Suicide Fatality Review Committee, which is established under the Health-General Article and overseen by the Maryland Department of Health (MDH). Additionally, local health officers and behavioral health directors—who are either state employees or closely integrated with MDH—are required members of these teams.

The bill creates significant legal protections, including exemptions from the Open Meetings Act and the Maryland Public Information Act, and establishes confidentiality and testimonial immunity. The OAG would be responsible for providing legal counsel to state entities regarding the implementation and enforcement of these privacy and disclosure standards.

The bill specifically restricts the admissibility of certain information in civil or criminal proceedings and provides that local team records are not subject to subpoena or discovery. This directly impacts judicial operations and the rules of evidence managed by the courts.
The bill requires the Director of the local department of social services (part of DHS's statewide network) to be a member of the local suicide fatality review team.

The bill requires the local Superintendent of Schools (overseen by MSDE) to be a member of the local suicide fatality review team, involving the public education system in the review of youth-related suicide data and policy.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill includes emergency medical services (EMS) providers as required members of local teams. MIEMSS is the state agency responsible for overseeing and regulating the EMS network that these providers belong to.
The bill lists state law enforcement officers as potential members of local suicide fatality review teams, which could involve the Maryland State Police in local multi-agency case reviews.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates new local advisory bodies and requires their coordination with the existing State Suicide Fatality Review Committee, which falls under this category of state-authorized committees and boards.

bill_summary: This emergency bill requires the Prince George’s County Board of Education and the County Superintendent to provide full-time salaries and benefits to all individuals employed as one-to-one student aides beginning in the 2027-2028 school year. It mandates quarterly reporting on special education services, requires annual professional development for special education staff, and directs the Maryland State Department of Education to hire a third-party auditor to conduct a comprehensive performance and financial audit of the county's special education department for fiscal years 2021 through 2025.
responsible_party: Prince George’s County Board of Education, Prince George’s County Superintendent, and the Maryland State Department of Education
stakeholders: Students with special needs in Prince George's County Public Schools, one-to-one student aides, and special education employees.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a significant new spending mandate for Prince George's County by requiring full-time salaries and benefits for one-to-one student aides. The Maryland State Department of Education will incur costs to contract with a third-party auditor for a multi-year audit. Specific dollar estimates for these expenditures are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary implementing agency, the Department is responsible for hiring a third-party auditor to evaluate Prince George's County Public Schools, receiving and publishing quarterly special education updates, and certifying compliance. Additionally, the State Superintendent of Schools is authorized to withhold funds from the local school system for non-compliance with the act's record production requirements.

The bill requires a comprehensive audit of special education due process filings and resolution timelines; the OAH is the independent agency responsible for adjudicating these contested cases, which includes special education disputes, via its Administrative Law Judges.

The bill mandates that one-to-one student aides in Prince George's County receive full-time salary and benefits equivalent to other employees, which directly impacts the administration of collective bargaining and labor relations for public school personnel overseen by this board.

The Department of Disabilities is the principal agency for coordinating and improving the delivery of services to residents with disabilities; the bill's focus on the delivery of Individualized Education Programs (IEPs) and the provision of one-to-one aides for students with disabilities is a core policy focus for this agency.

The Board of Public Works oversees and approves significant state procurement contracts; the requirement for the Department of Education to hire a third-party auditor to conduct a performance and financial audit would involve a contract that likely requires the Board's approval.

The OLA conducts performance and fiscal compliance audits of local school systems; the scope of the third-party audit mandated by this bill regarding special education services, financial data, and staffing within Prince George's County Public Schools is highly relevant to OLA's statutory oversight role.

The audit required by the bill includes analysis of student outcomes such as graduation rates, chronic absenteeism, and discipline; the MLDS Center is the state's repository for linking and analyzing the student performance data necessary for these longitudinal evaluations.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Education and the State Superintendent; they would likely be involved in drafting the audit contract and providing legal guidance on the enforcement mechanisms and fund withholding provisions of the bill.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency for the state; it would oversee the budget execution related to the Department of Education's new oversight duties and the fiscal implications of withholding state funds from the local school system.

This office utilizes data-driven strategies and performance metrics to enhance the responsiveness of state government; the bill's requirements for transparency dashboards, objective performance thresholds, and a corrective action plan based on audit metrics align with GOPI's mission.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, including the Department of Education; this bill represents a significant policy initiative concerning educational accountability and equity, and involves the appointment of various reporting requirements within the executive branch.

The office focuses on the well-being of Maryland's children and improving access to education and health services; this bill's aim to ensure accountability and service delivery for students with special needs directly impacts the children and families supported by this agency.

Synopsis: Defining "danger to the life or safety of the individual or of others" for purposes of the involuntary admission of individuals with mental disorders to a facility or Veterans' Administration hospital and the emergency evaluation of individuals with mental disorders.
Title: Mental Health Law - Danger to the Life or Safety of the Individual or of Others - Definition (Right to Treatment)
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/24 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Health Care Facilities -see also- Clinics; Hospices; etc
Mental and Behavioral Health -see also- Aut; Cogn; Dev; etc.

bill_summary: This bill defines the phrase 'danger to the life or safety of the individual or of others' as it relates to the involuntary admission and emergency evaluation of individuals with mental disorders. The definition includes a substantial risk of bodily harm, criminal justice involvement, inability to provide for basic needs like food and medical care, or a substantial deterioration of judgment that prevents an individual from making rational decisions regarding their treatment.
stakeholders: Individuals with mental disorders, mental health professionals, healthcare facilities, and law enforcement agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note with specific dollar estimates was not provided in the text. However, the broadening of the criteria for involuntary admission may lead to an increase in emergency evaluations and inpatient treatments, which could increase operational expenditures for the Maryland Department of Health and other psychiatric facilities.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MDH is the primary state agency responsible for behavioral health services and the administration of Maryland's mental health laws. It oversees both state-run and private facilities where involuntary admissions and emergency evaluations occur, which are directly impacted by the revised definition of 'danger' in this bill.

Administrative Law Judges at the OAH conduct the mandatory hearings for individuals who have been involuntarily admitted to mental health facilities. A change in the definition of the criteria for admission directly affects their adjudicative process and caseload.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The OPD is legally mandated to provide representation for indigent individuals in involuntary commitment proceedings. Expanding the definition of 'danger' is likely to increase the number of eligible individuals and the complexity of their defense in such cases.

State law enforcement is often tasked with responding to emergency evaluation petitions and transporting individuals to facilities. The bill's updated definition of danger may increase the frequency of these interventions.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and represents the state in matters related to the enforcement and interpretation of mental health laws, including involuntary admissions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS manages individuals in the correctional system, many of whom have mental health disorders. The bill specifically includes 'conduct that will result in criminal justice involvement' as part of the definition of danger, directly impacting how the department identifies and refers individuals for treatment.
The Judiciary is involved in the legal oversight of emergency petitions and civil commitments. Changes to these standards require operational and training updates within the court system.

The bill explicitly names 'Veterans' Administration hospitals' as facilities for involuntary admission under the new definition. DVMF advocates for veterans' health care and would be involved in ensuring veterans are appropriately served under these laws.
As the state's fiscal agency, DBM will be impacted by the increased costs associated with higher rates of involuntary admissions, including staffing at state facilities and legal costs for hearings.

The department coordinates services for residents with disabilities, including those with mental health disorders. This bill affects policy regarding inclusive treatment and integrated settings for those facing involuntary admission.
DHS works with vulnerable populations, including adults and children in need of protective services, who are frequently the subjects of emergency evaluations and mental health interventions.
DJS manages youth in the justice system who often require mental health evaluations. The bill's broadened definition of danger could impact the assessment and placement of youth in DJS custody.

Involuntary admission involves the loss of personal liberty. MCCR is concerned with ensuring that such processes do not disparately impact protected classes and that the expanded criteria do not lead to discriminatory practices.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MIEMSS oversees the statewide EMS network, which is responsible for the prehospital care and transport of individuals during mental health crises and emergency evaluations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP coordinates strategies to reduce crime and recidivism. The bill's focus on preventing 'criminal justice involvement' via mental health intervention aligns with the office's public safety policy goals.

The Department of Aging supports older adults who may face mental health crises and for whom the criteria for 'unable to provide for basic needs' is particularly relevant regarding involuntary admission.
The Maryland State Library Agency's primary focus is on library coordination and funding, which is not impacted by changes to mental health commitment laws.

bill_summary: This bill, known as Ralph's Act, requires the Developmental Disabilities Administration to grant eligibility for services to certain individuals who recently relocated to Maryland from another state. To qualify, an individual must be a dependent of an immediate family member who has lived in Maryland for at least two years, have received home- and community-based services in another state for at least ten years, and moved to Maryland following the death or incapacitation of their caretaker. The bill mandates an expedited 30-day review process and requires that eligible individuals be placed in the Crisis Resolution category for waiver services.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health, Developmental Disabilities Administration
stakeholders: Individuals with developmental disabilities moving to Maryland, their immediate family members living in Maryland, and the Maryland Department of Health.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will increase state expenditures by expanding the population eligible for developmental disability services and requiring those individuals to be placed in the highest priority category (Crisis Resolution) for funding. The Department will also incur administrative costs for the mandated 30-day expedited review process. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the bill text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the Developmental Disabilities Administration, which is a division within the Maryland Department of Health. The agency is responsible for establishing the expedited review process, determining eligibility, and providing the mandated services.

As the principal agency responsible for coordinating services for Marylanders with disabilities, this department would be heavily involved in the policy development and inter-agency coordination required by the bill.

The bill will likely have a significant fiscal impact due to the provision of new services and the personnel required to manage the expedited 30-day review process. DBM oversees state budget execution and personnel management.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives. This bill introduces a specific policy change regarding state residency requirements and service eligibility for vulnerable populations.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and would likely be involved in drafting the regulations for the expedited review process and interpreting residency laws as they relate to eligibility.

Individuals denied eligibility under this new process may appeal the decision through the Office of Administrative Hearings, which handles contested cases for state agencies including the Department of Health.

The bill affects individuals whose caregivers have died or become incapacitated, a situation often involving older adults. The Department of Aging coordinates long-term care advocacy and support for caregivers.

DHS provides services to residents in economic need and those requiring protection from abuse or neglect. There may be overlap in eligibility verification and social service coordination for the relocated individuals.
GOPI utilizes data-driven strategies to enhance the efficiency of state government. The bill's mandate for a 30-day expedited determination process is a performance metric this office might monitor.

Synopsis: Applying certain provisions of law establishing that certain noncompete and conflict of interest provisions in certain employment contracts are null and void as being against the public policy of the State to employees of certain employers that relocate, reorganize, or otherwise cease to have the majority of its employees or principal place of business located in the State.

bill_summary: This bill expands existing legal protections against noncompete and conflict of interest clauses in employment contracts. It specifies that such provisions are null and void for employees of an employer that employs more than 30 people in Maryland if the employer relocates its principal place of business or the majority of its employees outside of the state. These protections apply to employment contracts executed on or after October 1, 2026.
stakeholders: Maryland employees and employers with more than 30 employees who relocate their operations or a majority of their workforce outside the state.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text. The bill regulates private employment contracts and does not explicitly state any revenue changes or spending mandates; thus, specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Labor and Employment Article, specifically regarding noncompete and conflict of interest clauses. The Department of Labor is the primary agency responsible for enforcing state labor laws and protecting worker rights, making it the central agency for implementation and oversight of these changes.

As the chief legal officer for Maryland, the OAG is responsible for interpreting state laws and representing the state in legal matters. This bill establishes that certain contract provisions are 'null and void as being against the public policy of the State,' which may require the OAG to provide legal guidance or defend the state's policy in court.

The bill's new provisions are triggered when an employer relocates or ceases to have the majority of its employees in Maryland. As the state's primary economic development and business retention agency, Commerce is directly impacted by policies affecting business relocation and the competitive landscape for Maryland employers.

The bill declares certain employment contract clauses null and void. Disputes between employers and employees regarding the validity of these clauses will likely be litigated within the state's judicial system, affecting the workload and legal environment managed by the Judiciary.

The bill specifically references employees required to be licensed under the Health Occupations Article and those providing direct patient care. While these employees were already partially covered by existing law, the MDH oversees the regulatory boards for these professionals and has a significant interest in the labor conditions affecting healthcare delivery.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives. Changes to labor policy and business retention strategy are core executive functions, and the Governor would be responsible for the overall execution of such a shift in public policy.

Synopsis: Prohibiting the State or a unit of local government from approving the use of a building or structure as an immigration detention facility by a private entity unless certain zoning authority applies; establishing a certain penalty for a certain violation; and authorizing the Attorney General to bring a civil action to enforce the Act.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits state and local governments from approving the use of buildings as private immigration detention facilities unless the specific use is expressly permitted by local zoning authority. It defines these facilities based on features such as involuntary confinement and perimeter security. The bill authorizes the Attorney General to bring civil actions for enforcement and establishes a civil penalty of up to $10,000 per day for violations. The provisions apply retroactively to existing agreements.
responsible_party: Maryland Attorney General and local government zoning authorities
stakeholders: Private entities operating or planning to operate immigration detention facilities, local governments, and individuals held for federal civil immigration violations.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are unavailable. The bill establishes a civil penalty of up to $10,000 for each day a private entity operates in violation of the zoning requirements, representing a potential revenue increase. State and local governments may incur indeterminate costs related to enforcement and zoning administration.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly authorizes the Attorney General to bring civil actions to enforce the zoning requirements and seek injunctive relief against private entities operating immigration detention facilities in violation of the Act.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary department responsible for the Correctional Services Article of the Annotated Code of Maryland, DPSCS has significant interest in laws governing detention facilities and the standards applied to their operation within the state.

The bill centers on zoning authority and land-use classifications. The Department of Planning provides technical assistance and policy guidance to local governments regarding land use planning and zoning, making them relevant to the implementation of these requirements.
The bill creates new civil causes of action, establishes daily civil penalties of up to $10,000, and authorizes injunctive relief, which directly impacts court caseloads and judicial administration.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP serves as the primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategies. This bill affects detention policy and public safety regulations, falling within their strategic advisory scope.

DGS manages state-owned facilities and real estate leasing. The bill's prohibition on the State approving buildings for use as immigration detention facilities could impact DGS's management of state property and leasing agreements.

The Board of Public Works oversees and approves significant state contracts, including the lease or transfer of state property. The bill's restrictions and its retroactivity clause could impact existing or future contracts under the Board's purview.
As the state's fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for assessing the fiscal impact of legislation and would be involved in the budgetary implications of new enforcement actions by the Attorney General.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives. This emergency bill involves significant state-local relations and high-profile immigration policy, requiring executive oversight and coordination.

bill_summary: This emergency bill requires the Secretary of Public Safety and Correctional Services to adopt minimum mandatory standards for the care and custody of civil detainees in immigration detention facilities. It expands the authority of the Maryland Commission on Correctional Standards to inspect these facilities, requires healthcare and security personnel to report violations, and allows the Attorney General to seek civil penalties of up to $10,000 from private operators for noncompliance. The Commission is also authorized to close facilities that are found to be life-threatening or health-endangering.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services and the Maryland Commission on Correctional Standards
stakeholders: Civil detainees in immigration detention facilities, private entities owning or operating detention facilities, health care practitioners, security guards, and State and local correctional agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures will increase to provide the Maryland Commission on Correctional Standards with the staff and resources necessary to oversee and inspect immigration detention facilities. General fund revenues may increase from civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation per day imposed on private entities. Additionally, facilities must reimburse the Commission for the cost of performance audits. If a facility is ordered to close, the responsible State, local, or federal entity must pay for the transfer and maintenance of detainees. A formal Fiscal Note with specific dollar estimates was not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS is the primary agency responsible for this bill. The Secretary of Public Safety and Correctional Services is tasked with adopting the mandatory regulations, and the Maryland Commission on Correctional Standards (MCCS), which resides within the department, is given broad new oversight, inspection, and enforcement powers over immigration detention facilities.

The bill explicitly authorizes the Attorney General to bring civil actions against private entities for violations of the new standards, including seeking injunctive relief and significant civil penalties. The OAG also works with the Commission to petition courts for compliance orders.

The Governor oversees the Executive Department, including DPSCS. The bill requires annual reporting to the Governor on compliance issues and recommendations for both correctional and immigration detention facilities.

The bill mandates hearings regarding the cessation of operations for facilities found to be life-threatening or health-endangering. As the central panel for administrative disputes, OAH would likely conduct these hearings or review appeals from inspection reports.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill specifically authorizes the Maryland Commission on Correctional Standards to establish a new permanent advisory board on immigration detention facilities to assist in carrying out the duties mandated by the Act.

The Commission may conduct inspections in conjunction with the Maryland Department of Health. Additionally, MDH oversees the licensing boards for health care practitioners who are now legally required to report violations or face disciplinary action.

The bill requires certified security guards to report violations and security breaches. Since the Maryland State Police is the regulating body responsible for the certification and discipline of security guards under the Business Occupations and Professions Article, they are impacted by the enforcement provisions.

The bill expands the scope of the Maryland Commission on Correctional Standards, requiring additional inspections, auditing, and reporting, which will have a notable fiscal and personnel impact requiring DBM oversight during budget planning.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the Governor's primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategy, GOCPP is relevant to the development and implementation of new standards governing detention facilities within the state.

The bill requires the establishment of standards regarding 'individual rights' for civil detainees. This aligns with the Commission's mission to enforce anti-discrimination laws and protect civil rights in state-regulated environments.
The bill provides for judicial enforcement, allowing the Commission and Attorney General to petition circuit courts for orders requiring compliance or the closure of facilities.

The BPW oversees state expenditures and contracts. The bill involves potential state expenses related to the transfer and maintenance of detainees if a facility is ordered closed, which may require BPW's fiscal oversight.
The Office of Appointments may assist in recommending or vetting individuals to serve on the newly authorized advisory board for immigration detention facilities.

bill_summary: The bill expands Maryland's school bus transition program to include propane-powered school buses alongside zero-emission vehicles. It renames the state's transition grant program and fund, directs the Department of the Environment and Department of Transportation to provide technical assistance, and allows county boards of education to enter into contracts for propane-powered school buses starting in fiscal year 2030.
stakeholders: Maryland county boards of education, private school bus contractors, and public school students.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill expands the scope of the Zero-Emission Vehicle School Bus Transition Fund to include propane-powered buses, utilizing funding from state appropriations, interest earnings, and legal settlements. Although the bill enables grants and alters school board contracting options, specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not provided.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill designates the Department of the Environment as the lead agency responsible for implementing and administering the Zero-Emission Vehicle and Propane-Powered School Bus Transition Grant Program and Fund.

The Maryland State Department of Education is explicitly required to consult on the administration of the program and fund, and it oversees the county school boards directly impacted by the bus procurement changes.

The bill explicitly tasks the Department of Transportation with jointly providing technical assistance to county boards of education and contractors for the transition to propane-powered school buses.
The State Treasurer is specifically mandated to hold the Zero-Emission Vehicle and Propane-Powered School Bus Transition Fund and manage its investments and interest earnings.
The bill requires the Comptroller to account for the newly renamed and expanded Zero-Emission Vehicle and Propane-Powered School Bus Transition Fund.
The department is responsible for supervising the state's budget and will oversee the fiscal management and appropriations for the expanded grant program and special fund.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the primary implementing agencies (MDE, MSDE, and MDOT) regarding the new regulations and the management of legal settlements that may fund the program.
The Board of Public Works oversees and approves significant state expenditures and contracts, which may include large-scale procurement or grants related to school bus transitions.
The OLA is responsible for conducting fiscal compliance audits of the state agencies and the special fund created or altered by this legislation.

bill_summary: This bill increases the mandatory retirement age for certain members of the State Police Retirement System from 60 to 62 years of age. It also raises the maximum age for participation in the Deferred Retirement Option Program (DROP) from 60 to 62 and allows current DROP participants to extend their participation, subject to certain service and age limitations.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of State Police and the Board of Trustees for the State Retirement and Pension System

bill_summary: This bill prohibits manufacturers from selling or distributing various products containing intentionally added per- and polyfluoroalkyl (PFAS) chemicals, such as cleaning products, cookware, cosmetics, and textiles, by specified dates in 2028 and 2029. It establishes a registration system where manufacturers must disclose PFAS content to the Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) and pay registration fees. The bill also creates the Maryland PFAS Chemicals Protection and Remediation Fund to support state efforts in monitoring, preventing, and remediating PFAS contamination through grants and loans to public and private entities.
stakeholders: Manufacturers, distributors, and retailers of consumer goods; Maryland consumers; and communities or water systems affected by PFAS contamination.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes the Maryland PFAS Chemicals Protection and Remediation Fund, which will receive revenue from new manufacturer registration fees and administrative penalties of up to $15,000 per violation and $25,000 per day for noncompliance with administrative orders. These funds will cover MDE's administrative costs and provide grants and loans for PFAS remediation projects. Specific fiscal estimates are not provided in the bill text beyond a reference to a previous $500,000 appropriation in 2024 for fire-fighting foam take-back programs.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency for environmental protection, MDE is responsible for implementing the PFAS product phase-outs, managing the new registration system and fees, conducting product testing, and administering the Maryland PFAS Chemicals Protection and Remediation Fund.

MDH is a required consultative partner for MDE in identifying 'currently unavoidable uses' of PFAS and in the administration of the remediation fund. Additionally, the fund is used to conduct community health studies.
MDA must be consulted regarding the administration of the remediation fund. The fund is specifically authorized to provide emergency relief to farm operations impacted by PFAS contamination.

DNR is a required consultant for the remediation fund's administration. The fund is used to monitor PFAS in surface waters and fish tissue, and must be coordinated with DNR-managed programs like the 2010 Trust Fund.
The OAG is authorized to investigate compliance with PFAS prohibitions, request documentation from manufacturers, and bring civil actions to collect penalties and recover remediation costs.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch's policy implementation and is responsible for proposing budget appropriations for the PFAS take-back program and fund expenditures.
The State Treasurer is responsible for holding the new remediation fund separately, investing its assets, and ensuring interest earnings accrue to the fund.
The Comptroller is tasked with accounting for the Maryland PFAS Chemicals Protection and Remediation Fund and ensuring proper fiscal tracking of penalties and fees.
The Chesapeake Bay Trust is explicitly named as a mandatory consulting entity for the Department of the Environment in the administration of the remediation fund.
MDOT is affected by regulations on fire-fighting foam at airports and ports, as well as the regulation of automotive cleaning products used on motor vehicles.
OAH would likely adjudicate administrative appeals from manufacturers regarding orders, penalties, or registration requirements issued by MDE.
MES provides technical services for wastewater and landfill management, which are specifically identified in the bill as areas for PFAS research and remediation projects funded by the new program.
The bill's prohibitions and registration requirements significantly impact manufacturers, distributors, and retailers of various consumer goods within the state.
DBM oversees the fiscal management and personnel needs for state agencies tasked with implementing the new regulatory and grant-making functions established by the bill.
MDEM coordinates disaster recovery and resilience; the remediation fund provides emergency relief to households impacted by PFAS contamination.
DGS is the central procurement authority; the ban on various PFAS-containing products (cleaning supplies, furniture, cookware) directly affects state facility management and purchasing.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits the sale, distribution, and manufacturing of lab-grown meat for human consumption in Maryland. The Secretary of Health is also authorized to seize or condemn any lab-grown meat produced or sold in violation of the law.
stakeholders: Manufacturers, distributors, and retailers of meat products; Maryland consumers; and the Maryland Department of Health.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided. The bill establishes a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per violation, which would result in an indeterminate revenue increase for the state. The Maryland Department of Health will incur administrative and enforcement costs, including the potential seizure of prohibited products, though specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill adds a new subtitle to the Health – General Article. The Secretary of Health is responsible for enforcement, including the authority to seize or condemn prohibited lab-grown meat products.

This bill directly impacts the meat industry and agricultural policy in Maryland. The Department of Agriculture regulates food quality and is tasked with promoting the economic viability of traditional farming and agribusiness, which this ban supports.

The bill prohibits the manufacturing and sale of a specific food-technology product, which affects the state's economic development strategies, particularly within the biotechnology and food manufacturing sectors.

TEDCO supports early-stage technology-based businesses and the commercialization of technology. A ban on lab-grown meat would restrict innovation and investment in this emerging biotechnology sector in Maryland.
The bill establishes civil penalties to be collected via civil actions in the District Court, impacting court operations and the judiciary's administrative functions.
The OAG would provide legal counsel to the Department of Health and Department of Agriculture regarding the enforcement of this ban and would represent the state in civil penalty actions.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, coordinates policy initiatives, and would be responsible for signing this legislation and overseeing its implementation across departments.
DBM is responsible for fiscal planning and oversight. This bill has potential fiscal impacts related to enforcement costs and revenue from civil penalties.

The MDTA is an instrumentality responsible for toll facilities and has the power to finance and build transportation projects, which often requires land acquisition through eminent domain. This bill would limit that authority.

The Department of General Services is the state's central real estate and procurement agency, responsible for land acquisition for state-owned facilities. This bill restricts the agency's capacity to acquire specific types of property for public use.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Agricultural & Resource-Based Industry Development Corp.

The Governor oversees the executive branch and its instrumentalities, all of which are subject to this new prohibition on the use of eminent domain.

bill_summary: This emergency bill authorizes merchants to round the total price of cash transactions and allows employers to round wages paid in cash to the nearest five-cent increment. Under the bill, totals ending in 1, 2, 6, or 7 cents are rounded down to the nearest five cents, while totals ending in 3, 4, 8, or 9 cents are rounded up. Transactions totaling less than 5 cents may be rounded up to 5 cents. The bill's provisions preempt any conflicting local regulations or ordinances.
stakeholders: Maryland merchants, consumers, employers who pay wages in cash, and employees who receive cash wages
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the text; therefore, specific dollar estimates are unavailable. The financial implications include indeterminate impacts on business revenues, consumer expenditures, employee wages, and state sales tax collections resulting from the authorized rounding of cash totals.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Labor and Employment Article regarding wage payments and the Business Regulation Article. The Secretary of Labor is the designated official to adopt regulations for rounding cash transactions and oversees the enforcement of wage payment laws which this bill impacts.

The OAG's Consumer Protection Division is responsible for enforcing laws that protect consumers from unfair or deceptive trade practices. Rounding cash transactions directly impacts consumer costs and merchant disclosures, falling under the OAG's regulatory and legal oversight.

As the state's chief tax collector, the Comptroller oversees the collection of sales and use taxes. Rounding total prices in cash transactions may create discrepancies in revenue reporting and tax audits, requiring guidance from this agency.

The bill impacts the operational practices of all merchants in the state. As the primary economic development agency, the Department of Commerce is concerned with the regulatory environment and its effects on the business community.

Individuals with disabilities who rely on cash or live on fixed incomes may be impacted by changes in transaction rounding. The department coordinates services and advocacy for this demographic.

bill_summary: This bill expands the definition of "large load customers" under Maryland's electricity regulations to include all data centers, regardless of their specific power demand or capacity. It requires electric companies to submit specific rate schedules for these customers to the Public Service Commission (PSC) to ensure that data centers cover the costs of any electric transmission or distribution infrastructure required to serve them. The legislation is intended to prevent residential ratepayers from bearing the financial risks or subsidizing the infrastructure costs associated with high-energy-demand data center facilities. Additionally, the bill adjusts the deadlines for electric companies to submit these rate schedules and for the PSC to adopt necessary regulations.
stakeholders: Data center developers and operators, investor-owned electric companies, electric cooperatives, municipal electric utilities, and residential electricity ratepayers in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text. However, the bill specifies that large load customers, including data centers, are responsible for covering the costs associated with electric system buildouts required to interconnect and serve them. This mechanism is designed to protect residential retail electric customers from financial risks and ensures that cost allocations do not result in unreasonable subsidies by other customer classes.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary regulatory body responsible for implementing the bill, including approving specific rate schedules for large load customers and adopting mandatory regulations to carry out the act.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates high-level policy initiatives, including those related to energy regulation, economic development, and consumer protection.

fiscal_impact_summary: Calvert County property tax revenues will decrease by an indeterminate amount if the county implements the tax credit. No specific dollar estimates are available as the credit is permissive and its amount and duration are determined by the county governing body. There is no impact on state revenue or expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a new property tax credit in Calvert County for former tobacco barns. The Property Tax Assessment Appeals Board is the independent agency responsible for hearing appeals regarding property tax assessments and credits, directly impacting its administrative review workload if the credit or the underlying agricultural use assessment is disputed.

As the highest level of administrative review for tax-related disputes, the Maryland Tax Court would be responsible for adjudicating appeals related to the eligibility and valuation of properties applying for this tobacco barn tax credit.

The bill requires that the property be used for an activity recognized as an 'approved agricultural activity' to qualify for the tax credit. As the primary agency for agricultural policy and support, the Department provides the framework for defining such activities and supporting the transition from tobacco farming.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Agricultural & Resource-Based Industry Development Corp.
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MARBIDCO's mission is to support the sustainability and profitability of Maryland's agricultural industry, including assisting farmers in transitioning from tobacco and preserving agricultural assets like barns. This tax credit directly aligns with their goal of ensuring rural business viability.

The Rural Maryland Council addresses challenges in Maryland's rural counties, including Calvert County. This legislation affects the economic development and quality of life for rural residents and agricultural property owners in the region.

The Governor's Office oversees state policy initiatives and the executive branch. This bill involves changes to the Tax-Property Article and state-level recognition of agricultural activities, requiring executive coordination.

The Department of Planning promotes sustainable growth and resource management. Tax credits for maintaining agricultural structures like tobacco barns intersect with the department's mission of land use planning and agricultural preservation.

Synopsis: Requiring the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore City or the governing body of a county to give written notice of certain property tax credits for which a taxpayer may be eligible through the property tax bill.
Title: Property Tax Credits - Notice Through Property Tax Bill
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/24 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Mayor and City Council of Baltimore City and the governing bodies of Maryland counties to include a written notice with property tax bills informing taxpayers of property tax credits for which they may be eligible. It also specifies that if a property tax bill is sent to a third party rather than the taxpayer, that recipient must notify the taxpayer of the potential credits in writing.
responsible_party: Mayor and City Council of Baltimore City and the governing bodies of Maryland counties
stakeholders: Maryland property owners, local governments, and third-party tax bill recipients such as mortgage companies
fiscal_impact_summary: The formal Fiscal Note is not included in the bill text, so specific dollar estimates are unavailable. However, the bill creates a mandate for local governments to provide additional notices, which will likely increase administrative and printing expenditures. Furthermore, local property tax revenue may decrease if the notices successfully increase the number of taxpayers who apply for and receive tax credits.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency provides administrative review for property tax assessment disputes, including tax exemptions and various property tax credits, which are the primary subject of the bill's notice requirements.

This agency is the highest level of administrative review for tax disputes, including factual determinations regarding assessments and property tax credits affected by the bill's notice and reporting provisions.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the OAG provides legal counsel regarding the interpretation and implementation of the Tax - Property Article and the enforcement of statutory notice requirements.
As the state's principal tax official and revenue collector, the Comptroller has a general interest in tax policy and state-wide reporting requirements for property tax credits.

The department advocates for older adults, who are a primary target demographic for many property tax credits; the bill's requirement for mandatory notice on tax bills directly impacts the utilization of these benefits by seniors.

The agency assists veterans in securing state benefits, which often include specific property tax credits for disabled veterans and their families that would be subject to the bill's notice requirements.
The department coordinates services and benefits for residents with disabilities, many of whom are eligible for the property tax credits that must now be explicitly noticed on property tax bills.
The agency manages programs related to homeownership and community revitalization, which are often supported by the specific property tax credits addressed in the bill's requirements.

The department oversees the agricultural community, which benefits from specific property tax credits (e.g., for agricultural use or preservation) included under the scope of this bill's notice provisions.

Synopsis: Requiring each public high school in the State to maintain an injury log for injuries that occur during school athletic activities, subject to certain requirements; and requiring each local school system to submit an annual report on high school athletic injuries to the State Department of Education beginning on or before July 1, 2027.

Status: In the House - Hearing 3/10 at 1:00 p.m.

bill_summary: This bill requires each public high school in Maryland to maintain a standardized injury log for all injuries that occur during school-related athletic activities, including practices, competitions, and conditioning. It mandates that local school systems submit an annual aggregated report of these injuries to the Maryland State Department of Education beginning in 2027.
stakeholders: Public high school student-athletes, coaches, certified athletic trainers, school nurses, and local school systems.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the bill text. However, the bill creates administrative mandates for public high schools to document and retain injury records for five years and requires local school systems to compile and submit annual reports, which may result in increased operational or administrative costs.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency overseeing Maryland's public education system, the Department of Education is responsible for receiving annual injury reports from local school systems, prescribing the manner of reporting, and collaborating on the adoption of regulations and standardized forms.

The bill explicitly requires the Maryland Department of Health to collaborate with the Department of Education and the Maryland Public Secondary Schools Athletic Association to adopt regulations and standardized reporting forms for athletic injuries.

As an independent unit within the Department of Education focused on school safety, the Center is relevant to the bill's mission of tracking and reviewing athletic injuries for compliance and safety purposes to foster a safe learning environment.

As a state agency that operates high school programs for students through age 21, the Maryland School for the Deaf would be required to maintain standardized injury logs for its athletic activities and follow the reporting requirements mandated for public high schools.

The Office of the Attorney General would likely provide legal counsel in the drafting of regulations and ensure that the reporting and recordkeeping protocols comply with federal and state student privacy laws, such as FERPA, as mentioned in the bill.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM would evaluate the fiscal impact and potential resource requirements for the Department of Education to manage the collection and aggregation of statewide athletic injury data.

DoIT would potentially be involved if the Department of Education requires the creation or management of a centralized digital infrastructure to facilitate the standardized reporting of injury logs from local school systems.

Synopsis: Providing that the exemption for owner-occupied residential real property in a bankruptcy proceeding includes certain real property held in a revocable trust; and altering the amount of the exemption for owner-occupied residential real property in a bankruptcy proceeding.
Title: Bankruptcy Proceedings - Exemptions From Execution - Residential Real Property
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/05 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Elderly Persons (65+) -see also- Elder Abuse and Neglect

bill_summary: This bill modifies Maryland's bankruptcy laws regarding owner-occupied residential real property exemptions. It expands the exemption to include residential property held in a revocable trust and establishes new exemption limits: $300,000 for individuals who are at least 60 years old and are either veterans or have a certified disability, and $150,000 for other individuals. It caps the total exemption for multiple individuals in the same proceeding at $300,000 and requires annual adjustments to these amounts based on the Consumer Price Index beginning in fiscal year 2028.
stakeholders: Maryland residents filing for bankruptcy, homeowners, veterans, individuals with disabilities, settlors of revocable trusts, and creditors.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text, so specific dollar estimates for state and local impacts are unavailable. The bill increases the value of real property that may be exempted from execution in bankruptcy proceedings and provides for annual inflation-based adjustments to these limits, which impacts the assets available to creditors.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a significantly higher homestead exemption of $300,000 for individuals aged 60 and older, directly impacting the housing security and financial protection of Maryland's senior population during bankruptcy proceedings.

The bill provides a specific $300,000 homestead exemption for individuals with certified disabilities, which aligns with the department's mission of ensuring that people with disabilities have access to secure housing and can maintain community living.

The bill creates a higher $300,000 homestead exemption for veterans who are at least 60 years old, directly affecting the advocacy and support services provided by the department regarding veterans' housing and benefits.

The bill amends the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article of the Maryland Code, which is the statutory framework the Administrative Office of the Courts supports, particularly regarding the legal process for exemptions from execution on property.

The bill's expansion of homestead exemptions to include property held in revocable trusts and its increase in exemption limits support the department's core mission of ensuring state residents have access to safe, secure, and stable housing.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the OAG is relevant for the interpretation and enforcement of these changes to debtor-creditor law and the novel application of exemptions to residential property held in revocable trusts.

The Comptroller acts as the state's principal tax collector; an increase in the value of exempted assets in bankruptcy may impact the agency's ability to recover delinquent state taxes and other revenues from individual debtors.

The bill's focus on protecting the homes of individuals in financial distress serves as a preventative measure against homelessness, which is a primary focus area for the department's social service and economic assistance programs.

The team is tasked with identifying strategies to enhance economic mobility; the bill's changes to bankruptcy exemptions represent a policy tool for protecting household wealth and economic stability for vulnerable residents.

As the agency responsible for long-term fiscal planning and revenue supervision, DBM is minimally impacted by potential changes in state debt recovery that result from altered bankruptcy exemption thresholds.

Synopsis: Imposing a limit of four on the number of terms a person may serve in the General Assembly; providing that a certain term limit does not apply to terms that began before the 2030 gubernatorial election; and specifying how service for a partial term shall be considered for purposes of the term limits.
Title: General Assembly - Term Limits
Status: In the House - First Reading House Rules and Executive Nominations

NarrowSubjects.Name: General Assembly -see also- AELR Cmte; LegislativePolCmte

bill_summary: This bill proposes an amendment to the Maryland Constitution to limit individuals to four terms of service in the Maryland General Assembly. It specifies that terms beginning before the 2030 gubernatorial election do not count toward the limit and that serving two or more years of a partial term is considered a full term for the purpose of the limit.
stakeholders: Current and future members of the Maryland General Assembly, candidates for legislative office, and Maryland voters.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. The bill would incur administrative costs associated with adding the proposed constitutional amendment to the ballot for the November 2026 general election.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Board of Elections is responsible for administering the statewide referendum where voters will decide on the proposed constitutional amendment during the 2026 general election.
The Governor's Office is responsible for receiving the official election returns and formally proclaiming the amendment as part of the Maryland Constitution following a successful vote.
Establishing term limits for the General Assembly will impact the duration of service and future pension eligibility for legislators under the state retirement systems managed by this agency.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the state government and is typically involved in reviewing the legal sufficiency of constitutional amendments and drafting ballot questions.
The Secretary of State serves as the principal custodian of Maryland's official records and laws, including the certification and recording of changes to the State Constitution.

Synopsis: Requiring certain junk dealers, scrap metal processors, and antique dealers to register and provide a description including certain information of purchased telecommunications equipment with a certain law enforcement official; prohibiting certain junk dealers, scrap metal processors, and antique dealers from purchasing telecommunications equipment other than by check mailed to the seller's address; etc.
Title: Telecommunications Infrastructure - Protections
Status: In the House - First Reading Economic Matters

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.
Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.
Equipment -see also- Charging; Med. Equip.; MV Equip; etc.
Law Enforcement -see also- SRO; Sheriffs; State Police
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

bill_summary: This bill regulates the trade of telecommunications equipment by requiring junk dealers, scrap metal processors, and antique dealers to register transactions with local law enforcement, adhere to a 30-day holding period before disposal, and pay sellers only by mailed check. Additionally, it criminalizes the reckless or malicious damage of telecommunications infrastructure, establishing specific felony and misdemeanor penalties for violations.
responsible_party: Maryland Sheriffs, designated local law enforcement officials, and State licensing authorities for junk dealers.
stakeholders: Junk dealers, scrap metal processors, antique dealers, telecommunications service providers, and law enforcement agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are unavailable. The bill establishes fines of up to $2,000 for dealer violations and up to $5,000 for the destruction of telecommunications infrastructure, which may result in an indeterminate increase in state and local revenue. There may be increased administrative costs for law enforcement registration and enforcement.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends Title 17 of the Business Regulation Article, which governs the licensing and regulation of junk dealers and scrap metal processors, both of which are under the jurisdiction and oversight of the Maryland Department of Labor.

The bill requires junk dealers and scrap metal processors to register telecommunications equipment purchases with local law enforcement and creates new criminal penalties for the destruction of infrastructure, which involves the investigative and enforcement duties of the State Police.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes new criminal offenses, including a felony for destroying telecommunications infrastructure, which may impact the state's correctional facilities and parole and probation services.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The creation of new misdemeanor and felony charges related to telecommunications infrastructure and equipment will result in additional cases for the Office of the Public Defender representing indigent clients.

The introduction of new criminal penalties and regulations for scrap dealers will lead to an increase in civil and criminal litigation within the Maryland judicial system, requiring support from the Administrative Office of the Courts.

The OAG will be responsible for providing legal counsel to the Department of Labor regarding the new regulations and representing the state in any appeals related to the new felony and misdemeanor offenses.

As the agency responsible for the state's telecommunications strategy and infrastructure security, DoIT has a significant interest in legislation aimed at protecting the physical integrity of telecommunications systems.
The PSC regulates public utilities and certain telecommunications services; this bill specifically addresses the protection of infrastructure belonging to these regulated entities.
The bill provides for the revocation of state junk licenses for violations; such administrative actions typically involve hearings presided over by Administrative Law Judges from the OAH.

Synopsis: Establishing a temporary to-go event permit in Worcester County; authorizing the Board of License Commissioners for Worcester County to issue a temporary to-go event permit to a holder of a Class B beer, wine, and liquor license under certain circumstances; establishing a Class C per diem municipal to-go beer, wine, and liquor license in the county; authorizing the Board to issue a Class C per diem municipal to-go beer, wine, and liquor license to a municipality in the county; requiring the Board to adopt certain regulations; etc.
Title: Worcester County - Alcoholic Beverages - Temporary To-Go Event Permit and Class C Per Diem Municipal To-Go Beer, Wine, and Liquor License
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/23 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Age -see also- Age of Maj; Children; Elderly; Inf&Tod.; etc
Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes

bill_summary: This bill establishes a temporary to-go event permit for Class B beer, wine, and liquor license holders and a Class C per diem municipal to-go beer, wine, and liquor license in Worcester County. These authorizations allow for the sale and consumption of alcoholic beverages in approved to-go cups within designated special event areas for a period not exceeding seven consecutive days.
responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Worcester County
stakeholders: Class B alcoholic beverage license holders, municipalities in Worcester County, and residents or visitors attending special events.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates new local revenue sources through a $20 daily fee for temporary to-go event permits and a $45 daily fee for Class C per diem municipal licenses. Revenue from these fees is distributed to the county's general fund, with 75% allocated to the municipality if the licensed premises are located within municipal limits. A formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the bill text, so specific total dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's principal regulator of the alcohol industry, the Comptroller's Office is responsible for overseeing the industries affected by these new local permits and ensuring compliance with state-level revenue and regulatory standards.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and is responsible for appointing the members of local boards, such as the Board of License Commissioners for Worcester County, who will implement and manage these new permits.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state-authorized boards and commissions regarding the interpretation and enforcement of alcoholic beverage laws and the constitutional validity of local licensing regulations.

The Maryland State Police enforce criminal and traffic laws related to alcohol consumption and public safety, which are critical concerns for special events involving to-go alcohol consumption in high-traffic tourist areas like Worcester County.

Worcester County, which includes Ocean City, is a major tourism hub; the creation of municipal to-go alcohol zones directly impacts the state's tourism strategy, visitor experience, and the promotion of regional heritage and recreational events.

As the state's primary economic development agency, Commerce has an interest in local licensing tools and municipal event strategies that enhance the economic vitality and job creation within Maryland's tourism and hospitality sectors.

Decisions made by local boards of license commissioners regarding the issuance, denial, or regulation of these new permits are subject to judicial review in the state court system, impacting the judiciary's administrative and operational scope.

Synopsis: Requiring membership in the Correctional Officers' Retirement System for certain local detention center officers of Allegany County in the event Allegany County becomes a participating governmental unit in the Correctional Officers' Retirement System; and providing that certain local detention center officers who join the Correctional Officers' Retirement System and receive certain service credit shall no longer be members of the Employees' Pension System.
Title: Correctional Officers' Retirement System - Allegany County
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/18 at 1:00 p.m.
bill_summary: This bill requires local detention center officers in Allegany County to join the Correctional Officers’ Retirement System (CORS) if the county elects to participate as a governmental unit. It provides for the transfer of service credit from the Employees’ Pension System (EPS) to CORS for eligible individuals and stipulates that these officers will no longer be members of the EPS once the transfer is completed.
responsible_party: Allegany County and the Board of Trustees for the State Retirement and Pension System
stakeholders: Local detention center officers of Allegany County and the Allegany County government
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will likely increase pension expenditures for Allegany County if it chooses to join the Correctional Officers’ Retirement System, as CORS typically provides higher benefits than the Employees’ Pension System. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland State Retirement Agency is the primary body responsible for administering the state retirement and pension systems. This bill directly affects its operations by mandating membership in the Correctional Officers’ Retirement System for Allegany County officers and requiring the agency to manage the transfer of service credits and assets from the Employees’ Pension System.

The State Treasurer serves as the chief financial agency and custodian of the funds managed within the State Retirement and Pension System. They would oversee the management and investment of the retirement assets being transferred and credited under this bill.

The Department of Budget and Management is the principal personnel and fiscal agency for the state. It oversees employee benefits policies and retirement system fiscal planning, which are impacted by the expansion of the Correctional Officers’ Retirement System to new local government participants.

The Office of the Attorney General acts as the chief legal representative for state agencies like the State Retirement Agency. It would provide legal guidance on the interpretation of the new statutory requirements for mandatory membership and the legality of the service credit transfers.

Synopsis: Designating the Freedom Flag, designed and created by Richard Nicholas Melito of Richmond, Virginia, to memorialize the victims of the events of September 11, 2001, as the State symbol of remembrance for the attacks of September 11.
Title: State Designations - Symbol of Remembrance for September 11 - Freedom Flag
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/17 at 1:00 p.m.

BroadSubjects.Name: State Government - Agencies, Offices, and Officials

bill_summary: This bill designates the Freedom Flag, which was designed and created by Richard Nicholas Melito of Richmond, Virginia, as the official Maryland State symbol of remembrance for the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001.
stakeholders: Maryland citizens and victims and families affected by the September 11 terrorist attacks
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text; however, the designation of a State symbol typically does not have a significant fiscal impact on state or local government revenues or expenditures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Secretary of State is the principal custodian of the state's official records and handles the processing of laws and commissions, including the documentation of official state symbols.

The Maryland State Archives maintains the Maryland Manual On-Line and is responsible for the preservation of state historical records. The agency will need to update state symbol records and history to include the Freedom Flag.
As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees policy initiatives and the administration of state laws, including the formal adoption and use of new state designations.

The State House Trust oversees the management and use of the public areas of the State House and surrounding grounds, and would be involved if the new symbol of remembrance is displayed at the historic site.

The Department of General Services manages state-owned facilities and procurement. It would handle the logistical aspects if the state decides to procure or physically display the newly designated flag at state office buildings.

Synopsis: Altering the definition of "solar permitting software" for purposes of provisions regarding permitting and inspections of residential solar energy systems; altering from August 1, 2025, to August 1, 2027, the date by which certain counties and municipalities must implement certain solar permitting software; requiring, on or before August 1, 2027, certain counties and municipalities to authorize remote inspections of certain residential solar energy systems; etc.
Title: Residential Solar Energy Systems - Local Inspections and Permitting
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/03 at 1:00 p.m.
