bill_summary: This bill mandates that all Maryland counties and municipalities implement automated solar permitting software and authorize remote inspections for residential solar energy systems by August 1, 2027. It caps total solar permitting fees at $200 and remote inspection fees at $100, while prohibiting manual reviews of applications processed via the software. The bill also authorizes the Attorney General to seek judicial enforcement for noncompliance.
responsible_party: Maryland Energy Administration, the Maryland Office of the Attorney General, and Maryland local governments
stakeholders: Residential solar energy system installers, homeowners, and local government permitting and inspection departments
fiscal_impact_summary: Local government revenues are expected to decrease due to the imposition of a $200 cap on residential solar permitting fees and a $100 cap on remote inspections. Implementation of the required automated software may result in additional expenditures for counties and municipalities, though the Maryland Energy Administration may provide financial support if funds are available. A formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text, so specific aggregate dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly defines 'Administration' as the Maryland Energy Administration (MEA). MEA is responsible for determining if solar permitting software is maintained and has the authority to delay or suspend implementation requirements if state or federal funding is insufficient to support local jurisdictions.
The bill grants the Attorney General explicit authority to seek judicial enforcement against any county or municipality that fails to comply with the new solar permitting and inspection requirements.

The bill requires solar permitting software to automate plan reviews according to the Maryland Building Performance Standards and electrical codes, which are traditionally overseen and regulated by the Department of Labor.

The bill impacts local government permitting and land-use processes. The Department of Planning provides guidance to local governments on sustainable growth and land use, making the regulation of residential solar infrastructure relevant to their coordination with municipalities.

The implementation of the bill's requirements by local governments is contingent upon the availability of state or federal funds provided through the Maryland Energy Administration. DBM would oversee the allocation and execution of such state funds.

Synopsis: Increasing from 1 year to 3 years the statute of limitations for the prosecution or suit for enforcement of local consumer protection codes for which equitable relief, a fine, or a penalty is provided.
Title: Statute of Limitations - Prosecution or Enforcement of Local Consumer Protection Codes
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/05 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

bill_summary: This bill establishes a three-year statute of limitations for the prosecution or enforcement of local consumer protection codes. The three-year period begins when local authorities knew or reasonably should have known of the violation.
responsible_party: Local consumer protection agencies and the Maryland Judiciary
stakeholders: Local governments, Maryland consumers, and businesses subject to local consumer protection regulations
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill may lead to an indeterminate increase in local revenue from fines and penalties by extending the time available for authorities to initiate enforcement actions. State expenditures for the judiciary may increase slightly to accommodate additional cases. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill alters the statute of limitations for the prosecution and enforcement of local consumer protection codes. As these cases are adjudicated within the Maryland judicial system, the Administrative Office of the Courts is responsible for ensuring the courts properly implement and manage these procedural changes.

The Office of the Attorney General is the primary state agency responsible for consumer protection and serves as the chief legal representative for the state. While the bill specifically targets local consumer protection codes, the OAG's role in enforcing consumer laws and providing legal counsel to state and local entities makes this legal change highly relevant to their mission.

Synopsis: Establishing the Maryland Commission on Women's Health Advancement to study the feasibility of establishing a State women's hospital in Southern Maryland and a statewide clinical network to advance women's health; requiring the Commission by January 1, 2027, to submit to the Governor and the General Assembly an initial action plan, including a timeline, milestones, and specific research objectives; etc.
Title: Maryland Commission on Women's Health Advancement - Establishment
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/24 at 1:00 p.m.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Maryland Commission on Women’s Health Advancement to study the feasibility of building a State women’s hospital in Southern Maryland and developing a statewide clinical network to address women's unique health challenges throughout their lives.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and the Maryland Health Care Commission
stakeholders: Women in Maryland, healthcare professionals, patient advocates, and residents of Southern Maryland
fiscal_impact_summary: According to the Fiscal Note, State general fund expenditures will increase by at least $211,800 in FY 2027 to hire a health policy analyst and cover contractual services for data analysis. Costs are expected to continue through FY 2033, with estimates ranging from approximately $201,500 to $218,800 annually. There is no impact on State revenues or local government finances.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a commission within the Health - General Article and requires the Maryland Department of Health (MDH) to jointly provide staffing. The fiscal note indicates MDH general fund expenditures will increase to hire a health policy analyst to support the commission.

The bill explicitly mandates that the Maryland Health Care Commission (MHCC) jointly staff the commission. Additionally, the commission must collaborate with MHCC to assess financial viability and initiate a Certificate of Need for the proposed hospital.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Maryland Commission on Women's Health Advancement as a temporary body to conduct a special study and provide recommendations on women's health infrastructure, which directly falls under this agency's summary.

The Governor is responsible for appointing the majority of the commission's members, including the chair. The commission must also submit an initial action plan, annual interim reports, and a final report directly to the Governor.
The Attorney General (or their designee) is explicitly named as a member of the commission, and the fiscal note confirms the office can serve using existing budgeted resources.

The bill requires a representative from the Morgan State University School of Community Health and Policy to serve on the commission. The fiscal note confirms the university can fulfill this role with existing resources.
The bill requires a representative from the University of Maryland School of Public Health to serve on the commission. The fiscal note indicates this can be handled with existing resources.

The bill requires the Governor to appoint over 20 specific members from various professional backgrounds and geographic regions. The Office of Appointments is responsible for recruiting and vetting these candidates.

The commission is tasked with studying the feasibility and financial viability of a new State hospital. As the regulator of hospital rates and revenues in Maryland, HSCRC's work is directly impacted by the introduction of new hospital infrastructure.
The bill has a notable fiscal impact on the state budget, requiring new personnel (a Health Policy Analyst) and contractual services for financial assessments, which DBM oversees.

The Department of Human Services houses the existing Maryland Commission for Women. The new commission's study of women's health gaps and disparities overlaps with DHS's mission to protect and assist vulnerable populations and women.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Health & Higher Educational Facilities Authority
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The commission must assess the funding and financial viability for a State women's hospital. MHHEFA assists health care organizations with financing capital projects through bond markets, making them a relevant stakeholder in future implementation.
The commission's membership must include insurance professionals to provide insight into equitable financing and sustainable spending for hospital services, areas regulated and monitored by the MIA.

The bill specifically addresses healthcare gaps in Southern Maryland and underserved populations, including required expertise from the Maryland Rural Health Association, which aligns with the Council's mission to address health access challenges in rural counties.

Synopsis: Requiring the Maryland Medical Assistance Program and certain insurers, nonprofit health service plans, health maintenance organizations, and managed care organizations to provide coverage to victims of domestic violence for aesthetic services and restorative care related to scars or scarring determined to be medically necessary for the treatment of physical injuries caused by domestic violence.
Title: Maryland Medical Assistance Program and Health Insurance - Required Coverage for Aesthetic Services and Restorative Care for Victims of Domestic Violence (Healing Our Scars Act)
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/13 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Domestic Violence -see also- Child Abuse & Neglect
Health Insurance -see also- ACA; HMOs; MCOs
Health Maintenance Organizations -see also- Manage Care Orgs
Managed Care Organizations -see also- Health Maint Orgs

bill_summary: The Healing Our Scars Act requires the Maryland Medical Assistance Program and private health insurance carriers to provide coverage for aesthetic services and restorative care for victims of domestic violence. This mandate covers medically necessary treatments for scarring or physical injuries resulting from domestic violence, provided the services are performed by a licensed physician.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and Maryland Insurance Administration
stakeholders: Victims of domestic violence, the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid), managed care organizations, and private health insurance carriers
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a new insurance mandate for aesthetic and restorative services, which is expected to increase expenditures for the Maryland Medical Assistance Program and private health insurance carriers. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid), which is administered by the Secretary of Health, to provide coverage for aesthetic services and restorative care for victims of domestic violence.

The bill amends the Insurance Article to require health insurers, nonprofit health service plans, and HMOs to provide specific coverage. The MIA is the primary regulator responsible for ensuring these entities comply with such mandates.

As the agency responsible for developing the state budget and supervising budget execution, DBM is impacted by the fiscal requirements of expanding Medicaid coverage and any potential impact on the state's employee health insurance costs.
The MHBE administers the state's health insurance marketplace. New coverage mandates for insurers and HMOs affect the requirements for plans offered on the Exchange.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and the Maryland Insurance Administration and would be involved in legal oversight and enforcement related to the new insurance requirements.

DHS serves as the state's primary social service provider for victims of abuse and neglect. This bill directly benefits the population they serve by ensuring access to medically necessary restorative care.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP coordinates public safety strategies and manages funds for victim services. The bill's focus on domestic violence victims aligns with the office's mission to support victim services and policy development.

bill_summary: This bill establishes collective bargaining rights for employees of controlled-environment agricultural operations, such as greenhouses. It mandates the Secretary of Labor to adopt regulations governing bargaining units, election procedures, and dispute resolution. Additionally, the bill requires these employers to provide paid 5-minute rest breaks for every hour the heat index inside the facility reaches or maintains at least 90 degrees Fahrenheit.
stakeholders: Employees and employers of controlled-environment agricultural operations
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. The bill creates administrative costs for the Maryland Department of Labor to oversee collective bargaining processes and enforce heat protection standards. Private employers in the greenhouse industry will also face increased labor costs due to the mandate for paid rest breaks.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill designates the Secretary of Labor as the primary official responsible for establishing and overseeing collective bargaining procedures for greenhouse workers. This includes adopting regulations for bargaining units, conducting elections, certifying representatives, and investigating/enforcing labor violations. Additionally, the department's Maryland Occupational Safety and Health (MOSH) division is indirectly involved through the heat protection requirements.

The bill impacts 'controlled-environment agricultural operations' (greenhouses), which are a subset of the agricultural community supported and regulated by the Maryland Department of Agriculture. The establishment of collective bargaining and mandatory heat-related rest breaks directly affects the operations and economic viability of these agricultural businesses.

The Office of the Attorney General will be required to provide legal counsel to the Department of Labor during the development of new regulations for collective bargaining and heat protection, and may be involved in representing the state in any legal challenges or enforcement actions resulting from the bill.

The bill creates significant new regulatory and enforcement duties for the Department of Labor, which will likely require additional personnel (FTEs) and budgetary resources to manage elections, investigations, and oversight. DBM is responsible for the fiscal planning and personnel management related to such agency expansions.

The bill authorizes the Secretary of Labor to investigate violations and take enforcement actions. Such actions are typically subject to administrative appeal, where an Administrative Law Judge from OAH would likely preside over the contested case.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees the Department of Labor and the Department of Agriculture. The implementation of new labor rights for a specific industry aligns with the office's role in coordinating policy initiatives and overseeing state agency operations.

bill_summary: The Public Health Reform Act reorganizes Maryland's public health infrastructure by requiring the Maryland Department of Health to establish the Maryland Medical Reserve Corps and the Public Health Workforce Development Fund. The bill provides county health officers with greater autonomy regarding staff appointments and contracting for non-state-funded positions, modifies the composition and oversight responsibilities of the Commission on Public Health, and mandates that the Department of Legislative Services develop a process for evaluating the health equity impacts of legislation.
stakeholders: County health departments, health officers, public health employees and trainees, medical reserve volunteers, and the Maryland Community Health Resources Commission.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes the Public Health Workforce Development Fund as a special, nonlapsing fund to support education and training, with revenue derived from State budget appropriations, interest earnings (diverted from the General Fund), and transfers from the Population Health Improvement Fund. Local health departments may experience administrative and fiscal flexibility for positions funded independently of the State. A formal Fiscal Note with specific dollar estimates was not provided in the text, and specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health is the primary agency responsible for the bill's implementation. It must organize the Maryland Medical Reserve Corps, consult on electronic health records procurement, manage relationships with local health officers, and provide quarterly updates to the Commission on Public Health. The bill also establishes the Public Health Workforce Development Fund, which involves the Maryland Community Health Resources Commission (an entity within the Department).

The Secretary of Budget and Management is added as a member of the Commission on Public Health. Furthermore, the bill removes the requirement for DBM approval for certain local health department appointments that are fully funded without state money, directly impacting the department's personnel oversight role.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Service and Civic Innovation
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill alters the membership of the Maryland Corps Program Advisory Board by adding a health officer. DSCI administers the Maryland Corps Program, which was established by the SERVE Act of 2023 (which this bill amends), making the agency directly relevant to the program's governance changes.

The HSCRC is explicitly authorized by the bill to transfer money from the Population Health Improvement Fund to the newly established Public Health Workforce Development Fund to support education and training for the public health workforce.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill significantly reforms the Commission on Public Health, altering its membership, leadership selection, staffing, and sunset date. It also modifies the Maryland Corps Program Advisory Board. These bodies fall under this collective agency designation.

The Governor is responsible for appointing several members of the Commission on Public Health and an additional health officer to the Maryland Corps Program Advisory Board. The Governor's Office also oversees the executive branch departments (MDH, DBM, DoIT) that are central to this reform act.

The Secretary of Information Technology is added as a member of the Commission on Public Health. Additionally, the bill involves procurement of electronic health records systems, which aligns with DoIT's role in statewide IT strategy and infrastructure.
The State Treasurer is required to hold the Public Health Workforce Development Fund separately and invest its money. This is a notable administrative and fiscal responsibility for the office.
The Comptroller is responsible for accounting for the Public Health Workforce Development Fund, a new special fund established by the bill.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for the State and would provide legal counsel to the Maryland Department of Health and the various commissions mentioned regarding the implementation of the Public Health Reform Act.

The bill requires a faculty member from a public health program at a historically Black college or university (HBCU) to serve on the Commission on Public Health. As Maryland's preeminent urban research university and an HBCU, Morgan State University is a primary stakeholder for this representation.

The Commission on Public Health includes representatives from State academic institutions with expertise in public health systems. USM institutions are likely sources for these experts and staffing support for the Commission.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the notification procedures for Maryland counties and municipal corporations when filing for judicial in rem tax foreclosures on vacant and abandoned properties. It replaces the specific requirement to mail notice within five days of filing a complaint with a requirement to serve the complaint on each interested party in accordance with the Maryland Rules.
stakeholders: Local governments and interested parties, such as owners and lienholders, of vacant and abandoned real property subject to tax foreclosure.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates for state or local revenue and expenditures are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. The bill alters procedural notice requirements for local governments performing tax foreclosures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill changes the procedural requirements for notice in judicial in rem tax foreclosure actions filed in the Circuit Courts, replacing specific statutory mailing requirements with a mandate to serve the complaint according to the Maryland Rules.

This bill impacts the legal mechanism for foreclosing on vacant and abandoned properties, which is a key tool for community revitalization and addressing housing blight—core components of the department's mission.
As the chief legal officer for the state, the OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies regarding changes to tax property law and judicial service requirements.

The department is responsible for promoting sustainable growth and land use planning; the foreclosure process for vacant and abandoned properties is directly linked to municipal land management and revitalization planning.

Synopsis: Authorizing the holder of a Class 3 winery license to acquire bulk wine from the holder of a Class 4 limited winery license; and authorizing the holder of a Class 4 limited winery license to sell and deliver bulk wine to the holder of a Class 3 winery license.

bill_summary: This bill allows Class 3 winery license holders to purchase bulk wine from Class 4 limited winery license holders and authorizes Class 4 limited winery license holders to sell and deliver bulk wine to Class 3 winery license holders.
stakeholders: Class 3 winery license holders and Class 4 limited winery license holders
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. The bill authorizes transactions between existing winery licensees, which is expected to have a minimal fiscal impact on the state. The annual license fee for Class 3 wineries remains capped at 750 dollars.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is the primary regulator of the alcohol industry in Maryland and is responsible for tax collection, enforcement of alcohol laws, and oversight of license holders, including wineries.

Class 4 limited wineries are farm-based agribusinesses that utilize Maryland agricultural products. The Department of Agriculture is responsible for promoting the economic viability and sustainability of these entities.

The OAG provides legal counsel and representation to the state agencies responsible for regulating alcoholic beverages and helps ensure the proper implementation of amendments to the Alcoholic Beverages and Cannabis Article.
The Department of Commerce is Maryland's primary economic development agency, focused on business retention and expansion within the state's winery and agribusiness sectors.
Maryland's wineries are key cultural and recreational attractions that drive tourism. Changes to winery operations and supply chain flexibility can impact the tourism economy and brand promotion.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Agricultural & Resource-Based Industry Development Corp.
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MARBIDCO provides financial support and services to agricultural businesses, including wineries, to help them maintain profitability and acquire necessary facilities.
The Council supports the interests of rural counties where many Class 4 limited wineries are located and works to improve the quality of life and economic opportunities in these areas.

bill_summary: This bill expands the duties of the Maryland Health Insurance Coverage Protection Commission, requiring it to study and make recommendations to stabilize the individual and group health insurance markets. The Commission's tasks include conducting an actuarial analysis for a potential public health insurance option, exploring the merger of individual and small group markets, investigating interstate purchasing pools, and identifying methods to control prescription drug costs and support federally qualified health centers.
responsible_party: Maryland Health Insurance Coverage Protection Commission
stakeholders: Individual and small group health insurance consumers, Managed Care Organizations (MCOs), Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs), and state, county, and local government health insurance purchasers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill mandates several complex studies and an actuarial analysis, which are expected to increase state expenditures for consulting and administrative costs. Specific dollar estimates were unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly alters the statutory duties of the Maryland Health Insurance Coverage Protection Commission, which is a state commission tasked with conducting the studies and making the recommendations mandated by the legislation.

The MIA is the primary regulator of the state's health insurance market. The bill requires studies on market stability, merging the individual and small group markets, reinsurance funds, and capital requirements for managed care organizations, all of which fall under MIA's regulatory authority.

The bill mandates an actuarial analysis comparing Medicaid rates to commercial rates, explores the regulation of Managed Care Organizations (MCOs), and addresses the sustainability of Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs), all of which are central to the Department of Health's mission.
The bill specifically requires the Commission to study and make recommendations on whether to reinstate the Maryland Health Insurance Plan (MHIP) to help stabilize the state's insurance market.

The MHBE manages the individual health insurance marketplace (Maryland Health Connection). The bill's focus on individual market stability and the potential merging of the individual and small group markets directly impacts the Exchange's core operations.

The bill requires a study on the pooling of state, county, and local government health insurance purchasers. DBM manages state employee health benefits and would be a primary stakeholder in any effort to leverage state purchasing power or combine buying pools.

The MHCC is responsible for health system planning and improving access to care. The bill's focus on market stability, public option analysis, and prescription drug cost control aligns with the Commission's planning and policy research mandates.

The Governor oversees the executive branch and commission activities. The findings of these studies would likely influence the Governor's future health policy initiatives and state budget proposals regarding healthcare funding and market subsidies.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and would be required to analyze the legal feasibility of proposed interstate compacts and regulatory changes discussed in the bill.

Synopsis: Replacing references to a bus lane monitoring system with references to a bus obstruction monitoring system; and prohibiting a person from stopping, standing, or parking a vehicle in a bus stop zone if a transit vehicle is present, subject to certain exceptions.

bill_summary: This bill renames 'bus lane monitoring systems' to 'bus obstruction monitoring systems' and prohibits vehicles from stopping, standing, or parking in bus stop zones when a transit vehicle is present, with certain exceptions for authorized vehicles and active passenger loading. It authorizes transit and law enforcement agencies to use automated systems to enforce these regulations and establishes a civil penalty of up to 75 dollars for violations.
responsible_party: Maryland Transit Administration, Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority, local law enforcement agencies, and the District Court
stakeholders: Maryland motorists, transit users, and transit agencies
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes a civil penalty not exceeding 75 dollars for violations. Revenue from uncontested citations is paid to local political subdivisions, while contested case penalties are paid to the District Court. Specific total fiscal estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires the District Court to prescribe uniform citation forms and sets procedures for contested cases, trial elections, and the collection of civil penalties. The Administrative Office of the Courts provides the operational and technological support for these judicial functions.

The bill prohibits obstructing bus stop zones, which is a significant factor in ensuring accessible boarding and transportation for individuals with disabilities. The Department of Disabilities coordinates services and policies to improve such community living and transportation accessibility.

As the parent agency for MTA, MVA, and SHA, MDOT oversees the state's transportation network. This bill directly modifies vehicle laws and enforcement mechanisms regarding bus lanes and bus stops, which are core to MDOT's operational mandate.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office coordinates public safety strategies and manages funds for law enforcement. The implementation of new automated monitoring and enforcement systems for bus obstructions falls within its purview of advising on criminal justice and public safety policies.

The bill explicitly names the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority (WMATA) as an authorized agency to use bus obstruction monitoring systems. WMATA is a significant interstate agency in which Maryland holds membership.

The bill specifies that violations recorded by these monitoring systems may not be considered in the provision of motor vehicle insurance coverage, which affects MAIF as an insurer of last resort for Maryland residents.

The Maryland Insurance Administration regulates the insurance market and ensures compliance with state laws, including the bill's provision that these specific civil penalties cannot be used for insurance underwriting or rating purposes.

The Maryland State Police is authorized to issue citations and review recorded images from monitoring systems to verify violations. The bill involves enforcing motor vehicle and criminal laws across the state.

The MTA is specifically authorized by the bill to use bus obstruction monitoring systems (onboard or fixed) to enforce dedicated bus lanes and bus stop zones. This is a primary tool for their operational efficiency and safety.

MDTA maintains its own police force and coordinates with MDOT on transportation projects. Its law enforcement personnel may be involved in the inspection or adjudication of citations generated by these monitoring systems.
The MVA is responsible for refusing or suspending vehicle registrations if civil penalties for bus obstruction violations are not paid, as authorized under the bill.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the MDOT and its administrations (MTA, MVA, SHA) regarding the implementation of the new monitoring systems and the legal admissibility of recorded images as evidence.
The bill requires road signs alerting drivers to monitoring systems to be placed in accordance with the Maryland Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, which is managed by the SHA.

bill_summary: This bill authorizes pharmacists to prescribe and dispense HIV preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) medications following a training program. It mandates that the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid), managed care organizations, and private health insurance carriers provide coverage for FDA-approved HIV prevention drugs (PrEP and PEP) and associated services—such as lab testing, visits, and vaccinations—without requiring prior authorization, step therapy, or any cost-sharing (copayments, coinsurance, or deductibles). Additionally, the State Board of Pharmacy must establish a stakeholder workgroup and a pharmacist notification plan regarding these new authorities.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Health and the State Board of Pharmacy
stakeholders: Pharmacists, individuals seeking HIV prevention services, private health insurance carriers, managed care organizations, and the Maryland Medical Assistance Program.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes a mandate for the Maryland Medical Assistance Program and private insurers to cover HIV prevention drugs and related clinical services without cost-sharing or prior authorization starting January 1, 2027. The bill text specifies that Medicaid coverage is subject to the limitations of the State budget. Because a formal Fiscal Note with specific revenue or expenditure estimates was not provided with the bill text, specific dollar estimates of the fiscal impact on the State or local governments are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health is the primary agency responsible for administering the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid), which the bill requires to provide FDA-approved HIV prevention drugs. Additionally, MDH oversees the professional boards, including the Board of Pharmacy, Board of Physicians, and Board of Nursing, which are involved in developing the training and protocols required by the bill.

The Maryland Insurance Administration is the primary regulator for private insurers, nonprofit health plans, and health maintenance organizations. The bill mandates that these entities eliminate prior authorization, step therapy, and cost-sharing for HIV prevention drugs and related services, which the MIA will be responsible for enforcing.

The Department of Budget and Management is responsible for the state's budget execution and managing state employee benefits. This bill has a notable fiscal impact on the state budget via Medicaid expenditures and the cost structure of the State Employee Health Benefits Plan due to the elimination of cost-sharing for HIV prevention treatments.

The Maryland Health Benefit Exchange administers the state's health insurance marketplace. It must ensure that the private health plans offered through the exchange comply with the bill's new requirements prohibiting cost-sharing and prior authorization for HIV prevention drugs.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the establishment of a stakeholder workgroup to make recommendations regarding collaborative practice agreements and statewide protocols for pharmacists to assess patients and prescribe HIV prevention drugs.

The Maryland Health Care Commission is responsible for health system planning and improving access to care. The bill's aim to expand access to HIV prevention through pharmacies and insurance reform aligns with the Commission's role in planning for the state's health system needs.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the legal counsel for the Department of Health and the Insurance Administration. It will likely provide legal support in drafting and reviewing regulations needed to implement the bill's pharmacy and insurance mandates.

bill_summary: This bill clarifies that Maryland teachers holding a 10-year National Board Certification (NBC) awarded on or before December 31, 2021, are eligible for specific salary increases under the State's teacher career ladder. It establishes tiered salary increases for the renewal and maintenance of these 10-year certifications, ensuring they are treated similarly to 5-year certifications. The bill's provisions apply retroactively to July 1, 2026.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Education, the Accountability and Implementation Board, and local County Boards of Education
stakeholders: Public school teachers with 10-year National Board Certifications and Maryland county school systems.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill mandates shared State and local expenditures to fund salary increases for teachers with 10-year National Board Certifications ($8,000 for renewal, $7,000 for first maintenance, and $6,000 for second maintenance). These costs are distributed between the State and counties according to a wealth-based formula defined in the Education Article. Because the bill applies retroactively to certificates held on or before July 1, 2026, there may be immediate fiscal requirements for back-pay or salary adjustments. Specific aggregate dollar estimates from a Fiscal Note are unavailable in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Education Article regarding the 'career ladder' for public school teachers, which is a core component of Maryland's education policy. MSDE is responsible for overseeing the public education system, certifying educators, and setting the standards for the career ladder.

The bill specifies the calculation for the 'State share' of teacher salary increases. DBM is the principal fiscal agency responsible for developing the state budget and managing personnel policies, including the fiscal impact of state-mandated salary increases.

The bill explicitly states that salary increases associated with the renewal of a 10-year National Board Certification (NBC) are subject to collective bargaining. PERB is the agency responsible for overseeing and adjudicating collective bargaining for public school system personnel.

OLA conducts performance and fiscal compliance audits of local school systems and state education programs. They would be responsible for auditing the proper distribution and expenditure of the state and local shares of the salary increases mandated by this bill.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the annual state budget, which must include the funding formulas for the State's share of teacher salary increases as defined in this legislation.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, including MSDE. They would likely be consulted on the interpretation of the new certification definitions and the legal implications of the bill's retroactive application clauses.

As the state's chief financial officer, the Comptroller is responsible for the distribution of state revenues to local entities, including the distribution of the state share of teacher salary increases to county boards.

The Treasurer's Office manages the disbursement of state funds and acts as a member of the Board of Public Works, which oversees significant state fiscal policies and expenditures related to local education aid.

bill_summary: This bill establishes a five-year pilot program in Howard County that authorizes the use of surveillance camera systems to enforce laws against illegal dumping. The bill defines the citation process, outlines defenses, provides for District Court trials, and enables the Motor Vehicle Administration to refuse or suspend vehicle registrations for unpaid penalties.
responsible_party: Howard County Police Department or a department designated by the Howard County Executive
stakeholders: Motor vehicle owners in Howard County, Howard County government, the Howard County Police Department, the Maryland District Court, and the Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a civil penalty of up to $1,000 for illegal dumping violations, which will generate an indeterminate revenue increase for Howard County. Howard County will also incur expenditures related to the procurement, installation, and maintenance of surveillance systems and the administration of the citation mailing process. The District Court and Motor Vehicle Administration may experience minor administrative workload increases. Because a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text, specific total dollar estimates for revenue and expenditures are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Administrative Office of the Courts supports the District Court, which is responsible for prescribing citation forms, scheduling trials, and remitting penalties collected from Howard County's illegal dumping citations.
The Motor Vehicle Administration is explicitly mandated to refuse or suspend the vehicle registration of individuals who fail to pay citations or appear for trial in the District Court.

As the parent agency of the Motor Vehicle Administration, the Department of Transportation oversees the enforcement of registration sanctions and manages state highways, which are potential sites for illegal dumping.
The bill requires the District Court to remit collected fines and penalties to the State through a system coordinated with the Comptroller of Maryland.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the state agencies involved, including the Judiciary and the Motor Vehicle Administration, regarding the implementation of the pilot program and privacy protections.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office coordinates public safety policy and manages funding for initiatives related to crime prevention and the reduction of illegal dumping in Maryland communities.
The Department of Budget and Management oversees state fiscal planning and budget execution, including the tracking of revenues from civil penalties collected via the pilot program.

As the agency responsible for managing state-owned facilities, the Department of General Services may be impacted if state-owned properties in Howard County are designated as dumping sites monitored by the pilot program.
The Department of Natural Resources manages state parks and public lands; it may be involved if its properties in Howard County are impacted by illegal dumping or designated for surveillance.
The Department of the Environment is the state's primary agency for environmental protection and is responsible for enforcing laws regarding land quality and litter control.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid) and certain private health insurers to provide coverage for approved elopement response devices and associated supports for individuals at risk of wandering due to cognitive, developmental, or neurological conditions. It mandates that state programs categorize these devices—which include GPS trackers and window sensors—as medical devices or assistive technology, and requires the Maryland Department of Health to establish privacy safeguards, data standards, and seek federal financial participation.
stakeholders: Individuals with cognitive, developmental, or neurological disabilities; individuals diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease or related dementia; children under 21 eligible for EPSDT services; health insurance carriers and health maintenance organizations; and healthcare providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill mandates coverage for elopement response devices under Medicaid and private insurance plans, which will result in increased state expenditures and potential premium impacts. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note with figures was not provided in the text; however, the bill explicitly states that Medicaid coverage is subject to the limitations of the state budget and requires the Maryland Department of Health to maximize federal financial participation through state plan or waiver amendments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Health is the primary agency responsible for the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid), which is mandated by the bill to cover elopement response devices. The department must also approve these devices, establish medical necessity criteria, set prior authorization standards, and develop data privacy and minimization requirements.

The bill requires the Department of Health to consult with the State Department of Education to enable school-based billing and cost allocation for elopement response devices. The agency manages the Charlotte Hall Veterans Home and assists older veterans with securing benefits; as a state-operated program for older adults and individuals with disabilities, it must comply with the bill's mandate to recognize these devices as medical equipment.

As a state agency providing comprehensive support services and education to students with disabilities, the school's programs must comply with the bill's mandate to recognize and provide elopement response devices as assistive technology or medical equipment when documented in a qualifying plan.

bill_summary: This bill requires health insurance carriers to provide standing referrals for mental health care services to members during pregnancy and for one year following childbirth. bill_summary: This bill allows members of the U.S. Foreign Service and their spouses to practice their professions in Maryland using a valid license from another jurisdiction if they are assigned to the state. Qualifying individuals must be in good standing, have practiced within the last two years, and notify the relevant Maryland licensing authority. The bill excludes the practice of law and occupations already covered by existing interstate licensing compacts.
responsible_party: Maryland State licensing authorities, including the Maryland Department of Labor, Department of Agriculture, Department of Health, Department of the Environment, and various professional licensing boards.
stakeholders: Members of the U.S. Foreign Service and their spouses.

bill_summary: This bill establishes consumer protections for patients using third-party financing for health care services. It requires health care providers (excluding hospitals) and veterinarians to provide patients with written disclosures and treatment plans before discussing financing options and mandates refunds for unprovided services within 15 days. The bill prohibits providers from applying for financing on a patient's behalf, promoting financing to patients while they are under the influence of substances or undergoing treatment, or billing financiers more than 30 days before services are rendered. Violations are classified as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices under the Consumer Protection Act.

stakeholders: Health care providers (excluding hospitals), licensed veterinarians, and patients seeking or using third-party financing for medical or veterinary services.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the bill text. The Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General is responsible for preparing disclosure forms and enforcing the provisions of the bill, which may increase administrative expenditures. State revenue may increase indeterminately through civil penalties assessed for violations under the Consumer Protection Act.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General to prepare and publish a mandatory health care financing disclosure form. Additionally, the Attorney General is authorized to adopt regulations to carry out the subtitle, and violations of the bill are classified as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices under the Consumer Protection Act enforced by the OAG.

bill_summary: The Pregnancy Outcome Protection Act prohibits the investigation, civil liability, or criminal prosecution of individuals for experiencing a pregnancy loss, including miscarriages, stillbirths, and self-managed abortions. It also protects healthcare providers from liability for supporting patients in these circumstances and restricts the disclosure of medical records related to pregnancy loss. Additionally, the bill establishes that pregnancy loss does not constitute probable cause for a search warrant and allows for a private right of action and criminal penalties against those who violate these protections.
stakeholders: Individuals who experience pregnancy loss, healthcare providers, doulas, and law enforcement agencies
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not available. The bill establishes criminal fines for violations, including up to 5000 dollars for standard offenses and up to 100000 dollars for offenses involving deception, which could result in an indeterminate increase in state revenue. There may also be indeterminate costs for the state and local governments associated with law enforcement training and potential civil litigation.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems

As a primary law enforcement agency, Maryland State Police is considered an 'investigating entity' under the bill. The legislation explicitly restricts law enforcement's ability to investigate pregnancy loss, obtain search warrants related to it, and subjects them to civil liability and criminal penalties for violations.

The OAG serves as the chief legal representative for the state and provides counsel to state agencies and the Governor. It would be responsible for advising investigating entities (such as DHS and DJS) on compliance with this act and representing the state in civil or criminal appeals related to pregnancy loss investigations.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP is the primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategies. The bill establishes a new private right of action for individuals subject to prohibited investigations and creates new misdemeanor penalties. This impacts the judicial system by introducing new civil and criminal case types and affecting search warrant procedures.

The bill adds new sections to the Health - General Article and regulates 'Providers,' which include health care professionals and various facilities (hospitals, clinics, crisis centers) regulated by MDH. MDH is responsible for setting health policy and overseeing the conduct of health care institutions and practitioners impacted by these new reporting and liability prohibitions.

The bill explicitly names the Social Services Administration and Child Protective Services within DHS as 'investigating entities.' It places specific legal prohibitions on their ability to investigate individuals for pregnancy loss, impacting their operational procedures in cases of potential neglect or abuse.

DJS is explicitly named as an 'investigating entity' in the bill. The legislation prohibits the department from subjecting individuals to investigation for pregnancy loss unless specific conditions are met, directly affecting its intake and investigative protocols for youth.

DBM is responsible for the state budget and personnel. As several state agencies (MDH, DHS, DJS, MSP) face operational changes and potential civil liability under this bill, DBM would be involved in overseeing the fiscal impact and resource allocation necessary for implementation.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates major policy initiatives. This bill introduces a significant new policy framework (Pregnancy Outcome Protection Act) affecting multiple executive departments and law enforcement protocols.

bill_summary: The Keeping Affordable Housing Affordable Act alters disclosure requirements for the resale of condominium units and homes within homeowners associations (HOAs). As the principal fiscal agency, the Department of Budget and Management would oversee any budget adjustments or personnel allocations required for the Department of Health and the Board of Pharmacy to administer and enforce the expanded scope of practice and record-keeping requirements.

The bill specifically includes provisions for pharmacists to order vaccinations in response to a public health emergency, which falls within the coordinating duties of the Maryland Department of Emergency Management.

bill_summary: This bill requires Maryland nonprofit hospitals (excluding those in counties with fewer than 50,000 residents) to provide community benefits equal to either 100% of their tax-exempt benefits or at least 5% of their net patient revenue if charity care is at least 4% of net patient revenue. It mandates annual reporting to the Health Services Cost Review Commission (HSCRC), which must report noncompliance to the Attorney General and the Comptroller. The Comptroller is authorized to revoke a hospital's tax-exempt status for failure to comply. The bill also establishes daily civil monetary penalties for hospitals that fail to submit their annual community benefit reports on time.
responsible_party: Health Services Cost Review Commission (HSCRC), Maryland Comptroller, and the Maryland Attorney General
stakeholders: Maryland nonprofit hospitals, hospital patients, the Health Services Cost Review Commission, and Maryland taxpayers
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are unavailable. However, the bill text identifies potential financial impacts including an indeterminate increase in state revenue through civil monetary penalties ($600 to $11,000 per day depending on hospital size) and the potential revocation of tax-exempt status for noncompliant hospitals. Nonprofit hospitals may also face increased expenditures to meet the mandated community benefit spending thresholds.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The HSCRC is the primary implementing agency for this bill. It is responsible for establishing a workgroup, adopting regulations, collecting community benefit reports from hospitals, evaluating compliance, reporting non-compliance to the Comptroller and Attorney General, and levying civil monetary penalties.

The bill explicitly requires the Comptroller to receive reports from the HSCRC, verify hospital non-compliance with community benefit standards, and revoke or reinstate the tax-exempt status of nonprofit hospitals based on those findings.

The bill requires the HSCRC to submit reports identifying non-compliant hospitals to the Attorney General. Additionally, the OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like the HSCRC and Comptroller in enforcing regulations and defending against potential litigation.

The HSCRC is an independent regulatory agency located within the Maryland Department of Health. The bill's requirements directly impact hospital regulation and the administration of the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid), which is cited in the bill's definition of indigent care.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards

The OAH would likely handle contested cases and appeals regarding civil monetary penalties imposed by the HSCRC for failure to file required community benefit reports.

bill_summary: Known as the Bring Back Main Street Act, this bill requires Maryland counties with populations over 150,000 and Baltimore City to allow multifamily and mixed-use developments as a permitted use on parcels zoned for commercial or recreational use that have existing water and sewer service. A 'permitted use' designation allows these developments to be approved without public hearings or discretionary zoning actions, provided they meet site plan requirements. The bill restricts local governments from imposing specific density, setback, or parking requirements that are more stringent than those defined in the act. It also prohibits private land-use restrictions, such as HOA bylaws or deed covenants, from unreasonably limiting these developments, except for properties listed on or eligible for the Maryland Register of Historic Properties.
responsible_party: Local planning and zoning departments in Maryland counties with a population of more than 150,000 and Baltimore City
stakeholders: Property owners, residential and commercial developers, residents in populous Maryland counties, and local government zoning officials
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. The bill imposes a mandate on local governments in counties with more than 150,000 residents and Baltimore City to modify their zoning regulations and approval processes. Financial implications may include indeterminate administrative costs for updating local codes and potential changes to local property tax revenues resulting from the development of high-density residential or mixed-use properties on land previously restricted to commercial or recreational use.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Land Use Article and impacts statewide land use policy, which the Department of Planning oversees. Furthermore, the bill explicitly exempts historic properties determined by the Director of the Maryland Historical Trust, an entity within the Department of Planning.

As the primary agency for housing and community development, the bill's focus on promoting multifamily and mixed-use developments to revitalize communities and increase housing supply is central to the department's mission.

This multi-agency initiative focuses on sustainable development and planning visions. The bill's mandate for higher-density multifamily and mixed-use development in areas with existing infrastructure aligns with the initiative's goals of smart growth and reducing environmental footprints.

The bill focuses on 'Main Street' revitalization and mixed-use developments with retail components, which directly relates to the Department of Commerce's goals of economic development and business retention.

The bill requires that parcels for these new developments be serviced by water and sewer systems, which are regulated and overseen by the Department of the Environment. It also addresses impervious pavement requirements.
The OAG will likely provide legal counsel regarding the interpretation of 'unreasonable limitations' on property use restrictions and the preemption of local zoning laws.
Mixed-use and multifamily developments significantly impact state transportation networks, traffic volume, and the coordination of multi-modal transit services.
Increased density and mixed-use development on commercial/recreational lots will impact vehicle traffic patterns and signal management on state-numbered highways maintained by the SHA.
The MTA is impacted because multifamily and mixed-use developments often correlate with increased demand for public transit services and the planning of transit-oriented development.
The bill mentions 'disability accommodation' as a valid reason for maintaining mandatory impervious pavement and relates to accessible housing through multifamily development expansion.
The bill represents a significant change in state housing and land use policy, which falls under the Governor's executive branch oversight and policy coordination responsibilities.

The bill prohibits private 'restrictions on use' that impose unreasonable limitations on development, which may lead to increased litigation in the state court system to define and enforce these provisions.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill's allowance for mixed-use development including retail components provides potential economic opportunities and new physical locations for small and minority-owned businesses.
The bill addresses housing availability and urban revitalization, which are tied to the team's mission of reducing child poverty and enhancing economic mobility.
MEDCO assists with real estate development and financing for projects that promote economic prosperity; mixed-use developments allowed under this bill could fall within their operational scope.
The commission oversees anti-discrimination laws in housing; changes to multifamily housing accessibility and zoning can impact the equitable delivery of housing resources.

Synopsis: Clarifying the Consumer Price Index used to determine the cost-of-living adjustments for retirees of the State Retirement and Pension System in certain years.

bill_summary: This emergency bill clarifies the calculation of cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) for retirees of the State Retirement and Pension System by specifying that the missing October 2025 Consumer Price Index (CPI) value, which was not published due to a federal government shutdown, be calculated as the average of the September 2025 and November 2025 CPI values. This methodology provides a 12-month data set for determining COLA rates effective July 1, 2026, and July 1, 2027.
responsible_party: State Retirement Agency and the Board of Trustees for the State Retirement and Pension System
stakeholders: Retirees of the Maryland State Retirement and Pension System
fiscal_impact_summary: The Fiscal Note indicates that the bill likely has no discernible effect on State pension liabilities and contribution rates. While the proposed methodology for estimating the missing October 2025 CPI data point results in a slightly higher COLA rate (approximately 0.067 percentage points higher than one alternative interpretation of current law), this impact is considered negligible because many retirees are subject to COLA caps and any resulting changes in liabilities are amortized over 10 to 15 years. There is no impact on State or local revenues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the administrative body responsible for the operation and management of the State Retirement and Pension System (SRPS), the SRA is the primary agency that will implement the new methodology for calculating cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) and managing retiree benefits.

DBM is the principal fiscal and personnel agency for the state. It manages state employee benefits and develops the state budget, which is impacted by the actuarial liabilities and contribution rates of the pension system.

The State Treasurer acts as the chief financial agency for the management of state funds and traditionally serves as a key member and/or chair of the Board of Trustees for the State Retirement and Pension System.
The Comptroller is the state's chief financial officer and principal tax collector, and typically serves as a member of the Board of Trustees for the State Retirement and Pension System.

The OAG serves as the primary legal representative for the state and provides legal counsel to all state agencies, including the State Retirement and Pension System, regarding the interpretation and implementation of pension laws.

The OLA is responsible for conducting fiscal compliance audits of all executive branch agencies, including the Maryland State Retirement Agency, ensuring that pension calculations and benefit adjustments comply with statutory requirements.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the annual state budget, which must account for the financial health and funding requirements of the state retirement system.

The Maryland Stadium Authority is explicitly listed in the bill as a governmental unit eligible to participate in the Employees' Pension System, and its participation would be subject to the clarified requirements.

bill_summary: This bill alters the membership structure of the Baltimore County Board of Education. The board will continue to include one student member, keeping the total membership at 12.
stakeholders: Voters and residents of Baltimore County, the Governor of Maryland, and candidates for the Baltimore County Board of Education.
fiscal_impact_summary: The total number of board members remains at 12, so expenditures for member compensation are expected to remain stable. The transition from seven to nine electoral districts may involve administrative costs for the local board of elections. agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor is the primary authority responsible for appointing members to the Baltimore County Board of Education. As the unit within the Executive Department that vets and recommends candidates for state boards and commissions, this office will manage the process of filling the reduced number of appointed seats on the Baltimore County Board of Education.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Maryland Public Service Commission (PSC) as an independent unit of State government with authority over its own administrative operations. It requires the PSC to create an independent personnel management system, allows it to determine employee compensation and hire independent consultants, and exempts the commission from State and local taxation as well as most State procurement laws. The bill also mandates annual independent audits and requires the PSC to submit its operating budget to the Department of Budget and Management for informational purposes.
stakeholders: Employees of the Public Service Commission, the Maryland Department of Budget and Management, the Office of Legislative Audits, and regulated public service companies.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. The bill has an indeterminate fiscal impact, likely increasing expenditures for annual independent certified audits and potentially altering personnel costs as the PSC shifts to an independent compensation and management system. The commission's exemption from State and local taxes and procurement laws further contributes to the indeterminate financial impact.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary subject of the bill, which establishes its authority as an essential government function and grants it significant administrative, budgetary, procurement, and personnel independence.

The bill removes the Commission's employees from the State Personnel Management System and changes the Commission's budget submission to DBM to 'informational purposes,' significantly altering DBM's oversight of the agency's fiscal and personnel matters.
The bill exempts the Commission from most of the State's general procurement laws (Division II), for which DGS serves as the central procurement authority.
The bill explicitly mandates that the Commission is subject to audit and examination of accounts and transactions by the Office of Legislative Audits.

As the agency responsible for standardizing collective bargaining and labor laws for state employees, PERB would be impacted by the creation of an independent personnel management system for the Commission.

The Commission is an independent unit within the Executive Branch. Changes to its administrative operations, personnel system, and how its budget is presented to the Governor impact the executive branch's structure.
The bill alters the legal and structural framework of a state agency and specifies the organization of lawyers representing Commission staff, impacting the OAG's general role as chief legal officer.

The bill specifies that Commission employees remain subject to Divisions II and III of the State Personnel and Pensions Article, meaning they will continue to be members of the State Retirement and Pension System managed by this agency.
The bill explicitly exempts the Public Service Commission from state and local taxation, which relates to the Comptroller's role as the state's chief tax collector.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Heirs Protection Program and the Heirs Protection Fund to assist heirs in securing record title to inherited homes and preventing tax sales. Administered by the State Tax Sale Ombudsman, the program provides grants to legal services organizations for free legal assistance and direct grants to heirs for probate fees and inheritance taxes. The bill also expands eligibility for the Homeowners' Property Tax Credit and the Homestead Property Tax Credit to include heirs who are not yet listed as the record title holder for up to three taxable years.
responsible_party: State Tax Sale Ombudsman (Department of Assessments and Taxation)
stakeholders: Heirs and legatees of deceased homeowners, low-income, elderly, or disabled residents, legal services organizations, and Maryland county governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes the Heirs Protection Fund, which is financed by a mandated annual State appropriation of $250,000 from interest on overdue State property taxes and a collective annual payment of $500,000 from county governments. Additionally, the expansion of the Homeowners' and Homestead property tax credits to include non-title-holding heirs will likely result in a decrease in State and local property tax revenue, though specific dollar estimates for the credit expansion are not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the State Tax Sale Ombudsman to collaborate with the Registers of Wills to develop probate guides for heirs. Furthermore, the Ombudsman is authorized to provide grants to heirs specifically to pay probate fees and inheritance taxes, which are collected by the Registers of Wills.

The bill establishes the Heirs Protection Fund and specifically tasks the State Treasurer with holding the fund separately and investing its money. The Treasurer also manages the allocation of state interest earnings, which are impacted by the creation of this new special fund.

The Comptroller is tasked with accounting for the newly established Heirs Protection Fund. Additionally, the bill affects the accrual of interest on state money to the General Fund, which the Comptroller manages as the state's chief financial officer.

The bill mandates that the Governor include a specific annual appropriation of $250,000 from interest on overdue state property taxes in the budget for the Heirs Protection Fund. The Ombudsman's office, which administers the program, is also located within a principal executive department overseen by the Governor's Office.
As the agency responsible for budget development and supervision, DBM will oversee the execution of the mandatory $250,000 appropriation and the fiscal management of the new Heirs Protection Fund.

The OAG will be responsible for providing legal counsel to the Ombudsman and the Department regarding the implementation of the Heirs Protection Program, the administration of grants to legal services organizations, and the interpretation of new tax credit eligibility rules for heirs.
The bill specifically allows the Ombudsman to prioritize 'elderly' heirs for grants to pay probate fees and inheritance taxes, aligning with the department's mission to support older adults.
The bill allows the Ombudsman to prioritize 'disabled' heirs for grants under the Heirs Protection Program, which is relevant to the department's role in supporting residents with disabilities.

As the body that hears appeals from final decisions of state taxing authorities, the Tax Court may be required to adjudicate disputes arising from the new eligibility requirements for the Homeowners' and Homestead property tax credits for heirs.

The bill's purpose is to prevent tax sales of dwellings and allow heirs to remain in their homes, which directly supports the department's goals of ensuring safe, secure housing and community stability.

bill_summary: House Bill 1153 prohibits health insurance carriers and managed care organizations from downcoding medical claims—unilaterally changing service codes to lower-paying ones—without a clinical documentation review. The bill requires carriers to provide written notice and justification to health care providers before downcoding, allows providers to appeal these decisions, and mandates that final downcoding determinations be made by board-certified or eligible physicians. Additionally, it establishes a fine of up to $10,000 per violation and requires carriers to report downcoding data to the Maryland Insurance Commissioner.
responsible_party: Maryland Insurance Commissioner and the Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Health care providers (including physicians, hospitals, and freestanding medical facilities), health insurance carriers, nonprofit health service plans, health maintenance organizations (HMOs), managed care organizations (MCOs), and participants in the Maryland Medical Assistance Program.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are unavailable. The bill establishes a fine of up to $10,000 for each violation. Financial implications likely include increased administrative costs for the Maryland Insurance Administration and the Maryland Department of Health, as well as potential increases in reimbursement expenditures for the Maryland Medical Assistance Program and state-regulated health plans due to restricted downcoding practices.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulator of health insurance in Maryland, the Insurance Administration is responsible for enforcing the new prohibitions on downcoding, collecting quarterly reports from carriers on downcoding activities, and administering the fines of up to $10,000 per violation.

The bill explicitly amends the Health - General Article to apply the new downcoding protections to Managed Care Organizations (MCOs) within the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid), making the department responsible for oversight of these standards within the state's Medicaid system.

The bill classifies final decisions to downcode a claim leading to nonpayment as 'coverage decisions' under Title 15, Subtitle 10D of the Insurance Article, which are subject to the administrative appeal process often adjudicated by this office.

As the agency that manages the State Employee Health and Welfare Benefits Program, DBM is impacted by changes in claim reimbursement procedures and coding standards used by the carriers that provide benefits to state employees.

The bill regulates the reimbursement practices of health maintenance organizations and insurers, many of which offer plans through the Maryland Health Connection marketplace administered by the Exchange.

The commission regulates hospital rates and financial stability; because the bill specifically includes hospitals in the definition of 'health care providers' protected from downcoding, it impacts hospital reimbursement and revenue integrity.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Maryland Insurance Administration and the Department of Health and would be involved in defending regulatory actions or interpreting the new legal definitions created by the bill.

The commission's role in improving access to health care and increasing accountability in the health system is relevant to regulations that impact provider reimbursement and the financial viability of health services.

bill_summary: This bill limits the use of restrictive housing (solitary confinement) in Maryland correctional facilities by redefining it as confinement for 20 or more hours a day. It restricts placement to a maximum of 15 consecutive days and 20 total days within a 60-day period, while requiring at least 4 hours of out-of-cell time daily. Crucially, the bill prohibits placing members of 'vulnerable populations'—including youth under 22, seniors over 55, pregnant individuals, and those with mental or physical disabilities—in restrictive housing for any duration. The Correctional Ombudsman is tasked with monitoring implementation and reporting results in 2028 and 2030.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services and the Office of the Correctional Ombudsman
stakeholders: Incarcerated individuals (particularly youth, seniors, and those with disabilities), correctional facility staff, and the Correctional Ombudsman.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. Financial implications include potential increases in state and local expenditures for staffing to facilitate the mandated 4 hours of daily out-of-cell time, facility modifications to provide less restrictive environments, and administrative costs for the Correctional Ombudsman to conduct reviews and surveys.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services

The bill regulates the use of restrictive housing for minors and individuals under the age of 22, directly impacting the department's management and rehabilitation of youth within the juvenile justice system.
