bill_summary: This bill establishes a 5-year oyster rotational harvest pilot program in the Lower Choptank, Lower Main Stem Chesapeake Bay, Herring Bay, and Lower Chester areas of the Chesapeake Bay. Managed by the Department of Natural Resources (DNR), the program requires specific oyster bars to be opened for harvest on a rotating basis, mandates that commercial harvesters replace oyster shells in volumes equal to their catch, and requires the DNR to conduct extensive environmental surveys and monitoring before and after harvests. The DNR must report its findings and recommendations to the Governor and General Assembly by December 1, 2031.
stakeholders: Tidal fish licensees with oyster authorizations (commercial harvesters), the Department of Natural Resources, and the Chesapeake Bay environmental community.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. However, the bill mandates that the Department of Natural Resources implement a new pilot program involving detailed environmental surveys, continuous monitoring of water and habitat quality, and the preparation of a comprehensive report, which will likely result in increased state expenditures for personnel and resources.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Natural Resources is the primary agency responsible for implementing, managing, and monitoring the rotational harvest pilot program for oysters, as well as reporting findings to the Governor.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, and the bill requires the Department of Natural Resources to report its findings and recommendations under the pilot program to the Governor by December 1, 2031.
The pilot program requires monitoring of water quality and environmental impacts within the Chesapeake Bay, which falls under MDE's mandate for environmental protection and restoration.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Council on the Chesapeake Bay
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This council advises the Governor on the management and restoration of the Chesapeake Bay, and a pilot program altering oyster harvesting practices in sanctuaries would be within its advisory scope.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Natural Resources and would likely be involved in drafting regulations or addressing legal aspects of opening sanctuary areas to harvesting.
The Department of Agriculture supports the seafood industry and oversees the Rural Maryland Council, which is interested in the economic health of rural communities impacted by oyster harvesting.

DBM is responsible for the state's budget and personnel; the Department of Natural Resources may require additional fiscal resources to conduct the surveys, monitoring, and reporting mandated by the bill.
The bill impacts the economic viability of the oyster harvesting industry, which is part of the Department of Commerce's mission to stimulate Maryland's economy and promote its assets.
MDP promotes sustainable growth and resource management; the pilot program's focus on rotational harvesting is a component of long-term sustainable management of the Bay's natural resources.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Agricultural & Resource-Based Industry Development Corp.

The MFCA manages facilities for the distribution of seafood; changes in oyster harvest levels could impact the volume and efficiency of Maryland's seafood supply chain.
The RMC addresses challenges in rural counties, many of which rely on the oyster industry for economic activity and historical cultural heritage.
This multi-agency initiative coordinates efforts between DNR and MDE to protect the Chesapeake Bay, aligning with the pilot program's goals of balancing harvesting with environmental monitoring.

bill_summary: This bill classifies female genital mutilation (FGM) as child abuse, requiring professionals like healthcare providers and educators to report suspected cases. It prohibits performing, attempting, or conspiring to perform FGM on minors, as well as transporting minors out of state for such procedures. The bill increases criminal penalties to a felony punishable by up to 10 years in prison and a $10,000 fine, mandates the revocation of professional licenses for health practitioners convicted of the offense, and allows victims to bring civil actions for damages. Furthermore, the Maryland Department of Health must develop educational materials and submit annual reports on FGM statistics starting in 2027.
stakeholders: Minors at risk of female genital mutilation, healthcare practitioners, law enforcement agencies, educators, and human service workers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill increases the maximum criminal fine for female genital mutilation to $10,000 and expands reporting and prosecution requirements, which may lead to an indeterminate increase in State revenue from fines and indeterminate expenditures for incarceration and administrative reporting. The Maryland Department of Health will also incur costs to develop and distribute educational materials. Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are unavailable as the note was not provided with the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates the Department to develop and distribute educational materials on female genital mutilation, produce an annual report for the General Assembly, and ensure health occupation boards revoke the licenses of convicted individuals.

The bill alters the definition of child abuse to include female genital mutilation, impacting the agency's child protective services and reporting duties. The Social Services Administration within DHS must also be consulted for the required annual report.
Educators are listed as mandated reporters for suspected abuse/FGM, and the Department of Health is required to distribute educational materials specifically to schools.
Police officers are mandated reporters for suspected abuse/FGM. The agency is also a recipient of the mandated educational materials and must be consulted for the annual data report.
The bill creates a new civil cause of action for victims and increases criminal penalties for felonies that will be adjudicated in the state's circuit courts.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and the various health occupation boards that are now required to perform mandatory license revocations.
Staff at juvenile detention centers are specifically designated as mandated reporters for suspected abuse, which now includes female genital mutilation.
DBM oversees the fiscal implementation and potential personnel/resource needs for the Department of Health to fulfill the educational and reporting mandates.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency is responsible for the incarceration of individuals convicted under the increased felony penalties established by the bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the coordinating body for public safety and victim services, this office may be involved in the policy development and funding for programs related to FGM prevention.
OAH may be required to adjudicate contested cases related to the mandatory revocation of health professional licenses mandated by the bill.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive agencies (MDH, DHS, MSP) tasked with implementing the reporting, educational, and enforcement provisions of the bill.

bill_summary: This bill clarifies and limits the reasons a vehicle may fail a Vehicle Emissions Inspection Program (VEIP) test or inspection. responsible_party: Maryland Department of Transportation (Motor Vehicle Administration) and the Maryland Department of the Environment
stakeholders: Motor vehicle owners in Maryland and emissions testing facilities.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text. The bill defines the specific grounds for vehicle emissions test failure, which clarifies regulatory standards for the Vehicle Emissions Inspection Program.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Motor Vehicle Administration is the primary agency responsible for administering the Vehicle Emissions Inspection Program (VEIP). This bill directly modifies the statutory criteria for failing a vehicle during an inspection, requiring changes to MVA's operational policies and test software.

The Maryland Department of the Environment is responsible for air quality and emissions standards. This bill limits the grounds for failing a vehicle during an emissions test to compliance with applicable standards, missing equipment, or misfueling, which directly affects MDE's regulatory enforcement and policy framework for the program.

The Maryland Department of Transportation is the parent agency of the Motor Vehicle Administration. This legislation affects the administration and statutory requirements of the Vehicle Emissions Inspection Program, which is a major component of MDOT's regulatory and operational duties.

Maryland Environmental Service often provides operational and technical environmental services, including the management of various state facilities. The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to all state agencies. They would be responsible for advising the MVA and MDE on the legal interpretation of these new restrictions and ensuring that regulations align with the clarified grounds for failure specified in the bill.

The Office of Administrative Hearings conducts hearings for residents who contest actions taken by the MVA, such as vehicle registration issues resulting from failed inspections. Because this bill clarifies and limits the reasons a vehicle can fail inspection, it impacts the legal basis for administrative appeals related to VEIP.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits law enforcement agencies from establishing or maintaining quotas for arrests, citations, investigations, or warrants, and forbids using these metrics as the basis for officer evaluations, compensation, discipline, or promotion. It authorizes law enforcement officers to report the use of quotas to the Office of the Attorney General (OAG), which is then required to provide a standard reporting form, investigate all reports within one year, and issue cease and desist orders to agencies found to be in violation of the law.
stakeholders: Maryland law enforcement officers, state and local law enforcement agencies, and the Office of the Attorney General
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the text. However, the bill creates new administrative and investigative mandates for the Office of the Attorney General, including the development of a reporting system, the conduct of investigations into quota allegations, and the adoption of regulations, which will likely increase state expenditures. Additionally, local law enforcement agencies are prohibited from offering financial rewards or benefits based on quotas, which could impact local personnel spending.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates the Office of the Attorney General to create a reporting form for law enforcement quotas, investigate officer reports within one year, issue cease and desist orders for violations, and adopt implementing regulations.

As the primary state law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police is directly subject to the bill's expanded prohibitions on using quotas for arrests, citations, investigations, and warrants in officer evaluations and discipline.
The MDTA maintains a large police force for toll facilities and bridges that would be subject to the bill's restrictions on the use of quotas and the Attorney General's investigative oversight.

The Department oversees the Natural Resources Police, whose officers make arrests and issue citations; the agency must comply with the bill's prohibitions on using these metrics as the basis for personnel actions.
The MTA operates a transit police force that is subject to the bill's provisions regarding the use of law enforcement quotas for performance evaluation and discipline.
The MAA operates the police force for BWI Thurgood Marshall Airport, which is subject to the bill's constraints on law enforcement quotas and the investigative authority of the Attorney General.
The Port Administration oversees maritime police officers who would be covered by the bill's prohibition on the use of quantitative enforcement data as the basis for compensation or discipline.
The DGS manages the Maryland Capitol Police, a law enforcement agency that must comply with the bill's restrictions on arrest and citation quotas.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services

The University System's various campus police departments are law enforcement agencies that must adhere to the bill's requirements regarding quotas and reporting.
As an independent state university with its own police force, Morgan State must ensure its law enforcement evaluations comply with the bill's quota prohibitions.
The college's police force is subject to the bill's rules regarding the reporting of quotas to the Attorney General and the prohibition of using enforcement metrics for discipline or promotion.

The board oversees labor relations and collective bargaining for state employees; the bill's prohibition on using quotas for compensation and discipline directly impacts the criteria used in labor disputes and unfair labor practice investigations.

bill_summary: Known as Bentley's Law, this bill requires individuals convicted of homicide by motor vehicle or vessel while impaired to pay periodic restitution to the minor children of the victim. Restitution payments continue until the child reaches age 18 and graduates from high school, with the court determining the amount based on the child's financial needs, standard of living, and custody arrangements.
stakeholders: Individuals convicted of impaired driving resulting in death, minor children of the deceased victims, and surviving parents or guardians.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill requires courts to order private restitution from offenders to the children of victims; it does not provide for a direct state appropriation or revenue change. agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates that the court order restitution in specific criminal cases and establishes detailed criteria and procedures the judiciary must follow when determining the amount and timing of these payments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategies, this office is relevant to the development and implementation of new restitution policies aimed at supporting victims of crime.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for the state and represents the state in criminal appeals; they also provide legal counsel regarding the implementation of new criminal procedure laws like this restitution mandate.

The Maryland State Police is the primary agency responsible for enforcing motor vehicle laws and investigating DUI-related homicides, which are the specific offenses that trigger the restitution requirements in this bill.

MDOT, through the State Highway Administration and Motor Vehicle Administration, manages highway safety and driver licensing related to the underlying offenses (homicide by motor vehicle) mentioned in the bill.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies involved in implementing this law and coordinates policy initiatives related to criminal justice and public safety.

Synopsis: Requiring, to make a claim under a warranty for certain agricultural equipment, a consumer to provide written notice to certain parties to report a nonconformity, defect, or condition occurring in certain agricultural equipment; requiring certain parties to correct the nonconformity, defect, or condition in a certain manner; and requiring certain parties to provide a consumer with the opportunity to replace agricultural equipment or receive a refund under certain circumstances.
Title: Consumer Protection - Agricultural Equipment Warranties
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/10 at 1:00 p.m.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Agricultural Equipment Warranty Enforcement Act, which creates lemon law protections for purchasers of new agricultural equipment. It requires manufacturers or dealers to repair nonconforming equipment within 30 days at no cost to the consumer and mandates equipment replacement or a full refund if repairs are unsuccessful after a reasonable number of attempts.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General, Consumer Protection Division
stakeholders: Purchasers of agricultural equipment (farmers), agricultural equipment manufacturers, factory branches, and authorized dealers.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is unavailable for this text. The bill defines violations as unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices, making them subject to enforcement and civil penalties under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act. Additionally, courts may award consumers up to $10,000 in damages if a manufacturer or dealer is found to have acted in bad faith.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Agricultural Equipment Warranty Enforcement Act and makes any violation an unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practice under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act. The OAG's Consumer Protection Division is responsible for enforcing these laws and pursuing penalties.

The bill specifically regulates equipment used in the business of farming. As the primary agency supporting the economic viability of the agricultural community, the MDA is impacted by regulations affecting farmers' ability to maintain and repair critical machinery.

The Council is tasked with addressing challenges in rural counties and advocating for rural interests. This 'lemon law' for agricultural equipment directly impacts the financial stability and operational efficiency of rural farming businesses.

The bill creates a new cause of action, allowing consumers to bring civil actions in court for warranty violations. This may result in a notable increase in litigation related to agricultural equipment disputes.
The bill regulates the business practices of manufacturers, factory branches, and authorized dealers of agricultural equipment, which are commercial entities operating within the state's economy.

The bill requires manufacturers to refund license and registration fees to consumers under certain circumstances. Additionally, it references specific vehicle definitions within the Transportation Article managed by the MVA.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives; this bill introduces a significant new consumer protection framework that aligns with agricultural and economic policy priorities.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Commission on Blueprint Fiscal Sustainability and Student Achievement to evaluate the implementation and financial sustainability of the Blueprint for Maryland's Future education reform. The commission is charged with studying school funding formulas, the educator career ladder, and the efficiency of various student achievement models. It must submit an interim report by December 31, 2026, and a final report by December 1, 2027.
stakeholders: Maryland public school students, parents, teachers, local school boards, and county governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text. The bill text indicates that the Maryland State Department of Education and the Accountability and Implementation Board must provide staff support for the commission. Additionally, commission members are entitled to reimbursement for travel expenses as provided in the state budget.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Education is mandated to provide staffing for the Commission and the State Superintendent of Schools is a designated member.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill establishes a new temporary commission to study and make recommendations on the fiscal sustainability and implementation of the Blueprint for Maryland's Future.
The Chair of the Interagency Commission on School Construction is a designated member of the commission, reflecting the Blueprint's impact on school facilities.
The Secretary of Higher Education is a designated member of the commission, as the Blueprint includes significant components related to postsecondary education and teacher preparation.
The Secretary of Labor is a member of the commission, representing the agency's role in the workforce and career-readiness aspects of the Blueprint.
The Governor jointly designates the chair of the commission and the body is required to report its findings and recommendations to the Governor.
The Chair of the Governor's Workforce Development Board is responsible for appointing a member of a local workforce development board to the commission.
As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM is significantly impacted by a commission dedicated to the fiscal sustainability of the state's largest educational investment.
The OAG serves as the primary legal representative for state agencies and commissions and may be called upon for legal counsel during the commission's study process.

Synopsis: Requiring the Interagency Commission on School Construction, when calculating a school's Gross Area Baseline, to allocate square footage to accommodate certain aquatic facilities; requiring each local school system to develop a certain facilities plan before the start of a certain school year; and requiring the Interagency Commission to collaborate with each school system on developing a certain facilities plan.
Title: School Construction - Gross Area Baseline Calculation - Aquatic Facilities
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/11 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Intergovernmental Cooperation -see also- AdmAgn; Cmts; etc.
Public Schools -see also- Primary Schools; Secondary Sch

bill_summary: This bill requires the Interagency Commission on School Construction to include square footage for aquatic facilities, used for athletic education and competition, when calculating a school's Gross Area Baseline. It also mandates that each local school system, in collaboration with the Commission, develop a facilities plan identifying student access to pools or aquatic facilities before the 2026-2027 school year.
responsible_party: Interagency Commission on School Construction and local school systems
stakeholders: Maryland public school students, local school systems, and the Interagency Commission on School Construction
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the bill text. However, the bill is likely to increase state and local expenditures for school construction projects by expanding the Gross Area Baseline calculation to include aquatic facilities, thereby increasing the maximum state share of eligible construction costs.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly names the Interagency Commission on School Construction as the primary agency responsible for allocating square footage for aquatic facilities and collaborating with local school systems to develop facilities plans.

As the agency providing leadership and oversight to the 24 local school systems, MSDE is relevant because those local systems are required to develop new facilities plans for aquatic access under this bill.

The Maryland Stadium Authority is responsible for the design and construction of public schools through major state programs like the 21st Century School Buildings Program. Changes to the Gross Area Baseline for schools would directly impact their project planning and budgets.

By requiring the inclusion of aquatic facilities in school baseline calculations, the bill will likely increase the state's capital expenditure for school construction, requiring DBM to manage significant fiscal impacts and budget planning.

The Board of Public Works oversees and approves significant state expenditures and procurement contracts for school construction and capital projects; changes in baseline calculations would affect the project costs presented for their approval.

DGS provides operational support and manages state-led construction and procurement. While schools are largely local, DGS's role in state-funded building standards and facility planning makes them relevant to changes in baseline calculations.

Synopsis: Suspending the imposition of the State transfer tax from July 1, 2026, to June 30, 2029.
Title: State Transfer Tax - Temporary Suspension
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/03 at 1:00 p.m.
bill_summary: This bill suspends the State transfer tax for instruments of writing recorded with a clerk of the circuit court or filed with the Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation from July 1, 2026, through June 30, 2029.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Assessments and Taxation and Clerks of the Circuit Court
stakeholders: Real estate buyers and sellers, and state programs such as Program Open Space that are funded by transfer tax revenue.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will result in a significant decrease in State revenue from July 1, 2026, to June 30, 2029, by suspending the State transfer tax. Specific dollar estimates from a Fiscal Note are not included in the provided text, but the suspension of the 0.5 percent tax will impact funding for programs traditionally supported by these revenues.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's chief financial officer and principal tax collector, the Comptroller is responsible for monitoring state revenues and enforcing tax laws. Suspending the State transfer tax directly impacts revenue collection and financial reporting managed by this agency.

The State transfer tax is the primary funding source for Program Open Space and the Rural Legacy Program, which the Department of Natural Resources administers to conserve land, manage state parks, and restore the Chesapeake Bay. A suspension would significantly impact their budget and conservation operations.

The Maryland Agricultural Land Preservation Foundation (MALPF) is largely funded by the State transfer tax. Suspending the tax would eliminate the primary revenue stream used by the department to preserve farmland and maintain the economic viability of the agricultural industry.

DBM is responsible for estimating revenues and developing the state's budget. The multi-year suspension of the transfer tax would require significant adjustments to revenue forecasts and the allocation of funds for various state programs.

The clerks of the circuit courts, supported by the Administrative Office of the Courts, are responsible for recording instruments of writing and collecting the State transfer tax. This bill changes the administrative and financial procedures for recording property transfers.

The Treasurer's Office manages and protects state funds and oversees the issuance of state bonds, some of which may be supported by transfer tax revenues. The Treasurer also serves on the Board of Public Works, which oversees the programs funded by this tax.

The Department of Planning provides policy guidance and coordinates land use and preservation programs, such as Program Open Space, which are funded by the State transfer tax. The suspension would impact long-term resource management planning.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the state budget. This bill represents a significant change in fiscal policy that would affect the Governor's environmental and economic priorities.
The Board of Public Works approves significant state land acquisitions and contracts funded by transfer tax revenues, particularly for Program Open Space and agricultural preservation.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies regarding tax laws and would likely be involved in advising the Comptroller and the Judiciary on the legal implementation of the tax suspension.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Agricultural & Resource-Based Industry Development Corp.
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MARBIDCO partners with state agencies to facilitate rural land preservation, which is supported by programs funded through the State transfer tax. A suspension could impact the availability of grants or joint preservation efforts.

Synopsis: Establishing requirements for consumer reporting agencies that use algorithmic systems to assemble or evaluate consumer credit information on consumers for the purpose of furnishing consumer reports to third parties; and requiring the Commissioner of Financial Regulation of the Maryland Department of Labor to establish certain assessment thresholds for algorithms, mandate regular training for human reviewers, and implement a certain whistleblower protection program.
Title: Consumer Protection - Consumer Reporting Agencies - Use of Algorithmic Systems
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/10 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.
Job Training -see also- Continuing Ed; Vocational Rehab
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records
Technology -see also- AeroT; BioT; EnergyT; InfoT; MedT; etc
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: This bill establishes comprehensive regulations for consumer reporting agencies that use algorithmic systems to process consumer credit information. It mandates that agencies provide plain-language explanations for evaluations, maintain a public registry of algorithms, and adhere to strict accuracy standards, including an error rate of less than 0.5% and data input accuracy of 99.9%. Agencies must conduct quarterly third-party bias audits, provide human review for automated decisions, and offer non-algorithmic options for consumers. Additionally, the Commissioner of Financial Regulation is required to oversee these standards, provide reviewer training, and implement whistleblower protections for agency employees.
responsible_party: Commissioner of Financial Regulation of the Maryland Department of Labor
stakeholders: Consumer reporting agencies, Maryland consumers, and employees of consumer reporting agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the bill text. The legislation creates new regulatory and oversight duties for the Commissioner of Financial Regulation, including the establishment of assessment thresholds, the implementation of a whistleblower protection program, and the mandate for regular reviewer training. These activities are expected to increase state expenditures for administrative oversight and enforcement, although specific dollar estimates are currently unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly tasks the Commissioner of Financial Regulation within the Department of Labor with establishing assessment thresholds for algorithms, mandating training for reviewers, implementing a whistleblower protection program, and adopting regulations.

As the primary legal representative for the state and enforcer of consumer protection laws, the OAG would be responsible for providing legal counsel to the Commissioner of Financial Regulation and potentially litigating enforcement actions under the Commercial Law Article.

The bill addresses algorithmic discrimination and harmful bias based on protected characteristics, which falls directly within the mission of the Commission to enforce anti-discrimination laws and promote civil rights compliance.
Regulatory decisions or penalties imposed by the Commissioner of Financial Regulation on consumer reporting agencies would likely be subject to adjudication by the Office of Administrative Hearings.

The bill involves technical oversight of algorithmic systems, data governance, and AI-generated content detection. DoIT, as the lead agency for state IT strategy, may provide technical guidance on these standards.
The bill establishes significant regulatory requirements and audit costs for consumer reporting agencies, which are businesses operating within the state's economic landscape.

Consumer reports are frequently used to determine eligibility for housing; improvements in report accuracy and reductions in bias would impact the Department's mission to ensure access to secure housing.

As the principal fiscal and personnel agency, DBM would oversee the fiscal impact and potential staffing needs of the Department of Labor to implement the assessment thresholds and whistleblower program.

Synopsis: Authorizing the suspension or revocation of a shellfish aquaculture harvester permit or shellfish aquaculture harvester registration card for certain violations; and prohibiting a person whose registration or permit card has been suspended or revoked in accordance with the Act from engaging or working in any aquaculture activity during the suspension or revocation.
Title: Shellfish Aquaculture - Penalties - Suspension or Revocation of Permit or Registration Card
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/04 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Natural Resources -see also- Coal; For&Pks; Rivers; etc.
Penalties and Sentences -see also- Death Penalty

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the Maryland Department of Natural Resources to suspend for up to five years or revoke shellfish aquaculture harvester permits and registration cards for specific violations, such as harvesting oysters in prohibited areas, using illegal gear, or harvesting outside of permitted hours. It establishes a mandatory administrative hearing process before penalties are imposed and prohibits individuals with suspended or revoked permits from participating in any aquaculture activity during the penalty period.
stakeholders: Shellfish aquaculture harvester permit holders, harvester registration card holders, and the shellfish aquaculture industry in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates for revenues and expenditures are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the bill text. However, implementation is expected to result in an increase in administrative expenditures for the Department of Natural Resources to conduct hearings and manage the suspension or revocation of permits and registration cards.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary agency responsible for managing Maryland's fisheries and waterways, DNR is the issuing authority for shellfish aquaculture harvester permits and registration cards. The bill directly empowers the department to suspend or revoke these credentials for specific violations and mandates that it conduct administrative hearings.

The bill requires that before a permit or registration card is suspended or revoked, the Department must hold a hearing in accordance with the Administrative Procedure Act. OAH typically conducts these contested case hearings for executive branch agencies like DNR.

The OAG provides legal counsel to DNR and would represent the agency in the required administrative hearings and any subsequent judicial reviews in circuit court resulting from the suspension or revocation of permits.

The bill specifically allows individuals aggrieved by the Department's final decision to seek judicial review. This would increase the potential caseload for the state's circuit courts, which are supported by the Administrative Office of the Courts.

While DNR leads aquaculture regulation, the Department of Agriculture supports the economic viability of farming and agribusiness, including aquaculture. Changes in penalty structures for aquaculture harvesters affect the broader agricultural industry the department oversees.

Synopsis: Requiring qualified providers to inform patients of certain information and obtain signed, written informed consent before performing a procedure to terminate a pregnancy.
Title: Public Health - Abortion - Informed Consent
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/19 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.
Records -see also- Land Records; Vital Records

bill_summary: This bill requires qualified healthcare providers to inform patients of the nature of an abortion procedure and its potential risks—including depression, infection, hemorrhage, breast cancer, danger to subsequent pregnancies, infertility, and regret—and obtain a signed, written informed consent form before the procedure is performed.
stakeholders: Pregnant individuals seeking abortion services and qualified healthcare providers in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. The bill creates administrative requirements for healthcare providers to obtain and maintain written informed consent records, but it does not explicitly state any revenue changes or state/local expenditure mandates.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill adds requirements to the Health – General Article of the Maryland Code, which is primarily administered by the Maryland Department of Health. The department regulates public health and the medical professionals (qualified providers) who are mandated to provide this informed consent and maintain patient records.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the OAG provides counsel to the Maryland Department of Health and the General Assembly regarding the implementation and enforcement of health-related laws, including constitutional considerations related to abortion services and informed consent requirements.

The MHCC is tasked with promoting informed decision-making and improving access and accountability in health care. This bill directly relates to the clinical process of informed decision-making between patients and providers regarding surgical and medical procedures.

If providers fail to comply with these new statutory informed consent requirements, they may face disciplinary actions from their respective licensing boards (under MDH), which are adjudicated by Administrative Law Judges at the OAH.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, including the Department of Health, and coordinates high-level policy initiatives related to public health and reproductive services.

Synopsis: Requiring a medical examiner in receipt of notice that a deceased individual was Muslim to release the body of the deceased within 48 hours after the completion of the autopsy.
Title: Medical Examiner - Release of Body - Requirements for Muslims
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/10 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Death -see also- Homicide; Murder; Wrongful Death

bill_summary: This bill requires a medical examiner to release the body of a deceased Muslim individual within 48 hours after the completion of an autopsy, provided the medical examiner receives notice of the individual's faith through specific documentation, such as a will, notice from next of kin, or confirmation from an imam or mosque.
responsible_party: Medical Examiners and the Maryland Department of Health
stakeholders: Muslim residents of Maryland, their families and next of kin, imams, mosques, and state or local medical examiners.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the provided text does not include the formal Fiscal Note. The bill mandates a 48-hour timeline for the release of bodies of deceased Muslim individuals following an autopsy, which is expected to have a minimal fiscal or administrative impact on state or local government operations.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health oversees the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner (OCME), which is the agency directly responsible for performing autopsies and releasing deceased individuals. This bill mandates specific timeframes for the OCME to release the bodies of deceased Muslims.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like the Department of Health. It would be responsible for advising the medical examiner on the legal sufficiency of the various forms of notice described in the bill and ensuring compliance with religious freedom laws.

The GOCI manages faith-based commissions and coordinates between the state government and religious communities. It may be involved in establishing standards or communication protocols between the medical examiner and imams or mosques as specified in the bill.

The Register of Wills is the state entity responsible for the safekeeping and probate of wills. Since a will is a primary document used to notify the medical examiner of the deceased's religious status, this agency may be involved in verifying such documents.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees the Department of Health and its units, including the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, ensuring that statutory mandates regarding the treatment of deceased residents are implemented.

Synopsis: Authorizing the people to petition to a vote a proposal to add to, amend, and repeal the public general laws or the Maryland Constitution under certain circumstances and establishing the Initiative process; and requiring that the amendment be submitted to the qualified voters of the State at the next general election in November 2026 for adoption or rejection.
Title: Election Law - Initiative Process
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/04 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Voting -see also- Absentee and Mail-In Voting

bill_summary: This bill proposes a constitutional amendment to establish an initiative process in Maryland, allowing registered voters to petition for the addition, amendment, or repeal of public general laws or the Maryland Constitution. To qualify for the ballot, a petition must gather signatures from at least 10% of the total votes cast in the most recent gubernatorial election, with no more than 50% of signers coming from a single county or Baltimore City. If certified, the proposals are submitted to voters at the next general election.
responsible_party: Secretary of State, Attorney General, and the Governor
stakeholders: Maryland registered voters, the Maryland General Assembly, the Secretary of State, the Attorney General, and the State Board of Elections
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates administrative costs for the Secretary of State to verify and certify initiative petitions and for the Attorney General to review proposal summaries. There will be additional costs for the State Board of Elections to include initiative proposals on general election ballots. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill requires the Governor to make the final determination of the number of votes cast for and against initiative proposals, to issue official proclamations declaring proposals effective, and to resolve irreconcilable conflicts between multiple successful proposals with advice from the Attorney General.

The Secretary of State is designated as the primary administrative authority for the initiative process, responsible for receiving the text of proposals, determining the validity of petition signatures, and certifying proposals for inclusion on the ballot.

As the agency responsible for supervising and administering elections and managing the statewide voter registration system, the Board of Elections would be tasked with placing initiative proposals on general election ballots and providing the registration data necessary to verify the 10% signature threshold required by the bill.

The bill mandates that the Attorney General approve the accuracy of petition summaries and provide legal advice to the Governor regarding irreconcilable conflicts between successful initiative proposals.

The creation of a statewide initiative process will have significant fiscal and personnel impacts, including costs for signature verification and ballot printing, which fall under the fiscal oversight and budget planning responsibilities of this department.

As the central depository for Maryland's permanent government records, the Archives would be responsible for preserving the resulting changes to the Public General Laws and the Maryland Constitution enacted through the initiative process.

Synopsis: Stating the authority to construct, permit, and operate in the State an energy generating system that produces energy from natural gas; authorizing investor-owned electric companies and electricity suppliers in the State to construct, acquire, or lease, and operate, their own generating facilities and construct, acquire, or lease, and operate, certain transmission facilities; authorizing certain investor-owned electric companies to recover certain investments and costs in a certain manner; etc.
Title: Public Utilities - Energy Generation and Transmission
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/10 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.
Energy Matters -see also- Fuel; NuclearMatt; PwrPlnts; etc.
Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes
Renewable Energy Sources -see also- Geotherm; Solar; etc.
Utilities -see also- Recycl; Refuse; Sewage; Teleph; Water

bill_summary: This bill authorizes the construction and operation of natural gas power plants in Maryland. It permits investor-owned electric companies and electricity suppliers to build, own, or lease their own generation and transmission facilities. The legislation establishes a process for utility companies to recover their investments and costs through customer electricity rates or surcharges, provided certain conditions are met, such as obtaining a favorable credit rating assessment for large-scale projects. It also expresses legislative support for nuclear energy and calls for faster grid connection processes for new thermal power sources.
stakeholders: Investor-owned electric companies, electricity suppliers, residential and commercial utility customers, and PJM Interconnection, LLC.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill allows investor-owned electric companies to recover 'all prudently incurred' generation and transmission costs, including capital, operation, and fuel costs, through electricity rates or nonbypassable surcharges. This creates a mechanism for significant infrastructure investment funded by ratepayers. While the bill text does not provide specific dollar estimates for state revenues or expenditures, it establishes a regulatory framework for utility-led energy generation that would be overseen by the Public Service Commission.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission (PSC) is the primary regulatory body for public utilities in Maryland. This bill directly amends the Public Utilities Article, granting the PSC new authorities and responsibilities regarding the permitting, construction, and operation of natural gas and nuclear generating facilities, as well as overseeing cost recovery through electric rates and nonbypassable surcharges.

The Office of the People's Counsel is the statutory advocate for residential utility consumers. Since the bill allows investor-owned utilities to recover generation and transmission costs through rates and surcharges, the OPC would be heavily involved in representing consumer interests in the resulting PSC proceedings.

The MEA is the state's lead agency for energy policy and planning. The bill's significant shifts in energy generation policy—specifically the explicit authorization of natural gas facilities and support for nuclear energy—directly impact the MEA's mission to coordinate energy planning and advise the Governor and General Assembly.

The MDE is responsible for enforcing state and federal environmental laws. The construction and operation of new natural gas or nuclear power plants authorized by this bill would require significant environmental permitting for air emissions, water use, and potential hazardous waste management.

The DNR, through its Power Plant Research Program (PPRP), conducts the scientific and environmental reviews of power plant applications for Certificates of Public Convenience and Necessity (CPCN). The bill's promotion of new thermal and nuclear generation would increase the DNR's workload in reviewing these projects.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Public Service Commission and other state agencies. The new regulatory frameworks for cost recovery, credit rating assessments, and utility-owned generation proposed in the bill would require significant legal oversight and potential representation in litigation.

The bill establishes significant new state policies regarding energy independence and specific support for nuclear and natural gas power. As the office responsible for overseeing policy initiatives and the executive branch, this impacts the Governor's energy and environmental agenda.

The MCEC's mission is to advance clean energy and energy efficiency. While natural gas is a fossil fuel, the bill explicitly categorizes nuclear energy as 'clean energy' and supports its development, which aligns with the financing and promotional role of the MCEC.

The Department of Planning coordinates land use and resource management. The construction of major new generation and transmission infrastructure involves significant land use planning and impacts on state development visions.

Large-scale energy infrastructure projects, such as the natural gas and nuclear facilities promoted in this bill, are significant drivers of economic development and capital investment in the state, which falls under the purview of the Department of Commerce.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a candidate for certain State offices and a person acting on behalf of a candidate for certain State offices from participating in certain campaign finance activities during a regular session of the General Assembly.
Title: Election Law - Campaign Finance Activities - Candidates for State Office
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/04 at 1:00 p.m.

bill_summary: This bill expands existing prohibitions on campaign finance activities during a regular session of the Maryland General Assembly to include candidates for the offices of Governor, Lieutenant Governor, Attorney General, Comptroller, State Treasurer, and member of the General Assembly. Prohibited activities include receiving, soliciting, or depositing contributions and conducting fundraising events.
stakeholders: Candidates for State office, campaign finance entities, and individuals acting on behalf of candidates.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill may result in an indeterminate increase in State revenue to the Fair Campaign Financing Fund from civil penalties collected for violations of the fundraising prohibition. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The State Board of Elections is the primary agency responsible for supervising elections and managing campaign finance compliance. This bill expands the existing session-fundraising ban to include all candidates for specified State offices, an area of law administered and enforced by the Board.

The Governor is specifically listed as an individual subject to the bill's expanded campaign finance prohibitions. As the executive head of the state, changes to the Governor's ability to conduct fundraising during the legislative session directly impact the office's principal.
The Lieutenant Governor is explicitly named in the legislation as an official subject to the restricted campaign finance activities during the General Assembly's regular session.

The Comptroller is one of the five constitutional officers directly impacted by the bill's prohibition on receiving, soliciting, or depositing campaign contributions while the legislature is in session.

The State Treasurer is explicitly listed as an individual subject to the bill's fundraising restrictions. The agency's principal would be directly regulated by the new candidate-specific prohibitions.

The Attorney General is a subject of the legislation. Furthermore, as the chief legal officer for the state, the agency provides counsel on the interpretation and enforcement of the Election Law article amended by this bill.

The Office of the State Prosecutor is responsible for investigating and prosecuting offenses related to the integrity of state officials and the electoral process, specifically including the enforcement of state election laws and session-fundraising bans.

The Office of Administrative Hearings provides an impartial forum for contested cases involving state agencies; it would be the venue for any appeals of civil penalties issued for violations of these campaign finance restrictions.

Synopsis: Authorizing a person charged with murder or manslaughter in any degree or a crime under Title 3, Subtitle 2 of the Criminal Law Article to assert the defense that the person acted in self-defense and need not prove that the person believed danger was imminent or immediate if the victim had previously committed a certain act against the person.
Title: Criminal Law - Self-Defense - Prior Acts by Victim
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/10 at 1:00 p.m.
bill_summary: This bill modifies the requirements for asserting a self-defense claim in criminal cases involving murder, manslaughter, or assault. It allows a defendant to claim self-defense without proving they believed danger was imminent or immediate if the victim had previously committed an assault or sexually assaultive behavior against them.
stakeholders: Criminal defendants who were previously victimized by their alleged victims, the Maryland court system, State's Attorneys, and the Office of the Public Defender.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the text, and the bill does not contain explicit financial implications such as fee changes or appropriations. Therefore, specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill modifies the legal standards for self-defense in criminal cases, which directly affects judicial proceedings, jury instructions, and the adjudication of violent crimes within the Maryland court system.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill significantly impacts the defense strategies available to indigent clients charged with murder, manslaughter, or assault, as it expands the statutory defense of self-defense based on prior acts by the victim.

The OAG represents the state in criminal appeals and provides legal counsel to state agencies; changes to the elements of self-defense will likely lead to extensive appellate litigation and require updated legal guidance.

bill_summary: The Data Center Planning and Transparency Act requires owners or operators of large-scale data centers (those with a demand of at least 20 megawatts) to submit detailed disclosure reports concerning their energy usage, environmental impact, noise levels, and community benefits to state and local authorities. The bill mandates that local jurisdictions with a population of at least 10,000 residents develop and adopt large-scale data center plans and implementing zoning regulations by June 30, 2027. Additionally, it prohibits state agencies from providing grants, loans, or sales and use tax exemptions to large-scale data centers unless the owner is in compliance with the disclosure requirements and the local jurisdiction has adopted the required planning and zoning framework.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of the Environment, Maryland Department of Planning, Maryland Department of Commerce, and local jurisdictions with at least 10,000 residents.
stakeholders: Owners and operators of large-scale data centers, local governments, Maryland state agencies, utility ratepayers, and residents of communities where data centers are located or proposed.

It also creates administrative responsibilities for the Department of the Environment and the Department of Planning to publish reports and plans. The bill requires local data center plans to consider impacts on Rural Legacy Areas, which are designated and managed under programs within the DNR.
The Comptroller oversees tax law enforcement and revenue collection; the bill's modification of the sales and use tax exemption for data centers directly affects these duties.
The bill restricts how units of State government may use appropriations for data center incentives, impacting DBM's role in supervising budget execution and fiscal planning.
The BPW must approve significant state expenditures and contracts. The bill’s restriction on financial assistance to data centers affects the criteria for approving such state funding.

The Treasurer manages state funds and sits on the Board of Public Works, which would be responsible for ensuring state funds are not disbursed in violation of the bill’s new restrictions.

The OAG would provide legal advice on the implementation of these new regulatory frameworks and represent the state in any legal challenges regarding the planning mandates or incentive restrictions.

As a provider of state-funded financial assistance to tech companies, TEDCO would be restricted from providing incentives to data centers that fail to meet the bill's transparency and planning criteria.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission to develop a model policy regarding the use of worn identification by law enforcement officers while on duty. bill_summary: This bill modifies the Maryland income tax credit for long-term care insurance premiums by reducing the maximum credit from $500 to $250 per insured individual and restricting the credit to insurance policies covering individuals who are at least 45 years old. fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to impact State income tax revenues by halving the maximum credit per individual and adding age-based restrictions, which may increase revenue relative to current law. Because the full text of the Fiscal Note with specific revenue projections was not provided, a precise dollar estimate is unavailable.

The bill requires the reporting of savings to the State’s Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid), which is administered by the Department of Health. The Department of Aging is dedicated to the well-being of older adults and long-term care advocacy. As this bill specifically targets residents aged 45 and older and concerns the financing of future care, it aligns directly with the department's core mission and service population.

As an independent administrative agency that hears appeals regarding tax assessments and credits, the Maryland Tax Court would be the venue for adjudicating any disputes between taxpayers and the state regarding the eligibility or amount of the credit.

The Office of Legislative Audits performs fiscal compliance and performance audits of executive agencies, including the Comptroller's Office, and may be tasked with verifying the accuracy of the data reported regarding the credit's utilization and Medicaid savings.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates the State Board of Education, which is the governing body for this department, to review and update public high school graduation requirements at least every five years and implement those changes for specific cohorts.

The bill explicitly requires the State Board of Education to coordinate and consult with this board to ensure graduation requirements align with career readiness and the state's workforce goals.

Periodic changes to graduation requirements will impact how the system links and analyzes student performance and workforce outcomes for the cohorts affected by the updated standards.
Changes to high school graduation requirements and college readiness standards directly affect the preparation and admission criteria for students entering the state's public university system.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the process for the partition of real property. It requires parties in a partition action to notify the court of any outstanding liens, such as mortgages or tax liens, if a title report is not required. It also changes how the purchase price for a cotenant's interest is calculated by subtracting the total amount of liens from the property's value before applying the ownership fraction. Additionally, the court must adjust the purchase price to account for necessary costs incurred by a cotenant, like taxes and maintenance, or income earned from the property, such as rent.
stakeholders: Cotenants of real property, litigants in partition actions, and lienholders including mortgage lenders and tax authorities.
fiscal_impact_summary: The formal Fiscal Note is absent from the provided text; however, the bill focuses on the adjudication of private property rights and the calculation of purchase prices in partition actions. agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill directly alters judicial procedures for partition of real property actions. It requires courts to receive and review lien notifications, calculate purchase prices based on specific lien deductions, notify cotenants of price adjustments, and conduct hearings to consider evidence of costs and income related to the property.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the Office of the Attorney General provides counsel to the Judiciary and state agencies on the interpretation and implementation of statutory changes to real property law and judicial proceedings.

fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to increase state and private healthcare expenditures by prohibiting utilization review and cost-control measures for specific prescription drugs. Specific dollar estimates from a Fiscal Note were not included in the provided text.

Synopsis: Requiring a citation issued for violations relating to public consumption of alcohol and possession of an open container to contain notice that fines for the violation may be prepaid; establishing a maximum fine for public consumption and open container violations and authorizing the Chief Judge of the District Court to establish a schedule for prepayment of the fines; establishing that prepayment of a fine is a plea of guilty; etc.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the citation process for violations related to public alcohol consumption and open container possession. It requires that citations for these offenses include a notice that fines may be prepaid, with prepayment serving as a plea of guilty. The bill establishes a maximum fine of $100 for these specific violations and directs the Chief Judge of the District Court to establish a prepayment schedule, while also outlining court procedures for cases where a person fails to prepay, request a hearing, or respond to a summons.
stakeholders: Individuals cited for public alcohol consumption or open container violations, Maryland law enforcement agencies, alcoholic beverages inspectors, the District Court of Maryland, and the Motor Vehicle Administration.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill sets a maximum fine of $100 for public consumption and open container violations, which is a reduction from the $500 maximum for other general alcohol-related code violations. While a formal Fiscal Note with specific dollar estimates is not included in the text, the lower fine cap suggests a potential reduction in revenue per citation. The District Court will incur administrative costs to establish a prepayment schedule and update citation forms, and a $5 court cost remains applicable to certain proceedings.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the Judicial Branch by requiring the Chief Judge of the District Court to establish a schedule for the prepayment of fines for public consumption and open container violations. It also mandates that the District Court prescribe the form of citation used for adults and manages the summons and trial scheduling for these code violations.

As the primary state law enforcement agency, Maryland State Police officers are authorized to issue citations for the alcohol-related violations mentioned in the bill. The changes to the citation form, the inclusion of prepayment notices, and the established maximum fines directly affect their enforcement procedures.

The bill specifically identifies forest or park wardens within the Department of Natural Resources as authorities empowered to issue these citations in state forestry reservations, parks, and recreation areas. The procedural changes regarding citation notices and prepayment apply to their enforcement activities.

The Maryland Transportation Authority (MDTA) maintains its own police force which is authorized to issue citations for public consumption and open container violations on toll facilities and MDTA property. The bill's changes to the citation and fine process apply to these enforcement actions.

The Comptroller is the primary regulator of the alcoholic beverages industry in Maryland. Since the bill modifies the penalties and procedures for the public consumption and possession of alcoholic beverages, it intersects with the agency's regulatory and enforcement scope.

The OAG serves as the chief legal representative for the state and provides legal counsel to the General Assembly and state agencies on the implementation of new criminal and civil code procedures, such as the prepayment system established by this bill.
The bill establishes a maximum fine of $100 for specific violations and allows for prepayment, which impacts state revenue projections and fiscal planning handled by DBM.

The Treasurer's Office is responsible for receiving and distributing state funds. Fines collected through these citations, as well as payments to the Criminal Injuries Compensation Fund mentioned in the bill, fall under the office's fiscal management responsibilities.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill references the Criminal Injuries Compensation Fund, which is managed by GOCPP. bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA) to implement a system to collect address information from vehicle insurance contracts to identify Maryland residents who have improperly registered their vehicles in other states. The MVA is authorized to conduct investigations, hire private contractors for assistance, and assess penalties of $150 for noncompliance and an additional $500 if the vehicle remains unregistered 60 days after notice. All penalties are to be deposited into the Transportation Trust Fund.
stakeholders: Maryland residents owning vehicles registered out-of-state, the Motor Vehicle Administration, and private investigative contractors.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates a new revenue stream for the Transportation Trust Fund through penalties of $150 and $500 assessed against residents with improperly registered vehicles. The MVA will incur costs to establish the data collection system and conduct investigations, which may be performed by private agents under contract. Specific aggregate dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are not available in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA) is the primary agency tasked with implementing the new system to collect insurance address information, conducting investigations into improper vehicle registration, assessing penalties for noncompliance, and potentially contracting with private parties for these services.

As the parent agency of the MVA, the Department of Transportation oversees motor vehicle registration and manages the Transportation Trust Fund, which is the designated recipient of the penalties collected under this bill.
The Office of Administrative Hearings typically adjudicates contested administrative decisions and penalties assessed by the MVA, such as those authorized by this bill for improper registration.

The Board of Public Works oversees significant state procurement contracts; its approval would likely be required if the MVA enters into substantial contracts with private parties to procure the services of independent agents.

The Department of Budget and Management oversees state agency expenditures and personnel; it would be responsible for managing the fiscal impact on the MVA's budget and the resulting revenue for the Transportation Trust Fund.
The State Treasurer acts as the custodian of state funds, including the receipt and distribution of penalties directed to the Transportation Trust Fund.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the MVA and would likely be involved in drafting or reviewing the new regulations, investigation protocols, and private contracts authorized by this bill.

fiscal_impact_summary: The bill mandates administrative reporting for municipalities and web publication duties for the State Board of Elections. As the agency responsible for the state's information technology strategy and digital services, DoIT may be required to support the State Board of Elections in updating its website infrastructure to handle the new intake and immediate publication requirements for municipal election data.

The Department of Budget and Management is responsible for supervising budget execution and state personnel. It would review any fiscal impact or staffing needs the State Board of Elections might have in order to comply with the new administrative and website management mandates.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the State Board of Elections. It would likely advise SBE on the legal requirements for municipal compliance and the board's responsibilities under the new law.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Maryland Office of the Inspector General (OIG) and an Advisory Board to provide oversight and appoint an Inspector General. The OIG is authorized to investigate waste, mismanagement, misconduct, fraud, and corruption within the executive branch of the State government, conduct audits, and issue subpoenas. It also extends whistleblower protections to State employees who report information to the OIG and allows for the transfer of existing staff and funding to the new office.
responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Inspector General and the Maryland Office of the Inspector General Advisory Board
stakeholders: Maryland State employees, Executive Branch agencies and units, and Maryland residents
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes a new state office, resulting in increased state expenditures for salaries, equipment, and operations as provided in the state budget. The Governor is authorized to transfer existing funds and positions from executive agencies to the OIG. While specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are absent in the provided text, the bill establishes a potential revenue source through misdemeanor fines of up to $2,000 for unauthorized disclosure of confidential investigation records.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor or a designee serves as a member of the Maryland Office of the Inspector General Advisory Board. Additionally, the Governor appoints one professional member to the board, receives annual and final investigative reports, and is authorized to transfer positions and funds from other executive units to the new Office of the Inspector General.

The Comptroller or a designee serves as a member of the Maryland Office of the Inspector General Advisory Board, which is responsible for appointing and overseeing the Inspector General. The board requires the Comptroller's participation for a quorum and a majority vote for leadership decisions.

DBM is the state's principal fiscal and personnel agency. It will be responsible for managing the transfer of funds and positions to the new office and overseeing the implementation of the expanded whistleblower protections in the State Personnel and Pensions Article.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a new permanent advisory board, the Maryland Office of the Inspector General Advisory Board, to appoint, oversee, and potentially remove the Inspector General.

The bill establishes legal frameworks for investigations and criminal referrals. It also explicitly includes the Inspector General alongside the Attorney General as a protected recipient of disclosures in the state's whistleblower statute.
The bill requires the Inspector General to obtain approval from a circuit court judge to issue subpoenas. This creates a new administrative interaction between the executive branch and the judiciary.

The bill mandates that the state maintain and equip office space for the Maryland Office of the Inspector General, a core responsibility of DGS. Additionally, the Inspector General's oversight of 'waste and mismanagement' often involves procurement and facility management audits.

The bill requires the Inspector General to take steps to avoid duplicative investigations or audits. As OLA is the primary agency responsible for auditing executive units, the two offices must coordinate closely to ensure oversight efficiency.

The Inspector General is required to establish a toll-free hotline and a public website to receive complaints and post reports, which typically requires coordination with and technical support from DoIT.

The Inspector General is mandated to notify the appropriate law enforcement agency if an investigation discovers evidence of criminal activity. As the primary state-level law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police would likely receive such referrals.
The bill contains specific protections ensuring that employees transferred to the new Maryland Office of the Inspector General do so without diminution of their retirement status or benefits.

bill_summary: This bill requires health insurance carriers to take responsibility for identifying primary and secondary payors and coordinating benefit amounts when multiple payors are involved in a claim. It reduces the time period for carriers to retroactively deny reimbursement to health care providers from 18 months to 9 months for claims involving other carriers, though the 18-month limit remains for coordination with Medicaid and Medicare. Carriers are also required to submit an annual report on these coordination activities to the Maryland Insurance Commissioner.
stakeholders: Health insurance carriers, managed care organizations, health care providers, and the Maryland Insurance Administration
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the Fiscal Note was not included in the source text. The bill creates new administrative requirements for health insurance carriers and requires oversight and reporting to the Maryland Insurance Commissioner. The reduction of the retroactive denial window from 18 to 9 months for specific coordination of benefits may impact the timing and volume of reimbursement recoveries for insurers and providers.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary regulator of the health insurance industry in Maryland, the Maryland Insurance Administration is responsible for enforcing the Insurance Article. This bill mandates new coordination of benefits protocols, alters retroactive denial timeframes, and requires carriers to submit annual activity reports directly to the Insurance Commissioner.

The bill explicitly names the Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid) as a payor and affects Managed Care Organizations (MCOs), which are overseen by the Department of Health. The changes to coordination of benefits and the 18-month retroactive denial window directly impact Medicaid operations and provider reimbursements.

This independent regulatory agency plans for state health system needs and increases accountability. Changes to carrier reimbursement rules and coordination of benefits practices affect the overall financial stability and efficiency of the healthcare delivery system they monitor.

The Exchange oversees the state's health insurance marketplace. The new requirements for benefit coordination and restrictions on retroactive denials will directly affect the operations and compliance of private insurance carriers offering plans on the marketplace.

As the central agency managing state employee benefits, DBM oversees the health insurance plans provided to state workers. Changes to carrier regulations regarding reimbursement and coordination of benefits may have fiscal and administrative impacts on the state's employee health programs.

The OAG serves as the chief legal representative for state agencies, including the Maryland Insurance Administration and the Department of Health. The office will provide legal guidance on the implementation and enforcement of the bill's new regulatory requirements for insurance carriers.

The OAH adjudicates contested administrative cases. New regulations concerning retroactive denials and coordination of benefits are likely to generate disputes between health care providers, insurance carriers, and state regulatory bodies that require formal administrative hearings.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and the state budget. Because the bill impacts major state programs like Medicaid and introduces new regulatory frameworks for the insurance industry, it is relevant to the office's policy coordination and fiscal planning responsibilities.
