bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of Health to develop and implement a standardized system for collecting, compiling, and reporting annual data on the costs associated with women's health care services, including prenatal care, birth, postpartum care, pregnancy care, abortion services, and menopausal care. The Department must submit an annual report to the General Assembly starting December 1, 2026, summarizing aggregated cost data, regional trends, and recommendations for cost efficiency, while ensuring all data is anonymized to protect patient privacy.
stakeholders: Maryland women and individuals seeking reproductive or menopausal health care; licensed hospitals; licensed health care providers; and the Maryland Department of Health.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. However, the bill creates a state mandate for the Maryland Department of Health to develop a standardized reporting system and produce annual reports, which will result in increased administrative expenditures. Additionally, licensed hospitals and health care providers will incur costs associated with complying with the new data reporting requirements.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: MDH is the primary agency responsible for implementing the bill's requirements, including developing the standardized reporting system, collecting cost data from healthcare providers and hospitals, tracking Medicaid expenditures for reproductive services, and submitting annual reports to the General Assembly.

As an independent agency within MDH focused on health system planning and data transparency, the MHCC's mission to provide accurate information on healthcare costs and quality aligns directly with the bill's goal to inform public policy and assess the effective use of funds.

The HSCRC regulates hospital rates and revenues; the bill's requirement for hospitals to report revenues, charges, prices, and utilization data for women's health services falls directly within the commission's regulatory oversight and expertise.

DBM is the state's principal fiscal agency; the bill's mandate to analyze the financial impact of specific health services on the state and monitor Medicaid expenditures for reproductive health directly concerns state budget execution and long-term fiscal planning.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and will be essential in ensuring the new reporting system and data sharing protocols comply with federal HIPAA regulations and state privacy laws.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives; the data collected under this bill is intended to inform high-level public policy decisions and evaluate the efficiency of state healthcare spending.

DoIT manages the state's information technology strategy and data governance; the creation of a standardized, statewide reporting system for health data collection would likely involve their oversight regarding technical standards and cybersecurity.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Suitland Development Authority in Prince George's County to oversee and implement a comprehensive revitalization plan for the area surrounding the intersection of Suitland Road and Silver Hill Road. The Authority is empowered to acquire and develop property through various methods including eminent domain (excluding owner-occupied residences), provide grants and loans, and coordinate with residents and businesses to promote economic growth, housing rehabilitation, and public safety. It establishes the Suitland Development Authority Fund and requires the Authority to become self-sustaining by fiscal year 2036.
stakeholders: Residents, commercial property owners, and business operators located within the Suitland Road and Silver Hill Road target area and buffer zone in Prince George's County.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes the Suitland Development Authority Fund, a special nonlapsing fund for administrative expenses, and authorizes the Governor to provide annual State budget appropriations. The Authority is mandated to be self-sustaining by fiscal year 2036. The Authority is granted exemptions from various state and local taxes, including sales and use tax on construction materials and transfer and recordation taxes, which may result in a decrease in state and local revenues. Property sold or leased by the Authority to private entities remains subject to local real property taxes. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Secretary of Housing and Community Development is a designated member of the Authority's Board of Directors. Furthermore, the Authority's mission to develop housing and revitalize neighborhoods directly aligns with the department's core function of community revitalization and affordable housing support.

The Secretary of Commerce is a designated member of the Authority's Board of Directors. The Authority's legislative purposes include promoting economic development and attracting new business activity, which are central to the department's mission.

The Secretary of Transportation is a designated member of the Authority's Board of Directors. The Authority is specifically tasked with supporting transportation-related development, including motor vehicle and pedestrian infrastructure, within its target revitalization area.
The bill explicitly requires the State Treasurer to hold the Suitland Development Authority Fund and invest its money in the same manner as other state funds.

The bill mandates that the Comptroller account for the Suitland Development Authority Fund. Additionally, the Authority is granted exemptions from various state taxes (Sales and Use, Transfer, and Recordation) which the Comptroller normally administers.

The Executive Director of the Maryland Economic Development Corporation (MEDCO) is a designated member of the Authority's Board of Directors, indicating a high level of coordination for economic development projects.
The Governor is responsible for appointing a member to the Authority's Board and possesses the discretionary authority to include an annual appropriation for the Authority in the State budget.

While the bill exempts the Authority from many standard state budget and management laws, DBM remains relevant as the agency overseeing the state's operating budget, into which the Governor may include appropriations for the Authority.
As the Suitland Development Authority is established as an instrumentality of the State, the OAG would typically provide legal counsel and representation for the agency.

The Authority is required to develop a comprehensive neighborhood revitalization plan. MDP provides the technical assistance and policy guidance on land use and sustainable growth that aligns with these planning requirements.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly states that the Authority is subject to the state's Minority Business Enterprise (MBE) Program, which this office monitors and implements across state agencies.

The bill specifically mentions the Authority is exempt from Title 4 of the State Finance and Procurement Article, which governs DGS, highlighting an operational distinction from typical state agencies.
The Authority is specifically exempted from certain provisions of the State Finance and Procurement Article related to the Board of Public Works, defining its administrative independence.
The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in vetting and recommending candidates for the member position on the Authority's Board that is appointed by the Governor.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Board of Contract Appeals
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Although the Authority is largely exempt from General Procurement Law, it remains subject to specific subtitles (like those regarding service contracts) that may fall under MSBCA's jurisdiction for dispute resolution.
MCCR is relevant as it enforces anti-discrimination laws in state contracts, and the Authority is explicitly made subject to the state's MBE procurement requirements.

bill_summary: This bill regulates the extension of credit to players by video lottery operation licensees, requiring the State Lottery and Gaming Control Commission to maintain a central registry of players with approved credit and adopt regulations for player protections. It increases the maximum administrative penalty for gaming and sports wagering violations from $5,000 to $50,000 per violation. The bill also reallocates 1% of fantasy competition and online sports wagering proceeds to the Problem Gambling Fund, prohibits the use of credit cards for online sports wagering, and caps wagers on a single sporting event at $100,000.
responsible_party: State Lottery and Gaming Control Commission
stakeholders: Video lottery operation licensees, fantasy competition operators, sports wagering licensees, and individuals participating in gaming activities.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill increases state revenue by redirecting 1% of total fantasy competition proceeds (previously retained by operators) to the Problem Gambling Fund. For online sports wagering, the bill redirects 1% of proceeds from the General Fund to the Problem Gambling Fund, resulting in a revenue-neutral shift between state funds. Potential revenue from administrative penalties increases significantly as the maximum fine per violation is raised from $5,000 to $50,000. Specific total dollar estimates are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not provided.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency is the primary regulator and implementer of the bill's provisions. It is tasked with adopting regulations for credit extensions, creating a central player credit list, enforcing significantly higher penalties for violations, and managing the distribution of gambling and fantasy competition proceeds.

The bill redirects 1% of fantasy competition and online sports wagering proceeds to the Problem Gambling Fund, which is administered by the Maryland Department of Health to support responsible gambling and treatment services.
The bill alters the distribution of proceeds away from the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund, which supports the state's public education system, to the Problem Gambling Fund.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is affected by the changes in revenue distribution between the General Fund, the Blueprint for Maryland's Future Fund, and the Problem Gambling Fund, which impacts state budget planning.

The Comptroller is the state's chief financial officer and tax collector responsible for managing state revenues and the distribution of funds; the bill changes the allocation of specific gaming-related revenues.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the State Lottery and Gaming Control Commission and would be responsible for advising on the new regulatory framework and enforcement of increased civil penalties.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the annual state budget; the bill impacts state revenue policy and the regulatory duties of agencies within the executive branch.

bill_summary: This bill allows campaign finance entities to use campaign funds for security-related expenditures, such as electronic security systems and personal security services, for candidates, elected officials, their immediate families, and staff. Such expenditures are authorized when a threat arises from the protectee's status or activities associated with the candidate or official. The bill sets a $10,000 lifetime limit on these expenditures per candidate or official, prohibits certain items like firearms, and requires documentation of threats and the eventual return or reimbursement for tangible security items.
stakeholders: Candidates for office, elected officials, immediate family members of candidates or elected officials, campaign staff, and campaign finance entities.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill authorizes campaign finance entities to make security expenditures from their own funds, subject to a lifetime cap of $10,000 per candidate or elected official. It also allows campaign entities to reimburse the State for security goods or services. Because a formal Fiscal Note is not provided with this text, specific aggregate State and local revenue or expenditure estimates are unavailable; however, the bill mandates record-keeping and reporting requirements for the State Board of Elections.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency is the primary regulator of campaign finance. The bill requires the Board to develop forms for reporting security expenditures and documentation for the verification of threats.

As a primary law enforcement agency, it would be responsible for verifying threats that necessitate expenditures. It also provides executive security services for which the state may be reimbursed under this bill.

The OAG serves as legal counsel to the State Board of Elections and law enforcement agencies. It would provide legal guidance on the interpretation and enforcement of these new provisions in the Election Law Article.

This office investigates and prosecutes criminal offenses related to state election laws and would be responsible for investigating potential fraud or misconduct regarding security expenditure reports.

The Governor and executive staff are defined as protectees. The bill allows campaign funds to be used for their security, impacting the administrative and campaign operations for the state's chief executive.
The Lieutenant Governor is an elected official and a protectee. This bill directly authorizes their campaign finance entity to pay for security services under specific threat conditions.
The agency provides security through the Maryland Capitol Police, who may be involved in verifying threats or providing security services that are reimbursable to the state under this act.

The Treasurer is an elected official and protectee. The office also manages the receipt and management of state funds, which would include reimbursements from campaign entities for state-provided security.
Judges are elected officials in Maryland. The AOC supports the judicial branch, and judicial candidates or officials would qualify as protectees who can use campaign funds for security.
As an elected official and protectee, the Comptroller is impacted. The agency also functions as the state's principal revenue collector and would handle reimbursements from campaign entities.
As the state's fiscal agency, DBM oversees budget execution and would be involved in managing the accounting process for campaign reimbursements to state agencies.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Board of Trustees of the Maryland State Retirement and Pension System to identify and divest from investments associated with the government of Israel, including sovereign debt, securities, and assets held in the government. stakeholders: State employees and retirees who are members of the Maryland State Retirement and Pension System, the Board of Trustees of the system, and the government of Israel.

The impact on investment returns is mitigated by provisions that excuse divestment if it violates fiduciary duties or if assets cannot be sold for fair market value.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the Board of Trustees for the State Retirement and Pension System, which this agency administers, to review investment holdings, take divestment actions regarding Israeli investments, and report to the General Assembly.

The State Treasurer serves as a key member of the Board of Trustees for the State Retirement and Pension System and acts as the state's chief financial officer responsible for the management and protection of state funds.
The Comptroller is a principal financial officer of the state and serves as a member of the Board of Trustees for the State Retirement and Pension System.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Board of Trustees and state agencies; they would be responsible for advising on the legal implications of divestment, fiduciary responsibilities, and the liability immunities established in the bill.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits commercial entities, including social media platforms, from publishing or advertising residential property for lease or sale unless they verify that the person offering the property is the legal owner or an authorized agent. Commercial entities are required to maintain these verification records for at least three years and must promptly remove any advertisements found to be in violation. A violation of these requirements is classified as an unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practice under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act.
responsible_party: Office of the Attorney General (Consumer Protection Division)
stakeholders: Commercial entities and social media platforms that list real estate, residential property owners, real estate agents, and prospective renters and homebuyers in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the bill text. However, the bill specifies that violations are subject to the enforcement and penalty provisions of the Maryland Consumer Protection Act, which implies potential revenue from civil penalties and potential expenditures for the Office of the Attorney General to investigate and prosecute violations. Specific dollar estimates for these impacts are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes that a violation of the ownership verification requirements is an unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practice under the Maryland Consumer Protection Act. The Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General is responsible for enforcing this Act and investigating complaints of consumer fraud or deceptive advertising.

stakeholders: Individuals with prior out-of-state or federal sex offense convictions, the Maryland court system, and state correctional facilities.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures may increase due to longer incarceration periods for repeat offenders, as the bill increases the maximum penalty from one year to three years for those with qualifying prior convictions. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill impacts the judicial branch by modifying sentencing criteria for fourth-degree sexual offenses and referencing Maryland Rules for the indictment and trial of subsequent offenders, which the AOC supports through operational and legal guidance.

The bill has a notable fiscal impact by increasing maximum prison sentences from one year to three years for certain repeat offenders, which increases the long-term expenditures associated with the state's correctional system managed by DBM.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency is directly impacted by the increase in maximum incarceration time for repeat offenders, which affects prison population management and the Division of Parole and Probation's supervision caseloads.

As the office overseeing the executive branch and coordinating policy initiatives, the Governor's Office is responsible for the overall strategy regarding public safety and the enforcement of state laws mentioned in the bill.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency is Maryland's primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategies; the bill's changes to sentencing for sex offenders fall directly within its policy development and advisory scope.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill significantly impacts the Office of the Public Defender as it increases potential sentences for their clients and requires additional legal work to verify and contest the validity of out-of-state convictions used for sentence enhancement.
As the primary law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police are relevant to the enforcement and record-keeping associated with the criminal statutes and sexual offenses modified by this bill.

The OAG represents the state in criminal appeals and providing legal counsel on the interpretation of state laws, including how out-of-state crimes are compared to Maryland statutes for sentencing purposes.

bill_summary: This bill requires hospitals to create a safe discharge labor plan before discharging or transferring a patient in active labor, excluding emergency transfers. The plan must include clinical justification, a travel safety assessment, and a signed patient acknowledgement of risks and symptoms. Hospitals must also provide annual staff training on maternal health and racial disparities, maintain records for 21 years, post patient rights, and submit annual reports to the Maryland Department of Health. Noncompliance can result in civil penalties ranging from $5,000 to $25,000 per violation.
stakeholders: Pregnant individuals, hospital staff (obstetric, labor, delivery, and emergency care), and Maryland hospitals.
fiscal_impact_summary: State revenue may increase due to civil monetary penalties of $25,000 for discharge violations and $5,000 for training or record-keeping failures. State expenditures will likely increase for the Maryland Department of Health to oversee compliance and reporting. Hospitals will face increased costs for training, administrative planning, and long-term record retention. Specific total dollar estimates are unavailable as no formal Fiscal Note was provided.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) is the primary regulatory agency identified in the bill. It is responsible for overseeing hospital compliance, investigating violations, imposing civil monetary penalties, referring practitioners to health occupations boards, and compiling annual reports on safe discharge labor plans for the General Assembly.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and the various health occupations boards (such as the Board of Physicians and Board of Nursing) that would be responsible for disciplining practitioners referred under the bill's enforcement provisions.

The Commission is responsible for planning for the state's health system needs and improving access to and quality of care. The bill's requirements for hospital discharge protocols and data reporting on maternal health and adverse events align with the Commission's role in promoting informed decision-making and accountability.

The University System of Maryland, through its medical schools and affiliated teaching hospitals (such as the University of Maryland Medical Center), would be directly impacted by the training requirements, clinical protocol changes, and record-keeping mandates for patients in active labor.

The HSCRC regulates hospital rates and revenues and monitors hospital financial stability. The bill's requirements for annual staff training and administrative record-keeping for 21 years represent additional operational costs for hospitals that may impact their financial oversight and rate-setting considerations.

DBM oversees the state's fiscal planning and budget execution. This bill would have a fiscal impact on the state budget due to the collection of civil monetary penalties and the potential need for additional personnel within the Department of Health to manage the new reporting and enforcement duties.

The Office of Administrative Hearings would be responsible for conducting impartial hearings if hospitals contest the civil monetary penalties or disciplinary referrals imposed by the Department of Health for violations of the safe discharge labor plan requirements.

fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates for revenue or expenditures are unavailable in the provided bill text. The Department of Health is highly relevant as it oversees the state's Medicaid program and the managed care organizations (MCOs) that are required to have a representative in the workgroup. Changing the definition of specialty drugs will significantly impact health policy and pharmacy benefit management under the department's purview.

The Maryland Health Care Commission is responsible for health system planning and promoting informed decision-making regarding the cost and quality of health services, making the definition of specialty drugs a core area of interest for their regulatory and planning functions.
The definition of specialty drugs directly affects the design, cost, and coverage of health plans offered on the Maryland Health Connection, which the Exchange is responsible for administering.

Synopsis: Authorizing a consumer to send certain notice relating to alleged identity theft debt to a creditor; requiring a creditor to conduct a certain investigation following receipt of notice and to provide certain notice or take certain actions under certain circumstances; authorizing a consumer to file a civil action under certain circumstances and authorizing a consumer to demand a jury trial; prohibiting collection of certain debt under certain circumstances; etc.

bill_summary: This bill establishes procedures for consumers to challenge debts resulting from identity theft by providing written notice and evidence to a creditor. Upon receipt of such notice, a creditor must pause debt collection and conduct an investigation within 30 days. If the debt is confirmed as identity theft debt, the creditor must permanently cease collection, dismiss any pending litigation, and notify credit reporting agencies to correct the consumer's records. The bill also authorizes consumers to file civil actions in circuit court for violations, allowing for the recovery of damages, court costs, and attorney's fees.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and the Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Maryland consumers, creditors, debt collectors, and the Maryland court system
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. Potential fiscal impacts include increased administrative and caseload costs for the Maryland Judiciary due to the authorization of new civil actions, as well as operational costs for creditors and debt collectors to comply with the mandated investigation and reporting procedures.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Office of the Attorney General is the primary agency responsible for enforcing Maryland's consumer protection laws. The bill specifically relates to consumer protection regarding identity theft and designates reports made to the OAG as valid evidence. Additionally, the OAG is responsible for issuing 'Identity Theft Passports,' which the bill identifies as a key piece of evidence for consumers contesting identity theft debt.

The bill creates a new civil cause of action that consumers can file in the Circuit Court and explicitly authorizes consumers to demand a jury trial. The Administrative Office of the Courts provides the operational and legal support for the judicial branch and will be responsible for managing the increased litigation and procedural requirements resulting from this bill.

The bill establishes strict requirements for 'creditors,' which includes debt collectors as defined by state law. The Department of Labor is responsible for the licensing and regulation of financial institutions and the debt collection industry in Maryland, making this bill highly relevant to their regulatory oversight of these entities.

The bill relies on police reports and law enforcement records as primary evidence for consumers to assert that a debt is related to identity theft. As the state's primary law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police will be responsible for investigating these crimes and providing the documentation required for consumers to utilize the bill's protections.

Older adults are frequent targets of identity theft. The Department of Aging, which advocates for the rights and well-being of seniors, would be directly interested in these new consumer protections to assist their constituents in resolving fraudulent debt issues.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office coordinates state strategies for public safety and victim services. The bill integrates criminal justice outcomes, such as guilty pleas or convictions for identity theft, as evidence in civil debt disputes, aligning with GOCPP's mission to address crime-related policy and support for victims.

Residents with disabilities can be particularly vulnerable to financial exploitation and identity theft. The department works to ensure programs and protections are inclusive, and would have a role in communicating these new legal rights to the population they serve.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies responsible for implementing and enforcing this legislation, including the Department of Labor and the Maryland State Police, and coordinates the broader policy initiatives related to consumer safety and public peace.

bill_summary: The bill exempts health benefit plans issued through Professional Employer Organizations (PEOs) from certain state requirements applicable to small employer health benefit plans. fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. The bill may have an impact on the administrative oversight responsibilities of the Maryland Insurance Administration and could potentially influence enrollment and carrier participation in the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange's SHOP program.

The Department of Labor regulates Professional Employer Organizations (PEOs) and employee leasing in Maryland. This bill specifically targets health benefit plans issued through PEOs and establishes new definitions and disclosure requirements for these entities.

The Maryland Health Care Commission is responsible for planning health system needs and monitoring the cost and quality of health services. Changes to the regulation and offering of small group health benefit plans fall under its broad mandate to improve access to care.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs

Legislative changes affecting the disclosure of health benefit costs and the structure of employee benefits are highly relevant to the small business community they support.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Maryland Insurance Administration and the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange, and will likely assist in the development of new regulations and the enforcement of the bill's disclosure requirements.

The Department of Health sets broad health policy for the state. While insurance regulation is handled by the MIA, the MDH has a vested interest in the availability and transparency of health benefits for Maryland residents.

The board is authorized to recommend projects that include specific allocations in the State's operating and capital budgets, directly impacting the fiscal planning and supervision roles of DBM.

It also prohibits residential rental property owners and managers from using algorithmic software or data analytics services to coordinate and set rental prices or lease terms across different ownership entities. responsible_party: Maryland Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Maryland consumers, retail merchants, residential rental property owners, property management companies, and developers of algorithmic pricing and data analytics software.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's chief legal officer and primary enforcement authority for the Maryland Consumer Protection Act, the OAG is responsible for investigating and prosecuting the unfair, abusive, or deceptive trade practices defined in this bill regarding algorithmic pricing and rent-setting coordination.

bill_summary: This emergency bill requires the Maryland Public Service Commission (PSC) to develop and implement a successor program to the current net energy metering (NEM) program. It sets a 3,000-megawatt capacity limit for the existing program and a combined 6,000-megawatt cap for both the current and successor programs. The PSC is mandated to conduct a formal proceeding with stakeholder input and submit a report by December 15, 2026, recommending a program structure that balances distributed generation incentives with grid maintenance, ratepayer costs, and energy equity.
stakeholders: Eligible customer-generators (owners/operators of solar, wind, biomass, and other distributed generation), electric utility companies, retail electricity ratepayers, renewable energy industry experts, and consumer advocates.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures will increase for the Public Service Commission to conduct the required proceeding and develop the mandated report by December 2026. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. Long-term fiscal impacts may include changes in state and local electricity expenditures and utility grid maintenance costs depending on the design of the successor program.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary agency responsible for the bill's implementation. It is mandated to develop and implement the successor net energy metering program, conduct a formal proceeding with stakeholders, and report its recommendations to the Governor and General Assembly.

The OPC represents residential utility consumers in proceedings before the Public Service Commission. Since the bill requires the PSC to evaluate ratepayer costs and energy equity in the new program, the OPC's advocacy for affordable and reliable utility services is directly involved.

The MEA coordinates state energy policy and promotes renewable energy. The development of a successor net energy metering program directly impacts the state's renewable energy goals and the distributed generation initiatives that the MEA manages and advises upon.

As the state's green bank, the MCEC facilitates the adoption of clean energy technologies. Changes to the financial structure of net energy metering will affect the economic viability of the distributed energy projects that MCEC helps finance.

Many agricultural operations in Maryland function as 'eligible customer-generators' using solar or biomass systems. The successor program will impact the economic viability of these on-farm renewable energy investments.

DGS manages state-owned facilities and leads sustainability and energy conservation initiatives for the government. As a manager of property that utilizes net energy metering, DGS is an affected customer-generator under the program's changes.

The MDE is responsible for the state's environmental protection and carbon reduction goals. Net energy metering is a key policy tool for promoting renewable energy, which directly supports the agency's mission to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and improve air quality.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Public Service Commission and the Governor. The agency will likely provide legal guidance during the PSC's formal proceeding and the development of the required legislative report.

The bill requires the Public Service Commission to submit a formal report on the successor program to the Governor. The office also oversees the executive branch agencies (PSC, MEA) responsible for the program's policy direction.

USM institutions are significant 'eligible customer-generators' through various campus-based distributed generation projects. Changes to the net energy metering program will impact their energy costs and sustainability targets.

MDOT operates numerous facilities, including airports and transit stations, that may utilize net energy metering. As a customer-generator, MDOT would be impacted by the successor program's tariffs and contracts.
As an independent state university and customer-generator, the university would be impacted by changes to the net energy metering program affecting its facility operations and energy budget.
As an independent public college, St. Mary's may participate in net energy metering for its campus facilities, making the successor program relevant to its operational and utility costs.

The Governor is required to include the specific funding for the program in the annual budget bill and oversees the executive departments responsible for implementation.

The State Treasurer acts as the custodian of the Opioid Restitution Fund and is responsible for holding the fund separately as the source of program financing.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Health and manages the unit responsible for recovering the settlement funds that constitute the Opioid Restitution Fund.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Opioid Restitution Fund Advisory Council is explicitly mentioned in the bill's amendments to the State Finance and Procurement Article as the body that must approve the use of funds for such research studies.

Public research universities within the University System of Maryland, such as the University of Maryland, Baltimore, often possess the neurosurgery programs and research facilities required to be 'eligible research institutions' under the bill.
The Commission coordinates policies and oversight for the Maryland research institutions that would apply for and receive these state clinical research grants.
As a state research university, Morgan State may qualify as an eligible research institution to conduct these clinical trials if it meets the neurosurgery and facility criteria.
OLA would be responsible for performing fiscal compliance audits on the Department of Health's administration and expenditure of the grant funds from the Opioid Restitution Fund.

Synopsis: Requiring a contractor to pay a subcontractor or supplier at least 95% of an undisputed amount to which the subcontractor or supplier is entitled within 10 days of receiving payment from the State.

bill_summary: This bill requires a contractor on a State procurement contract to pay a subcontractor or supplier at least 95% of an undisputed amount owed within 10 days of receiving payment from the State. If payment is withheld, the contractor must provide written notice to the subcontractor or supplier and a copy to the procurement officer, explaining the reason for the withholding.
responsible_party: Maryland State procurement officers and state agencies overseeing procurement contracts
stakeholders: State contractors, subcontractors, and suppliers involved in State procurement projects
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text. The bill regulates payment timelines between private contractors and their subcontractors or suppliers; therefore, specific dollar estimates for state or local fiscal impact are unavailable, though the direct impact on State expenditures is likely minimal.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's central procurement authority, the Department of General Services (DGS) oversees a vast number of contracts and procurement officers who will be responsible for receiving notices when contractors withhold payments from subcontractors or suppliers.

The Maryland Department of Transportation (MDOT) manages extensive capital projects and maintenance contracts involving numerous subcontractors and suppliers. Its procurement officers are directly impacted by the requirement to receive copies of withholding notices.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Small, Minority & Women Business Affairs
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office monitors the State’s socioeconomic procurement programs (MBE, SBR, VSBE). Since subcontractors and suppliers are often small or minority-owned businesses, the prompt payment requirements are central to this agency's mission of ensuring economic opportunities for these entities.

The Maryland Stadium Authority (MSA) manages large-scale construction projects for stadiums and public schools, which rely heavily on subcontractors. The agency's procurement operations must comply with the altered prompt payment standards.

As the state's principal tax collector and bill payer, the Comptroller's disbursement of progress and final payments to prime contractors triggers the 10-day timeline for those contractors to pay their subcontractors and suppliers.

The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) is the principal fiscal agency overseeing budget execution and personnel. It plays a key role in setting statewide procurement policies and fiscal planning affected by this legislation.

The Board of Public Works oversees and approves significant state procurement contracts and expenditures. This bill alters the statutory framework under which those state contracts are administered and enforced.

The University System of Maryland (USM) manages a large volume of infrastructure and service procurement. Its institutions must ensure their contractors adhere to the revised prompt payment and notification requirements for subcontractors.

The IAC oversees public school construction projects across the state. These projects involve complex tiers of contractors and suppliers who are directly affected by changes to prompt payment regulations in state finance and procurement law.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Board of Contract Appeals
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The MSBCA adjudicates contract disputes between the state and vendors. Alterations to payment obligations and dispute notification requirements (such as the 95% threshold) could lead to new administrative cases regarding contract performance and compensation.

The Office of the Attorney General (OAG) provides legal counsel to all state agencies on procurement matters and would be responsible for advising on the interpretation and enforcement of the revised prompt payment statute.

As a member of the Board of Public Works and the state's chief financial agency, the Treasurer's Office oversees the management of state funds and procurement approvals impacted by this regulatory change.

As an independent state agency with its own procurement authority, Morgan State University must ensure that its contractors and procurement officers comply with the new payment and notice standards for subcontractors.

Saint Mary's College is an independent unit of state government that engages in procurement activities; its contractors will be subject to the updated prompt payment regulations mandated by this bill.

Synopsis: Increasing the State minimum wage rate to $18 for calendar year 2028 for large employers and for calendar year 2029 for small employers; and increasing, beginning January 1, 2029, and January 1, 2030, for large employers and small employers, respectively, the State minimum wage rate in effect for certain periods of time based on annual growth in a certain consumer price index, as determined by the Commissioner of Labor and Industry.
Title: Labor and Employment - Minimum Wage - Increase (Maryland Raise the Wage Act)
Status: In the House - First Reading Government, Labor, and Elections

NarrowSubjects.Name: Salaries and Compensation -see also- Overtime; Reimb. Rates
Work, Labor, and Employment -see also- JobTrn; Leave; etc.

bill_summary: The Maryland Raise the Wage Act increases the State minimum wage to $18.00 per hour. For employers with 50 or more employees, the $18.00 rate takes effect January 1, 2028. For small employers, now defined as those with 49 or fewer employees, the $18.00 rate takes effect January 1, 2029. Starting in 2029 and 2030 respectively, the minimum wage will be adjusted annually based on the average percent growth in the Consumer Price Index for the Washington-Arlington-Alexandria metropolitan area, with annual increases capped at 5%.
stakeholders: Maryland employees, private employers, and Maryland State and local governmental units.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note with specific dollar estimates was not provided in the text. However, the bill specifies that 'Employer' includes governmental units, indicating an increase in state and local expenditures for employee wages. Additionally, the Commissioner of Labor and Industry is assigned new administrative duties to calculate and announce annual inflation-based wage adjustments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Commissioner of Labor and Industry, who is a part of this department, is explicitly mandated by the bill to calculate, determine, and announce annual state minimum wage increases based on growth in the Consumer Price Index.

As the principal personnel and fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for the state's personnel policies and budget development, both of which will be significantly impacted by mandatory minimum wage increases for state employees.

The bill has a notable fiscal impact on the department, as it oversees various service providers (e.g., for behavioral health and developmental disabilities) whose labor costs and state-funded reimbursement rates are directly tied to the minimum wage.

This bill is highly relevant to the department's mission of economic development and business retention, as changes to the state minimum wage significantly affect the business environment and labor market competitiveness.
As a major state employer, the University System will experience a significant fiscal impact due to increased wage requirements for a large number of student workers and entry-level staff.
As an independent state agency and employer, the university will face notable fiscal impacts resulting from the requirement to increase wages for its lower-paid staff and student employees.
The college is a state agency that employs many individuals, including student workers, who will be impacted by the higher minimum wage rates established by this bill.
The bill is relevant to the agricultural sector's economic viability, as it impacts labor costs for farming and agribusiness operations that the department is tasked with supporting.

MDOT and its modal administrations, particularly the Maryland Transit Administration, employ a large workforce and utilize contractors whose labor costs will be directly affected by the minimum wage increase.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and proposes the annual state budget, both of which must account for the significant fiscal and policy implications of increasing the state minimum wage.
The board's role in setting the statewide vision for workforce development and aligning it with economic goals is directly impacted by major changes to the state's minimum wage laws.
The board oversees collective bargaining for the public sector; increases in the state minimum wage often directly affect labor negotiations and pay scales for various public employee units.
As the state's chief financial officer and payor of state employees, the Comptroller's office must implement the payroll adjustments necessitated by the minimum wage increases.
The department relies on contracted service providers whose labor costs for providing social services will increase, potentially requiring funding adjustments from the state.
The department oversees programs where local agencies and providers employ aides and support staff at or near the minimum wage, leading to a fiscal impact on service delivery costs.
While local school systems are separate entities, the state minimum wage increase impacts the wages of support staff across the education system which MSDE leads and oversees.

Synopsis: Establishing certain civil penalties for violations of law involving the employment of minors; prohibiting employers from allowing the formation of a certain organization or entity under certain circumstances; authorizing certain private employees to petition the Public Employee Relations Board to resolve certain matters under certain circumstances; prohibiting Executive Branch units from applying for a waiver of the federal Fair Labor Standards Act; etc.

bill_summary: This bill increases labor protections in Maryland by establishing civil penalties for child labor law violations and prohibiting employers from forming certain labor organizations that bypass federal labor laws. It allows private sector employees to petition the State's Public Employee Relations Board to resolve labor disputes when federal oversight by the National Labor Relations Board is absent, delayed, or legally challenged. Additionally, the bill prohibits State Executive Branch units from seeking waivers to the federal Fair Labor Standards Act.
responsible_party: Maryland Public Employee Relations Board and the Commissioner of Labor and Industry
stakeholders: Private and public sector employees, Maryland employers, minors in the workforce, labor organizations, and State Executive Branch agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates new revenue streams from civil penalties: child labor violations may incur fines up to $16,035 (general) or $72,876 (willful/repeated) per violation, directed to the General Fund. Unfair labor practice violations involving private employees can result in penalties of $1,000 per employee, directed to a special fund for the Public Employee Relations Board. The prohibition on Fair Labor Standards Act waivers for State agencies may impact future expenditure flexibility. A formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text, so specific total dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Labor is responsible for enforcing state labor laws. The bill establishes significant civil penalties for child labor violations to be assessed by the Commissioner, a role residing within the Department of Labor, and increases these penalties annually based on the Consumer Price Index.

The bill significantly expands the jurisdiction and duties of the Board to include adjudicating labor relations and unfair labor practices for private sector employees in specific scenarios where the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) is unable to act or federal law is narrowed.

As the state's principal personnel agency, the Department of Budget and Management is impacted by the bill's provision prohibiting Executive Branch units from applying for waivers of the federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA).

The Office of the Attorney General would provide essential legal counsel to the Department of Labor and the Public Employee Relations Board regarding the implementation and enforcement of new civil penalties and the state's assumption of jurisdiction over private sector labor disputes.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates state policy initiatives. The bill restricts the ability of executive branch units to seek federal labor law waivers and involves a major expansion of state regulatory authority over private labor relations.

The bill establishes that orders issued by the Public Employee Relations Board regarding private employees are subject to judicial review in Circuit Court, which falls under the operational oversight of the Administrative Office of the Courts.

Synopsis: Prohibiting tissue banks and hospitals from denying a patient a physician-ordered autologous or directed blood donation under certain circumstances; authorizing a patient or an individual authorized to make medical decisions on a patient's behalf to request an autologous or directed blood donation; and authorizing tissue banks and hospitals to decline a request for a physician-ordered autologous or directed blood donation only under certain circumstances.
Title: Tissue Banks and Hospitals - Autologous and Directed Blood Donations
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/11 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Health -see also- COVID19; EnvHlth; MedCon; etc.
Health Care Facilities -see also- Clinics; Hospices; etc

bill_summary: This bill requires hospitals and tissue banks to permit autologous blood donations (the patient's own blood) or directed blood donations (blood from a specific designated donor) for medical procedures if ordered by a physician and if all safety and regulatory standards are met. It prohibits these institutions from denying such requests solely based on internal policy, though they may decline if compliance is not feasible due to medical, logistical, or regulatory constraints. Hospitals and tissue banks must also provide patients with clear information regarding blood donation options.
stakeholders: Patients, physicians, hospitals, and tissue banks (including blood banks).
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. The bill text indicates that it does not require institutions to establish new donation programs, which may limit direct expenditure increases, though the Maryland Department of Health would be responsible for oversight of these new requirements under existing licensure and permit frameworks.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) is the primary regulatory body for both tissue banks (under Title 17) and hospitals (under Title 19). The bill specifically amends Health-General articles that the Secretary of Health oversees, including the issuance of permits for tissue banks and the regulation of hospital protocols and informed consent standards.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of Health. It would be responsible for advising the Department on the implementation of these new regulations and representing the state in any legal challenges regarding the enforcement of autologous and directed blood donation mandates.

The MHCC is responsible for planning state health system needs and improving access to care. This bill introduces new requirements for facilities to provide information on donation options and ensures patient access to specific medical procedures (autologous/directed donations), aligning with the commission's role in promoting informed decision-making and accountability.

The OAH adjudicates contested cases involving state agencies. If the Department of Health takes enforcement action against a hospital or tissue bank for non-compliance with the new blood donation requirements, the OAH would provide the impartial hearing process for those disputes.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees the Department of Health and ensures that state laws are enforced. The office coordinates policy initiatives that may relate to healthcare access and patient rights as outlined in this bill.

bill_summary: This bill mandates that Maryland local governments provide a property tax credit to disabled veterans and their surviving spouses, changing the credit from an optional local authority to a state-mandated requirement. It expands eligibility to include veterans with a disability rating as low as 20% (previously 50%), provided their federal adjusted gross income is $100,000 or less, and increases the percentage of the property tax credit available based on the veteran's disability rating.
responsible_party: The Mayor and City Council of Baltimore City, and the governing bodies of Maryland counties and municipal corporations.
stakeholders: Disabled veterans with service-connected disabilities of at least 20%, surviving spouses of these veterans, and local Maryland county and municipal governments.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will result in a mandatory decrease in local property tax revenue for counties and municipalities by converting an optional tax credit into a mandate and expanding the eligible population. While specific dollar estimates from a Fiscal Note are unavailable in the provided text, the impact is a mandatory reduction in local government tax collections starting in fiscal 2027.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly impacts the benefits provided to disabled veterans and their surviving spouses by mandating and expanding property tax credits, aligning with the agency's mission to assist veterans in securing benefits.

As the agency responsible for hearing appeals related to property tax assessments and credits, this bill's changes to eligibility and mandatory credit levels will directly affect their adjudicatory workload and procedures.
The Maryland Tax Court serves as the highest level of administrative review for tax disputes, including those related to property tax assessments and credits affected by this legislation.
Public schools are primarily funded through local property taxes; the bill's mandate to increase property tax credits reduces the revenue available to local school systems overseen by the department.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM is responsible for revenue estimation and long-term fiscal planning, both of which are impacted by changes in mandated local tax credits and their fiscal notes.

The bill redefines and expands eligibility for tax relief for disabled individuals, specifically veterans, which intersects with the department's role in coordinating services and policies for Marylanders with disabilities.
The Comptroller functions as the state's chief financial officer and principal tax officer, providing oversight and reporting on changes to state tax laws and revenue streams.

The Governor oversees the executive branch and proposes the state budget; a mandate on local property tax credits affects the overall fiscal landscape and intergovernmental relations managed by the office.
The department supports homeownership and community vitality; increasing tax credits for disabled veterans impacts the affordability and security of housing for a vulnerable population.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and the General Assembly regarding the implementation and enforcement of tax laws and state mandates on local governments.

Synopsis: Repealing the authority of the State Board of Professional Counselors and Therapists to issue a temporary telehealth license; and exempting certain State licensure requirements for certain individuals who are licensed in another state and who provide counseling through telehealth to clients in the State.

Mental and Behavioral Health -see also- Aut; Cogn; Dev; etc.

bill_summary: This bill allows clinical professional counselors licensed in other states to provide telehealth services to their existing clients who have moved to Maryland for up to six months to ensure continuity of care. It repeals the existing authority of the Maryland State Board of Professional Counselors and Therapists to issue temporary telehealth licenses, replacing that regulatory process with a time-limited licensure exemption for qualified out-of-state providers.
responsible_party: Maryland State Board of Professional Counselors and Therapists
stakeholders: Licensed out-of-state clinical professional counselors, Maryland residents who have recently relocated and require continued counseling services, and the Maryland State Board of Professional Counselors and Therapists.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to result in an indeterminate decrease in special fund revenue for the Maryland State Board of Professional Counselors and Therapists due to the repeal of temporary telehealth license fees. This will be partially offset by a reduction in administrative expenditures as the Board will no longer be required to process these license applications. Specific dollar estimates were not provided in the bill text as the associated Fiscal Note was not included.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Health Occupations Article regarding the State Board of Professional Counselors and Therapists, which is a regulatory body within the Department of Health. The department is responsible for regulating health care professionals and overseeing the licensing of clinical counselors.

The Office of the Attorney General serves as the primary legal representative for all state agencies, including the Department of Health and its various licensing boards. They will be responsible for providing legal counsel regarding the new licensure exemptions and the repeal of temporary telehealth licenses.

As an independent regulatory agency within the Department of Health, the MHCC is responsible for health system planning and improving access to care. This bill's changes to telehealth regulations for continuity of care fall within their scope of monitoring health service availability and quality.

The Department of Budget and Management oversees state agency budgets and personnel. The repeal of the temporary telehealth license may impact the revenue generated by the State Board of Professional Counselors and Therapists through application and license fees.

The bill repeals Section 17-304.2, which specifically governed temporary telehealth licenses for out-of-state providers treating students at Maryland institutions of higher education. The commission coordinates policies for these institutions and their students.

The University System of Maryland's student population was a specific focus of the temporary telehealth licensing provision that is being repealed. The system office coordinates services and resources that impact student health and access to out-of-state providers.

As a state-governed university, Morgan State's students were previously eligible for care under the specific temporary telehealth license being repealed. The university has a direct interest in the regulatory changes affecting student access to mental health services via telehealth.

As an independent unit of the state government, the college is impacted by the repeal of the student-specific telehealth licensing provision and the transition to a general 6-month licensure exemption for out-of-state providers.

The OAH adjudicates contested cases for state agencies. If the Board of Professional Counselors and Therapists takes enforcement action against a provider or denies an exemption claim under the new criteria, the OAH would likely handle the administrative appeal.

Synopsis: Providing that a State's Attorney may not enter into a certain plea agreement in a prosecution for certain human trafficking offenses if the victim is a minor; and prohibiting a person convicted of a certain offense against a minor from knowingly operating or entering a certain place for children.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits State's Attorneys from entering into plea agreements that result in the dismissal or nolle prosequi of human trafficking charges involving minor victims. It also prohibits individuals registered as sex offenders for offenses against minors from knowingly entering or operating 'places for children,' defined to include playgrounds, theme parks, and children's museums. Violating the restriction on entering places for children is a felony punishable by up to 5 years in prison and/or a fine of up to $5,000.
responsible_party: Maryland State's Attorneys and the Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
stakeholders: Individuals registered as sex offenders for crimes against minors, Maryland State's Attorneys, and minors and their families in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes a new felony offense, which may lead to an indeterminate increase in state expenditures for incarceration (up to 5 years) and a potential increase in state revenue from criminal fines (not exceeding $5,000 per violation). Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note were not provided in the bill text.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: DPSCS is responsible for the Maryland Sex Offender Registry and the state's correctional facilities. This bill directly impacts the registry by creating a new felony for registered offenders who enter 'places for children' and may increase the prison population due to the new felony classification and the prohibition of plea agreements that dismiss charges.

The bill prohibits State's Attorneys from entering into plea agreements that result in the dismissal of charges for child sex offenses, which directly impacts judicial proceedings and court management of these cases. It also creates a new felony charge that will be adjudicated in the state court system.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Office of the Public Defender
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill restricts the ability of defense counsel to negotiate plea agreements for indigent clients charged with sex offenses against minors. It also creates a new felony for violating location restrictions, which will require legal representation by OPD staff.

As the primary state law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police would be responsible for enforcing the new criminal prohibition against registered sex offenders entering or operating specified 'places for children.'

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and represents the state in criminal appeals. This bill introduces significant changes to plea agreement laws and a new felony, which may require legal interpretation and appellate representation.
DNR manages Maryland's state parks, which frequently contain playgrounds—specifically defined in the bill as a 'place for children' where registered sex offenders are prohibited from entering.

DBM oversees state fiscal planning. The creation of a new felony and the restrictions on plea agreements are likely to increase the length of stay and the overall population in state correctional facilities, leading to a notable fiscal impact on the state budget.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP coordinates state public safety strategies and advises the Governor on criminal justice policy. The changes regarding plea agreements for sex offenders and new registry-related crimes fall within their policy domain.

The Governor oversees the executive branch, including the state agencies responsible for enforcing this law, and is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation that affects criminal law and public safety policy.

Synopsis: Requiring the Maryland Department of Health to develop a certain pamphlet relating to State and national crisis support resources; requiring certain health care providers and representatives of the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner to give the pamphlet to an individual under certain circumstances; and requiring the Department to conduct a review of certain trauma-informed care training.

bill_summary: Tiarra's Law requires the Maryland Department of Health to develop an informational pamphlet regarding the State's Crisis Response System and the 9-8-8 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This pamphlet must be distributed by health care providers and the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner to individuals upon request or in connection with a death, overdose, or behavioral health crisis. Additionally, the Department must review and report on trauma-informed care training for health care providers, focusing on family engagement and post-incident support.
stakeholders: Family members of individuals experiencing overdose or behavioral health crises, health care providers, emergency medical services personnel, and representatives of the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures are expected to increase for the Maryland Department of Health to develop informational pamphlets and conduct a review of trauma-informed care training. Distribution requirements will affect the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner and various health care providers. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the Fiscal Note was not provided.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill focuses on reducing racial inequities in public health and improving economic and social outcomes for families in crisis, which aligns with the Innovation Team's mandate to address child poverty and economic mobility.

MDH is the primary agency responsible for the Crisis Response System. The bill requires the Department to develop the informational pamphlet, conduct a review of trauma-informed care training, and report findings to the General Assembly. It also explicitly requires the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner, an MDH unit, to distribute the pamphlet.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill's requirements for 'health care providers' include emergency medical services providers licensed under the Education Article. MIEMSS oversees and regulates these providers and the statewide EMS network, making them critical to the implementation of the pamphlet distribution and training review.

The bill addresses the practices of first responders during overdose and behavioral health crises. As the state's primary law enforcement agency, MSP personnel frequently interact with families in these scenarios and would be subject to the training reviews and behavioral health coordination requirements.

DBM oversees the fiscal impact on state agencies. The requirement for MDH to develop and distribute new materials and conduct a comprehensive training review will have fiscal and personnel implications managed by DBM.

The bill mandates the Executive Branch to implement new public health protocols and coordinate with national crisis lifelines, which falls under the Governor's role in overseeing state policy and executive agencies.
The bill involves the state's 9-8-8 lifeline and its coordination with 9-1-1 and emergency responders. MDEM oversees the 9-1-1 Board and statewide disaster and emergency response coordination.

The OAG provides legal counsel to MDH and the Chief Medical Examiner regarding the implementation of the new distribution requirements and any potential liability issues related to crisis response resources.

The bill defines 'health care provider' by referencing the Education Article for EMS providers. MSDE also oversees behavioral health and safety programs in schools that may interface with the Crisis Response System.

The review of trauma-informed care training for health care providers may impact the curriculum and continuing education standards for medical and emergency personnel trained at Maryland's higher education institutions.
MDOT agencies like SHA and MTA have first responders who may be involved in behavioral health crises or overdose responses on state property, making them relevant to the training review.

Synopsis: Requiring that the average weekly wages from employments of a covered employee who, at the time of an accidental personal injury or last injurious exposure to an occupational disease, was concurrently employed by more than one employer be combined for purposes of computing the average weekly wages under certain circumstances; and requiring that the Subsequent Injury Fund reimburse an employer for certain compensation paid by the employer to an employee for permanent partial and total disability under certain circumstances.

bill_summary: This bill requires that when a worker who holds multiple jobs is injured or develops an occupational disease that prevents them from working any of those jobs, their average weekly wage for workers' compensation purposes must be calculated by combining the wages from all their employers. It also mandates that the Subsequent Injury Fund reimburse the employer or insurer for the extra benefit costs resulting from including wages from other jobs in the calculation for permanent disability cases.
responsible_party: Maryland Workers' Compensation Commission and the Subsequent Injury Fund
stakeholders: Workers with multiple concurrent employers, workers' compensation insurance carriers, self-insured employers, and the Subsequent Injury Fund.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill requires the Subsequent Injury Fund to reimburse employers or insurers for the portion of permanent disability benefits derived from an employee's concurrent employment wages. This is expected to increase expenditures for the Subsequent Injury Fund. Because the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text, specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the Subsequent Injury Fund to reimburse employers or their insurers for additional weekly compensation resulting from combining a covered employee's wages from multiple concurrent employers for permanent partial and total disability claims.

As the independent agency that administers the state's Workers' Compensation Law and adjudicates claims, the Commission is responsible for implementing the new method of computing average weekly wages for concurrently employed workers and overseeing the reimbursement process from the Subsequent Injury Fund.

The Injured Workers' Insurance Fund (operating as Chesapeake Employers' Insurance Company) is the third-party administrator for workers' compensation claims for State of Maryland employees. It will be responsible for calculating combined wages for state employees with concurrent employment and seeking reimbursement from the Subsequent Injury Fund.

The bill specifically amends Section 9-602(c) regarding the computation of the average weekly wage for individuals engaged for fire fighting by the Department of Natural Resources, ensuring their wages from other employment are factored in according to the new subsection.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, including the State Workers' Compensation Commission and the Subsequent Injury Fund, and represents the state in civil appeals related to workers' compensation claims.

As the central personnel agency for the state, DBM manages state employee benefits and policies; changes to workers' compensation payouts and the resulting fiscal implications for the state as an employer fall under its oversight.

bill_summary: This bill proposes a constitutional amendment to modernize the Maryland Constitution by replacing gender-specific language with gender-neutral terminology. It replaces terms such as 'man' and 'mankind' with 'person' and 'humanity,' and updates masculine pronouns like 'he,' 'him,' and 'his' with gender-neutral alternatives like 'they,' 'them,' 'their,' or specific role titles such as 'the Governor' or 'the Judge.'
responsible_party: The Maryland General Assembly, the Governor of Maryland, and the State Board of Elections
stakeholders: All citizens and voters of Maryland, as well as state government officials and employees whose roles are defined within the Maryland Constitution.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates for state or local fiscal impacts are unavailable as no formal Fiscal Note is provided in the bill text. The primary financial implication of the bill is the administrative cost to the State Board of Elections for preparing and including the constitutional amendment on the November 2026 general election ballot.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill proposes multiple amendments to Article II (Executive Department) of the Maryland Constitution, which governs the powers, duties, and descriptors of the Governor's office.
Article II, Sections 1A, 1B, 21, and 21A are specifically amended to modernize language and descriptors pertaining to the Lieutenant Governor.
Article VI (Treasury Department) is amended to modernize terminology for the Comptroller, and Article II is amended regarding the Governor's examination of the Comptroller's books.
Article VI (Treasury Department) is specifically amended to modernize terminology and duties for the State Treasurer.
Article V is amended to modernize the title and descriptors for the Attorney General. Additionally, the Attorney General is tasked with approving summaries for referendum petitions in Article XVI.
Article II, Sections 22 and 23 are amended regarding the Secretary of State's appointment and duties. The Secretary is also mentioned in Article XVI regarding ballot titles for referendums.
Article IX, Section 2 is amended to modernize the terminology and gendered language specifically describing the Adjutant General's office and duties.
Article IV, Section 41 is specifically amended to modernize descriptors for the Register of Wills.
The bill significantly amends Article IV (Judiciary Department), affecting constitutional language for judges, the Chief Judge of the District Court, and various court clerks.
The bill amends Article I (Elective Franchise) and requires the State Board of Elections to submit the constitutional amendment to the voters in the 2026 general election.
The bill updates the constitutional titles and descriptions of all three members of the Board of Public Works (Governor, Comptroller, and Treasurer).
As the custodian of Maryland's official records and the Constitution, the modernization of constitutional text is directly relevant to their preservation and documentation mission.
Article IX (Militia and Military Affairs) is amended; the National Guard operates under the Adjutant General, whose constitutional description is being modernized.

bill_summary: The Vincent Anthony Fisher III Act narrows the eligibility for individuals to request a reduction in their prison sentences. It specifically targets individuals who were between the ages of 18 and 24 at the time of their offense and have served at least 20 years. The bill adds a list of serious offenses—including various forms of murder, manslaughter, homicide by vehicle, and child abuse resulting in death—that make an individual ineligible to file a motion for a sentence reduction.

bill_summary: The Retail Energy Modernization and Consumer Choice Act authorizes residential electricity and gas suppliers to offer specialized products including time-of-use rates, contracts exceeding 12 months, and energy products bundled with emissions-free certificates or distributed energy resources.
