stakeholders: Residential electricity and gas customers, energy suppliers, electric and gas utility companies, and distributed energy resource aggregators.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text. However, the bill imposes administrative and regulatory mandates on the Public Service Commission to develop new rules by 2027 and requires electric and gas companies to implement consolidated billing and nondiscriminatory interconnection procedures, which likely involve significant implementation and operational costs.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission (PSC) is the primary regulatory body for electricity and retail gas supply in Maryland. The bill explicitly requires the PSC to adopt several sets of regulations, including those for consolidated billing, accounts receivable purchase protocols, cybersecurity standards, and interconnection procedures for distributed energy resources.

The Office of the People's Counsel is the statutory advocate for residential utility consumers in Maryland. Since this bill directly alters the pricing, terms, and consumer protection regulations for residential electricity and gas supply, the agency will be heavily involved in the resulting Public Service Commission proceedings.

The Maryland Energy Administration (MEA) advises on state energy policy and manages renewable energy programs. The bill's provisions regarding 'green power' products, emissions-free energy certificates, and distributed energy resources align closely with MEA's mission to promote renewable energy and efficiency.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Public Service Commission and enforces state consumer protection laws. The bill introduces new consumer protection rules and exemptions for energy marketing that may require legal interpretation or enforcement action by the OAG.

The Department of General Services is mentioned specifically in the bill as being exempt from certain regulations regarding residential electricity and green power sales, maintaining its current authority under existing law to manage certain energy sales and procurement.

The bill requires the Public Service Commission to establish cybersecurity standards and information exchange protocols for electricity suppliers and distributed energy resource aggregators, which falls under the broader expertise and strategic mandate of the Department of Information Technology.

The bill defines and regulates 'emissions-free energy' and products related to reducing greenhouse gas emissions. As the agency responsible for environmental protection and air quality, MDE is relevant to the environmental standards applied to 'green' energy products.

bill_summary: House Bill 1495 requires the Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration to issue only one registration plate for all classes of vehicles, rather than two. The bill specifies that registration plates must be displayed on the front of tractors and on the rear of all other vehicles. It also prohibits historic vehicle owners from knowingly violating their registration terms, with a warning system established for first-time offenses.
stakeholders: Maryland vehicle owners, the Motor Vehicle Administration, and state and local law enforcement agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to result in a decrease in state expenditures for the Motor Vehicle Administration due to reduced costs associated with manufacturing and distributing one registration plate per vehicle instead of two. There may also be an impact on law enforcement efficiency and revenue from automated license plate readers. Specific dollar estimates are not provided in the bill text, and a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided document.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates the MVA to change its vehicle registration process by issuing a single registration plate instead of two for all vehicle classes, and requires the MVA to verify compliance for Class L vehicle violations.
As the parent agency of the MVA, MDOT is responsible for the overall management of the state's transportation network and the administrative transition to a single-plate system.

The bill impacts law enforcement's ability to identify vehicles from both the front and rear. It also explicitly requires police officers to report violations of the new registration requirements to the MVA.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: License plates in Maryland are typically manufactured by Maryland Correctional Enterprises, a program within DPSCS. Moving from two plates to one for most vehicles would significantly reduce production volume and operational revenue/expenditure for this unit.

The MDTA operates toll facilities that utilize license plate recognition cameras for enforcement and billing; the removal of front license plates on many vehicles may impact the efficiency and accuracy of these systems.
The bill establishes a new violation and warning system for Class L (historic) vehicles, which must be tracked through the state's judicial and administrative hearing systems.

The transition to a single-plate system will have a notable fiscal impact on the state budget, specifically regarding reduced manufacturing costs and potential changes in registration fees or processing costs managed by DBM.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the MDOT and MVA and would be responsible for advising on the regulatory changes required to implement a single-plate system and enforcing the new Class L vehicle terms.

Synopsis: Altering the definition of "vulnerable individual" to exclude an individual who is riding a motorcycle for purposes of the prohibition on causing the serious physical injury or death of a vulnerable individual as a result of operating a motor vehicle in violation of certain rules of the road.
Title: Vehicle Laws – Causing Serious Injury or Death of Vulnerable Individual
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/12 at 1:00 p.m.

BroadSubjects.Name: Vehicle Laws - Rules of the Road

NarrowSubjects.Name: Death -see also- Homicide; Murder; Wrongful Death

bill_summary: This bill alters the definition of 'vulnerable individual' under Maryland's vehicle laws by excluding motorcyclists. By removing motorcycles from this category, the specific criminal and administrative penalties for causing serious physical injury or death to a vulnerable individual while violating traffic laws—which include mandatory court appearances, fines up to $2,000, community service, and driver's license suspensions—will no longer apply to incidents involving motorcyclists.
responsible_party: Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA) and the Maryland Judiciary
stakeholders: Motorcyclists, motor vehicle operators, the Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration, and the Maryland court system
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not included in the provided text, so specific aggregate dollar estimates are unavailable. However, the bill may result in an indeterminate decrease in State fine revenue (up to $2,000 per violation) and a reduction in administrative expenditures for the Motor Vehicle Administration due to fewer mandatory license suspension proceedings.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the agency overseeing the state's transportation network and the Transportation Article of the Maryland Code, MDOT is directly responsible for the policy and implementation of vehicle laws. The bill specifically alters definitions within the rules of the road that MDOT and its administrations manage.

The bill explicitly tasks 'The Administration' (referring to the MVA) with the mandatory suspension of driver's licenses for individuals convicted of causing serious injury or death to a vulnerable individual. The MVA will need to update its systems and procedures to reflect the change in definition for 'vulnerable individual.'

The bill mandates that individuals charged with this violation must appear in court and may not prepay fines. It also outlines specific sentencing options for the court, including fines, community service, and safety courses, directly affecting judicial operations and case processing.

As the primary law enforcement agency for enforcing motor vehicle laws and ensuring traffic safety on state highways, MSP officers would be responsible for charging individuals under this specific section of the Transportation Article. Changes to the definitions of offenses impact enforcement protocols and reporting.

OAH provides an impartial hearing process for contested cases involving state agencies, including driver's license suspensions initiated by the MVA. Mandatory license suspensions resulting from this bill could lead to an increase in administrative hearings.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the MDOT, MVA, and MSP, and would be responsible for advising these agencies on the legal interpretation and enforcement of the revised definition of 'vulnerable individual' and the associated penalties.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This office coordinates public safety strategies and advises the Governor on criminal justice matters. Changes to vehicle laws involving serious injury or death fall under their policy purview regarding public safety and recidivism reduction.

Synopsis: Requiring Charles County to establish a rent increase limit for units occupied by seniors that is no greater than the Consumer Price Index; and defining "senior" as an individual who is at least the age required to receive full Social Security retirement benefits.

bill_summary: This bill requires Charles County to establish an annual rent increase limit for rental units occupied by seniors, defined as individuals who have reached the age for full Social Security retirement benefits. The annual increase is limited to the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for the Washington Metropolitan Area.
stakeholders: Senior renters and landlords in Charles County.
fiscal_impact_summary: Charles County is required to implement rent stabilization for seniors, likely resulting in administrative expenditures for the county. Since no formal Fiscal Note was provided with specific figures, the exact financial impact is indeterminate.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill directly concerns the economic security and housing stability of Maryland's senior population. As an agency dedicated to protecting the rights and improving the quality of life for older adults, the Department of Aging is heavily impacted by policies that regulate senior-specific housing costs.

The Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development is the state's primary agency for affordable housing. While this bill mandates action at the county level, state housing policy and community vitality are directly influenced by rent stabilization measures, making this relevant to the agency's overarching mission.

The Office of the Attorney General (OAG) provides legal counsel to state agencies and enforces consumer protection laws. Changes to rental property law in the Real Property Article require legal oversight, interpretation, and potentially enforcement by the OAG to ensure compliance with state standards.

Landlord-tenant disputes and eviction proceedings are adjudicated within the state's District Courts. Establishing a specific rent increase limit for a specific demographic in Charles County creates a new legal standard that judges and court personnel must apply during judicial proceedings.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and policy initiatives. As this bill requires the Governor's signature to become law and involves a local mandate that could set a precedent for statewide senior housing policy, it is relevant to the executive's policy coordination role.

Synopsis: Prohibiting the Board of License Commissioners for Wicomico County from issuing a Class A beer, wine, and liquor license to a specific establishment with retail floor space of more 3,500 square feet; prohibiting the Board from issuing a Class A beer, wine, and liquor license for use at certain restaurants, subject to certain grandfather provisions; and prohibiting the Board from issuing more than one Class A beer, wine, and liquor license for use in a councilmanic kjdistrict.

bill_summary: This bill modifies the regulations for Class A beer, wine, and liquor licenses in Wicomico County. It prohibits the issuance of these licenses to establishments with more than 3,500 square feet of retail floor space and restricts the issuance of new licenses to restaurants (Class B license holders) beginning July 1, 2026, while allowing existing licenses to be renewed. Furthermore, it limits the distribution of these licenses to no more than one per councilmanic district and maintains a countywide cap of three total licenses.
responsible_party: Board of License Commissioners for Wicomico County
stakeholders: Current and prospective alcoholic beverage license holders in Wicomico County, including restaurant owners and retail establishment operators.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill maintains an annual license fee of $4,400 and keeps the maximum number of Class A beer, wine, and liquor licenses in Wicomico County at three. While it introduces new restrictions on establishment size and eligibility for restaurant owners, the cap on the total number of licenses suggests the overall fiscal impact on license revenue will be negligible. Specific dollar estimates for the net fiscal impact are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is the primary state agency responsible for regulating the alcohol industry and collecting state revenues. This bill directly alters alcoholic beverages licensing requirements, fees, and operational restrictions for Wicomico County, which falls under the Comptroller's regulatory and oversight purview.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to all state agencies, boards, and commissions. This includes the Board of License Commissioners for Wicomico County, which will require legal guidance on implementing the new prohibitions and grandfathering provisions established by this bill.

The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in appointing individuals to state boards and commissions, including the Board of License Commissioners for Wicomico County, which is the body tasked with issuing the licenses regulated by this bill.

The Department of Budget and Management oversees the state's budget and revenue estimation. As this bill modifies license fees ($4,400 per license) and the number of available licenses, it may have a fiscal impact on state or local revenues that DBM monitors.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch, including the local boards of license commissioners created under state law, and holds the ultimate authority for appointing the members who will enforce these new regulations.

bill_summary: This bill increases the maximum deposit amount a home improvement contractor may receive before or at the time of signing a contract from one-third to one-half of the total contract price.
responsible_party: Maryland Home Improvement Commission (Maryland Department of Labor)
stakeholders: Home improvement contractors and Maryland residential property owners
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill increases the maximum allowable deposit for home improvement contracts from one-third to one-half of the contract price. No specific state or local fiscal impact, such as revenue changes or expenditure mandates, is described in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Labor houses the Maryland Home Improvement Commission, which is responsible for the licensing and regulation of home improvement contractors. This bill directly amends the regulatory limits on deposits for home improvement contracts, making the Department of Labor the primary agency responsible for implementation, regulatory updates, and enforcement.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Department of Labor and its regulatory commissions. Additionally, the OAG enforces state consumer protection laws; changing the legal limit for home improvement deposits impacts how the Consumer Protection Division investigates and prosecutes potential violations.

The Office of Administrative Hearings adjudicates contested cases for state agencies, including disciplinary actions and disputes involving home improvement contractors and the Maryland Home Improvement Commission. Changes to the statutory cap on deposits would be a factor in administrative law proceedings regarding contract compliance.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a unit of State government that is required by law to adopt regulations to implement a program that is authorized or required under State law from collecting any fee or other payment under that program until the unit finalizes adoption of the regulations that implement the program.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits a unit of State government from collecting any fee or payment under a program authorized or required by law until the unit has finalized the adoption of the regulations necessary to implement that program.
stakeholders: Maryland State agencies and any individuals or entities required to pay fees or payments under State programs.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill could result in an indeterminate delay or loss of revenue for State agencies if required regulations are not finalized before program implementation. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's principal tax collector and regulator of the alcohol, tobacco, and motor fuel industries, the Comptroller's ability to collect fees and revenues is directly contingent on the finalization of the regulations governing those programs.

The Department of Labor licenses and regulates a vast array of professions and industries; this bill would prohibit the agency from collecting any licensing or regulatory fees until the required program regulations are officially finalized.

The Maryland Department of Health regulates health care professionals and facilities and administers the Medicaid program; this bill would halt fee collection for any health-related programs that do not have finalized implementing regulations.

The MDE issues numerous permits for pollution control and water systems; this mandate would prevent the agency from collecting permit fees until all regulations for the corresponding environmental programs are fully adopted.

MDOT and its administrations, particularly the Motor Vehicle Administration (MVA), collect extensive fees for driver licensing and vehicle registration; this bill prevents such collections until the underlying program regulations are complete.

The MCA is responsible for licensing and compliance within the cannabis industry; this bill would restrict the agency from collecting business licensing fees until its regulatory framework for medical or adult-use programs is fully finalized.

The MIA licenses insurance companies and producers and monitors financial solvency; this bill would prevent the collection of licensing or regulatory fees until the specific program regulations are finalized.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland State Lottery & Gaming Control Agency
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The agency regulates commercial gaming and sports wagering, which involves significant licensing fees; this bill would require finalized regulations as a prerequisite for collecting those payments from operators.

The DNR collects fees for hunting, fishing, and boating licenses and manages public lands; this bill would necessitate that all program regulations be finalized before these revenue-generating activities can proceed.

The MDA conducts regulatory activities involving pesticides, animal health, and food quality that often require fees; this bill would prohibit these collections until all necessary implementing regulations are finalized.

The PSC sets rates and regulates utilities and passenger transportation; this bill would prevent the Commission from collecting fees from utility companies or carriers until the specific program regulations are fully adopted.

The MSP handles various licensing duties, including handgun permits and specialized law enforcement certifications; this bill would stop the collection of any associated fees until the regulations for those programs are finalized.

MSDE certifies educators and licenses child care providers; this legislation would prohibit the collection of certification or licensing fees until the corresponding program regulations are finalized.

The Secretary of State manages the registration of charitable organizations and notaries public; this bill would prevent the collection of these registration fees until the governing regulations are finalized.

As the legal counsel for all state agencies, the OAG would be responsible for advising units on the legal finality of their regulations and ensuring compliance with this new restriction on fee collection.

As the state's principal fiscal agency, DBM would need to monitor the potential loss or delay of revenue across various state agencies if regulations are not finalized in a timely manner as required by this bill.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development to establish and manage a tiered certification program for all types of homeless shelters, including year-round, transitional, and emergency facilities. The Department must develop specific certification requirements, conduct on-site monitoring, and implement a grievance process for residents. Homeless shelters are prohibited from operating without a certificate after assigned deadlines, and the Department is authorized to issue penalties for non-compliance.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD)
stakeholders: Homeless shelter operators (including year-round, transitional, and emergency shelters), homeless individuals, shelter residents, and the Department of Housing and Community Development.
fiscal_impact_summary: The formal Fiscal Note is absent from the provided text, so specific dollar estimates are unavailable. However, the bill creates state expenditures for the Department of Housing and Community Development to staff and manage the new certification program, conduct on-site monitoring, and handle resident grievances. The bill also authorizes penalties for shelters operating without certification, which may generate indeterminate state revenue.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly mandates this department to establish, manage, and enforce a new state-wide homeless shelter certification program, including tiered classification, on-site monitoring, and the implementation of a grievance process.

As the state's primary provider for individuals facing homelessness and economic need, DHS manages the social services and local department networks that frequently interact with and utilize these shelter facilities.
The bill regulates 'medical or specialized care shelters' which provide health care and assistance with activities of daily living, areas typically overseen by the Department of Health.
The legislation defines and includes 'disaster or hazard emergency shelters' which are integral components of county emergency operations plans coordinated by MDEM.
The OAG will be required to provide legal counsel for the drafting of certification regulations and the enforcement of penalties, suspensions, and revocations.
DBM will oversee the fiscal and personnel adjustments necessary to fund the new certification, monitoring, and grievance functions within DHCD.
OAH would be responsible for adjudicating appeals from shelter operators regarding the denial, suspension, or revocation of certifications.
This office focuses on reducing child poverty and youth homelessness, both of which are directly impacted by the availability and standards of certified shelters.
Veterans are a significant portion of the homeless population; this agency advocates for their access to supportive services which are defined and regulated under the new certification system.
The department's focus on accessible housing and community living is relevant to the bill's requirements for specialized care shelters and the mobility needs of shelter residents.

bill_summary: This bill legalizes the purchase, possession, and use of consumer fireworks by individuals at least 18 years old, subject to specific safety and location restrictions, such as distances from structures and livestock. It requires retailers to be licensed by the State Fire Marshal and operate from specific permanent or temporary structures. The bill allows counties to opt out of the legalization and establishes a 16% sales and use tax on consumer fireworks, with the resulting revenue distributed among the 9-1-1 Trust Fund, the Senator William H. Amoss Fire, Rescue, and Ambulance Fund, and the State's General Fund.
responsible_party: State Fire Marshal and Comptroller of Maryland
stakeholders: Individuals aged 18 and older, fireworks retailers, livestock owners, county governments, and emergency service providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes a 16% sales and use tax on consumer fireworks beginning in fiscal year 2027. Revenues from this tax are distributed quarterly: 31% to the 9-1-1 Trust Fund, 31% to the Senator William H. Amoss Fire, Rescue, and Ambulance Fund, and 38% to the State General Fund. While a specific total revenue estimate is not provided in the bill text, the act creates a new revenue stream for state emergency funds and the general fund. Counties may see fiscal impacts related to enforcement or the decision to opt out of the bill's provisions.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes a new 16% sales and use tax on consumer fireworks. As the state's principal tax collector, the Comptroller is responsible for collecting this revenue and quarterly distributing it to the 9-1-1 Trust Fund, the Senator William H. Amoss Fund, and the General Fund.

The Office of the State Fire Marshal is a division of the Maryland State Police. The bill grants the Fire Marshal the authority to license permanent and temporary structures for firework sales, issue permits for display fireworks, and seize fireworks sold in violation of the law.

The Department of Emergency Management oversees the Maryland 9-1-1 Board and the Senator William H. Amoss Fire, Rescue, and Ambulance Fund. Both entities receive significant new funding (31% each) from the fireworks sales tax established by this bill.

DBM is responsible for revenue estimation and fiscal planning. This bill introduces a new tax stream and mandates specific distributions and a $16.5 million annual appropriation to the Amoss Fund, impacting state budget execution.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive agencies (MSP, MDEM, DBM) implementing these regulations and is responsible for proposing the annual state budget, which must include the mandated appropriations for the Amoss Fund.

The bill contains specific provisions regarding the discharge of fireworks near animal housing facilities and livestock, requiring written notification to owners or managers, which aligns with the department's role in protecting animal health and supporting the agricultural community.

As the state's chief financial agency, the Treasurer's Office is responsible for managing and protecting state funds, including the 9-1-1 Trust Fund and the Amoss Fund, which are recipients of the new tax revenue.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the State Fire Marshal, the Comptroller, and MDEM regarding the implementation and enforcement of the new firework regulations and tax distribution requirements.
The OAH would adjudicate any contested cases resulting from the State Fire Marshal's decisions to deny, suspend, or revoke licenses for permanent or temporary firework sales structures.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the State Fire Prevention Commission to adopt regulations to carry out the provisions related to consumer and display fireworks.

The bill establishes several misdemeanor offenses related to the illegal sale, possession, or discharge of fireworks, which will fall under the jurisdiction of the state court system managed by the AOC.
The use of consumer fireworks presents a fire risk to public lands, including state parks and forests managed by the DNR, particularly during periods of high fire danger.

The bill prohibits the discharge of consumer fireworks from within, into, or at motor vehicles, watercraft, and aircraft, which are modes of transportation regulated or operated by MDOT administrations.

stakeholders: Residents, property owners, and developers in Carroll County, as well as the Carroll County government.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill authorizes the establishment of district planning commissions, which would likely result in indeterminate local expenditure increases for Carroll County for administrative and staffing support. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the provided text did not include a formal Fiscal Note.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives, and the Governor is responsible for signing or vetoing legislation such as this bill concerning Carroll County planning.

Carroll County is a significant agricultural region; planning and zoning regulations developed by district commissions directly affect the department's mission to protect environmental resources and promote the economic viability of farming.
Land use planning and zoning are essential components of economic development and business attraction, which are primary responsibilities of the Department of Commerce.
Planning for the orderly growth of districts and the provision of facilities includes the oversight and leadership of public education systems, which fall under this department's purview.
District planning for growth and facilities involves environmental quality standards and infrastructure oversight, such as public water and sewer systems, which are regulated by MDE.

The bill's focus on zoning, subdivisions, and orderly growth directly intersects with the department's mission to ensure residents have access to safe, affordable housing and to support community revitalization.
Local land use planning and district zoning impacts the conservation and management of Maryland's natural resources, parks, and waterways within Carroll County.

As the principal agency for land use planning and policy guidance, this department oversees the implementation of the Land Use Article, which this bill proposes to amend to authorize new planning commissions.
The creation of district planning commissions to oversee growth and facilities affects the state's transportation network and the management of state highways in Carroll County.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the General Assembly and state agencies regarding the implementation and legal sufficiency of new land use and local government laws.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Council on the Chesapeake Bay
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The council advises on watershed restoration strategies, which are influenced by changes in local planning and zoning structures that impact the Chesapeake Bay's health.
The commission oversees the planning and funding of public school construction projects, which are directly impacted by local district planning for community growth and facilities.
As the custodian of state records and publisher of the Maryland Manual, the Archives is responsible for recording state laws and updating information regarding new local government bodies.
The bill's provision for district planning of facilities and services overlaps with the commission's regulation of public utilities, including water and sewage disposal.
The council advocates for the unique interests of rural counties like Carroll, focusing on agricultural sustainability, economic development, and resource management.
This multi-agency initiative relies on coordinated local planning to achieve statewide goals for sustainable development, community revitalization, and environmental protection.

bill_summary: This bill requires the State Highway Administration to prioritize funding for the construction and reconstruction of sidewalks and bicycle pathways that are part of, or adjacent to, highways subject to a complete streets policy or a Vision Zero program. It establishes that local governments must request funding through annual priority letters for inclusion in the Consolidated Transportation Program and adjusts cost-sharing ratios between the State and local governments for projects in sustainable communities and priority funding areas.
stakeholders: Local governments, pedestrians, cyclists, and the Maryland Department of Transportation.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill alters the funding and cost-sharing framework for sidewalk and bicycle pathway projects. Specifically, it allows the State to fund 100% of costs in sustainable communities or for projects addressing substantial safety risks (including right-of-way acquisition). In priority funding areas where local contributions are insufficient, the State may cover 75% of costs while the local government covers 25%. While these provisions change the allocation of expenditures between State and local entities, specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly tasks the Administration (SHA) with prioritizing funding for sidewalks and bicycle pathways based on Complete Streets and Vision Zero programs. SHA is also responsible for the construction, reconstruction, and cost-sharing of these facilities along urban highways.

As the parent agency of SHA, MDOT oversees the Consolidated Transportation Program (CTP), which is the vehicle through which local governments must now request sidewalk and pathway funding as mandated by this bill.

The bill uses the designation of 'priority funding areas'—which are overseen and managed by the Department of Planning—as a primary criterion for determining state-local cost-sharing ratios for sidewalk and bicycle pathway projects.

The bill utilizes the definition of 'sustainable communities' from the Housing and Community Development Article to determine when the State may fund 100% of the cost for sidewalk and bicycle pathway construction.
The bill alters the funding prioritization and state-local cost-sharing formulas for transportation infrastructure, impacting the state budget execution and long-term fiscal planning managed by DBM.

bill_summary: This bill adds correctional officers as eligible recipients for the Maryland Loan Assistance Repayment Program and the Maryland Police Officers and Probation Agents Scholarship Program, providing them with financial assistance for tuition and loan repayment in exchange for their service.

fiscal_impact_summary: The bill expands eligibility for two higher education financial assistance programs to include correctional officers, which will likely increase state general fund expenditures. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because the formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the bill text.

fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the text. The Office of the Attorney General enforces state consumer protection laws. Regulating and capping the fees that homeowners associations and condominium associations can charge new owners is a consumer protection matter within the OAG's jurisdiction.

Disputes regarding the legality or amount of capital contribution fees under these new statutory limits would be adjudicated in the Maryland court system, which this agency supports operationally and legally.

This agency is dedicated to ensuring affordable homeownership. Statutory limits on the financial burden for new owners in condominiums and homeowners associations directly relate to the department's mission of maintaining housing accessibility and affordability.

Synopsis: Requiring a mortgage servicer that receives certain insurance proceeds to deposit the proceeds into a certain interest bearing account; requiring a borrower to elect the use of the interest earnings on the insurance proceeds; requiring certain interest earnings to begin accruing by a certain date; authorizing a mortgage servicer to charge a fee for disbursement of interest earnings subject to certain limitations; and requiring certain methods and procedures for disbursement of insurance proceeds and interest earnings.

responsible_party: Office of the Commissioner of Financial Regulation
stakeholders: Mortgage servicers, borrowers with insurance claims for property damage, and federally insured banking institutions.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text. The bill creates a financial mandate for mortgage servicers to pay at least 2% interest on insurance proceeds to borrowers. The Office of the Commissioner of Financial Regulation would be responsible for oversight and enforcement, which may result in minor administrative costs, while borrowers receive a direct financial benefit from the interest earnings.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Financial Institutions Article of the Maryland Code regarding mortgage servicers. The Office of the Commissioner of Financial Regulation, which is located within the Department of Labor, is the primary regulatory and licensing authority for mortgage servicers and is responsible for enforcing the provisions of the subtitle being amended.

The OAG serves as the legal counsel to the Department of Labor and the Commissioner of Financial Regulation. Additionally, the OAG’s Consumer Protection Division may be involved in addressing consumer complaints or enforcement actions regarding the handling of insurance proceeds by mortgage servicers.

The bill impacts residential real estate and owner-occupied dwellings in Maryland. DHCD is the principal agency for homeownership and community development, and these regulations affect the financial stability and recovery of homeowners following property damage.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees the Department of Labor and signs the proposed annual budget which would include any fiscal impacts for the Commissioner of Financial Regulation to implement this new oversight.

Synopsis: Altering and establishing certain requirements related to the prevention, detection, and enforcement of unemployment insurance fraud in the State, including requirements related to the use of multifactor authentication under certain circumstances, reviews of claims for benefits, and the submission of proof of identification by claimants; authorizing the Maryland Department of Labor to recover overpaid benefits through State income tax withholding; etc.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Crimes and Punishments -see also- Penalties and Sentnc; etc.

bill_summary: This bill establishes comprehensive requirements for the prevention, detection, and enforcement of unemployment insurance (UI) fraud. It mandates the use of multifactor authentication for the Department of Labor's online UI portals, requires claimants to provide specific forms of identification, and necessitates mandatory reviews of claims involving duplicate bank accounts, addresses, or out-of-state IP addresses. Additionally, the bill increases the monetary penalty for fraud from 15% to 20%, extends UI disqualification for fraudulent claimants to 10 years, allows for the recovery of overpayments through State income tax withholding, and requires the referral of fraud cases to law enforcement. It also mandates the termination of government employees or contractors found to have committed UI fraud.
stakeholders: Unemployment insurance claimants, employers, the Maryland Department of Labor, law enforcement agencies, and government employees or contractors.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to result in an indeterminate increase in State revenue due to the increased fraud penalty (from 15% to 20%) and the authorization to recover overpaid benefits through State income tax refund withholding. State expenditures will increase to implement technological requirements like multifactor authentication, conduct mandated claim reviews, and fulfill new annual reporting obligations. Local fiscal impact may include increased costs for county law enforcement agencies tasked with investigating and prosecuting referred fraud cases. Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note were not available in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of Labor is the primary agency responsible for administering the state's unemployment insurance program. This bill directly mandates new operational requirements for the department, including multifactor authentication, specific claim review procedures, annual reporting on fraud, and enhanced enforcement and recovery mechanisms.

The bill authorizes the recovery of overpaid unemployment benefits through State income tax withholding and references procedures for withholding tax refunds under the Tax – General Article, which the Comptroller oversees as the state's principal tax collector.

DBM oversees the Central Collection Unit (CCU), which the bill explicitly authorizes to collect unemployment insurance overpayments caused by fraud. Additionally, DBM is the central personnel agency for the state; the bill's mandate to terminate government employees who commit unemployment fraud directly impacts its personnel management and policy duties.

The bill specifies that a final determination of unemployment fraud is grounds for immediate termination of a state employee, notwithstanding any terms of a collective bargaining agreement. As the agency responsible for administering collective bargaining and labor laws for state employees, PERB would be impacted by this statutory override of labor contracts.

The bill requires the use of multifactor authentication for the Department of Labor's publicly accessible websites and online portals. As the agency responsible for the state's information technology strategy and cybersecurity standards, DoIT would likely be involved in the technical implementation and security oversight of these requirements.

The bill discusses 'final determinations' after the exhaustion of administrative appeals. The OAH conducts hearings for contested cases involving state agencies, including the Department of Labor. New fraud review protocols and disqualification criteria would likely result in an increased volume or change in the nature of administrative hearings handled by this agency.

The bill requires the Secretary of Labor to refer final determinations of unemployment fraud to appropriate law enforcement agencies for prosecution. As the primary state law enforcement agency responsible for criminal investigations, MSP is a likely recipient of these referrals.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Labor and the Comptroller. The bill specifically mentions the Attorney General's role in advising on the validity of debts before they are certified for tax refund withholding.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and the Secretary of Labor. The bill requires the Department of Labor to submit an annual report on fraud prevention and enforcement efforts to the Governor.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: GOCPP coordinates the state's criminal justice strategies and manages funds for law enforcement. The bill's emphasis on referring fraud for prosecution aligns with GOCPP's mission to reduce crime and recidivism through interagency collaboration.

Synopsis: Renaming and transferring the State Clearinghouse for Missing Children to be the State Clearinghouse for Missing Persons; requiring the Department of State Police to study the Department's capacity to report about persons who have disappeared from, or are thought to be located in, Maryland to the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System; and requiring the Department to submit its findings to the Governor and the General Assembly by December 1, 2026.

stakeholders: Missing persons, families of missing persons, Maryland law enforcement agencies, and volunteer search organizations.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is absent from the provided text, so specific dollar estimates are unavailable. However, the bill's requirements for the Department of State Police to expand the Clearinghouse's scope and conduct a study suggest potential administrative and operational expenditure increases.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly mandates the Department of State Police to operate the State Clearinghouse for Missing Persons, publish statistics, develop fingerprinting programs, and conduct a study on reporting to the National Missing and Unidentified Persons System.

Expanding the clearinghouse from 'children' to 'persons' includes older adults and seniors, which aligns with the Department's mission to protect and advocate for Maryland's elderly population, particularly those who may go missing due to cognitive conditions.
The expansion of the clearinghouse to include all persons directly involves individuals with disabilities who may be at risk and require coordinated state services for location and recovery.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the primary coordinating body for public safety and criminal justice strategies, this office is relevant to the policy shift of expanding the state's missing persons reporting and tracking capabilities.

The OAG serves as the chief legal representative for the Maryland State Police and would provide legal guidance on the transfer of statutory authority and the regulatory requirements of the new State Clearinghouse for Missing Persons.

Synopsis: Requiring, if a merchant rounds up the price of a cash transaction for a good or service in a certain manner, the merchant to remit to the Comptroller the difference between the total price the customer is required to pay after the rounding occurs and the price before the rounding occurs; and requiring the Comptroller to distribute certain revenue to the General Fund of the State.

bill_summary: This bill requires merchants who round up the total price of a cash transaction to the nearest 5 cents to remit the difference between the rounded price and the original price to the State Comptroller, provided the customer did not consent to the rounding for a donation. The Comptroller is required to distribute this revenue to the State General Fund.
stakeholders: Merchants, cash-paying customers, and the State of Maryland
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will result in an indeterminate increase in State General Fund revenue from remitted cash transaction rounding differences. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable because no formal Fiscal Note was provided with the bill text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the state's chief financial officer and principal tax collector, the Comptroller is explicitly tasked by the bill with prescribing the manner of remittance for the rounded amounts and distributing the collected revenue to the General Fund.

DBM is the principal fiscal agency responsible for estimating revenues and overseeing budget execution; this bill introduces a new revenue stream for the General Fund.
The Treasurer's Office is responsible for receiving and distributing state funds; it would manage the funds collected under this bill once remitted to the General Fund.

The bill impacts every 'merchant' engaged in the sale of goods or services in Maryland. The Department of Commerce, as the primary business development agency, may need to coordinate with the Comptroller to inform businesses of the new regulation.

As the administrative body that hears appeals regarding final decisions of taxing authorities, the Maryland Tax Court would have jurisdiction over disputes between merchants and the Comptroller regarding the remittance of rounded cash transaction differences.

bill_summary: This bill expands existing laws regarding noncompete and conflict of interest clauses to include employees of certain large employers that relocate outside of Maryland. stakeholders: Maryland employees, Maryland employers with more than 30 employees that may relocate out of state, and legal practitioners specializing in employment law.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is absent from the provided text, and specific dollar estimates for revenue or expenditure changes are unavailable. The bill's financial impact is primarily private, affecting the enforceability of employment contracts for relocating businesses. agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Labor is the primary agency responsible for enforcing Maryland's labor and employment laws. This bill directly amends the Labor and Employment Article regarding the validity of noncompete and conflict of interest clauses in employment contracts.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the General Assembly and state agencies on the interpretation and enforcement of state laws. It would likely represent the state's interest in defending the public policy regarding voided noncompete clauses.

The Department of Commerce is Maryland's primary economic development agency. The bill's provisions regarding employer relocation outside the state directly impact the business climate and the agency's mission to retain and expand companies within Maryland.

The Maryland Judicial Branch will be responsible for adjudicating civil disputes where employment contracts containing noncompete or conflict of interest clauses are challenged as null and void under this new provision.

The Governor's Office oversees executive branch policy and legislative initiatives. This bill introduces a significant shift in labor policy by linking the validity of private employment contracts to an employer's relocation status.

MEDCO supports the state's economy by providing services for business retention and expansion. The bill's focus on employer relocation and its legal consequences for employment agreements is relevant to their economic mission.

The board coordinates partnerships and strategies to ensure residents have access to employment. Policies that nullify noncompete clauses promote labor mobility, which is a key interest of the state's workforce strategy.

It also expands the authorized uses of the Strategic Energy Investment Fund to include fuel assistance programs in addition to electric assistance for low-income households.
responsible_party: The Office of Home Energy Programs within the Maryland Department of Human Services
stakeholders: Low-income electric customers (at or below 200% of the federal poverty level), electric utility companies, and residential, commercial, and industrial ratepayers.

This team's mission to enhance economic mobility and reduce child poverty is directly related to the state's strategies for providing energy assistance to low-income residents.
The OAG provides legal counsel to the primary agencies (DHS, PSC, MEA) involved in the administrative transfer and the implementation of the bill's requirements.
The Governor oversees the executive departments involved in this reorganization and is responsible for the state budget that must reflect the transfer of program funding and personnel.

Synopsis: Establishing that a "qualified project" is a certain residential project that has been subject to retaliatory downzoning; requiring a local jurisdiction to allow the density of a certain qualified project to exceed the density otherwise authorized; and permitting a certain qualified project to consist of certain types of developments with certain density limits under certain circumstances.
Title: Land Use - Qualified Project - Retaliatory Downzoning
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/12 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.
Housing -see also- Apartments; Condos; Mobile & Manuf  Homes
Public Officials -see also- Atty Gen; Compt; Coun Admin; etc

bill_summary: This bill defines 'qualified projects' as residential developments targeted by 'retaliatory downzoning'—a situation where local officials publicly oppose a project and subsequently reduce its permitted density in a manner inconsistent with professional recommendations. Local jurisdictions are required to allow these projects to exceed standard density limits, permitting middle housing in single-family zones and significantly increased density in multifamily, mixed-use, and nonresidential zones, provided that 15% to 20% of the units are deed-restricted as affordable for at least 40 years.
responsible_party: Local jurisdictions (Maryland counties and municipal corporations)
stakeholders: Residential developers, local government officials, local planning and transportation departments, and residents in need of affordable housing.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text. Potential financial impacts include increased local administrative costs for processing development applications and changes to local property tax revenue resulting from increased density and mandatory affordable housing requirements.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Land Use Article, which the Department of Planning oversees. The agency is responsible for promoting sustainable growth through comprehensive land use planning and providing technical assistance and policy guidance to local governments, all of which are impacted by new mandates on density and retaliatory downzoning.

The bill mandates density bonuses for residential projects and includes specific requirements for affordable housing units and deed restrictions, directly aligning with this agency's mission to ensure access to safe and affordable housing.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the OAG would be involved in providing legal counsel on the interpretation of 'retaliatory downzoning' and defending the state's authority to override local zoning ordinances in these specific cases.

This multi-agency initiative coordinates efforts across Planning and the Environment to manage land use and sustainable development. The bill's density mandates for 'qualified projects' directly interact with the initiative's goals regarding land use and community revitalization.

The Governor's Office oversees policy initiatives and intergovernmental relations. This bill represents a significant state-level policy intervention into local government zoning authority, a matter of executive branch policy coordination.

DBM is responsible for the state's fiscal planning and would need to evaluate any fiscal note or resource requirements for state agencies tasked with monitoring compliance with these new land use provisions.

The creation of a legal definition for 'retaliatory downzoning' and new density rights is likely to lead to increased litigation between developers and local jurisdictions, impacting the workload of the state's judicial branch.

Synopsis: Altering the triennial assessment cycle for real property for property tax purposes to a 5-year cycle.
Title: Property Tax Assessments - 5-Year Assessment Cycle
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/03 at 1:00 p.m.
bill_summary: This bill alters the assessment cycle for real property in Maryland from a three-year (triennial) cycle to a five-year (quinquennial) cycle. It adjusts the phase-in of property value increases to occur in one-fifth increments over five years, rather than the current one-third increments over three years, and updates related administrative procedures for revaluations and appeals.
responsible_party: Maryland State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT)
stakeholders: Real property owners in Maryland, local governments including Baltimore City and Maryland's 23 counties, and the State Department of Assessments and Taxation.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill extends the real property assessment and phase-in cycle from three to five years. This change will likely result in a delay of property tax revenue growth for both the State and local governments, as value increases will be spread over a longer duration (five years instead of three). Specific dollar estimates for expenditures or revenue changes were not provided in the bill text, and a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the source material.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency is directly responsible for hearing appeals regarding real property valuations. Changing the assessment cycle from 3 to 5 years fundamentally alters their adjudication process, workload timing, and the statutory standards for the cases they review.

As the highest level of administrative review for tax disputes, the Tax Court will be responsible for interpreting and applying the new 5-year assessment cycle rules, phased-in value calculations, and appeal rights established by this bill.

The bill specifically amends Section 8-209 regarding farm and agricultural use land, changing the income averaging period used to determine tax classification from a 3-year to a 5-year period. This directly impacts the department's mission to support the economic viability of farming.

DBM is responsible for state revenue estimation and long-term fiscal planning. Moving from a 3-year to a 5-year assessment cycle will significantly change the timing and volume of property tax revenue projections, which are critical for state budget development.

The Treasurer manages state funds and oversees the issuance of State bonds. State property tax revenues are typically used to pay debt service on General Obligation bonds; changing the assessment cycle affects the predictability and timing of these funds.

The Board oversees significant state expenditures and bond issuances. Changes to the property tax assessment cycle affect the fiscal projections and revenue streams that support the state's capital projects and fiscal integrity, which the Board monitors.

As the state's chief financial officer and a member of the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller oversees state revenues and fiscal policy, both of which are impacted by changes to property tax assessment cycles and phase-in schedules.

The Governor is responsible for proposing the annual state budget and overseeing the executive branch agencies (like SDAT) that implement property tax laws. Changes to the assessment cycle impact the fiscal resources available for executive priorities.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies involved in tax administration and represents the state in civil appeals. This bill introduces new statutory requirements for assessments and appeals that may require legal interpretation or defense.

OLA conducts fiscal compliance audits and performance evaluations of state agencies. They would be responsible for auditing the transition and adherence to the new 5-year assessment cycle by the relevant tax agencies.

Changes to property tax assessment cycles affect the cost of homeownership and the administration of property tax credits, which are relevant to the department's mission of ensuring access to affordable housing.
While most tax disputes are handled administratively, changes to property tax law can result in litigation that eventually reaches the state's court system, requiring judicial branch support.

Synopsis: Altering the definition of "control" of a cannabis business and excluding from the definition certain management services agreements, franchise relationships, and options to purchase; prohibiting the Maryland Cannabis Administration from limiting the acquisition of a certain ownership interest in cannabis businesses; reducing the number of years that a cannabis licensee is prohibited from transferring ownership or control of the license; repealing certain criteria for a certain prohibition on cannabis advertising that targets minors; etc.

bill_summary: The Cannabis Reform and Opportunity Act alters Maryland's cannabis regulations by narrowing the definition of business 'control' to exclude certain management services, franchise agreements, and purchase options. It reduces the mandatory waiting period for transferring cannabis license ownership from five years to three years and relaxes outdoor advertising restrictions, allowing signs and billboards provided they are at least 500 feet from schools, child care centers, and other sensitive locations. Additionally, the bill doubles the maximum fine for unlicensed cannabis sales to $10,000 and establishes that each individually packaged product sold in violation constitutes a separate offense.
stakeholders: Cannabis licensees, business investors, management service providers, the Maryland Cannabis Administration, and unlicensed cannabis vendors.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided. According to the bill text, there is a potential for increased state revenue resulting from the increase in fines for unlicensed cannabis sales from $5,000 to $10,000 and the provision that each individually packaged product is a separate violation. The Maryland Cannabis Administration may also face increased administrative expenditures to process management services agreements and provide advisory opinions on advertisements.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Cannabis Administration is the primary agency responsible for implementing this bill. It is tasked with reviewing and approving management services agreements, providing advisory opinions on advertising compliance, publishing patient and sales data, and adopting implementing regulations.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Maryland Cannabis Administration regarding its regulatory duties. Additionally, the bill references consumer protection laws and franchise relationships, both of which fall under the OAG's enforcement and regulatory purview.

The OAH would be responsible for adjudicating contested cases arising from the Administration's new authority to deny management services agreements or issue adverse decisions regarding advertising compliance.

The bill increases criminal fines for the unlicensed sale of cannabis products and defines each package as a separate violation, which impacts the adjudication of these misdemeanor cases in the state court system.

As the primary state law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police would be responsible for investigating and issuing citations for the unlicensed sale of cannabis products, which are subject to the increased penalties defined in the bill.

The bill regulates advertising that makes therapeutic or medical claims, requiring scientific evidence and side-effect disclosures, which overlaps with the Department's mission to protect public health and safety.

The bill establishes buffer zones for outdoor cannabis advertising near primary and secondary schools as well as child care centers, which are entities under the leadership and oversight of the Department of Education.

The alterations to the definition of 'control' and ownership interest, as well as the changes to license transfer periods, directly affect the economic development and business environment of the state's cannabis industry.

DBM may be impacted by the need for additional personnel or resources within the Maryland Cannabis Administration to handle the review of management agreements and the provision of advertising advisory opinions.
The bill addresses the use of a licensee's trademarks and brands in advertisements; the Secretary of State's office is the custodian of trademark registrations in Maryland.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees the policy initiatives represented in this Act, particularly regarding the regulation of a significant state industry and public safety measures for minors.

bill_summary: This bill increases the maximum value of personal and residential property that a debtor may exempt from court-ordered judgments or during bankruptcy proceedings. It raises exemption limits for household goods, tools of a trade, and motor vehicles, and establishes a new $3,000 exemption for firearms. The bill also provides significantly higher exemption thresholds for individuals who are elderly, disabled, or disabled veterans, including an increase in the bankruptcy homestead exemption to $300,000 for general debtors and $600,000 for elderly or disabled debtors.
stakeholders: Individual Maryland debtors, creditors, elderly individuals, disabled veterans, and individuals with disabilities.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates for state and local fiscal impact are unavailable as the formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. The bill's changes primarily affect the amount of property available for collection in private civil judgments and bankruptcy, though it may require updated administrative procedures for Sheriffs and the Maryland Judiciary.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This bill directly amends the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article regarding exemptions from judgment, affecting court procedures, the issuance of writs of garnishment, and the role of the sheriff in appraising property.
The bill creates specific, higher exemption limits for individuals defined as 'elderly' (60+ years old) regarding motor vehicles and residential property in bankruptcy proceedings.
The bill establishes significant new financial protections and higher exemption thresholds for individuals with physical or mental disabilities regarding motor vehicles and residential property.
The bill explicitly references the Department of Health's rights to claim against retirement plans and its subrogation rights in personal injury and workers' compensation recoveries.

The bill addresses exemptions related to child support and alimony payments and specifies the conditions under which child support arrearages can be collected from a debtor's net recovery in legal claims.
The bill provides specific, increased exemption amounts for household furnishings and goods belonging to 'disabled veterans' as defined by the Tax - Property Article.
The bill alters how workers' compensation indemnity benefits and settlement proceeds are treated during the execution of a judgment, specifically concerning child support arrearages.
The bill significantly alters the exemptions allowed for motor vehicles necessary for a debtor's occupation, trade, or education, which impacts the administration of vehicle-related assets.

As the chief legal officer, the OAG provides counsel to state agencies on changes to the Courts and Judicial Proceedings Article and represents the state in matters involving these statutory exemptions.
The bill clarifies the exemption of assets within qualified retirement plans from the claims of creditors, with specific exceptions for claims made by the Maryland Department of Health.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Maryland Teachers & State Employees Supplemental Retirement Plans
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill impacts the protection of supplemental retirement plan assets (such as 401(k) and 457(b) plans) from creditor claims, which is a core part of the agency's administrative oversight.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill includes specific financial protections for disabled individuals; the agency advocates for the welfare of Maryland's deaf and hard of hearing residents who may be impacted by these changes.
The bill alters exemptions for owner-occupied residential property, mobile homes, and manufactured homes in bankruptcy proceedings, which relates to the agency's mission of ensuring secure housing.
The bill exempts payments under sections 24 and 32 of the Internal Revenue Code (related to child tax credits and earned income credits) from judgment execution.
The bill affects the treatment of money payable in the event of sickness, accident, injury, or death, as well as subrogation rights within health insurance contracts.
While primarily focused on living debtors, these exemption statutes frequently intersect with estate administration and the protection of assets from creditors within the probate process.

bill_summary: House Bill 1521 establishes a State income tax credit to incentivize financial contributions, volunteerism, and the employment of at-risk youth (ages 12 to 25) in designated high-crime or high-poverty zip codes, including all of Baltimore City and Baltimore County. The bill allows for a 50% credit for donations to certified organizations, a $25 daily credit for professional volunteering in schools, and a $1,000 credit per at-risk youth employed for a minimum duration.
stakeholders: At-risk youth, nonprofit organizations, local education agencies, business entities, and individual taxpayers in high-crime or high-poverty areas.
fiscal_impact_summary: State general fund revenues will decrease by an estimated maximum of $10,000,000 annually between fiscal years 2027 and 2033, as the bill caps the total amount of certified tax credits at this amount per taxable year. Although a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text, the bill explicitly limits the Department of Commerce to certifying no more than $10,000,000 in credits each year.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department of Commerce is the primary agency responsible for certifying eligible organizations, establishing the tax credit application process, certifying the credit amounts for taxpayers, and reporting annually to the General Assembly on the program's impact.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The office is explicitly required to consult with the Department of Commerce to certify eligible organizations and adopt regulations, and it serves as the lead agency for the public safety and juvenile crime prevention aspects of the bill.
As the state's chief tax collector, the Comptroller's office is responsible for administering the new income tax credits, processing claims, and managing the fiscal impact on state revenue.

The bill designates local education agencies and public schools as eligible organizations for contributions and volunteerism; it also targets youth who are chronically absent or have dropped out of school, which are metrics tracked by MSDE.

The bill's definition of at-risk youth includes individuals involved in prevention or diversion programs under the Human Services Article, as well as those aging out of foster care or experiencing homelessness, both of which fall under DHS jurisdiction.
The bill specifically targets youth involved in the juvenile justice system for support services, development programs, and employment initiatives to reduce juvenile crime.
The bill provides a tax credit for employers who hire at-risk youth, which directly relates to the Department of Labor's mission of supervising workforce development and enforcing labor laws.
The bill's focus on reducing child poverty, youth homelessness, and improving outcomes for underinvested communities aligns directly with the central mission and the ENOUGH Initiative of this office.
DBM oversees the state's revenue estimations and fiscal planning, which will be impacted by the $10 million annual cap on the tax credits established by this bill.

The bill requires that individuals claiming the volunteer credit must be accompanied by school safety personnel while on school grounds, which falls under the safety standards and personnel oversight of this agency.

The bill targets at-risk youth experiencing homelessness and promotes community revitalization in high-poverty ZIP codes, areas managed through DHCD's community investment and homeless solution programs.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Service and Civic Innovation
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: This agency promotes service and volunteerism to create workforce pathways, aligning with the bill's provisions for professional volunteerism and youth employment credits.

The bill's primary objectives of reducing child poverty and enhancing economic mobility for at-risk youth are the core priorities this team was established to address through novel policy initiatives.
The bill includes faith-based organizations as eligible recipients for supporting at-risk youth, a sector primarily engaged by GOCI through its community and faith-based commissions.

As the administrative support for the Governor, this office oversees the executive branch agencies (Commerce and GOCPP) tasked with implementing the bill and coordinates the broader policy initiative.

Synopsis: Repealing the exemptions for a motor vehicle that is owned by a motor vehicle rental or leasing company or that displays certain registration plates from liability for citations produced as a result of images recorded by a traffic control signal monitoring system or a speed monitoring system.
Title: Traffic Control Signal Monitoring and Speed Monitoring Systems - Exemptions From Liability - Vehicle Rental Companies
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/12 at 1:00 p.m.

BroadSubjects.Name: Vehicle Laws - Rules of the Road

NarrowSubjects.Name: License Plates -see also- Motor Vehicle Registration

bill_summary: This bill repeals the liability exemptions for motor vehicle rental or leasing companies and holders of certain special registration plates regarding citations produced by traffic control signal monitoring systems (red light cameras) and speed monitoring systems. It expands the definition of 'owner' to include all registered owners and lessees, regardless of the lease duration, thereby making these entities or their drivers subject to civil penalties for violations recorded by automated enforcement systems.
responsible_party: Maryland State Highway Administration, Maryland Transportation Authority, and local jurisdictions or police departments operating automated traffic monitoring systems.
stakeholders: Motor vehicle rental and leasing companies, lessees of rental vehicles, holders of special registration plates, and state and local government agencies that manage traffic monitoring programs.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill is expected to result in an increase in state and local revenue through the collection of civil penalties from previously exempt rental and leased vehicles and special registration plate holders. Specific dollar estimates for the fiscal impact are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note with numerical data was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: As the parent agency for the SHA, MVA, and MDTA, MDOT oversees the state's transportation network and the multi-modal administrations responsible for implementing and maintaining automated enforcement systems and vehicle registration records.

The SHA is specifically authorized in the bill to operate speed monitoring systems on Interstate 83 and Interstate 695. The repeal of liability exemptions for rental companies and special plate holders directly impacts their citation issuance and revenue collection processes.

The MDTA is explicitly mentioned as the operator of speed monitoring systems on the Intercounty Connector (MD Route 200). Changing the definition of 'owner' to include rental companies directly affects their enforcement operations and revenue stream.

The MVA manages the vehicle registration and titling database used to identify 'owners' for automated citations. They also oversee the special registration plates (manufacturers, dealers, etc.) for which the bill repeals liability exemptions.

Citations from automated monitoring systems are civil penalties that are often contested in the District Court system. Expanding the pool of liable parties (by removing exemptions) may lead to an increase in the volume of cases adjudicated by the Judiciary.

The OAG provides legal counsel to MDOT, SHA, and MDTA. They would be responsible for defending the state's enforcement procedures or handling potential litigation resulting from the removal of exemptions for rental and leasing companies.

DBM oversees state revenue and fiscal planning. This bill will likely have a fiscal impact by increasing citation revenue into state and local funds (like the Strategic Energy Investment Fund or General Fund) that were previously lost to exemptions.

The Maryland State Police are responsible for enforcing traffic laws and work in conjunction with automated systems to ensure public safety. Changes to liability definitions impact the overall traffic safety enforcement landscape in the state.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies (MDOT, MSP) implementing these programs and is responsible for the overall policy direction regarding traffic safety and state revenue from civil penalties.
