bill_summary: This bill expands the authority of the Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission to include the enforcement and seizure of unauthorized consumable products, specifically tianeptine, kratom, and phenibut. It prohibits retailers from distributing or advertising these products under certain conditions, grants the Commission the power to confiscate and destroy contraband, and establishes misdemeanor penalties and fines for violations.
stakeholders: Retailers (including manufacturers, wholesalers, and various food/drink establishments), consumers, the Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission, and the Maryland Department of Health.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes civil penalties ranging from $1,000 to $2,000 and misdemeanor fines of up to $5,000 for violations related to the sale and advertising of unauthorized products, which may increase State General Fund revenue. The Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission will incur costs associated with the enforcement, seizure, and destruction of unauthorized products. Specific total dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note are unavailable in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly references the Health – General Article for definitions of unauthorized consumable products (kratom, tianeptine, and phenibut) and requires the Department to report changes in the regulatory or approval status of these products to the Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission.

The bill explicitly authorizes the District Court to order the Comptroller to suspend or revoke certain tobacco and business licenses for violations. Additionally, the Field Enforcement Division is mandated to cooperate with the Office of the Comptroller.

As the chief legal officer, the OAG will likely provide legal counsel to the Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission and the Department of Health regarding the implementation of new seizure, confiscation, and summary forfeiture powers, and represent the state in related litigation.

The bill grants specific authority to the District Court to order the suspension or revocation of licenses and to adjudicate new misdemeanor offenses and summary forfeiture proceedings related to unauthorized consumable products.

The bill establishes that officers of the Field Enforcement Division are sworn police officers and mandates cooperation with other police and peace officers to enforce the prohibitions against unauthorized consumable products.
The bill specifies that the Field Enforcement Division may employ officers and employees as provided in the state budget, which is overseen and developed by DBM.

The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and the various agencies (such as the Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission and the Maryland Department of Health) responsible for enforcing the bill's provisions and reporting on product status.

bill_summary: This bill requires Maryland employers with 15 or more employees and all governmental units to provide employees who are parents, stepparents, or legal guardians with at least 20 hours of paid leave per year to attend school functions at their child's elementary or secondary school. Use of the leave is limited to two hours per month and requires the employee to provide proof of the school function within 48 hours.
stakeholders: Maryland employees who are parents or guardians of school-aged children, private employers with 15 or more employees, and State and local government agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will result in increased expenditures for State and local government units due to the requirement to provide additional paid leave to employees. Private sector employers with 15 or more employees will also face higher personnel costs. Because a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the bill text, specific dollar estimates for these impacts are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill amends the Labor and Employment Article and grants the Commissioner of Labor and Industry the authority to investigate violations, handle employee complaints, and issue orders to compel employer compliance with the new paid leave requirements.

As the central personnel and fiscal agency for the State of Maryland, DBM will be responsible for implementing this new paid leave benefit across the executive branch and managing the resulting fiscal impact on the state personnel budget.

The Office of the Attorney General will provide essential legal counsel to the Department of Labor regarding enforcement of the act and advise other state agencies on their compliance obligations as employers.

As the state's chief financial officer responsible for paying state employees, the Comptroller's office will need to update payroll systems to track and account for this specific category of paid leave.

The bill contains specific provisions regarding the interaction of the new leave requirement with collective bargaining agreements. PERB, which oversees labor relations for state and school employees, would be responsible for adjudicating disputes related to these agreements.
OAH would be responsible for conducting hearings and adjudicating appeals if an employer contests a compliance order issued by the Commissioner of Labor and Industry.

MSDE oversees the state's 24 local school systems, which are large governmental employers directly impacted by these leave requirements. Additionally, the leave is specifically designed for attendance at functions within the schools MSDE regulates.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Governor to withdraw Maryland from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) by January 1, 2027, and establishes specific conditions under which the State may rejoin. It eliminates the utility surcharge for EmPOWER energy efficiency programs and limits the rate for community solar energy bill credits to the electric company's standard offer service generation cost.
responsible_party: Governor of Maryland and the Maryland Public Service Commission
stakeholders: Maryland electric and gas utility customers, utility companies, community solar subscriber organizations, and state agencies receiving Strategic Energy Investment Fund proceeds.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will cause a significant loss of State special fund revenue due to the cessation of carbon allowance sales under RGGI. It also eliminates the EmPOWER surcharge on utility bills, which will reduce costs for ratepayers but remove the cost-recovery mechanism for energy efficiency programs. Specific financial estimates are unavailable as no formal Fiscal Note was included in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the Governor to withdraw the State from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI) by a specific date and provides criteria under which the Governor may rejoin. It also mandates specific notifications from the Governor to the Department of Legislative Services.

The bill amends the Environment Article regarding carbon dioxide emissions and the State's participation in RGGI, which is the primary regulatory framework managed by MDE for greenhouse gas reductions from power plants.

MEA manages the Strategic Energy Investment Fund (SEIF), which receives all proceeds from RGGI auctions. The bill's withdrawal from RGGI would cease these revenue streams, and rejoining would redirect them back to the SEIF.
The bill mandates the PSC to eliminate utility surcharges for the EmPOWER program and restricts the PSC's ability to set community solar tariffs above standard offer service rates.
The bill impacts utility rates for residential consumers by eliminating surcharges and changing community solar bill credits, areas where the OPC is the primary advocate for consumers.

The withdrawal from RGGI and elimination of EmPOWER surcharges have significant fiscal and personnel implications for state programs funded by these mechanisms, requiring DBM's oversight of the state's budget and fiscal planning.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the PSC and MDE regarding the implementation of statutory changes to the Public Utilities and Environment Articles and would handle legal aspects of withdrawing from the RGGI interstate memorandum.
The Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative is an interstate compact/agreement. Maryland's withdrawal directly affects its status and cooperation within this interstate body.
The bill's focus on eliminating energy efficiency surcharges and withdrawing from greenhouse gas initiatives directly impacts the MCEC mission to advance clean energy and energy efficiency products.
Changes to utility surcharges and energy policy affect the cost of doing business in Maryland, which falls under Commerce's role in economic development and business retention.
DHS manages energy assistance programs (like SNAP and OHEP) that are sometimes supported by funds derived from energy initiatives and RGGI proceeds.
DHCD administers energy efficiency and weatherization programs that are frequently funded through EmPOWER and RGGI proceeds.
This multi-agency initiative is focused on reducing the state's carbon footprint, a goal directly impacted by withdrawing from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative.

bill_summary: This bill creates the Complementary and Alternative Health Care Practice Act, which allows individuals to practice a wide range of alternative health services, such as acupressure, herbalism, and homeopathy, without being licensed or certified by the state. agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill creates a new title within the Health Occupations Article, which the Department of Health oversees, and impacts health policy and the regulatory landscape for numerous health professions in the state.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the statutory authority of nearly two dozen health occupation boards (e.g., Acupuncture, Nursing, Physicians, Massage Therapy, etc.) to create exceptions to their licensing requirements for alternative practitioners.

The OAG serves as the chief legal officer for the state and provides counsel to all the health boards and the Department of Health regarding the implementation and enforcement of this new authorization versus existing professional scopes.

The department coordinates services for residents with disabilities, many of whom may seek alternative therapies authorized under this bill for wellness and community living support.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Secretary of State is the principal state custodian for records related to condominiums and cooperatives. The bill directly impacts judicial procedures by allowing parties to appeal commission decisions to the courts, providing for the consolidation of related cases, and mandating that courts stay certain civil proceedings for at least 90 days if a dispute is filed with the commission.

The bill concerns the governance and operational support of common ownership communities, which is central to the agency's mission of ensuring safe, secure housing and community revitalization. The commission's duties, such as technical assistance for municipal infrastructure like stormwater management, align with the department's focus.

The bill requires at least one member of the local commission to be a licensed common ownership community manager. The Department of Labor is responsible for the licensing and regulation of various professions in Maryland, including community association managers.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel on state laws, including the Real Property Article. As the governing body for 12 public institutions of higher education, the University System of Maryland must ensure its member institutions implement the new tuition eligibility criteria and comply with the bill's reporting and policy adoption requirements.

Morgan State University is a public senior higher education institution directly impacted by the bill. It must update its tuition exemption policies, eliminate the tax-filing documentation requirement for eligible undocumented students, and report data to the Higher Education Commission.

As an independent public honors college, Saint Mary's College of Maryland is required to adopt policies to implement the bill's changes to tuition eligibility for undocumented students and maintain records for state reporting.

The Department of Budget and Management oversees state agency budgets and personnel. Changes in tuition eligibility for undocumented students may have a fiscal impact on the revenues of state institutions of higher education, which DBM monitors.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to state agencies, including public universities and the Maryland Higher Education Commission, regarding the implementation of statutory changes and compliance with state and federal laws.

The Maryland Longitudinal Data System Center links student and workforce data. Changes in the eligibility and documentation requirements for a specific student population (undocumented immigrants) affect the data collected and analyzed by the center.

The bill's eligibility criteria for tuition exemptions are based on attendance and graduation from Maryland public or nonpublic secondary schools, which are overseen by the Maryland State Department of Education.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Maryland Helping Everyone Afford Life-Saving Treatments and Health Care (HEALTH) Fund as a special, nonlapsing fund designed to assist individuals with costs for legally protected health care services that are subject to federal restrictions. The fund provides grants to health care providers and is financed through an annual distribution of $20 million from abandoned property proceeds, unspent funds from the Abortion Care Clinical Training Program Fund, and specific sales, use, and property tax revenues derived from insurers.
stakeholders: Maryland Medical Assistance Program enrollees, insured and uninsured individuals seeking health care services impacted by federal funding restrictions, and Maryland health care providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: Beginning in FY 2027, the bill redirects $20,000,000 annually from unclaimed property proceeds to the HEALTH Fund instead of the General Fund. It also requires that unspent money from the Abortion Care Clinical Training Program Fund be credited to the HEALTH Fund. Additionally, certain sales and use tax and State property tax revenues attributable to insurance companies are distributed to the Fund. The Maryland Health Benefit Exchange is responsible for administering the fund through grants and contracts, while the Comptroller and State Treasurer handle accounting and investments.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly designates the Executive Director of the Exchange to administer the HEALTH Fund, adopt regulations for its operation, provide grants to health care providers, and submit annual reports to the General Assembly.

The Comptroller, as the Administrator of abandoned property, is required to distribute $20 million annually from unclaimed funds to the HEALTH Fund. Additionally, the Comptroller is responsible for distributing specific sales and use tax revenue to the Fund.
The State Treasurer is required to hold the HEALTH Fund separately, invest its money in the same manner as other State funds, and serve as its custodian.

The bill requires that residual funds from the Abortion Care Clinical Training Program Fund, which is managed by the Department of Health, be credited to the HEALTH Fund at the end of each fiscal year. The Fund also provides assistance to Maryland Medical Assistance Program (Medicaid) enrollees.

The bill amends the Insurance Article and relates to premium taxes. As the regulator of Maryland's insurance market, the MIA oversees the entities subject to the taxes that will now contribute additional revenue to the HEALTH Fund.

As the principal fiscal agency, DBM is involved in the creation of new special funds and the oversight of revenue shifts from the General Fund. The bill also references definitions in the State Personnel and Pensions Article which DBM manages.

The OAG will provide legal counsel to the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange, the Comptroller, and the Treasurer regarding the administration of the new fund and the implementation of grants and regulations.
The Governor oversees the executive agencies involved (MHBE, MDH) and is responsible for the state budget, which will be impacted by the redirection of millions in tax and abandoned property revenue.
The OLA will be responsible for conducting fiscal compliance audits of the HEALTH Fund and its administration by the Maryland Health Benefit Exchange.

The bill involves the distribution and imposition of specific tax revenues (sales, property, and premium taxes); the Tax Court serves as the administrative review body for disputes regarding these taxes.
The bill includes provisions regarding the distribution of State property tax revenue; these local boards handle disputes related to property tax assessments that contribute to that revenue.

bill_summary: This bill, titled the Continuing the Next Generation Energy Act, modifies several aspects of Maryland's energy regulation and efficiency programs. Key provisions include lowering the threshold for 'large load' customers to qualify for specific rate schedules from 100 megawatts to 25 megawatts, adjusting multiyear rate plan requirements to prevent certain cost-recovery charges to customers, and updating greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets for utilities. Additionally, it requires the Public Service Commission to investigate transitioning to a third-party administrator for energy efficiency programs and mandates a study by the Power Plant Research Program to streamline permitting for energy development sites.
stakeholders: Electric and gas public service companies, large load industrial electricity customers, residential and commercial utility ratepayers, low-income energy program participants, and energy developers.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note with specific revenue and expenditure estimates was not included in the provided text. However, the bill likely results in administrative expenditures for the Public Service Commission to conduct new RFI and RFP processes and for the Power Plant Research Program to conduct a state-level energy permitting study. The bill also contains provisions that restrict utilities from filing for cost reconciliations that would increase customer charges and caps potential nuclear energy project cost increases at 15%.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Public Service Commission is the primary regulator and implementing agency for the bill's provisions, including overseeing rate schedules for large load customers, approving multiyear rate plans, regulating energy efficiency and conservation programs (EmPOWER Maryland), and conducting RFIs and RFPs for third-party administrators.

The bill references 'the Department' regarding low-income energy efficiency and conservation programs; in this statutory context, this refers to the Department of Housing and Community Development, which is responsible for administering these programs and submitting plans to the Commission.

The Department of Natural Resources houses the Power Plant Research Program (PPRP), which is explicitly mandated by Section 3 of the bill to lead a study on streamlining the permitting process for energy development and identifying priority energy sites.

The Maryland Energy Administration is statutorily required to be consulted on the design and adequacy of energy efficiency plans and to consult with the PPRP on the energy development permitting study.

The Department of the Environment is a mandated consultant for energy efficiency and conservation plans and is tasked with consulting on the energy permitting study. The bill's focus on greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets also directly aligns with the agency's core mission.

The Office of the People's Counsel is statutorily required to be consulted on the design and adequacy of energy efficiency plans and serves as the primary advocate for residential utility consumers who are directly impacted by the bill's rate and program changes.

The bill requires a study on streamlining state-level zoning and permitting structures for energy development, which falls under the Department of Planning's jurisdiction regarding sustainable growth and infrastructure development policy.

The Office of the Attorney General provides legal counsel to the Public Service Commission and other executive agencies as they navigate new regulatory frameworks, the RFP process for third-party administrators, and potential legal challenges to rate changes.

The Department of Budget and Management oversees fiscal personnel and planning, which may be affected by the bill's requirements for new studies, administrative transitions, and the fiscal implications outlined in the legislation's multi-year planning cycles.

The bill requires the Power Plant Research Program to report its findings on energy permitting to the Governor, and the legislation significantly alters state energy policy which is overseen by the Governor's executive branch.

The Board of Public Works may be required to review or approve the significant state contract resulting from the Public Service Commission's required request for proposals for a third-party administrator for energy efficiency programs.

fiscal_impact_summary: The Maryland Department of Health may experience increased operational expenditures to conduct investigations and product inspections. bill_summary: This bill establishes comprehensive operating and siting standards for data centers in Maryland. It requires the Department of the Environment to set regulations for sound levels, vibration controls, and backup power generation. Data centers located within 2,500 feet of a school are subject to additional requirements, including setbacks for electrical infrastructure, air quality monitoring, and mandatory funding for school HVAC filtration systems. Furthermore, the bill restricts the construction of data centers on high-quality agricultural land, eased land, and rural legacy areas, and it authorizes $10,000 civil penalties for violations.
stakeholders: Data center owners and operators, primary and secondary schools, local health departments, local approving authorities, and Maryland residents living near proposed or existing data center sites.
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note is not provided in the text; however, specific financial implications are identified. Data center operators who violate the new standards are subject to a civil penalty of $10,000 per violation. Additionally, operators near schools must fund the installation and annual maintenance costs of HEPA and MERV 13+ filters for the school's HVAC system. State and local government entities, particularly the Department of the Environment and local health departments, will likely incur indeterminate administrative costs related to regulation, monitoring, and the enforcement of emergency stop-work orders.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes Title 19 in the Environment Article, requiring the Department of the Environment to set regulations for sound, vibration, and air quality standards for data centers, and grants it enforcement powers including civil penalties and permit revocation.

The bill adds a new subtitle to the Land Use Article regarding data center siting and impacts sustainable growth policies and local zoning regulations which the Department of Planning oversees and provides technical assistance for.

The bill prohibits the construction of data centers on specific agricultural lands (Class I or II soil) and land encumbered by agricultural easements, which directly impacts the department's mission to protect farming and soil resources.
The bill prohibits the construction of data centers in Rural Legacy Areas, which are conservation areas defined and managed under the Natural Resources Article.

The bill mandates specific setbacks from school playgrounds and athletic fields, requires air filtration improvements in schools paid for by data center owners, and requires air quality monitoring at school intakes.
The bill empowers local health departments, which are overseen by the Maryland Department of Health, to issue emergency stop-work orders for violations of sound or air quality standards.
As the state's economic development agency, Commerce is impacted by the new operational and siting restrictions which affect the attractiveness and expansion of the data center industry in Maryland.

The bill mandates backup power requirements, Tier 4 emission standards, and on-site battery storage for large data centers, areas that fall within the agency's mission to manage energy efficiency and planning.

The bill sets setback requirements for electrical substations and high-voltage transmission lines (over 69 kilovolts), infrastructure that is generally under the regulatory and approval purview of the PSC.
This multi-agency initiative coordinates the Department of Planning and Department of the Environment on sustainable growth and land use, which are the primary areas of law modified by this bill.
The OAG will be responsible for providing legal counsel to the various implementing agencies and representing the state in any enforcement actions or appeals related to the new regulations.
The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch agencies (MDE, MDP, etc.) tasked with developing the new regulations and manages the intergovernmental relations affected by the land use changes.
DBM will oversee the fiscal impact and potential personnel needs of the Department of the Environment to implement and enforce the new regulatory framework.

MEDCO provides real estate development and advisory services for industry; the bill's requirement to evaluate decommissioned industrial or power plant sites directly relates to MEDCO's development mission.

bill_summary: The Maryland Enforcement Limits and Transparency (MELT) Act prohibits state and local government agencies, employees, and contractors from voluntarily assisting with federal immigration enforcement in ways that violate constitutional rights. The bill mandates that any cooperation with immigration authorities be documented and that affected individuals be notified. It grants the Maryland Attorney General investigative and enforcement powers, authorizes civil lawsuits for damages, and allows for the termination of state procurement contracts and the revocation of professional licenses for violations.
responsible_party: Maryland Attorney General, Maryland Board of Public Works, and State licensing authorities
stakeholders: Immigrants, state and local government employees, county sheriffs, state procurement contractors, and occupational or professional licensees
fiscal_impact_summary: A formal Fiscal Note with specific revenue and expenditure estimates is unavailable. However, the bill text explicitly establishes a civil penalty of up to $25,000 for each violation and allows the Attorney General to recover the costs of enforcement actions. State expenditures may increase due to new investigative and litigation responsibilities for the Office of the Attorney General, and there is a potential fiscal impact on state procurement if contracts are voided or modified due to noncompliance.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: Section 3-2703 explicitly designates the Attorney General as the primary authority responsible for investigating violations of the Act, issuing subpoenas, and bringing civil actions for enforcement and penalties.

Section 3-2704 grants the Board of Public Works the authority to void, decline to renew, or impose conditions on state procurement contracts for entities that violate the Act's immigration enforcement prohibitions.

As the primary state law enforcement agency, the Maryland State Police are directly subject to the Act's prohibitions on knowingly aiding in immigration enforcement and the new documentation and record-keeping requirements for interactions with immigration authorities.

The DNR includes the Natural Resources Police, who are state law enforcement officers subject to the Act's restrictions on immigration enforcement cooperation and related documentation duties.
DJS staff manage youth in the justice system and are subject to the Act's prohibitions on detaining or sharing information for the purpose of immigration enforcement without a judicial warrant.

The Act defines 'judicial warrants' involving state judges and commissioners and authorizes civil lawsuits for damages in state courts, impacting judicial administration and proceedings.

DHS employees handle sensitive personal information of vulnerable populations and are 'persons' subject to the Act's prohibitions on sharing such information with immigration authorities without a warrant.

The Commission serves as the regulatory board for higher education institutions and career schools, acting as a 'licensing authority' subject to the disciplinary and certification mandates of Section 3-2705.

bill_summary: The Maryland Generational Housing Act of 2026 requires local jurisdictions to authorize the development of at least one internal and one external accessory dwelling unit (ADU) on residential lots with a single-family detached home, regardless of density limits. The bill prohibits local governments from imposing development excise taxes or impact fees on ADUs smaller than 1,000 square feet and exempts ADUs occupied by family members from property taxes. It also restricts additional parking requirements and caps utility connection fees for units occupied by family members.
responsible_party: Local governments (counties and municipalities), utility providers, and the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (SDAT).
stakeholders: Single-family homeowners, qualified family members (parents, children, siblings, etc.), local governments, and utility providers.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill will result in an indeterminate decrease in local revenues due to the prohibition of development excise taxes and impact fees for ADUs under 1,000 square feet. State and local property tax revenues will decrease because of the exemption for ADUs occupied by family members. Additionally, local and private utility providers will experience a reduction in revenue due to capped connection fees and permitted shared meters. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly amends the Land Use Article, requiring local jurisdictions to authorize accessory dwelling units (ADUs) and excluding them from density calculations. This falls under the Department's mission to promote sustainable growth and provide policy guidance on land use.

As the primary agency for housing policy, DHCD is responsible for ensuring access to affordable housing. This bill, the 'Maryland Generational Housing Act of 2026,' aims to increase housing supply through ADUs, directly aligning with the Department's core mission.

The bill regulates water and sewer connection fees and mentions capacity charges related to septic systems. MDE regulates sanitary commissions and municipal authorities involved in these services, and provides oversight for environmental infrastructure.

The bill defines utilities to include private companies regulated under the Public Utilities Article. The PSC oversees these private companies, which would now be prohibited from charging certain fees for ADUs and must allow shared meters.

The bill specifically references septic system capacity as a factor in fee exemptions. MDH oversees local health departments and sets policies regarding environmental health, including the regulation and approval of septic systems.

The bill creates a new property tax exemption for ADUs occupied by qualified family members. PTAAB would be responsible for hearing appeals from property owners regarding the denial or valuation related to this specific exemption.

As the highest level of administrative review for tax-related disputes, the Maryland Tax Court would adjudicate appeals involving the new property tax exemption and local development excise tax prohibitions.

The bill's provision exempting certain ADUs from property tax has a fiscal impact on the State's revenue (specifically the portion of property tax used for debt service). DBM is responsible for estimating revenues and managing fiscal planning.

The Governor oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives like the 'Generational Housing Act.' The office would be responsible for the broader implementation of these housing and tax policies.
The OAG would provide legal counsel to the various state agencies (MDP, DHCD, MDE) as they implement the new statutory requirements and regulations for ADUs and utility fees.

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Maryland Labor Relations Act and creates the Maryland Labor Relations Board (MLRB) as an independent state agency to oversee collective bargaining for specific private sector employees. It grants employees the right to organize, join employee organizations, and engage in collective bargaining while prohibiting unfair labor practices by both employers and unions. The MLRB is empowered to supervise elections, certify exclusive representatives, and resolve labor disputes. The act is contingent on the repeal of the federal National Labor Relations Act or the federal government ceding jurisdiction to the state.
stakeholders: Private sector employees (excluding agricultural and domestic workers), private sector employers, and employee organizations (unions) in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: The creation of the Maryland Labor Relations Board as an independent unit of State government will increase state expenditures to cover salaries for a full-time chair, four board members, and associated administrative and travel costs. These expenditures will be determined through the annual state budget process. As a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the bill text, specific dollar estimates for these costs are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor is responsible for appointing the Chair and all four members of the newly established Maryland Labor Relations Board, with the advice and consent of the Senate. Additionally, the Board is required to submit an annual report to the Governor summarizing its cases and actions.

The bill explicitly tasks the Maryland Department of Labor with monitoring federal government actions regarding the National Labor Relations Act and notifying the Department of Legislative Services when specific contingencies are met to trigger the effectiveness of the Act.

The bill creates a new independent state agency, the Maryland Labor Relations Board, with members and a full-time chair entitled to compensation and reimbursement as provided in the state budget, which is managed and executed by DBM.
The Office of Appointments will assist the Governor in the recruitment, vetting, and recommendation of the five individuals to serve on the newly created Maryland Labor Relations Board.

As the chief legal officer for the state, the OAG would be responsible for providing legal counsel to the newly established Maryland Labor Relations Board and representing the state in legal matters arising from the Act's enforcement.

The bill prohibits employee organizations from discriminating against members based on protected classes such as race, sex, sexual orientation, and disability, which aligns with the anti-discrimination enforcement mandate of the MCCR.

bill_summary: The bill establishes the Maryland Justice Corps Program within the University System of Maryland, providing an alternative pathway to a license to practice law for graduates of the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law and the University of Baltimore School of Law. Participants commit to a three-year term with a public or private supervising organization, with priority given to those serving in underserved areas or legal fields. responsible_party: University System of Maryland, specifically the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law and the University of Baltimore School of Law
stakeholders: Graduates of the University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law and the University of Baltimore School of Law; public and private legal organizations; and Maryland residents in underserved communities.

The remaining 50% is paid by the supervising organization. The total fiscal impact is indeterminate as the number of participants is not capped in the bill and a formal Fiscal Note with total aggregate estimates was not included in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Maryland Justice Corps Program within the University System of Maryland (USM). The program provides an alternative pathway to a license to practice law. The Supreme Court of Maryland, which the Administrative Office of the Courts supports, is responsible for establishing the minimum qualifications for this alternative licensure and admitting successful participants to the Bar.

The bill has a significant fiscal impact as the State is required to pay 50% of the total cost of benefits for participants, which includes a $75,000 salary, a $15,000 housing stipend, and up to $30,000 for student loan debt annually. The office coordinates statewide efforts to improve the well-being and safety of Maryland's children, including initiatives to prevent child abuse and neglect in educational settings.

The bill expands the circumstances under which property owners must perform lead risk reduction measures, which will likely increase private-sector compliance expenditures. There may be minor administrative impacts on the Maryland Department of the Environment to oversee these modified standards.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) is the primary agency responsible for implementing and enforcing the Lead Risk Reduction in Housing Act. This bill directly amends the Environment Article, which MDE oversees, by altering the triggers for property owners to meet lead risk reduction standards.

The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) monitors elevated blood lead levels (EBL) and coordinates with local health departments for case management. Since the bill links housing risk reduction requirements to EBL test results, MDH is a critical stakeholder in the identification and notification process.

The Office of the Attorney General (OAG) provides legal counsel to MDE and MDH and represents the state in enforcement actions. Removing the requirement for an environmental investigation to find a defect before triggering remediation alters the legal burden and enforcement protocols for lead-based paint violations.

The Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH) adjudicates contested cases from state agencies, including MDE. Disputes between property owners and MDE regarding compliance with the modified risk reduction standard and notices of lead risk are heard by Administrative Law Judges at OAH.

The Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) manages programs for safe and affordable housing. While MDE handles lead-specific regulations, DHCD has a significant interest in housing quality standards and the impact of lead remediation requirements on the rental housing market.

The Judicial Branch manages civil litigation between landlords and tenants. Removing a prerequisite for requiring lead risk reduction measures may affect the volume and nature of civil suits brought by tenants seeking remediation or damages related to lead exposure.

Synopsis: Replacing the term "landlord" with "residential housing provider" and "tenant" with "resident" in the context of residential leases.
Title: Real Property - Residential Lease - Terminology
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/13 at 1:00 p.m.
bill_summary: This bill updates the terminology in Maryland's residential lease laws by replacing the terms 'landlord' and 'tenant' with 'rental property owner' and 'resident,' respectively. It also renames the Office of Tenant and Landlord Affairs to the Office of Resident and Rental Property Owner Affairs within the Department of Housing and Community Development and requires the state's code publisher to update all relevant cross-references and terminology.
responsible_party: Maryland Department of Housing and Community Development
stakeholders: Residential rental property owners and residents in Maryland.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill primarily involves changing statutory terminology. No specific revenue or expenditure figures are included in the bill text, and since a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the source material, specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill directly renames the 'Office of Tenant and Landlord Affairs' within DHCD to the 'Office of Resident and Rental Property Owner Affairs' and mandates the department to develop and publish the 'Maryland Residents' Bill of Rights'.

The bill extensively alters terminology used in District Court proceedings, including summary ejectment, rent escrow, and warrants of restitution. The Judiciary will be required to update forms, procedures, and legal citations across the court system.

The bill amends the Environment Article regarding lead-safe housing, changing terminology for 'change in occupancy', 'relocation expenses', and 'rent subsidy', which impacts MDE's regulatory and oversight functions.

The OAG's Division of Consumer Protection is responsible for enforcing many of the residential lease rights amended by this bill, including those related to security deposits and senior apartment conversions.

The bill amends the State Government Article regarding discriminatory housing practices and reasonable modifications for individuals with disabilities, directly impacting MCCR's enforcement of anti-discrimination laws.
The bill requires owners and rental property owners to file notices regarding cooperative housing and condominium conversions with the Secretary of State.
The bill amends the Public Utilities Article regarding utility termination, billing, and the rights of residents to establish new utility accounts when a rental property owner is in arrears.

The bill involves DHS in the process of deducting rent from temporary cash assistance for delinquent residents in public housing and mentions utility assistance eligibility for security deposit limits.
The bill amends the Health - General Article to update terminology for nursing home licensure applications involving rental property owners or management companies.
The bill updates terminology for smoke alarm requirements and installation orders, which are functions typically enforced by the State Fire Marshal housed within the Maryland State Police.
The bill impacts senior residents of rental facilities, specifically regarding lease extensions and protections during the conversion of senior apartment facilities to general population housing.
The bill updates terminology and rights for residents with disabilities, including protections during housing conversions and requirements for reasonable modifications.
The bill updates terminology for provisions allowing military members and their spouses to terminate residential leases upon receiving a change of assignment.
The bill amends terminology regarding weatherization benefits for low-income residents occupying leased or rented residences.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Governor's Office of the Deaf and Hard of Hearing
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill updates requirements for rental property owners to provide specialized notification appliances (smoke alarms) for residents who are deaf or hard of hearing upon request.
The bill requires rental property owners who know a resident has a pet to provide a link to a fact sheet published on the Department of Agriculture's website.
The bill involves Administrative Law Judges in issuing orders for relief in discriminatory housing practice cases where residents are affected.

Synopsis: Altering the definition of "rental dwelling unit" for purposes of provisions of law governing the reduction of lead risk in housing.
Title: Reduction of Lead Risk in Housing - Rental Dwelling Unit - Definition
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/13 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Hazardous and Toxic Substances -see also- Asbestos; Radiatn
Housing -see also- Apartments; Condos; Mobile & Manuf  Homes

bill_summary: This bill expands the definition of "rental dwelling unit" within the context of lead risk reduction in housing. It removes the requirement that a unit be "independent" and specifies that a unit qualifies if it has either direct provisions or "access to" permanent facilities for living, sleeping, eating, cooking, and sanitation.
stakeholders: Owners of rental properties, tenants in units with shared facilities, and the Maryland Department of the Environment.
fiscal_impact_summary: Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text. The expansion of the definition of rental dwelling units likely increases the number of properties subject to lead risk reduction standards, which could increase State revenue from registration fees and raise administrative and enforcement expenditures for the Maryland Department of the Environment.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Maryland Department of the Environment (MDE) is the primary agency responsible for implementing and enforcing lead risk reduction laws in housing. This bill directly amends the Environment Article to expand the definition of 'rental dwelling unit,' thereby increasing the number of properties subject to MDE's lead risk reduction regulations and enforcement actions.

The Maryland Department of Health (MDH) works closely with MDE on public health initiatives related to lead poisoning prevention. Expanding the scope of regulated rental units directly affects public health monitoring and services provided to residents at risk of lead exposure.

The Department of Housing and Community Development (DHCD) oversees housing safety and affordability. Changes to the lead risk regulations for rental units impact the standards and compliance requirements for the housing stock that DHCD supports, finances, and revitalizes.

The Office of the Attorney General (OAG) provides legal counsel to MDE regarding environmental regulations and represents the state in civil and criminal enforcement of lead risk reduction laws. A broader definition of rental units will likely result in increased legal workload and advisory needs.

The Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH) adjudicates contested cases from various state agencies, including MDE. An expansion of regulated rental units could lead to an increase in administrative appeals regarding lead risk enforcement actions.

The judiciary handles litigation involving landlord-tenant disputes, including habitability and lead risk compliance. Changing the definition of what constitutes a rental dwelling unit may impact the volume and nature of these cases in state courts.

The Department of Human Services (DHS) provides assistance to vulnerable populations who often reside in rental housing. The inclusion of units with shared facilities under lead risk regulations may impact the availability or standards of units used by participants in DHS programs.

The Governor's Office for Children is focused on child well-being and reducing child poverty. Lead poisoning is a significant health and economic barrier for children in underinvested communities, making this regulatory expansion relevant to their policy goals.

Synopsis: Repealing the authority of the State to engage in eminent domain; and repealing certain provisions of law relating to the State's eminent domain and condemnation authority.
Title: Eminent Domain and Condemnation Authority - Repeal (Property Rights Protection Act)
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/13 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Counties -see also- Chartered Counties; Code Counties; etc.

Article.Title: XI-B - City of Baltimore - Land Development and Redevelopment

bill_summary: The Property Rights Protection Act repeals the authority of the State of Maryland, its agencies, and local governments to exercise eminent domain and condemnation. It strikes numerous provisions from the Annotated Code of Maryland and proposes a constitutional amendment to explicitly prohibit the General Assembly from enacting laws that authorize the taking of private property for public use.
responsible_party: Maryland General Assembly, Maryland Board of Public Works, and all state and local government agencies and departments
stakeholders: Private property owners, state and local government agencies, public utilities, and the general public of Maryland
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill's repeal of eminent domain authority is expected to have a significant fiscal impact by requiring all future land acquisitions for public projects to be conducted through voluntary market transactions. This change likely increases project costs and may cause delays or cancellations for infrastructure such as roads and schools. Because a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text, specific dollar estimates for state and local expenditures or revenue changes are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Governor's Office oversees the executive branch and coordinates policy initiatives; the bill represents a fundamental policy shift regarding state power and initiates the constitutional amendment process.
The Comptroller is a member of the Board of Public Works, which oversees and approves all significant state property acquisitions and would be restricted from approving condemnations.
The State Treasurer is a member of the Board of Public Works, which oversees and approves all significant state property acquisitions and would be restricted from approving condemnations.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies and represents them in court; the repeal of eminent domain would fundamentally change legal procedures for state land acquisition and litigation.
The bill repeals the authority to condemn land under agricultural preservation easements and removes the Secretary's power to acquire property via condemnation.
As the fiscal agency, DBM oversees budget execution; the removal of eminent domain will significantly impact the cost and timeline of state capital and infrastructure projects.
The department advises on the acquisition of power plant sites and oversees economic development assets like racetracks which are specifically mentioned in the bill.
The bill repeals the authority of local school boards to bring condemnation proceedings for school purposes and affects the student member's voting rights on such matters.
The bill repeals condemnation authority for sanitary districts, water/sewer systems, and the acquisition of sites for hazardous waste cleanup or mine reclamation.
DGS is the central procurement and real estate authority for the state; the bill repeals its specific authority to value and acquire property through condemnation.
The bill repeals the department's authority to condemn property for health facilities and impacts the inspection of records for governmental entities with eminent domain powers.
The bill repeals the authority of the department and local housing authorities to use eminent domain for community development and housing projects.
The bill repeals DNR's authority to condemn land for forests, parks, wildlife management areas, and environmental restoration projects.
The department coordinates land use planning and site selection for power plants; the bill's removal of eminent domain impacts long-term infrastructure and growth management strategies.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill repeals the authority of the state and counties to condemn land for the construction of correctional facilities.
MDOT and its administrations rely heavily on eminent domain for highway, transit, airport, and port construction; the bill repeals vast sections of the Transportation Article.
The bill specifically repeals the authority to condemn property adjacent to Martin State Airport needed for the safe operation of the Maryland Air National Guard's fighter squadron.
The bill removes the ability to use eminent domain for highway safety improvements, which impacts traffic safety and the operational environment of the State Police.
The Secretary of State is the custodian of state records and manages the administrative process for the proposed constitutional amendments.
The judiciary handles all condemnation and eminent domain cases; the bill repeals the legal framework for these proceedings and eliminates a significant category of civil litigation.
The bill repeals multiple sections requiring BPW approval for condemnations and removes the board's authority to oversee acquisitions via eminent domain for state use.
The bill repeals the authority's power to exercise condemnation for property within the park corridor in Cumberland.
The bill repeals the commission's authority to condemn property and modifies provisions regarding the acquisition of life estates for homeowners within commission boundaries.
The bill repeals provisions allowing for the transfer of cannabis licenses to new premises if the original site is taken by condemnation.
The bill repeals MEDCO's authority to acquire real property for economic development projects through condemnation.
The bill impacts power plant site selection and energy infrastructure planning, which MEA coordinates for the state.
The bill repeals the service's authority to exercise eminent domain for the construction or operation of environmental projects.
The commission coordinates policies for public colleges and universities that would lose the authority to condemn property for institutional expansion.
The bill repeals the authority's power to condemn land for sports complexes, performing arts centers, and other facility sites.
As a state agency with its own board, the university would lose the authority to acquire property for campus use through condemnation.
The bill repeals eminent domain for utility infrastructure, which directly affects the cost, reliability, and planning of services for the residential utility consumers OPC represents.
The bill repeals the commission's oversight of utility condemnations and removes the authority of regulated gas, electric, and water companies to condemn rights-of-way.
The college would lose the authority to acquire property through condemnation, affecting its ability to manage its waterfront campus and institutional needs.
The system's institutions would lose the authority to condemn land for educational research, expansion, and facility development.

Synopsis: Establishing the Dog Breeder Accountability Fund as a special, nonlapsing fund; requiring, on or before July 1, beginning in 2028, a dog breeder to register annually with the Department of Agriculture and, at the time of registration, pay an annual registration fee of $150; requiring, beginning on July 1, 2029, and within 30 days after the birth of a litter, a dog breeder to apply to the Department for a puppy birth certificate for each puppy born in the litter; etc.
Title: Department of Agriculture - Regulation of Dog Breeders
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/11 at 1:00 p.m.

Transfer of Goods -see also- Goods&Svc; Leas&Rnt; RetailSale

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Dog Breeder Accountability Fund to promote breeder registration and support animal shelters. It requires dog breeders to register annually with the Department of Agriculture starting in 2028, apply for puppy birth certificates for each puppy born starting in 2029, and ensure puppies born on or after July 1, 2030, are microchipped. It prohibits breeders from selling or transferring puppies to the public unless they are registered and have the required birth certificates and microchips.
stakeholders: Dog breeders, animal shelters, spay/neuter programs, puppy buyers, and the Maryland Department of Agriculture.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill creates the Dog Breeder Accountability Fund, which will collect revenue from a $150 annual breeder registration fee and a $50 fee per puppy birth certificate application. The Department may also impose administrative penalties of up to $5,000 per violation. Fund expenditures are designated for animal shelters and spay/neuter programs (50%), administrative costs (30%), and education and enforcement (20%). Interest earnings are credited to the General Fund. Total fiscal estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes Title 17 under the Agriculture Article, making the Department of Agriculture the primary agency responsible for registering dog breeders, issuing puppy birth certificates, administering the Dog Breeder Accountability Fund, and maintaining a public registry.
The bill requires the State Treasurer to hold the newly established Dog Breeder Accountability Fund separately and to invest the money of the fund.
The bill requires the Comptroller to account for the Dog Breeder Accountability Fund.
The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies like the Department of Agriculture regarding the adoption of new regulations and the enforcement of administrative penalties established in this bill.

The Department of Agriculture is required to submit an annual report to the Governor regarding the implementation of the breeder registration program and the impact of the Dog Breeder Accountability Fund.

DBM is responsible for supervising the state budget and personnel. The creation of a new special fund and the administrative requirements placed on the Department of Agriculture would involve DBM in fiscal and potentially personnel planning.

The bill authorizes the Department of Agriculture to impose administrative penalties of up to $5,000 per violation. Contested cases involving these penalties would likely be adjudicated by the Office of Administrative Hearings.

Synopsis: Establishing a Class L beer, wine, and liquor license; authorizing a local licensing board to issue the license to a holder of a manufacturer's license; specifying that the license authorizes the license holder to sell or provide samples of certain beer, wine, and liquor for on-premises consumption under certain circumstances; and establishing an annual license fee of $250.00.
Title: Alcoholic Beverages - Class L Beer, Wine, and Liquor License - Established
Status: In the House - Hearing 2/23 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Fees -see also- Attys' Fees; Devt Fees & Taxes

bill_summary: This bill establishes a Class L beer, wine, and liquor license, which local licensing boards may issue to holders of manufacturer's licenses. The license permits holders to sell or provide free samples of beer, wine, and liquor (produced by the holder or another manufacturer) for on-premises consumption.
stakeholders: Alcoholic beverage manufacturers, local licensing boards, and consumers
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill establishes an annual license fee of $250 for the Class L license. While this will result in a revenue increase for local licensing boards, the total fiscal impact is indeterminate as the number of licenses to be issued is unknown and a formal Fiscal Note with aggregate estimates was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Comptroller is the state's principal tax collector and regulates the alcohol industry. This bill establishes a new Class L alcoholic beverages license for manufacturers, directly falling under the Comptroller's regulatory and revenue collection oversight.

The OAG provides legal counsel to state agencies, including those involved in the regulation of alcoholic beverages, and would be responsible for interpreting the new license's legal framework and representing the state in related litigation.

Many alcoholic beverage manufacturers in Maryland, such as farm-breweries and wineries, are part of the state's agricultural community. This bill affects their ability to sell products and provide samples on-site, impacting the economic viability of these agricultural businesses.

The Department of Commerce is responsible for stimulating the economy and supporting Maryland businesses. This new license provides a business expansion opportunity for manufacturers (breweries, wineries, and distilleries) to increase on-premises sales.

The OAH adjudicates contested cases for state agencies. Disputes regarding the issuance, suspension, or revocation of these new licenses by state-level regulators or local boards (where applicable for appeals) may be heard by Administrative Law Judges.

As the head of the executive branch, the Governor's Office oversees policy initiatives and coordinates intergovernmental relations. This bill involves changes to state law and local board authority that the Governor's staff would review and coordinate.

Synopsis: Requiring an order for guardianship of the person of a disabled person to allow for certain visitation; authorizing an interested person to file a certain petition for guardianship of the person of a disabled person on the grounds that the disabled adult's current guardian is medically or physically neglecting the adult; requiring a court to hear certain petitions within a certain amount of time; and authorizing an interested person to file a certain petition to appoint a temporary guardian of a disabled person.
Title: Estates and Trusts - Guardianship of the Person of a Disabled Person - Emergency and Temporary Guardianship Petitions
Status: In the House - Hearing 3/11 at 1:00 p.m.

NarrowSubjects.Name: Vulnerable Adults -see also- DevDisab; EldPers; PhysDisab

bill_summary: This bill modifies procedures for the guardianship of disabled persons, requiring court orders to include visitation schedules for relatives unless detrimental to the disabled person. It authorizes petitions for emergency or temporary guardianship based on allegations of medical or physical neglect by an existing guardian. The bill mandates expedited court hearings, requiring rulings within one business day for emergency petitions and seven calendar days for temporary petitions, and adjusts the standard of proof for emergency services to a preponderance of the evidence.
responsible_party: Maryland Judiciary and the Maryland Department of Human Services
stakeholders: Disabled adults under or potentially under guardianship, their families and relatives, court-appointed guardians, and the Maryland legal and social service systems.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures will increase due to the requirement that the State pay attorney fees for indigent individuals in guardianship proceedings. The Maryland Judiciary may also experience an impact on resources due to the newly established expedited hearing schedules for emergency and temporary guardianship petitions. Specific dollar estimates are unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not provided with the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill mandates significant changes to Maryland court procedures regarding the guardianship of disabled persons, including requirements for access schedules for relatives, strict expedited timelines for rulings on emergency and temporary petitions (1 business day and 7 calendar days respectively), and expedited appellate reviews.

Local departments of social services, which operate under DHS, are primary entities responsible for filing guardianship petitions and serving as guardians of last resort for disabled adults. The bill specifically requires the court to appoint attorneys who have contracted with DHS for indigent individuals in these proceedings.

The Secretary of Aging is specifically authorized by the bill to serve as an emergency guardian for disabled persons. The department oversees Area Agencies on Aging that support and advocate for older adults and people with disabilities, who are the primary subjects of these guardianship provisions.

The OAG provides legal counsel to the Department of Human Services and the Department of Aging. Its attorneys represent these agencies and their local directors in court proceedings involving guardianship, protective services, and compliance with the new expedited procedural requirements.

The bill involves guardianships related to medical treatment and authorizes representatives from local departments of health to assist law enforcement during authorized forcible entries. It also references health care standards and advance directives regulated under the Health - General Article.

The bill requires the State to pay reasonable attorney's fees for indigent persons in guardianship proceedings when payment is not the responsibility of a specific agency. DBM oversees the state budget and would manage the fiscal impact of these increased legal costs.

The bill mandates that law enforcement officers transport certain disabled adults to medical facilities and accompany other officials when a court authorizes forcible entry into a premises to provide protective services.

bill_summary: This bill requires the Maryland Office of the Comptroller, in consultation with the Public Service Commission and PJM Interconnection, LLC, to conduct a study and report on the feasibility and potential fiscal impact of exempting electricity used for agricultural purposes from the state sales and use tax. The study must specifically address electricity used for raising livestock or poultry, soil preparation and irrigation, and the management of seeds and crops. A report of the findings and fiscal estimates is due to the General Assembly by December 15, 2026.
stakeholders: Maryland farmers, agricultural producers, and electric utility companies.
fiscal_impact_summary: The bill mandates a study and report on the fiscal impact of a potential tax exemption; however, the provided text does not include a formal Fiscal Note with specific revenue or expenditure estimates. State administrative costs may increase slightly to conduct the study and prepare the report, but specific dollar estimates are unavailable.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly requires the Office of the Comptroller to lead the study and report to the General Assembly regarding the proposed sales and use tax exemption for electricity used for agricultural purposes.

The bill requires the Comptroller to consult with the Public Service Commission to conduct the study, specifically regarding usage and billing information from electric companies which the Commission regulates.

The subject of the study—electricity used for livestock, soil preparation, and crop management—directly pertains to the agricultural community and the economic viability of farming, which the department oversees.
As the state's principal fiscal agency, the department is concerned with the fiscal impact estimates required by the study, as tax exemptions affect state revenue and long-term fiscal planning.

bill_summary: This bill establishes additional oversight mechanisms for the Blueprint for Maryland's Future. It shortens the terms of Accountability and Implementation Board (AIB) members from six to four years and places the board under the jurisdiction of the Inspector General for Education. The bill establishes a Stakeholder Advisory Council to evaluate the classroom-level effectiveness of policies and a Joint Oversight Committee of the General Assembly to monitor implementation. Furthermore, it creates an appeals process through the Office of Administrative Hearings for local school systems contesting the withholding of funds by the AIB and mandates triennial performance audits of the AIB by the Office of Legislative Audits.
stakeholders: Local school systems, public school administrators, teachers, students, parents, and Maryland State education agencies.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures increase to support triennial performance audits by the Office of Legislative Audits and administrative hearings conducted by the Office of Administrative Hearings. Additional operational costs will be incurred by the Department of Legislative Services to staff the new Joint Oversight Committee and the Stakeholder Advisory Council. While no specific appropriation is provided in the bill, it establishes a $1,000,000 threshold for the Joint Oversight Committee to review AIB decisions regarding the withholding of education aid. Local school systems may experience a fiscal impact if they successfully appeal and recover withheld State education funds.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The Department is the primary agency responsible for the Blueprint for Maryland's Future implementation, and the bill establishes new legislative oversight over its implementation and enforcement decisions.

The bill designates the Office of Administrative Hearings as the body to adjudicate appeals from local school systems regarding decisions by the Accountability and Implementation Board to withhold Blueprint funding.
The bill mandates that the Office of Legislative Audits conduct a performance audit of the Accountability and Implementation Board at least once every three years beginning in 2026.
The Governor is responsible for appointing members of the Accountability and Implementation Board, and the bill alters their terms and the appointment cycle for these members.

agency_relevance.agency_name: Executive Commissions, Committees, Task Forces, and Advisory Boards
agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future Stakeholder Advisory Council as a new advisory body under this category to offer expertise to the General Assembly.
The Comptroller must be notified of the Accountability and Implementation Board's final decisions regarding the release or withholding of education aid funds for accounting and payment purposes.
The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in the recruitment and vetting of members for the Accountability and Implementation Board, whose membership terms are restructured by this bill.

As the chief legal representative for state boards, the OAG would provide legal counsel and representation to the Accountability and Implementation Board during the new administrative appeal processes.

Synopsis: Prohibiting a person from placing an advertisement for a sugary beverage on certain property unless the advertisement includes a certain warning.

bill_summary: This bill prohibits the placement of advertisements for sugary beverages on property owned by the State, a county, or a municipal corporation unless the advertisement includes a specific health warning label. The label must be in bold, boxed, and highly visible, warning that added sugar can contribute to obesity, type 2 diabetes, and tooth decay. The bill applies to beverages containing added sugars or nonnutritive sweeteners like aspartame or stevia.
responsible_party: Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General
stakeholders: Manufacturers and advertisers of sugary beverages, State and local government agencies that manage advertising space on public property, and Maryland residents.
fiscal_impact_summary: State General Fund revenues may increase by an indeterminate amount due to civil penalties of up to $1,000 per day for each violation. State and local government entities could experience an indeterminate impact on advertising revenue if beverage companies choose not to place advertisements on government-owned property to avoid the warning label requirement. Specific dollar estimates from a formal Fiscal Note were not provided in the text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill explicitly tasks the Consumer Protection Division of the Office of the Attorney General with enforcing the new advertising requirements and imposing civil penalties for violations.

As the primary manager of state-owned facilities and the central procurement authority, DGS must ensure that all advertisements and vending contracts on state property comply with the required health warnings.
The MTA manages extensive advertising space on state-owned transit vehicles and facilities, all of which would be subject to the bill's mandatory labeling requirements.

The MSA manages large state-owned sports and entertainment complexes where sugary beverage advertisements are a significant presence; the agency will be responsible for ensuring compliance with label mandates.

As the parent agency for several modal administrations that manage state property with advertising space (such as MTA and MAA), MDOT oversees the implementation of these regulations across its network.
The bill focuses on public health outcomes like obesity and diabetes, and it designates the required text as a 'Maryland State Health Warning,' making MDH a key stakeholder and policy expert.
The MAA operates BWI and Martin State Airport, which are state-owned properties featuring significant commercial advertising that would require the specified warning labels.
DNR manages half a million acres of state-owned public lands and parks where advertisements on vending machines or signage must now include the health warning.
The Board of Public Works approves significant state procurement and concession contracts, including those for food and beverage services on state property that involve advertising.
The bill applies to advertisements on county property, which includes local public schools; MSDE would likely provide guidance and oversight to ensure compliance within school systems.
USM governs various state-owned university campuses where sugary beverage advertisements on vending machines or at athletic venues would need to comply with the bill.
As a state agency managing its own urban campus, Morgan State must ensure all advertisements for sugary beverages on its state-owned property include the required warning labels.
As an independent state honors college, SMC must ensure that advertisements on its state-owned campus property meet the new health labeling standards.
The MPA manages state-owned maritime terminals where beverage advertisements or vending machines must comply with the bill's labeling mandate.
The MFCA manages state-owned wholesale food distribution facilities; any advertisements for sugary beverages within these centers would require the specified health warning.
The OTD manages state welcome centers; any beverage advertisements or signage in these state-owned facilities must include the required labeling.
Since the bill applies to municipal and county-owned property, the Maryland State Library Agency will likely coordinate with local library systems to ensure their signage and vending machines comply.

Synopsis: Establishing a Real Estate Advisory Committee in the Department of General Services to conduct a review of certain real estate transactions and make certain recommendations; requiring certain real estate transactions submitted to the Board of Public Works for approval to include certain information; and requiring the Advisory Committee, by January 1 each year, to submit an annual report to the Governor and the General Assembly to include a list of certain real estate transactions by the State.
Title: Procurement - Department of General Services - Real Estate Advisory Committee
Status: In the House - First Reading Government, Labor, and Elections

NarrowSubjects.Name: Commerce and Business -see also- ElectrComm; ForeignTr; etc.
Real Estate -see also- Agents and Brokers

bill_summary: This bill establishes the Real Estate Advisory Committee within the Department of General Services to review and make recommendations on state real estate transactions, including leases and property purchases, that have an expected cost exceeding $500,000 per year. It requires state agencies to provide comprehensive cost-benefit analyses, parking assessments, and renovation justifications for these transactions, and mandates the committee to publish an annual report on the status and costs of state real estate holdings.
stakeholders: State agencies involved in property leasing or acquisition, the Department of General Services, the Board of Public Works, and private property owners or developers engaged in real estate transactions with the State.
fiscal_impact_summary: State expenditures will increase for the Department of General Services to provide staff support for the new committee and to reimburse committee members for travel expenses. State agencies will also experience an increase in administrative workload to prepare the required cost-benefit analyses and documentation for transactions exceeding $500,000. Specific dollar estimates were unavailable as a formal Fiscal Note was not included in the provided text.

agency_relevance.relevance_explanation: The bill establishes the Real Estate Advisory Committee within the Department of General Services (DGS). The DGS Secretary chairs the committee, and the department is responsible for providing staff, managing real estate transaction reviews, and publishing annual reports and data on its website.

The bill directly impacts the Board's approval process for real estate transactions. It requires that all transactions submitted to the Board include the Advisory Committee's recommendations and detailed cost-benefit analyses, justifications, and renovation data.

The Governor is responsible for appointing two members to the Real Estate Advisory Committee and receives an annual report from the committee regarding state real estate transactions and agency compliance.

As a member of the Board of Public Works, the Comptroller is part of the final approval body for the real estate transactions governed by this bill and will utilize the new documentation and recommendations required for submission.

As a member of the Board of Public Works, the State Treasurer is part of the final approval body for the real estate transactions governed by this bill and will utilize the new documentation and recommendations required for submission.

DBM oversees budget execution and long-term fiscal planning. Because real estate transactions over $500,000 per year have significant fiscal impacts, DBM is relevant to the coordination of these major state expenditures and the cost-benefit analyses required by the bill.

The OAG provides legal counsel to DGS, the Board of Public Works, and other state agencies. They would likely review the legality of the new advisory process and the required procurement documentation.

The Office of Appointments assists the Governor in vetting and recommending candidates for state boards and commissions, which would include the gubernatorial appointments to the new Real Estate Advisory Committee.
